entry.title: Q1. Make Array Elements Equal to Zero | Easy | LeetCode Weekly Contest
entry.content:
🌐 中文版：繁體中文
Intro This is my first record of doing a LeetCode Weekly Contest. I jumped on today on a whim, so by the time I was ready to compete there wasn’t much time left. But I’m still a rookie, so I just focused on the first problem to test the waters, and stopped after finishing it.
Problem statement
Difficulty: Easy Statement: given an integer array nums, you first pick a starting point curr where nums[curr] = 0. From the starting point you can choose to move left or right, then repeat the following steps:
If curr goes out of the range [0, n-1], the process stops Move left or right by decrementing/incrementing curr: increasing curr moves right, decreasing curr moves left After moving, once nums[curr] > 0: decrement nums[curr] by one reverse the current direction of movement take one step in the new direction
A run is considered valid if, once the movement ends, all element values are zero. Return the total number of valid selections. SolutionInitial ideaFirst we need to iterate over the given array nums and find the starting points (there may be several). Then, starting from a start point, we walk left or right to judge whether it’s valid. During the traversal, as soon as we hit a value greater than 0 we start walking in the opposite direction, until we reach the far end or another value greater than zero. My solutionclass Solution {public: bool isValid(vector<int>nums, int start, bool direct){ int n = nums.size(); int curr = start; while(curr >=0 && curr < n) { if(nums[curr] ==0){ if(direct) curr++; else curr--; } else{ nums[curr]--; direct = !direct; if(direct) curr++; else curr--; } } for(auto it=nums.begin(); it!=nums.end(); ++it){ if(*it !=0){ return false; } } return true; } int countValidSelections(vector<int>& nums){ //select starting position int n = nums.size(); int found = 0; for(int i = 0; i< n;i++){ if(nums[i]==0){ if(isValid(nums,i,true)){ found++; } if(isValid(nums,i,false)){ found++; } } } return found; }};
Here I split it into two functions. The main function countValidSelections uses a loop to find the starting points first, and once it finds one it calls isValid twice with different directions. In isValid, we walk back and forth over the elements within the range curr >= 0 && curr < n. Once we hit an element with value zero, we keep walking in the current direction, and if we hit a value greater than 0 we decrement nums[curr] by one and take one step in the reverse direction. After traversing all elements, we check whether every element is now zero; if so it’s valid, otherwise invalid. Back in the main function, if the path is valid we increment the found variable. After trying the different starting points, we can return found. Execution result
The runtime cost was very high.
ComplexityTime complexity $O(n^2)$
countValidSelections: runs at most $n$ times, and for each starting position isValid is called twice. isValid: in the worst case the while loop traverses the whole array, so $O(n)$, and before returning there’s another loop checking whether every element is 0, which also needs $O(n)$. So the overall time complexity is $2 \times (O(n) + O(n)) = O(4n) = O(n)$ per start, times up to $n$ starts. Space complexity $O(n)$Each call to isValid creates a copy of the array nums, so $O(n)$. In each iteration of countValidSelections, isValid is called twice, but these copies are local and short-lived, so they don’t accumulate. So the overall space complexity is $O(n)$.

entry.title: 2019 Communications Dept. Graduation Project
entry.content:
🌐 中文版：繁體中文
Preface:Honestly, when first choosing an advisor I didn’t think much about it; I just wanted a relaxed one. I remember my thinking was “for our school, prepping for grad school to transfer to a better school ASAP matters more,” so I didn’t pick a harder topic/advisor, lol. So in the end I found the most relaxed advisor in the whole department, whose project topic was Arduino every year (probably to save money and time, and because it barely needs teaching). 6 project students split into 3 groups of 2. “Arduino + App remote control”, with other topics you package yourself.Since the tech is simple and the architecture clear, it seemed the competition was about creativity and ideas. One afternoon, my teammate and I were going to buy drinks, and I suddenly had a flash of inspiration: wouldn’t it be cool if the bubble-tea cups and drinks on the market could be auto-mixed and wirelessly controlled!!!So our project, the “Smart Drinks machine,” was born. ConceptWe split the goal into a few parts and solved them one by one:App + Wifi connection + a method to move the drink + the machine bodySince the method of moving and mixing drinks is key and affects the whole body design, we first designed the drink-mixing method (how to do it, how to design it). Dispensing and mixing method:We planned to use a container to hold the drink ingredients, with a hole in the container’s bottom, and a cardboard glued below the bottom, also with a hole, but the container hole and cardboard hole are initially misaligned. A servo motor controls the rotation angle to align the cardboard hole with the container hole, and the contents fall out naturally.
So with this dispensing method, the container must have a certain height, so the body design must consider this. Predictably, the drink cup must move along the bottom to dispense, and finally add water. Movement method:Design an X/Y axis slide (like the moving bar on top of a claw machine) to let the drink cup move back/forth and left/right.After roughly planning how to dispense and move, we started designing the body. Body design:We cut and assembled using cheap, eco-friendly pine boards.
Since we had no woodworking experience, we spent a long time on the woodwork (woodworking has been added to the handyman skill set), lol. Then we built the top dispensing can and servo motor:
Dispensing can: any can (with a lid), with a hole in the bottom and a hole in the red lid (you can design the hole shape yourself)
Then cut a fan-shaped hole slightly larger than the red lid’s hole in a cardboard or foam board, and pass a small screw through the cardboard and container board (for easy rotation)
Servo motor: fixed on the side of the upper board, glued to the cardboard
To prevent the container from rotating when the servo motor turns, use hot glue to fix the wire and the dispensing can to the board.
With that, the dispensing-can structure is basically done; then repeat it 3 times, since we set up 3 dispensing cans.We started building the most troublesome part, the X/Y axis slide:Materials: stepper motor x 2, screw shaft x 2 (or just order lead screws online), bearing seat x 4, cable ties, bearings x2, iron rod x 2Cut suitable wood, drill holes, insert the iron rod and the screw shaft + stepper motor (*before inserting the screw shaft you must insert a bearing to avoid the screw shaft spinning the board out when it turns), and finally insert the bearing seats to carry the X axis; the X axis is done the same way.
The biggest problem we hit was: the X axis was too heavy to support, so the whole bearing seat would jam and couldn’t turn. We later temporarily solved it with a small toy car for support.
With that, the drink-machine body was also done!!
Hardware wiring: Components used: - NodeMCU- Arduino Mega board- L298N x 2- 4-channel relay- 1-channel relay- servo x4- stepper motor x2- submersible pump x2- power supply (can use multiple battery boxes instead)
Idea: the NodeMCU receives commands to control 4 relay switches, each relay connects to an Arduino board’s power, each Arduino board corresponds to one drink, with pre-flashed code inside the Arduino; when powered on it automatically runs the dispensing and drink-mixing program. ps. The figure above only implements one Arduino board.ps. Each Arduino board must connect to a relay controlling a submersible pump.
The water-pipe position is the drink’s start and end point (dispense ingredients, return to position, add water).
NodeMCU wiring: - 4-channel relay- connected to 4 Arduino power jacks respectively- the 4 Arduino boards each route out the L298N control pins to control the slide's XY axes- the 4 Arduinos route out other pins to control 4 servo motors- a certain pin of each of the 4 Arduinos routes out to the submersible pump's signal line.
Watch the voltage distribution
Arduino code: Arduino code:#include <Stepper.h>#include <Servo.h>#define STEPS 200 //define the stepper motor's steps per revolution#define WATER 24 //pump motor pin//steps: how many steps the motor needs for one revolution. If the motor labels the degrees per step,//divide 360 by that angle to get the needed steps (e.g. 360/3.6=100).Stepper Y(STEPS, 8, 9, 10, 11);Stepper X(STEPS, 4, 5, 6, 7);Servo goal;int pos;void setup(){ goal.attach(12); goal.write(0); X.setSpeed(160); // set the motor speed to 140RPM, max 150~160 Y.setSpeed(160); // voltage 7.5V pinMode(WATER,OUTPUT);}void loop(){ // Y.step(17000);//+ inward - outward //cocoa:17000 //milk tea: 17000 //tea: none delay(500); X.step(-24000);//inward //cocoa:-7500 //milk tea:-20000 //tea: -20000 delay(1000); for (pos = 0; pos <= 120; pos += 1) { //cocoa:140 //milk tea: 40 //tea:120 goal.write(pos); delay(15); } for (pos = 120; pos >= 0; pos -= 1) { goal.write(pos); delay(15); } delay(1000); X.step(22000); // delay(500); // Y.step(-17000); delay(1000); digitalWrite(WATER, HIGH); delay(5000); digitalWrite(WATER, LOW); delay(5000);//while(1) { }}
To dispense a drink from the back row, you must first move the Y axis to the back row, then move the X axis to a fixed point, then the servo motor turns to dispense, then move the X axis back to position, move the Y axis to the start position to add water, and finally start the pump to finish.
The program must adjust the delay times based on the container positions, ingredient-dispensing time, and water amount, and the front row doesn’t need to move the Y axis.
NodeMCU code: #define RELAY1 D7 //CHOCOLATE#define RELAY2 D8 // COFFEE#define RELAY3 D5 // Tea#include <ESP8266WiFi.h>#include <WiFiClient.h> #include <ESP8266WebServer.h>String command; //String to store app command state.const char* ssid = "專題";ESP8266WebServer server(80);int counter = 0;void setup() {pinMode(RELAY1, OUTPUT); pinMode(RELAY2, OUTPUT); pinMode(RELAY3, OUTPUT);Serial.begin(115200); // Connecting WiFiWiFi.mode(WIFI_AP); WiFi.softAP(ssid);IPAddress myIP = WiFi.softAPIP(); Serial.print("AP IP address: "); Serial.println(myIP); // Starting WEB-server server.on ( "/", HTTP_handleRoot ); server.onNotFound ( HTTP_handleRoot ); server.begin(); }//chocolatevoid relay1(){ delay(1000); digitalWrite(RELAY1,HIGH); delay(180000); digitalWrite(RELAY1,LOW); delay(5000); }//milk tea or coffeevoid relay2(){ delay(1000); digitalWrite(RELAY2,HIGH); delay(180000); digitalWrite(RELAY2,LOW); delay(5000); }//teavoid relay3(){ delay(1000); digitalWrite(RELAY3,HIGH); delay(145000); digitalWrite(RELAY3,LOW); delay(5000); }void loop() { server.handleClient(); command = server.arg("State"); //command below only changes when the phone changes state if (command == "L") { relay1(); /*chocolate*/ } else if (command == "R") { relay2(); /*milk tea */ } else if (command == "I"){ relay3(); /*tea*/ } else if (command == "F"){ counter ++; Serial.println(counter); }}void HTTP_handleRoot(void) {if( server.hasArg("State") ){ Serial.println(server.arg("State")); } server.send ( 200, "text/html", "" ); delay(1);}
Phone side
I didn’t know how to write a mobile app back then :(, so I used the simple MIT App Inventor to make it.
Actual operation Fill the containers with ingredients Fill the water container with water Turn the power supply on Connect the phone to the Wifi AP Open the app and choose the drink you want Wait for the machine to finish
Overall view There’s also an LED marquee ClosingThis project has many things that could be improved, from equipment selection to motor stability.Although Arduino really is simple, with enough ideas the possibilities are endless. Future development The top ingredient cans could be designed to be detachable A stirring module could be designed (a DC motor with a popsicle stick or something, lol) Waterproofing design Redesign the app with Android Studio, for more flexibility Directly buy a module combining ESP8266 and a relay (I only found out later this exists) Voice recognition, no app needed Heater: to brew with both cold and hot water

entry.title: 🧪Notes - 5G Core Network: Mobility Management
entry.content:
🌐 中文版：繁體中文
User identifiers and location identifiersUser identifiers split into permanent and non-permanent:
Permanent identifiers Once bound to a user they aren’t modified, offering a degree of privacy 1. SUPI2. Generic Public Subscription Identifier (GPSI)3. Permanent Equipment Identifier (PEI) Non-permanent identifiers Used to temporarily identify a user; 3GPP periodically changes the identifier 1. 5G Globally Unique Temporary Identifier (5G-GUTI)2. SUCI Location identifiers include the Tracking Area Identity (TAI) and Tracking Area Code (TAC).
SUPIThe SUPI is a permanent identifier; every subscribed user in the 5G system is allocated a 5G SUPI, used to identify that subscriber within the 3GPP system.The SUPI is stored in UDM/UDR (an NF), functioning like 4G’s IMSI.The SUPI can contain IMSI information or a network-specific identifier for private networks. IMSI format:
Field MCC MNC MSIN
Length 3bit 2~3bit <=10bit
PLMN PLMN
In roaming scenarios: the SUPI must carry the home network’s address info: MNC, MCC When interworking with an EPC network: the SUPI is always based on IMSI
Generic Public Subscription Identifier (GPSI)The GPSI is a permanent identifier, used to identify a 3GPP subscription within non-3GPP networks.The GPSI-to-3GPP mapping is stored in the subscription data; the GPSI can serve as a public identifier both inside and outside the system.The GPSI can be an MSISDN or another external identifier. Permanent Equipment Identifier (PEI)The PEI is a permanent identifier, for a 3GPP UE accessing the 5G network.For different UE types and use cases, the PEI may have different formats.When sending the PEI, the UE can carry instruction info corresponding to the format used by that PEI.If the UE supports at least one 3GPP access technology, its PEI must use the IMEI or IMEISV format. 5G Globally Unique Temporary Identifier (5G-GUTI)The 5G-GUTI is a non-permanent identifier, temporarily allocated to the UE by the AMF (during the registration procedure), used to identify that UE.The same 5G-GUTI is used for different access methods (3GPP, non-3GPP).
Structure of the 5G-GUTI: <5G-GUTI>:=<GUAMI><5G-TMSI> (:= is the symbol for "defined as")<GUAMI>: used to identify one or more AMFs<5G-TMSI>: used to uniquely identify the UE Structure of the GUAMI: <GUAMI>:= <MCC><MNC><AMF Region ID><AMF Set ID><AMF Pointer><AMF Region ID>: used to identify a region<AMF Set ID>: uniquely identifies a set of AMFs within an AMF region<AMF Pointer>: uniquely identifies an AMF within an AMF set
The 5G-S-TMSI is a shortened form of the GUTI, used in radio signaling (paging or service-request procedures) to improve transmission efficiency.
Structure of the 5G-S-TMSI: <5G-S-TMSI>:= <AMF Set ID><AMF Pointer><5G-TMSI>
The 10 least-significant bits of the 5G-TMSI are used by the NG-RAN to determine the UE’s paging occasion
so these 10 least-significant bits should be evenly distributed, making different UEs’ paging occasions evenly distributed
MCC MNC AMF Region ID AMF Set ID AMF Pointer 5G-TMSI
12bit 8/12bit 16bit 4bit 4bit 32bit
PLMN PLMN AMF ID AMF ID AMF ID
GUAMI GUAMI GUAMI GUAMI GUAMI
5G-S-TMSI 5G-S-TMSI 5G-S-TMSI
5G-GUTI 5G-GUTI 5G-GUTI 5G-GUTI 5G-GUTI 5G-GUTI
SUCIThe SUCI is a non-permanent identifier, a privacy-protecting identifier formed from an encrypted form of the SUPI (Subscription Permanent Identifier).Since each subscriber’s SUPI is permanent and unique, transmitting it directly poses a privacy risk. The UE (USIM or ME) can generate the SUCI based on ECIES, or even the Null-Scheme.When the AMF receives the SUCI, it triggers the authentication procedure, after which a decryption algorithm (SIDF) in the UDM/SIDF decodes the received SUCI into the SUPI to complete subsequent authentication. TAI & TACBoth are location identifiers.TAI: Tracking Area IdentityTAC: Tracking Area Code
Format:
MCC MNC TAC
12bit 8/12bit 20bit
PLMN ID PLMN ID TAC
TAI TAI TAI
Security architecture and proceduresWhen a UE moves within the RAN or between different networks, it needs to mutually authenticate with the network to ensure both sides are trustworthy.Mutual authentication between the UE and network needs the support of the 5G security architecture.The 5G security architecture should include: - mitigating and reducing attacks- supporting authentication and authorization mechanisms- supporting key-related functions
Features of the security architecture A security architecture independent of the access method (3GPP, non-3GPP), using a unified authentication method and key architecture Enhanced security (4G → IMSI → insecure | 5G → SUCI/SUPI → secure) Differentiated authentication: 5G supports USIM, certificates, username/password, and other authentication methods Service-based architecture and open-interface security
The NFs involved in the security architecture include: ARPF, AUSF, SEAF, SIDF
ARPF: deployed together with UDM responsible for storing the root key $Ki$ and related subscription data computes 5G authentication vectors
AUSF: provides the EAP authentication server function, performing EAP authentication to derive the anchor key
SEAF: deployed together with AMF responsible for deriving the lower-layer NAS and AS keys from the anchor key, and completing the 5G AKA authentication-result comparison function
SIDF: deployed together with UDM responsible for decoding the SUCI into the SUPI
Security procedures
The UE initiates a request, sending a SUCI or 5G-GUTI message to the SEAF The SEAF sends the SUCI or SUPI (if the 5G-GUTI is valid) to the AUSF of the home network After the AUSF completes authentication, it sends a message to the home network’s UDM The UDM receives the SUCI, decodes it into the SUPI, selects the corresponding authentication algorithm based on the subscriber data, and completes identity authentication through the subsequent procedure
The authentication algorithms 5G currently supports: EAP-AKA’ and 5G AKA - 3GPP TS 33.501 Referenceshttps://cat.chriz.hk/2019/12/5g-security-architecture.html

entry.title: 🧪Notes - 5G Network Function Interfaces and Protocol Stacks
entry.content:
🌐 中文版：繁體中文
The N2 interface (control interface and protocol stack)$5G Access,Network \stackrel{N2}{\longleftrightarrow} 5GC(AMF)$
Management procedures: not related to a specific UE, like setting up or resetting the N2 interface Procedures related to a single UE: NAS transport procedures, UE context management, PDU-session resource-related procedures, handover management, etc. Uses the NG-AP protocol (regardless of access network type: 3GPP RAN or N3IWF non-3GPP), which is an application-layer protocol The AMF has a unique N2 termination point for a UE Since the SMF and AMF are decoupled, NG-AP supports the AMF relaying N2 SM messages between the 5G RAN and 5GC
SCTP guarantees transport between the Access Network and 5GC
The control-plane interface and protocol stack between the UE and 5GCFor each connection method a UE uses (3GPP, non-3GPP), the UE has an N1 NAS connection, with a unique N1 termination point located in the AMF.
Non-access stratum (NAS)A protocol layer that originally existed in 3G/UMTS, a functional layer between the user equipment and the core network.It has the following functions:
mobility managementcall controlsession managementidentity managementNAS reference
N1 NAS can be used for:
UE registration management connection management session management
The NAS protocol within the N1 interface splits into: NAS-MM, NAS-SM NAS-MMUsed for the UE to interact with NFs other than the AMF
session-management messages UE policy location services
NAS transports session-management messages, SMS, UE policy, location services, and other protocol procedures FeaturesHandles the NAS procedures between the UE and AMF, including:
handling the UE’s registration management (RM) and connection management (CM): providing a secure message link and access control between the UE and AMF applicable to other types of NAS messages (NAS-SM, SMS, etc.), which can be transmitted simultaneously with RM/CM NAS messages the same NAS protocol is used for different access methods (3GPP, non-3GPP) the UE has one N1 NAS connection for each access method
NAS-SMSupports handling session management between the UE and SMF
establishment, modification, and release of the PDU session’s user plane SM messages are established and processed within NAS-SM (the content isn’t parsed by the AMF) the NAS-MM layer handles sending/receiving SM messages between the UE and AMF, and provides security protection (protecting message integrity)
The control-plane interface and protocol stack between 5GC NFsIn the 5G core, an NF Service Producer provides services to an NF Service Consumer via a service-based interface. The 5G core defines the following control interfaces as service-based interfaces: - Nsmf- Nudm- Nnrf- Nnssf- Nausf- Nnef- Nsmsf- Nudr- Npcf- N5g-eir- Nlmf These service-based interfaces use HTTP 2.0 and JSON as application-layer protocols; all 3GPP network functions must support TLS.If the PLMN doesn’t provide another network-security solution, TLS must be used.In the future, QUIC/UDP may be used as an optimized solution.
The N4 interface and protocol stack$SMF\stackrel{N4}{\longleftrightarrow}UPF$ N4 sits between the SMF and UPF, with control-plane and user-plane functions.N4 defines the following procedures: Control-plane procedures - N4 session management: for the SMF to establish, update, and delete N4 session context on the UPF- N4 reporting procedures: for the UPF to report events (e.g. traffic usage) to the SMF- N4 node-level procedures: establishment, update, association, and release of the N4 node between SMF and UPF; the UPF reports N4 node-level events to the SMF- SMF charging-suspend procedures:
User-plane proceduresForwarding traffic between the SMF and UPF:When the user is in the CM-IDLE state, the UPF can forward downlink data to the SMF, which then decides the paging policy.
PFCP $\longleftrightarrow$ PFCP
UDF $\longleftrightarrow$ UPF
IP $\longleftrightarrow$ IP
L2 $\longleftrightarrow$ L2
L1 $\longleftrightarrow$ L1
Control Plane $\longleftrightarrow$ User Plane
The user-plane interface and its protocol stack$Access,Network\stackrel{N3}{\longleftrightarrow}UPF$$UPF \stackrel{N9}{\longleftrightarrow}UPF$The N3 and N9 interfaces carry data between the 5G RAN and UPF, and between UPF and UPF, respectively.
PDU (Protocol Data Unit) layer: responsible for carrying PDUs in the PDU session between the UE and the Data Network

entry.title: Executing Remote Operations with AWS IoT Jobs: A Hands-On Tutorial
entry.content:
What is a Job? A Job is a remote operation that is sent to and executed on one or more devices connected to AWS IoT. For example, you can define a Job that instructs a set of devices to download and install application or firmware updates, reboot, rotate certificates, or perform remote troubleshooting operations.
How to create a Job?You must create a job document first.
The Job Document is a description of the remote operations to be performed a Job
Target When you create a Job, you specify a list of targets that are the devices that should perform the operations. The targets can be things or thing groups or both. The Jobs feature sends a message to each target to inform it that a Job is available.
Job Execution A Job execution is an instance of a Job on a target device. The target starts an execution of a Job by downloading the Job document. It then performs the operations specified in the document, and reports its progress to AWS IoT.
Prepare to run a remote operation using Jobs Setup download location (Device Client)
mkdir -p /home/ubuntu/workshop_dc/downloadLocation Check if the process successful sudo tail -F /var/log/aws-iot-device-client/aws-iot-device-client.log
AWS IoT Job using embedded-c SDKLaunch an EC2. AMI: ubuntu t2.micro
Networking:
VPC CIDR: 10.1.0.0/16 Public Subnet: 10.1.0.0/24
Connect to the instance and install the necessary packages Installationsudo apt-get install vim git curlgit clone https://github.com/aws/aws-iot-device-sdk-embedded-c.git --recurse-submodulescd aws-iot-device-sdk-embedded-cmkdir -r build/bin/sudo apt-get install libssl-dev
Create Things Create Thing Enter Thing Name, press “Next” Select Auto-generate a new certificate
Policy
Make sure that the certificate you create have bind to policy with enough permisssioniot: Connectiot: Receiveiot: Publishiot: Subscribe
Download Certificate Upload certificate to EC2 scp -i <local ssh private key> <cert_name>pem.crt admin@ec2-XX-XXX-XXX-XXX.compute-1.amazonaws.com:/home/admin/aws-iot-device-sdk-embedded-c/build/bin/certificates/
Upload private key scp -i TestKeyAccess.pem debace3e049b44eb15d67fad8ab17763cc575604f4d4a1451cc62cd4ef1498ed-private.pem.key ubuntu@ec2-54-167-159-68.compute-1.amazonaws.com:/home/ubuntu/aws-iot-device-sdk-embedded-c/build/bin/certificates
Upload certificates scp -i TestKeyAccess.pem debace3e049b44eb15d67fad8ab17763cc575604f4d4a1451cc62cd4ef1498ed-certificate.pem.crt ubuntu@ec2-54-167-159-68.compute-1.amazonaws.com:/home/ubuntu/aws-iot-device-sdk-embedded-c/build/bin/certificates
Upload AmazonRootCA1.pem scp -i TestKeyAccess.pem AmazonRootCA1.pem ubuntu@ec2-54-167-159-68.compute-1.amazonaws.com:/home/ubuntu/aws-iot-device-sdk-embedded-c/build/bin/certificates
AWS IoT Jobs Demo Ref: https://aws.github.io/aws-iot-device-sdk-embedded-C/202012.00/docs/doxygen/output/html/jobs_demo.html
sudo apt install curl libmosquitto-dev mosquitto
Create Jobaws iot create-job --job-id t12 --targets <YOUR_THING_ARN> \ --document '{"url":"https://cdn.kernel.org/pub/linux/kernel/v5.x/linux-5.8.5.tar.xz"}'
Execute Job on the target device run the demo program with device credentialsjobs_demo_mosquitto -n device1 -h abcdefg123.iot.us-east-1.amazonaws.com \ --certfile bbaf123456-certificate.pem.crt --keyfile bbaf123456-private.pem.key
Build the demo programcd /aws-iot-device-sdk-embedded-c/demos/jobs/jobs_demo_mosquittomake
./jobs_demo_mosquitto
./jobs_demo_mosquitto -n <Thing Name> -h <YOUR_IOT_ENDPOINT> \ --certfile bbaf123456-certificate.pem.crt --keyfile bbaf123456-private.pem.key
Endpoint: a2t2vimlyuhccy-ats.iot.us-east-1.amazonaws.com ./jobs_demo_mosquitto -n ThingforExecuteJobs -h a2t2vimlyuhccy-ats.iot.us-east-1.amazonaws.com --certfile ~/aws-iot-device-sdk-embedded-c/build/bin/certificates/debace3e049b44eb15d67fad8ab17763cc575604f4d4a1451cc62cd4ef1498ed-certificate.pem.crt --keyfile ~/aws-iot-device-sdk-embedded-c/build/bin/certificates/debace3e049b44eb15d67fad8ab17763cc575604f4d4a1451cc62cd4ef1498ed-private.pem.key
Check AWSIoTLogv2

entry.title: Reflections on a Year and a Half as an AWS Cloud Support Engineer
entry.content:
🌐 中文版：繁體中文
Background I currently work as a Cloud Support Engineer at Amazon Web Services in Taiwan, but in two days I’m leaving. So before I go, I wanted to write down and look back on the work and life of the past year and a half.
I applied for the AWS Cloud Support campus recruitment position in the first semester of my second year of grad school (October 2021). At the time I was originally looking for the R&D alternative military service, but once I heard AWS had an opening, I sent in my resume just to see what would happen. I got the Online Assessment notice about a day later. The OA was really just basic computer knowledge, probably just used to filter CS vs non-CS majors (?). Then came the phone interview. Back then the campus recruitment let you rank your preferences. What I originally wanted was the Security or Deployment profile, but during the interviews I found most of the questions were troubleshooting-related, so Security was a fail, and in the Deployment final loop I got grilled in the last technical round too. Later I switched to interviewing for DMS (Developer and Mobile Services). Even though it was a field I wasn’t familiar with at all, thankfully I passed the interview in the end. After finishing my master’s degree and my military service, I finally started at the end of March 2023. This was the first full-time job of my life. OnboardingThe first few months are employee training plus learning the services your team needs to know. This stage really demands absorbing all kinds of knowledge quickly. Every day there was something new to learn, very full-on, and you had to pick up a technology or tool fast. These months might have been the happiest: learning things and getting paid for it. But the foundation really does get laid during this time, so in those first few months I spent a while deploying and wiring up services in our internal lab environment. For example, implementing API Gateway Private Integration, experimenting with Lambda Provisioned Concurrency, that sort of thing. Life back then was pretty relaxed. I’d bring my MacBook Pro to the office, grab any seat (Agile Desk, Shared Desk), open the AWS Console, jump into us-east-1, and start practicing and operating resources. The nice thing about a cloud company is that the local employees’ hardware doesn’t have to be great, since you just connect to some Region to get your work done. When I got tired I’d go make some tea or coffee, look out the window at Taipei 101 or the Tao Zhu Yin Yuan building, and take it in. Day-to-day work During onboarding you also learn how to resolve cases. This job is a lot like being a disaster-relief worker: the person opening a case is often already facing a damaged production environment, so at that point you might need to hop on a call with the customer, pin down the problem, and try to solve it. If it’s something we can’t solve, the problem can be escalated to a stronger internal team to investigate (they have permission to use certain investigation tools), and sometimes you also need to talk to internal service teams to understand the details. Different cases also have different levels of urgency, so you have to stay alert at all times. You might be taking it easy one moment and suddenly an urgent case comes in (and of course there are also customers who open a non-urgent case as urgent). A single sentence might mean a call, and then you’re watching the customer’s screen as they operate, investigating. I also feel really lucky I got to work alongside a group of absolute experts here. Some of my questions were probably dumb to them, but they’d answer enthusiastically, so you could learn all kinds of things without worry, and there was room to make mistakes. It was a team you could feel at ease being part of. Cloud Support is shift-based, so weekends need people on duty too. After all, AWS Support’s whole pitch is 24/7, 365 days, uninterrupted service. So as the Taipei timezone is wrapping up for the day, Dublin in Ireland takes over and keeps handling incoming cases, then it’s Seattle’s turn, and the next day it comes back to Taipei. So cross-country collaboration is pretty frequent here too.
You might randomly get pinged by someone in India with a question lol
For larger customers, you’d usually need to meet and collaborate with the Technical Account Manager (TAM) or Solutions Architect (SA) responsible for that customer. There’s bound to be friction in that, and how you digest it is up to the individual (hard to say, lol). Daily lifeIn the morning, after everyone finished their cases, we’d go to Yongji Road for a cheap lunch, chatting over the meal about who ran into which customer again. Thursday afternoons we’d enjoy the afternoon tea the company ordered. Then it was back to work until the end of your shift. I also feel like there was quite a lot of leave, plus comp time, so I actually took time off to travel fairly often. And you don’t have to worry while you’re off: if a customer comes back, someone will always pick it up for you. A couple of afternoon-tea photos from a few weeks back. The company has quite a few events too, though whether you have time to join is another matter. Even though this job doesn’t require overtime, those 8 hours felt pretty intense to me personally. I once had an afternoon with three back-to-back customer meetings, which really makes your head explode. CSA to CSEIn campus recruitment I mainly applied for CSA (Cloud Support Associate), because I had no cloud experience at the time, so you start in this position. But actually, a while after training ends you go through the process of converting to CSE. During this period you still need to resolve more cases and get more familiar with the services’ characteristics. This change of position really only affects your title and salary; what you actually do is still the same: troubleshooting for customers. SMEOutsiders might only know about AWS Certificates, but for people inside AWS, SME (Subject-Matter Expert) is the more important thing. It usually means you’re extremely familiar with a service, enough to be an expert in it. It’s a kind of proof of your ability, and an effective data point to demonstrate you have certain skills, which can help somewhat with collaboration or promotion.
Reference: https://aws.amazon.com/tw/certification/certification-sme-program/
Why leave?It’s hard to explain in a sentence. All I can say is that my personality isn’t quite suited to Support, and there was a gap from what I expected coming in. Overall, since it’s about serving customers, it felt more like a service industry: dedicated to providing good service and meeting most of the customer’s requests. But I’d expected to be solving interesting technical problems, whereas here any problem is possible, and no day is predictable in what you’ll hit. Most problems might be ones you’ve repeatedly seen before, or ones with little technical substance. If you want a stable work life, this job is pretty good, but this was my first job, and I wanted to learn more, not be confined to specific AWS services. Another thing is how hard it is to change tracks. The longer you do Support, the more the development and research skills you used to have gradually fade. After work I didn’t really have the energy to learn new things either; I just wanted to release the negative energy I’d absorbed during those 8 hours (which is why I say it’s probably more personality-related: I’m not well suited to the service industry). So the things I once knew gradually faded, and that gave me an inexplicable panic. I could already picture myself failing to switch jobs after 30. Relocation would be a harder path here, and I probably wouldn’t stay until that happened. Promotion is a matter of opinion, so I won’t comment… :( A fun part: sleeping over at the officeThere were still plenty of fun times at the company. A while back I took on the challenge of staying overnight at the office. In the evening I ordered pizza with coworkers and we chatted for ages. That kind of joyful atmosphere is really great. After everyone left, I went back to my seat.
It was my first time sleeping over at the office. Even though the other AWS building has showers, I figured I’d just take the MRT home at 6 am and shower then. After 8 pm the office emptied out, and I did some LeetCode at my desk. Once I was done, in the middle of the night I watched the launch-day livestream of the Elden Ring DLC. Roughly every hour Security would come by on patrol. I’d heard a rumor before: there was once an employee who slept at the office too, but he was studying there, and once he’d passed every AWS certification he bailed. Sounds like a weirdo like me. The Xinyi District night view in the evening is pretty beautiful too.
Call it leaving as deep a memory as I could at this company. What’s nextSince I decided to leave, I also stopped seeing the therapist. I can only say that quitting cures all ills. The faded knowledge is gradually returning to my body, my mood has gradually brightened, and I’ve started getting back into my old regular exercise habits. In my spare time I even submitted a paper to IEEE CNS, and now I’m doing LeetCode. Life is very nourishing. But overall, I’d still highly recommend using AWS services. The engineers inside all have the spirit of Customer Obsession and Deep Dive, and being a customer is a very fortunate thing. The friendships, connections, and resources this job brought are all extremely precious, and I learned a lot of cloud-service knowledge I didn’t have before, plus many serverless and architectural deployment approaches. It was a very precious year. Before I leave the day after tomorrow, I’m still a bit emotional about saying goodbye to this place. I hope all my coworkers can find where they belong. Goodbye, Amazon Taiwan.

entry.title: 🐞Building a Web Crawler with Amazon Lambda
entry.content:
🌐 中文版：繁體中文
PrefaceThis post is from reproducing a customer issue. To solve the customer’s problem, I tried to install Selenium Chromedriver and BeautifulSoup, package them into a Lambda Layer, and build a Lambda based on that layer, but kept getting a “Chromedriver file not found” error. After pit after pit of troubleshooting, this savior suddenly appeared: https://stackoverflow.com/questions/69047401/selenium-docker-container-runs-on-ec2-but-not-on-aws-lambda. Based on this article and the corresponding GitHub https://github.com/rchauhan9/image-scraper-lambda-container/tree/master, it mainly builds the Lambda via a container image, but before doing so you first package the needed packages and environment into an image. But since the company Mac can’t install Docker, I first spun up an EC2 for most of the work. The examples and the knowledge needed to build this post all reference the AWS official docs.
The whole flow is roughly as follows. I drew the flowchart with mermaid, referencing this blog and the official doc tutorial:https://shannonhung.github.io/posts/first-blog.html#%E5%89%8D%E8%A8%80https://mermaid.js.org/syntax/flowchart.html
graph LR A(Create and configure EC2) --> B(Configure VPC) B(Configure VPC) --> C(Connect to EC2) C(Connect to EC2) --> D(Install Docker) D(Install Docker) --> E(Build image) E(Build image) --> F(Test container) F(Test container) --> G(Push to repository) G(Push to repository) --> H(Build Lambda)
Installing EC2Name: TestWebScrappingAMI: Amazon Linux 2Region: us-east-1Access Key: "CWAccess.pem"
Configuring the networkIPv4 CIDR: 10.1.0.0/16Subnet: TestSubnet1CIDR: 10.1.0.0/24RouteTable: 10.1.0.0/16 | local0.0.0.0/0 | Internet GatewaySecurity GroupTCP 443 Source: 0.0.0.0/0TCP 80 Source: 0.0.0.0/0TCP 22 Source: 0.0.0.0/0
After creation, connect to EC2 ssh -i "CWAccess.pem" ec2-user@ec2-3-83-139-226.compute-1.amazonaws.com
Installing DockerFor the install docs here, refer to the AWS official guide:https://docs.aws.amazon.com/zh_cn/AmazonECS/latest/developerguide/create-container-image.html sudo yum update -ysudo amazon-linux-extras install dockersudo service docker startsudo usermod -a -G docker ec2-user# log back into the terminal at this pointdocker info
Building the Docker imageFirst create a few files in the home directory:
requirements.txt entry.sh app/app.py
requirements.txt requests==2.25.0selenium==3.14.0beautifulsoup4==4.9.3Pillow==8.0.1boto3botocore

app/app.py mkdir appcd appvim app.py import jsonfrom selenium import webdriverfrom selenium.webdriver.chrome.options import Optionsfrom selenium.webdriver.support.ui import WebDriverWaitfrom selenium.webdriver.common.by import Byfrom selenium.webdriver.support import expected_conditions as ECdef handler(event, context): chrome_options = Options() chrome_options.add_argument('--disable-dev-shm-usage') chrome_options.add_argument('--disable-domain-reliability') chrome_options.add_argument('--disable-extensions') chrome_options.add_argument('--disable-features=AudioServiceOutOfProcess') chrome_options.add_argument('--disable-hang-monitor') chrome_options.add_argument('--disable-ipc-flooding-protection') chrome_options.add_argument('--disable-notifications') chrome_options.add_argument('--disable-offer-store-unmasked-wallet-cards') chrome_options.add_argument('--disable-popup-blocking') chrome_options.add_argument('--disable-print-preview') chrome_options.add_argument('--disable-prompt-on-repost') chrome_options.add_argument('--disable-renderer-backgrounding') chrome_options.add_argument('--disable-setuid-sandbox') chrome_options.add_argument('--disable-speech-api') chrome_options.add_argument('--disable-sync') chrome_options.add_argument('--disk-cache-size=33554432') chrome_options.add_argument('--hide-scrollbars') chrome_options.add_argument('--ignore-gpu-blacklist') Driver Initiated") response = { "statusCode": 200, "body": json.dumps(html, ensure_ascii=False) } return response
vim Dockerfile
Dockerfile # Define global argsARG FUNCTION_DIR="/home/app/"ARG RUNTIME_VERSION="3.9"ARG DISTRO_VERSION="3.12"# Stage 1FROM python:${RUNTIME_VERSION}-alpine${DISTRO_VERSION} AS python-alpineRUN apk add --no-cache \ libstdc++# Stage 2FROM python-alpine AS build-imageRUN apk add --no-cache \ build-base \ libtool \ autoconf \ automake \ libexecinfo-dev \ make \ cmake \ libcurlARG FUNCTION_DIRARG RUNTIME_VERSIONRUN mkdir -p ${FUNCTION_DIR}RUN python${RUNTIME_VERSION} -m pip install awslambdaric --target ${FUNCTION_DIR}# Stage 3FROM python-alpine as build-image2ARG FUNCTION_DIRWORKDIR ${FUNCTION_DIR}COPY --from=build-image ${FUNCTION_DIR} ${FUNCTION_DIR}RUN apk update \ && apk add gcc python3-dev musl-dev \ && apk add jpeg-dev zlib-dev libjpeg-turbo-devCOPY requirements.txt .RUN python${RUNTIME_VERSION} -m pip install -r requirements.txt --target ${FUNCTION_DIR}# Stage 4FROM python-alpineARG FUNCTION_DIRWORKDIR ${FUNCTION_DIR}COPY --from=build-image2 ${FUNCTION_DIR} ${FUNCTION_DIR}RUN apk add jpeg-dev zlib-dev libjpeg-turbo-dev \ && apk add chromium chromium-chromedriverADD https://github.com/aws/aws-lambda-runtime-interface-emulator/releases/latest/download/aws-lambda-rie /usr/bin/aws-lambda-rieRUN chmod 755 /usr/bin/aws-lambda-rieCOPY app/* ${FUNCTION_DIR}COPY entry.sh /ENTRYPOINT [ "/entry.sh" ]CMD [ "app.handler" ]
Build the image docker build -t awsLambdacrawler .
Once built, check whether it succeeded with: docker images
Testing the containerdocker run -p 9000:8080 <IMAGE_ID>
The output will look like this Now open another terminal to invoke and test the request curl -XPOST "http://localhost:9000/2015-03-31/functions/function/invocations" -d '{}'
Then create an ECR Repository (on the local MacBook) aws ecr create-repository --repository-name cx-lambda --image-scanning-configuration scanOnPush=true docker tag awsLambdacrawler:latest <ENTER YOUR CONTAINER REPOSITORY URI>:latest
Then on the local MacBook, get the ECR password aws ecr get-login-password
Copy the password docker login <YOUR AWS ACCOUNT ID>.dkr.ecr.<YOUR REGION>.amazonaws.com (http://amazonaws.com/)>
username: AWS password: the password just copied
Push the image to the repository docker push <YOUR AWS ACCOUNT ID>.dkr.ecr.<YOUR REGION>.amazonaws.com (http://amazonaws.com/)
Check it in the ECR console Creating the LambdaGo to Lambda Console > Create Function > Container Image Function Name: ScrappingfromImageContainer image URI: 125657041963.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/cx-lambda:latest
Configuring Lambda network accessIf you want the Lambda function to connect to the external network, unlike EC2, you need to attach the Lambda to your own VPC, put the Lambda in a private subnet, and that private subnet’s route table must have its default route set to a NAT Gateway.Because when Lambda connects to a VPC it creates an ENI, and that ENI by default only takes a private IP, so a NAT Gateway is needed to translate between public and private IPs, and it connects to the NAT Gateway via a feature called V2N.
If interested, refer to these two official docs, which detail Lambda’s networking mechanism:https://docs.aws.amazon.com/zh_tw/lambda/latest/dg/foundation-networking.htmlhttps://aws.amazon.com/tw/blogs/compute/announcing-improved-vpc-networking-for-aws-lambda-functions/
As a flowchart it looks like this:
flowchart LR subgraph Custom VPC direction LR c1(Lambda) ---> a2(NATGateway) subgraph Public Subnet direction LR a2(NATGateway) end subgraph Private Subnet direction LR c1(Lambda) end end
private route Configuring Lambda permissionsRemember to add the VPCAccessExecutionRole permission to the Lambda. Then test the code. But first go to Configuration > General Configuration > Timeout and raise the timeout.
Timeout: 20 sec
Testing the Lambda Success

entry.title: Buffer Overflow Vulnerability Experiment
entry.content:
IntroductionBuffer Overflow Vulnerability is one of the most common and severe security vulnerabilities in the field of software and system security. In the complex software systems of today’s digital age, the threat from hackers or malicious users is ever-present. Buffer Overflow Vulnerability is one of the most concerning threats among them due to the significant threat it poses to computer systems. In simple terms, a buffer overflow vulnerability occurs when code attempts to store data in a predefined size of memory block known as a buffer. If the amount of data input exceeds the maximum capacity of the buffer, the excess data will overflow into adjacent memory areas, potentially overwriting instructions or data that control program execution, leading to unexpected behavior. The fundamental cause of buffer overflow vulnerabilities is negligence and errors in program design. When developers fail to handle user input correctly, especially when they do not perform sufficient validation and restrictions on the input, it may lead to such vulnerabilities. Attackers often exploit these unchecked inputs by sending specially crafted malicious data, triggering buffer overflow attacks. This attack method has been around for many years and has caused numerous serious security incidents throughout history. In the past, several well-known buffer overflow vulnerabilities have been widely reported, some of which have had profound impacts on global information security. For example, the infamous Code Red and Nimda worms utilized buffer overflow vulnerabilities to rapidly infect tens of thousands of hosts. Similarly, the Slammer worm exploited a buffer overflow vulnerability in Microsoft SQL Server, causing a sudden surge in global internet traffic. These events emphasize the need for the entire tech industry to take buffer overflow vulnerabilities seriously.
SQL Slammer - https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SQL_Slammer
So, this article aims to conduct a simple experiment on buffer overflow vulnerabilities to provide at least a conceptual understanding. Environment SetupIn terms of environment setup, we use the Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL) platform to configure the development environment and use Ubuntu 20.04 LTS as the development environment. We will install the necessary tools in this environment, including Python3, Pwntool, and the PEDA plugin for GDB debugging. WSL provides a feature to run Linux distributions on Windows systems, enabling us to perform Linux-related development work in a Windows environment. Ubuntu 20.04 LTS is a stable and common Linux distribution widely used in development and testing environments. Before configuring the environment, we need to ensure that WSL is installed and running. Installation instructions for WSL can be found in the Microsoft official documentation or relevant online tutorials.
https://learn.microsoft.com/zh-tw/windows/wsl/install
Next, we need to install Python3 and Pwntool in WSL. Pwntool is a common Python library used in CTFs, specifically designed for exploit development. Before installing Pwntool, we need to make sure that git is installed in WSL. If not installed, it can be done using the following commands: sudo apt updatesudo apt install git Next, we can install Pwntool as follows: sudo apt install python3 python3-pippip3 install --upgrade pippip3 install pwntools
Now we have completed the installation of Python3 and Pwntool in WSL. Finally, we will configure the GDB DEBUG environment, using the PEDA plugin to assist us in practicing buffer overflow vulnerabilities. git clone https://github.com/longld/peda.git ~/pedaecho "source ~/peda/peda.py" >> ~/.gdbinit
Lastly, here is a simple C program buffer_test.c used as the target for demonstrating the buffer overflow vulnerability. The program includes a uname() function that uses the gets() function to receive user input, but it does not perform sufficient validation on the input, potentially leading to a buffer overflow vulnerability. buffer_test.c #include <stdio.h>void target(){ printf("Oh No! Your Hacker.\n");}void uname(){ char str[16]; printf("input your name: \n"); gets(str); printf("Hello, %s \n", str);}int main(){ setvbuf(stdin, NULL, _IONBF, 0); //Clear buffer setvbuf(stdout, NULL, _IONBF, 0); uname(); return 0;}
The program contains the risky input function gets, used for practicing Buffer Overflow.
Experimental StepsCompile the ProgramFirst, we need to compile the code named buffer_test.c for further experimentation. During compilation, we need to disable the Stack Canary protection mechanism using the following command: gcc buffer_test.c -o buffer_test -fno-stack-protector -no-pie
-fno-stack-protector : Disable the Stack Canary protection mechanism.
Check Protective MeasuresBefore starting the experiment, it is necessary to confirm the security protective measures of the target program. The checksec command can quickly check the relevant security measures of the target executable: checksec buffer_test
Confirm the TargetBefore launching an attack, we need to identify the target. In this experiment, our goal is to execute the target function, so we need to find the memory address of that function and overwrite the function’s return address. Confirm Function Memory AddressUse GDB to query the memory address of the target function: gdb buffer_testgdb-peda$ disas target
From the above image, the starting address of this function is 0x0000000000401196 . Knowing the address of the function, the next step is to understand how to overwrite the ret address from input. TestingBefore launching an actual attack, let’s run the program in GDB and observe its behavior: gdb-peta$ r // Run it first
The program will prompt the user to input a name, and after entering the name, it responds with "Hello, {name}". Since the array in the original program that holds user input is only 16 bytes (RBP ~ RBP-16), we can observe its behavior by inputting data exceeding 16 bytes.
As shown in the image, when input exceeds 24 bytes, a buffer overflow occurs, and a crash occurs after the v character. This indicates that we need at least 24 bytes of input to successfully overwrite the function’s return address.
So, it can be covered with 8 Bytes to overwrite the ret address.
RBP shows only up to ‘qrstuvwx’, meaning it crashed when input reached 24 bytes.
Actual Overwriting with Python為了進行實際的攻擊，將使用 Python 撰寫攻擊腳本。這個腳本將使用 Pwntools 函式庫來進行攻擊，蓋過程式中的函式返回位址，使之執行 target 函式。 To carry out the actual attack, a Python script will be used to overwrite the program’s function return address. This script will use the Pwntools library to perform the attack and execute the target function. The attack script attack.py is as follows: #!/usr/bin/env python# coding=utf-8from pwn import *r = process('./demo')r.recvuntil('input your name:') targer_address = p64(0x400667)r.sendline(b'A' * 24 + targer_address)r.interactive()
In the attack script, the process() function is used to execute the buffer_test program. Then, the recvuntil() function is used to wait for the program to display the prompt “input your name:”, after which the pre-calculated address of the target function is added to the input data. Finally, the interactive() function is used to enter interactive mode to observe the results of the attack.
recvuntil(): receive until, can receive a specific string, and execute the xx command when the target string is reached.
p8()、p32()、p64()
p32: pack data (32-bit integer) for data // u32: unpack p64: pack data (64-bit integer) for data // u64: unpack
Convert to address
sendline(payload): send payload and newline interactive()： enter interactive mode, used to execute local or remote executables
Execute the Attack ScriptFinally, we run the attack script to perform the attack: python3 attack.py
After a successful attack, the program will execute the target function and display the message “Oh No! Your Hacker.” This proves that we have successfully exploited the buffer overflow vulnerability. Successfully executed the target function!
Remember to ensure compliance with relevant laws and regulations when applying the knowledge gained in real-world environments, and only conduct security testing and exploitation in legally authorized situations.
Referenceshttps://mks.tw/2976/%e8%b3%87%e8%a8%8a%e5%ae%89%e5%85%a8-%e5%be%9e%e6%af%ab%e7%84%a1%e5%9f%ba%e7%a4%8e%e9%96%8b%e5%a7%8b-pwn-buffer-overflow

entry.title: C++ Problem-Solving Power Tool - STL (Standard Template Library) | LeetCode
entry.content:
🌐 中文版：繁體中文
What is the STL (Standard Template Library)?In C++, the STL is a collection of containers. Different containers implement different data structures, and they’re actually implemented with heavy use of C++ templates.Algorithms are implemented on top of these data structures, and the STL also provides operations on containers, with different data-structure containers having different ways of operating on them.
A template, simply put, is a predefined structure that can be used with different data types. For example, I write an array template, but it can be int[], float[], double[], or char[].template <typename T> is the usual way to define a template. Think of the stuff inside the angle brackets as the compiler doing copy-paste for you.
STL componentsThere are 6 main components:
Container Algorithm Iterator Function object (functor) Adaptor Allocator
For problem solving, the key things to focus on are containers and iterators, plus algorithms like sort, which usually exist as functions and are mostly one-off computations. But on LeetCode you mostly have to implement things yourself, so I won’t go into detail on those.
STL containersContainers are usually the data-structure part, existing as variables, and can continuously interact with and maintain data.
The container types usable on LeetCode are: Vector, List, Stack, Queue, PriorityQueue (Binary Heap), Set/MultiSet, Unordered Set, Map/MultiMap, Unordered Map STL iteratorsAn iterator is used to visit all elements of a container in order, and also to refer to a specific element in a container, which can express a search result or the endpoint of a range. Below is an example #include <iostream>#include <vector>#include <algorithm>using namespace std;int main(){ int n, i; vector<int> v; while (cin >> n) { v.resize(n); for (i=0; i<n; i++) { cin >> v[i]; } sort(v.begin(), v.end()); for (vector<int>::iterator it=v.begin(); it!=v.end(); ++it) { cout << *it << "\n"; } } return 0;}
From: https://hackmd.io/@sa072686/cp/%2F%40sa072686%2FS11uDpiuH
You can see that inside the for loop we can use vector<int>::iterator to declare an iterator it, which starts from the beginning of the vector and increments by 1 while not equal to the end. A few key points to observe here:
An iterator is declared as container_type::iterator Iterators support ++ or -- operations Containers that support iterators can basically all use .begin() to get the first element and .end() to get the position one past the last element, which is a nonexistent empty slot, matching the STL’s left-inclusive, right-exclusive rule Using the dereference operator * you can get the value at the iterator’s current address
Most of the time, understanding it as a pointer is fine (a pointer is a special case of an iterator; it’s also an iterator).
auto type deductionFrom the example above you’ll notice one thing: declaring an iterator is really verbose, so there’s a lazy trick, using auto to let the compiler do automatic type deduction. The compiler decides the variable’s type based on the type of the initial value. You can rewrite the for loop like this vector<int> v;for (auto it=v.begin(); it!=v.end(); ++i){ //...}
For vector, this is a random-access iterator. What is random access? Random AccessIf a container can be accessed in $O(1)$ complexity, then it has the random access property. For problem solving, the iterators you’ll use differ by container type. See the table below.
Iterator Type Description Container
Bidirectional iterator Read and Writes forward and backward list,set,multiset,map,multimap
Random access iterator Read and Write with random access vector,deque,array,string
Common STL containersVectorThink of it as a dynamic array
You can access and modify elements in $O(1)$ time Modifying an element in the middle of the collection is $O(n)$. It’s generally recommended to swap the value to be deleted to the end first, then delete it.
# include <vector>
Vector initialization// declare an int vectorvector<int> v;// declare a vector of type T with length Nvector<T> v(n);// declare an int vector of length N initialized to 0vector<int> v(n,0);// initialize a vector from the data in a setvector<T> v(s.begin(), s.end());//Subvectorvector<T> sub(v.begin(),v.begin()+5);//2D vectorvector<vector<T>> v2d;//declare a 2D vector of size nxmvector<vector<T>> v_2d1(n, vector<T>(m));
Common Vector operationsv.empty();v.size();v.front();v.back();v.push_back(); // push obj to the end of the vectorv.pop_back(); // remove the obj at the end of the vectorv.insert(); // insert at a specified positionv.insert(v.begin(), target); // add target to the frontv.insert(v.begin() + n, target); // add target to an arbitrary position, n <= v.size()v1.insert(v1.end(), v2.begin(), v2.end()); // insert v2 at the very end of v1v.reverse(first, last); // reverse the vector from first to lastv.erase(); // remove the element at a specified positionv.clear(); // clear all elements
For the last v.erase(), if you don’t care about order you can use swap(v[n], v.back()); // swap position n with the last position
There are some more operations // Traversalfor(int i = 0; i < v.size(); ++i) { cout << v[i] << endl;}auto it = find(v.begin(), v.end(), val); // find the position where val first appears.v.count(v.begin(), v.end(), val); // count how many times val appears in the range
Traversal can also be written in the form below, but this involves iterators, which are covered later. for(auto it = v.begin(); it != v.end(); ++it) { cout << *it << endl;}
ListOperations like moving or deleting are all $O(1)$ #include <list>
// delcare list containerlist<int> l;
Common operations: l.empty();l.size();l.push_back();l.pop_back();l.push_front();l.pop_front();
Moving a value from one list into another l.splice(iterator pos, list& x); // splice all of x's elements into l at position pos.l.splice (iterator pos, list& x, iterator i); // move a single element i from x into l at position pos.l.splice (iterator pos, list& x, iterator first, iterator last); // move x's elements from first to last into l at position pos.
StackProperty: LIFO (Last-In-First-Out). A Stack is a finite sequence of objects, and the items that can be deleted, retrieved, and modified in the sequence are only the most recently inserted obj. #include <stack>// declare a stackstack<T> s;// common functionss.empty(); // test whether the stack is empty. Returns true if empty, false otherwise.s.size(); // return how many elements are currently in the stack.s.push(); // add an element to the stack.s.pop(); // remove the current topmost element of the stacks.top(); // get the current topmost element of the stack
QueueProperty: FIFO (First-In-First-Out), so insertion can only happen at the tail, and deletion, retrieval, and modification are only allowed from the head. #include <queue>// declare a queuequeue<T> q;// common functionsq.empty(); // test whether the queue is empty. Returns true if empty, false otherwise.q.size(); // return how many elements are currently in the queue.q.push(); // add an element to the queue.q.pop(); // remove the current frontmost element of the queue (i.e. the earliest to enter).q.front(); // get a reference to the current frontmost element of the queue
PriorityQueueIt’s actually a heap structure, often used in Dijkstra’s algorithm #include <queue>// declare a priorityqueuepriority_queue<T> pq; // defaults to the largest on toppriority_queue<T, vector<T>, greater<T> > pq; // change to sort from small to large// define your own compare function// sort from small to large, opposite of sort's cmpauto cmp = [](int& a, int& b) { return a > b;};priority_queue<int, vector<int>, decltype(cmp)> pq(cmp);// common functionspq.empty(); // test whether the priority queue is empty. Returns true if empty, false otherwise.pq.size(); // return how many elements are currently in the priority queue.pq.push(); // add an element to the priority queue.pq.pop(); // remove the current highest-priority element of the priority queue.pq.top(); // get a constant reference to the current highest-priority element. Note that PQ’s pop and push complexity is $O(\log n)$ make heap operationsThere’s a space-saving method: use make_heap to turn a vector into a heap, which makes the space complexity $O(1)$ vector<int> nums{1, 3, 5, 2, 4, 6};make_heap(nums.begin(), nums.end()); // default is max-heapmake_heap(nums.begin(), nums.end(), less<int>()); // max-heapmake_heap(nums.begin(), nums.end(), greater<int>()); // min-heap// pop, because pop_heap only moves the element to the end,// you still need pop_back()pop_heap(nums.begin(), nums.end()); // for max-heappop_heap(nums.begin(), nums.end(), greater<int>()); // for min-heapnums.pop_back();// push, you need to put the element at the end firstnums.push_back(val);push_heap(nums.begin(), nums.end()); // for max-heappush_heap(nums.begin(), nums.end(), greater<int>()); // for min-heap// sort_heapsort_heap(nums.begin(), nums.end()); // ascending sortsort_heap(nums.begin(), nums.end(), greater<int>()); // descending sort
Set and MultiSetA Set is a set By default a set sorts from small to large, and the elements in a set container are unique, with no duplicates.A multiset allows duplicate elements. unordered_set is an unsorted set. unordered_multiset is an unsorted multiset. #include <set>// declare a setset<T> s;set<T> s{1, 2, 3, 4, 5}; // with initial valueset<T> s(vector<T>); // can take a vectorset<T> s(vector.begin(), vector.end()); // import data from vector, convenient for lookupsset<T,greater<T>> s2; // sort from large to smallmultiset<T> st;// common functionss.empty();s.size();s.insert();auto it = s.insert(val); // can get the position after insertions.erase(); // can take a key or an iterator; if a key is passed it deletes duplicate keys// so you must first use find to get the iterator of the value, to ensure only one is deleteds.erase(s.find(value));s.clear();s.count(); // how many elements there are; since a set allows only one, this is effectively checking existence. multiset returns the count.s.find(); // returns an iterator, so you still need to check whether it's s.end();// convert set to vectorvector<T> v(s.begin(), s.end());// Traversalfor(const auto& item : s) { // declaring as const assumes item's value won't be modified in the function. cout << item << endl;}for(auto it = s.begin(); it != s.end(); ++it){ cout << *it << endl;}for (auto it = s.rbegin(); it != s.rend(); ++it) { cout << *it << endl;}// get the first and last elementcout << *s.begin() << endl; // get the value of the first elementcout << *s.rbegin() << endl; // get the value of the last element, can't use end() directlycout << *(--s.end()) << end; // must use the one before end()
Map and MultiMapA Map is like a lookup table, using key-value pairs to implement a one-to-one mapping
By default it also sorts from small to large multimap allows multiple identical key-value pairs. unordered_map is an unsorted map. unordered_multimap is an unsorted multimap.
Simple example: #include <map>using namespace std;int main(){ map<string, int> m; // maps from string to int // set the corresponding values m["one"] = 1; // "one" -> 1 m["two"] = 2; // "two" -> 2 m["three"] = 3; // "three" -> 3 cout << m.count("two") << endl; // 1 -> has a mapping cout << m.count("ten") << endl; // 0 -> no mapping}
#include <map>//declare a mapmap<T, U> m;map<T, U, greater<T>> m; // sort from large to small// common functionsm.empt();m.size();m.insert();m.erase(); // delete an elementm.clear(); // clear all elementsm.count(); // return how many elements there arem.find(); // return an iteratorm.swap(x); // swap the data of m and x; m and x must be the same type// Traversal by referencefor (const auto& item : m) { cout << item.first << ":" << item.second << endl;}// Traversal by reference with namefor(const auto& [key, value] : m) { cout << key << ":" << value << endl;}// Traversal by iteratorfor (auto it = m.begin(); it != m.end(); ++it) { cout << it->first << ":" << it->second << endl; // use prev() to get the one before the iterator cout << prev(it)->first << ":" << prev(it)->second << endl;}// get the first and last elementcout << m.begin()->first << endl; // get the value of the first elementcout << m.rbegin()->first << endl; // get the value of the last element, can't use end() directlycout << (--m.end())->first << end; // must use the one before end()
Map’s underlying implementation uses a red-black tree, so its mappings are sorted by key, which is why insertion, lookup, and deletion are all $O(\log n)$.unordered_map’s underlying implementation uses a hash table and is unordered, so the complexity is $O(1)$.
When using unordered_map, you look up the value by the hash produced from the key. Since it’s a hash, there’s a collision problem.
As we know a Bucket is a slot in the container’s internal hash table to which all the element are assigned based on the hash value of their key . Buckets are numbered from 0 to bucket_count.
If the number added exceeds bucket_count, the map automatically enlarges the bucket slots and recomputes the hash of all items.
When the Load Factor(load_factor) reaches a certain threshold, the container increases the number of buckets and rehashes the map.
Using the code below enlarges the buckets to n and recomputes the hash table. m.refresh(n); If we know the size in advance, we can use the following function to reserve buckets up to n directly, avoiding exceeding the threshold and needing to enlarge the container. Reserving n buckets in advance also helps avoid hash collisions. m.reserve(n);
Reference[1] https://hackmd.io/@sa072686/cp/%2F%40sa072686%2FS11uDpiuH[2] https://jasonblog.github.io/note/c++/stl_rong_qi_4e0029_-_ji_ben_jie_shao.html[3] https://hackmd.io/@meyr543/BkgMaiV6Y#Vector[4] https://blog.csdn.net/weixin_42292229/article/details/125523668[5] https://ikaminyou.medium.com/leetcode-%E5%88%B71500%E9%A1%8C%E5%BF%83%E8%B7%AF%E6%AD%B7%E7%A8%8B-8614284f03da

entry.title: Binary Search | Easy | LeetCode#704 Binary Search
From Parallel Computing to Federated Learning | Study Notes
entry.content:
🌐 中文版：繁體中文
What is parallel computing?Today’s deep neural network models have a huge number of parameters, and a big model also means more computation.
Big Model + Big Data -> Huge computation cost !
A year’s worth of computation on a single GPU can be done at once on 20 GPUs in parallel, reducing the time cost. Linear PredictorTo be continued Federated learningIt’s best to first have a foundation in parallel computing and distributed machine learning. You can refer to this video series: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gVcnOe6_c6Q&t=124s
Background Problem background: Google wants to train a model using data on users’ mobile devices.
A possible solution: collect user data, upload it to a centralized learning platform, and train the model there.
The challenge faced: users refuse to upload data, especially sensitive data, to Google’s servers.
This kind of problem scenario also occurs at European/American enterprises with strict personal-privacy protection, or in medical environments. Distributed learning and federated learning The process of one iteration:
The worker node requests parameters from the parameter server The server returns the parameters The worker node computes the gradient locally based on the returned parameters The worker node returns the gradient to the parameter server The parameter server updates the parameters via the gradient
In this process, the worker’s data never leaves the node, and the server can’t see user data. This architecture solves the problem scenario above.
Federated learning is a kind of distributed learning, but it still differs from traditional distributed learning in several ways:
Users have control over their devices and data, whereas in traditional distributed learning the workers are controlled by the server Worker nodes are unstable, since worker nodes are usually mobile devices (e.g. phones) with varying computing power, some fast and some slow Federated learning has a high communication cost, usually due to low communication bandwidth or a large distance between the worker node and server The data stored on a worker node isn’t IID (independent and identically distributed) Federated learning’s node load is unbalanced: user A’s phone takes photos every day, user B’s phone takes a photo once every 10 days
Do more computation, less communication. Since communication is costly, a common research direction is to reduce the number of communication rounds.
Gradient descentWhat the worker does Receive the model parameters $w$ from the server Compute the gradient $g_{i}$ from the model parameters $w$ and local data Send $g_{i}$ to the server
What the server does Receive the gradients $g_{1},…,g_{m}$ from different worker nodes Compute $g=g_{1}+…+g_{m}$ Update the model parameters: $w \leftarrow w - \alpha \cdot g $ (this is gradient descent)
$\alpha$ is the learning rate
After the server finishes, the next iteration can proceed, until the algorithm converges. Federated Averaging Algorithm (FedAvg) Unlike the gradient-descent algorithm above, this is a communication-efficient algorithm. The first step is the same: the parameter server sends parameters to the worker nodes. But the subsequent steps start to differ. What the worker doesSuppose this is the $i$-th worker node
Receive the model parameters $w$ from the server Repeat the following:a. Compute the gradient $g$ from the model parameters $w$ and local datab. Do gradient descent locally: $w \leftarrow w - \alpha \cdot g$
a. and b. repeat for several epochs; one epoch processes the local data once, so repeating a, b N times is N epochs.
Send $\widetilde{w_{i}} = W$ back to the server (here $\widetilde{w_{i}}$ is the $w$ after local gradient descent)
With that, the node has finished computing. What the server does The server receives $\widetilde{w_{i}}$ ~ $\widetilde{w_{m}}$ from $m$ workers Average or weighted-average: $w \leftarrow \cfrac{1}{m}(\widetilde{w_{i}} + … +\widetilde{w_{m}} ) $
The new model parameters are $m$.
So gradient descent has the worker return the gradient for the server to compute the model parameters, while FedAvg has the worker compute the local model parameters first and upload them directly, with the server averaging.
For the same amount of communication, FedAvg converges faster. FedAvg sacrifices the worker nodes’ computation for fewer communication rounds.
For the same number of epochs (one pass over the data by the worker, used to measure computation), FedAvg converges more slowly. Communication-Efficient Algorithms Approximate Newton’s algorithms Primal-dual algorithms One-shot averaging
Communication is a big problem in distributed machine learning, and many algorithms aim to reduce the number of communication rounds, basically trading lots of computation for fewer communication rounds. Privacy protectionIn distributed learning or federated learning, architecturally only the gradient is uploaded from local to the server, and user data stays local. Does this mean user privacy is safe? Actually not, since the gradient itself is computed from user data via a function: Let’s look at how the stochastic gradient is derived. First, a least squares regression is:

The top $l(w,x_{i},y_{i})$ is the least squares regression’s loss function, defined as the inner product of the data and model parameters, minus the label $y_{i}$, then squared. Computing the gradient means taking the derivative with respect to $w$, giving a vector, and the term in front of this vector,
(
X

) is a real number, so it can be seen as scaling the original user data $X_{i}$. So the gradient is just a transformation of the original data, with no data-protection effect. The original data can be reconstructed from the gradient, so a privacy risk exists.
And in federated learning, both the server and workers can see the model parameters after each iteration, so federated learning leaks even more privacy.
How to defend?This brings up differential privacy, whose concept is adding noise to the gradient or model parameters. But if the noise isn’t strong enough, the original data can still possibly be reversed; and if the noise is too strong, the loss function may fail to keep converging, so the model doesn’t learn well either. Defending against Byzantine faults and malicious attacksByzantine faults are related to the Byzantine Generals Problem, a distributed-systems problem: if a node in a distributed system fails without going down, it drags down the other nodes in the system. Think of it as one of us being a traitor. If a node is malicious and modifies its own data and labels, it can send problematic gradients to the server, training a problematic model. This attack is called a Data Poison Attack, doable even in traditional neural networks, while the attack specifically targeting distributed machine learning is a model poisoning attack, which usually swaps local labels for wrong ones, naturally producing a wrong model. One defense is for the server to take a gradient uploaded by a worker, update the model parameters, and compute accuracy on the server or a test machine; if a worker sends a wrong gradient, the test accuracy will necessarily drop. But this defense isn’t well-suited to federated learning, because the server can’t see user data, and workers’ statistical distributions differ, so even a non-malicious worker could cause accuracy to drop, and the server averages the model parameters anyway. Current defenses are all based on user data being IID (independent and identically distributed), but federated learning’s reality is that user data isn’t IID, and individual workers’ statistical distributions differ, so current defenses aren’t very practical. Summary Federated learning is a kind of distributed learning Its purpose is to let multiple users collaboratively train a model without sharing data, with user data never leaving local (the point is protecting user privacy) Federated learning’s unique challenges: non-IID data slow communication
So important directions are:
Building communication-efficient algorithms Defending against data leakage (attacks are easy, defense is hard) Building mechanisms to prevent Byzantine faults
Reference[1] https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=STxtRucv_zo&t=6s[2] https://zh.wikipedia.org/zh-tw/%E7%8B%AC%E7%AB%8B%E5%90%8C%E5%88%86%E5%B8%83

entry.title: DevOps Skill Tree Knowledge Roundup |【Notes Index】
entry.content:
🌐 中文版：繁體中文
PrefaceThis records the common knowledge points for DevOps interviews, mainly notes organized from this GitHub repository: DevOps Exercises and ByteByteGo’s GitHub repo.
It may take a long time to finish organizing everything.
DevOps GeneralWhat is DevOps? DevOps is a culture and set of practices combining Development (Dev) and Operations (Ops), aiming to shorten the software delivery cycle and increase release frequency while keeping systems stable. Its core spirit is automation, continuous feedback, and cross-team collaboration. What are some core DevOps practices?
CI/CD: continuous integration and continuous delivery/deployment IaC (Infrastructure as Code): manage infrastructure with code (Terraform, CloudFormation) Monitoring and observability: metrics, logs, traces Automated testing Version control (everything goes into Git, including config and infrastructure)
What is CALMS? A framework for measuring an organization’s DevOps maturity: Culture, Automation, Lean, Measurement, Sharing. How does SRE relate to DevOps? SRE (Site Reliability Engineering) can be seen as a concrete implementation of DevOps, using software-engineering methods to solve operations problems. Core concepts include SLI/SLO/SLA, error budget, and eliminating toil. Python Basic Data Types OOP / Class Raise Exceptions Regex Async File Manipulation OS lambda decorator Flask
Article: Python for DevOps |【DevOps Skill Tree】 (this section has its own article, see the link)
NetworkingWhat are the seven OSI layers? Physical → Data Link → Network → Transport → Session → Presentation → Application. A common mapping bottom-up: “cable → MAC/switch → IP/router → TCP/UDP → …”. In practice the TCP/IP four-layer model (Link, Internet, Transport, Application) is used more. What’s the difference between TCP and UDP?
TCP: connection-oriented, reliable (three-way handshake, ACK, retransmission, flow control, congestion control), ordered. Used by HTTP, SSH, file transfer. UDP: connectionless, no delivery or order guarantee, but low latency and low overhead. Used by DNS, streaming, games, VoIP.
What is CIDR? Classless Inter-Domain Routing, representing a network with IP/prefix length, e.g. 10.0.0.0/16 means the first 16 bits are the network address, holding 2^(32-16)-2 host addresses. /24 = 256 addresses (254 usable). What does ARP do? Address Resolution Protocol, resolving an IP address to a MAC address. Within a LAN, to send a packet to an IP, a host broadcasts ARP asking “who has this IP?”, and the owner replies with its MAC. arp -a shows the ARP cache. What is NAT? Network Address Translation, translating private IPs to public IPs (and vice versa), letting many internal machines share one public IP to reach the internet. Common in home routers and cloud NAT Gateways. What’s the DNS resolution flow? Browser → local cache → recursive DNS (e.g. 8.8.8.8) → Root → TLD (.tw) → authoritative DNS, resolving the IP level by level. The recursive server doesn’t store records itself but queries all the way to the authoritative server for you. Common records: A (IPv4), AAAA (IPv6), CNAME (alias), MX (mail), NS (name server), TXT. What’s ICMP for? A network-layer control and error-reporting protocol; both ping (Echo Request/Reply) and traceroute are based on ICMP. What’s the DHCP flow (DORA)? Discover → Offer → Request → Ack; the client broadcasts to find a DHCP server, and the server offers an IP lease. VLAN vs SDN?
VLAN: logically isolated broadcast domains carved out on the same physical switch. SDN (Software-Defined Networking): separates the network’s control plane (decisions) from the data plane (forwarding), controlled centrally by software; OpenFlow is a representative protocol.
LinuxA few key directories in the Filesystem Hierarchy Standard (FHS)? /etc (config files), /var (variable data like logs), /usr (user programs), /home (user home directories), /bin /sbin (executables), /proc /sys (kernel virtual filesystems), /dev (device files), /tmp (temporary). What do Linux permissions 755 / 644 mean?
