Each digit is octal rwx: r=4, w=2, x=1. 755 = owner rwx, group r-x, other r-x (common for directories or executables); 644 = owner rw-, others read-only (common for regular files). Special permissions: SUID, SGID, sticky bit. Common I/O redirection usage? cmd > file # stdout overwritecmd >> file # stdout appendcmd 2> file # stderrcmd > file 2>&1 # both stdout+stderr to filecmd1 | cmd2 # pipe, cmd1's stdout as cmd2's stdin
Common systemd commands? systemctl status/start/stop/restart/enable <service>systemctl list-units --type=servicejournalctl -u <service> -f # view service logs systemd is the modern Linux init system (PID 1), managing services, mounts, and the boot process. The boot process (roughly)? BIOS/UEFI → Bootloader (GRUB) → load Kernel → mount initramfs/initrd → run init (systemd, PID 1) → start the various targets/services → login. (See also: initrd vs initramfs) Common performance-analysis tools?
CPU/overall: top, htop, vmstat, mpstat Memory: free -m, /proc/meminfo Disk I/O: iostat, iotop Network: ss, netstat, iftop, tcpdump Combined: dstat, sar
What is the OOM Killer? When system memory is exhausted, the kernel picks a process to kill by oom_score to free memory. Logs are in /var/log/messages or dmesg. You can adjust a process’s likelihood of being picked via /proc/<pid>/oom_score_adj. Shell ScriptingWhat is a shebang? The script’s first line #!/bin/bash, telling the system which interpreter to run it with. What are $?, $#, $@, $0? $? the previous command’s exit code (0=success), $# number of arguments, $@ all arguments, $0 the script name, $1..$n the n-th argument. Difference between [ ] and [[ ]]? [ ] is POSIX test, [[ ]] is a bash extension supporting &&, ||, regex =~, and is safer without needing to quote variables. A common example? #!/bin/bashset -euo pipefail # stop on error, error on undefined vars, fail if any pipe failsfor f in *.log; do [ -f "$f" ] || continue echo "processing $f"doneif grep -q "ERROR" app.log; then echo "found error"fi
What do set -e, set -u, set -o pipefail do? The three safety switches: -e aborts on command failure, -u errors on using an undefined variable, pipefail makes a pipeline fail if any command in it fails. Strongly recommended for production scripts. SecurityThe principle of least privilege? Grant each user/service/program only the minimum privileges needed for its task, to limit the blast radius after a compromise. Symmetric vs asymmetric encryption?
Symmetric: same key for encrypt/decrypt (AES), fast, but key exchange is the challenge. Asymmetric: public key encrypts, private key decrypts (RSA, ECC), solving key exchange but slow. In practice they’re combined: use asymmetric to exchange a symmetric key, then use symmetric to transfer data (that’s how TLS works).
Difference between hashing and encryption? Hashing is one-way and irreversible (SHA-256), used to verify integrity or store passwords (with salt); encryption is reversible, used for confidentiality. Common web attacks? SQL Injection, XSS (cross-site scripting), CSRF (cross-site request forgery), SSRF, path traversal, command injection. Defenses: parameterized queries, input validation, output encoding, CSP, least privilege. How should secrets be managed? Don’t hardcode them in code or commit them to Git. Use a dedicated secrets-management service (AWS Secrets Manager, HashiCorp Vault, K8s Secret with encryption at rest), restrict access with RBAC, and rotate regularly. What is defense in depth? Don’t rely on a single line of defense, but layer protections (network ACL, firewall, WAF, host hardening, app-layer validation, encryption), so if one layer is breached there’s another behind it. CertificatesWhat is a TLS certificate? A digital document issued by a Certificate Authority (CA) binding “public key ↔ domain,” used to verify a server’s identity and establish an encrypted connection. Browsers trust root CAs and verify down through the certificate chain. The TLS handshake flow, roughly? ClientHello (supported TLS versions, cipher suites, random) → ServerHello (chosen suite, certificate, random) → verify the certificate → exchange/negotiate a session key → then transfer data with symmetric encryption. (See also: this skill tree’s DMS Troubleshooting notes have a more detailed handshake explanation) Difference between a self-signed and a CA-signed certificate? A self-signed certificate has no trusted CA backing, so browsers warn; it suits internal/testing. Production services should use a trusted CA (the free Let’s Encrypt works). What to do when a certificate expires? Reissue/renew it. In production, use cert-manager (K8s) or certbot (Let’s Encrypt) to auto-renew so you don’t forget. Git git commands branch merge rebase git internal principles troubleshooting
Article: Git for DevOps Notes |【DevOps Skill Tree】 (this section has its own article, see the link)
CI/CDDifference between CI and CD?
CI (Continuous Integration): developers frequently merge code into the mainline, with automatic build and test on each merge, to catch integration problems early. CD: either Continuous Delivery (automated to an “always deployable” state, with deployment being a button press) or Continuous Deployment (even the button is gone; anything passing tests goes to production automatically).
Stages of a typical pipeline? checkout → build → unit test → static analysis/scan → package image → push registry → deploy to staging → integration/E2E tests → deploy to production. Blue-green vs canary deployment?
Blue-Green: maintain two environments at once, switch all traffic at once, and instantly switch back if something breaks. Canary: route a small portion of traffic to the new version first, watch the metrics, then gradually ramp up.
Common CI/CD tools? Jenkins, GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, CircleCI, Drone, Argo CD (GitOps-style continuous deployment for K8s). What is GitOps? Declare the “desired system state” in Git and use a tool (Argo CD, Flux) to continuously reconcile the actual state to the declaration in Git. Git becomes the single source of truth, and deploying = changing Git. ContainerDifference between a container and a VM? A VM virtualizes the whole hardware and runs its own OS kernel, offering strong isolation but heavy; a container shares the host’s kernel and only packages the app and its dependencies, so it starts fast, is lightweight, and achieves high density. Relationship between an image and a container? An image is a read-only template (layered); a container is a running instance of an image (a writable layer stacked on top of the image). What’s the benefit of Docker’s layers? Each Dockerfile instruction is a layer, layers can be cached and shared across images, so changing one line only requires rebuilding the later layers, also saving storage and transfer. What container states are there? created, running, paused, stopped/exited, removed. Docker network modes?
bridge (default, a built-in virtual bridge within a single host) host (uses the host network directly, no isolation) none (no network) overlay (across hosts, for Swarm/K8s)
What is OCI? Open Container Initiative, which defines open standards for containers (image spec, runtime spec) so Docker, containerd, Podman, etc. can interoperate. A few Dockerfile optimization points? Multi-stage builds to shrink the image, use layer cache well, put frequently-changing instructions later, use a small base image (alpine/distroless), .dockerignore to exclude unnecessary files, and don’t run as root. KubernetesThis section has its own complete article, covering cluster architecture, Pod, Deployment, Service, Ingress, StatefulSet, Storage, Networking, RBAC, Helm, Security, etc.:
Article: Kubernetes for DevOps Notes |【DevOps Skill Tree】
Cloud GeneralDifference between IaaS / PaaS / SaaS? The responsibility boundary from most to least: IaaS (rent hardware/VMs, like EC2, you manage the OS and up) → PaaS (rent a platform, like App Engine or RDS, you only manage code and data) → SaaS (use software directly, like Gmail). The public cloud’s shared responsibility model? The cloud provider is responsible for “security of the cloud” (physical data center, underlying hardware, virtualization layer), and the customer for “security in the cloud” (OS updates, applications, data, IAM configuration, network rules). Horizontal vs vertical scaling?
Vertical (Scale Up): make a single machine bigger (more CPU/RAM), with an upper limit and single-point risk. Horizontal (Scale Out): add more machines to share the load, the mainstream cloud approach, paired with a load balancer.
Region vs AZ? A Region is a geographic area (like us-east-1); within a Region are multiple mutually-isolated AZs (Availability Zones) with independent power/networking, and deploying across AZs achieves high availability. VirtualizationHypervisor Type 1 vs Type 2?
Type 1 (bare-metal): runs directly on hardware (VMware ESXi, Xen; KVM is strictly a hybrid), good performance, used in data centers. Type 2 (hosted): runs on top of a host OS (VirtualBox, VMware Workstation), convenient, used on desktops.
What is KVM? Kernel-based Virtual Machine, a virtualization technology that turns the Linux kernel into a hypervisor, usually paired with QEMU for hardware emulation. (See also: the Proxmox VE series uses KVM + LXC) Can VMs and containers be used together? Yes, and it’s common: run K8s nodes inside cloud VMs, then run containers on the nodes, combining strong isolation (VM layer) with lightweight deployment (container layer). AWS Regions & AZs IAM / VPC / EC2 / ELB / Auto-Scaling / S3 / Route53 / Lambda / API Gateway / SNS / SQS / MQ / CloudFormation / ECS / EKS / Fargate …
Article: AWS for DevOps Notes |【DevOps Skill Tree】 (this section has its own article, see the link)
TerraformWhat is Terraform? How is it different from CloudFormation? Terraform is HashiCorp’s IaC (Infrastructure as Code) tool, describing infrastructure declaratively in HCL and supporting multi-cloud (AWS/GCP/Azure…); CloudFormation is AWS-only. Terraform’s core flow? terraform init # initialize, download providersterraform plan # preview the changes it will maketerraform apply # actually applyterraform destroy # tear down
What is the state file? Why does it matter? terraform.tfstate records the actual state of the resources Terraform manages, used to diff desired vs actual. For team collaboration you must use remote state (S3 + DynamoDB lock, Terraform Cloud) to avoid conflicts or overwrites from concurrent changes. What’s a module for? Package a reusable set of resources into a module, parameterize it, and reuse it across environments (dev/staging/prod), essentially a function for IaC. Difference between plan and apply? plan only computes and shows the diff (read-only, safe); apply actually creates/modifies/deletes resources. In a proper flow, CI runs plan first for human review, and only applies after approval. System DesignWhat aspects do you consider when designing a system? Scalability, availability, reliability, latency, consistency, cost, operability. Usually you estimate from the requirements (QPS, data volume, read/write ratio), then decide the architecture. Common components for horizontal scaling? Load balancer (LB), a stateless application layer (easy to scale out), caching (Redis/CDN), database read/write splitting and sharding, and message queues (peak shaving, decoupling). Common caching strategies and problems? Cache-Aside, Write-Through, Write-Back. Watch out for cache penetration, cache avalanche, and cache breakdown, plus eviction strategies (TTL, LRU). How do you improve availability? Eliminate single points (SPOF), redundancy across AZs/Regions, health checks + automatic failover, retries and circuit breakers, rate limiting and graceful degradation. What does a CDN do? Caches static content to edge nodes near users, reducing latency and origin load. Distributed SystemThe CAP theorem? A distributed system can only have two of three among Consistency (C), Availability (A), and Partition tolerance (P) when a network partition occurs. Since partitions are unavoidable (P is mandatory), in practice it’s a trade-off between C and A (CP or AP). What is eventual consistency? It doesn’t guarantee reading the latest value each time, but after no new writes, all replicas eventually converge to a consistent state. Many high-availability systems (DynamoDB, DNS) use it. Consensus algorithms? Let multiple nodes agree on a value even with node failures. Representatives: Paxos, Raft (easier to understand, used by etcd/Consul). Why does idempotency matter? The same request produces the same result whether run once or many times. Distributed systems have retry mechanisms, and a non-idempotent interface (like a duplicate charge) causes big problems, usually deduplicated with a unique request ID. Byzantine fault tolerance (BFT)? A fault-tolerance mechanism that tolerates nodes not just “going down” but also “lying / sending malicious messages,” which is what blockchains need. Most internal systems only need to tolerate crashes (non-Byzantine). MLOpsWhat is MLOps? Applying DevOps practices to the machine-learning lifecycle: automating and versioning data processing, training, evaluation, deployment, and monitoring, so models can go live reliably and reproducibly and keep iterating. What does an ML pipeline add over ordinary CI/CD? Two more changing artifacts: data and models. You need data version control (DVC), feature engineering, model training and evaluation, a Model Registry, and model monitoring after deployment. What is model drift / data drift? Online data distribution diverges over time from the training distribution (data drift), degrading model performance (model/concept drift). You need to monitor metrics and retrain when drift occurs. Common ways to deploy a model? Wrap it as a REST/gRPC service (FastAPI, TF Serving, TorchServe), batch inference, or edge deployment. Pair with A/B testing or shadow deployment to validate a new model. HardwareA few key CPU concepts? Core count, threads (hyperthreading), clock speed (GHz), cache (L1/L2/L3), architecture (x86 / ARM). More cores suit parallel work, higher clock suits single-threaded work. Difference between BIOS and UEFI? Both are boot firmware. UEFI is the modern replacement for BIOS: it supports >2TB disks (GPT), boots faster, and has a graphical interface and Secure Boot. Common RAID levels?
RAID 0: striping, fast but no fault tolerance (one dies, all lost) RAID 1: mirroring, fault-tolerant but halves capacity RAID 5: distributed parity, at least 3 disks, tolerates 1 failure RAID 10: 1+0, balancing performance and fault tolerance
SSD vs HDD? SSD has no mechanical parts, fast random access, shock-resistant; HDD is cheaper with a lower cost per unit capacity. Put databases/caches on SSD, cold data/backups on HDD. MiscWhich HTTP methods are idempotent? GET, PUT, DELETE are idempotent (repeated calls give the same result); POST is non-idempotent (creates duplicates). Keep this in mind when designing APIs and retry mechanisms. The three pillars of observability? Metrics (numeric indicators, Prometheus), Logs (event logs, ELK/Loki), Traces (distributed tracing, Jaeger/OpenTelemetry). (See also: Prometheus + Grafana on Proxmox) Difference between an L4 and an L7 load balancer?
L4 (transport layer): forwards based on IP/Port, fast, unaware of application content. L7 (application layer): routes intelligently based on HTTP header/path/cookie (e.g. path-based routing, TLS termination).
Blue-green / rolling / canary deployment in one line each? Blue-green = switch the whole batch, rolling = replace batch by batch, canary = route a small portion of traffic first to test the waters.

entry.title: FreeRTOS_Note
entry.content:
AWS FreeRTOS FreeRTOS includes libraries for connectivity, security, and over-the-air (OTA) updates. FreeRTOS also includes demo applications that show FreeRTOS features on qualified boards.
FreeRTOS is an open-source project. You can download the source code, contribute changes or enhancements, or report issues on the GitHub site at https://github.com/FreeRTOS/FreeRTOS.
FreeRTOS - ArchitectureFreeRTOS contains two types of repositories
single library repositories Each single library repository contains the source code for one library without any build projects or examples.
package repositories Package repositories contain multiple libraries, and can contain preconfigured projects that demonstrate the library’s use.
FreeRTOS Kernel conceptsThe FreeRTOS kernel is a real-time operating system that supports numerous architectures. Basic components including:
A multitasking scheduler. Multiple memory allocation options (including the ability to create completely statically-allocated systems). Intertask coordination primitives, including task notifications, message queues, multiple types of semaphore, and stream and message buffers. upport for symmetric multiprocessing (SMP) on multi-core microcontrollers.
No malloc() but pvPortMallocWhen RTOS objects are created dynamically, using the standard C library malloc() and free() functions is not always appropriate for a number of reasons:
They might not be available on embedded systems. They take up valuable code space. They are not typically thread-safe. They are not deterministic. For these reasons, FreeRTOS keeps the memory allocation API in its portable layer.
Reference[1] What is FreeRTOS? - https://docs.aws.amazon.com/freertos/latest/userguide/what-is-freertos.html[2] What is FreeRTOS? - FreeRTOS architecture - https://docs.aws.amazon.com/freertos/latest/userguide/what-is-freertos.html#freertos-architecture[3] FreeRTOS kernel fundamentals - https://docs.aws.amazon.com/freertos/latest/userguide/dev-guide-freertos-kernel.html[4] Architecute Image Ref - https://blog.naver.com/kim1417/221540814246

entry.title: 🧪 Building an HTTP Server Step by Step with Winsock
Hands-On Practice: AWS IoT Device Shadow
entry.content:
Intro - What is AWS IoT Device Shadow?In real world, sometime it is difficult to get the actual device state in real time in such IoT scenarios. A device shadow can overcome this challenge, Device Shadow can consider a virtual virtual representation of a device which managed by the IoT Things resource created in AWS IoT Core.
The Shadow document is a JSON or a JavaScript notation doc that is used to store and retrieve the current state information for a device. You can use the shadow to get and set the state of a device over MQTT topics or HTTP REST APIs, regardless of whether the device is connected to the internet.
Shadow Document{ "state": { "desired": { "color": "green" }, "reported": { "color": "blue" }, "delta": { "color": "green" } }}
Refer to the json above, you can check there 3 state properties in shadow document.
desired Apps specify the desired states of device properties by updating the desired object
reported Devices report their current state in the reported object.
delta AWS IoT reports differences between the desired and the reported state in the delta object.
You can consider the flow of Shadow a finite state machine, for AWS IoT Core, it will also check if there are delta event, that means there difference between Desired and Reported states
So how can we update the state of a shadow? The answer is clear,
By subscribing/publishing messages to the certain MQTT topics
Shadow Topic
ShadowTopicPrefix value Shadow type
$aws/things/thingName/shadow Unnamed (classic) shadow
$aws/things/thingName/shadow/name/shadowName Named shadow
Topic Client operations allowed
ShadowTopicPrefix/delete Publish/Subscribe
ShadowTopicPrefix/delete/accepted Subscribe
ShadowTopicPrefix/delete/rejected Subscribe
ShadowTopicPrefix/get Publish/Subscribe
ShadowTopicPrefix/get/accepted Publish/Subscribe
ShadowTopicPrefix/get/rejected Subscribe
ShadowTopicPrefix/update Publish/Subscribe
ShadowTopicPrefix/update/accepted Subscribe
ShadowTopicPrefix/update/rejected Subscribe
ShadowTopicPrefix/update/delta Subscribe
ShadowTopicPrefix/update/documents Subscribe
For detail explanation about these shadow topics, see the documentation - https://docs.aws.amazon.com/zh_tw/iot/latest/developerguide/device-shadow-mqtt.html
The state changes of Device Shadow Take this picture for example, the update flow is:
The MQTT client publishes a $aws/things/myLightBulb/shadow/update message to the server. The message carries the desired state {"state": {"desired":{"color":"green"}}} IoT Server responds with $aws/things/myLightBulb/shadow/accepted, indicating that the update message has been received. At the same time, it publishes $aws/things/myLightBulb/shadow/delta to notify the device to update, and then publishes $aws/things/myLightBulb/shadow/update/document as update record After receiving the message, the Device performs the corresponding update operation and publishes a message $aws/things/myLightBulb/shadow/update {"state"{"report":{"color":"green"}}} to the IoT Server after completion. Notification updated After receiving the post-update message, IoT Server responds with $aws/things/myLightBulb/shadow/accepted to indicate that the update message has been received. Publish another $aws/things/myLightBulb/shadow/update/document as an update record
Expermient for IoT ShadowDevice SetupSince I don’t have any IoT Device currently available, I simulate the device by launching a EC2 instance.
AMI: Ubuntu 22 LTS Type: t2.Micro Subnet: 10.1.0.0/24
Then connect to the EC2 instance by using SSH, and run the following command sudo apt updatesudo apt install -y python3-pipmkdir certs/
Setup in AWS IoT CoreThere are 3 things to setup in AWS IoT Core
Create certificate Create IoT Policy and associated with the certificate Create Things object and associate with the certificate
ThingsThis is a thing named ESP32 for testing purposes, it have associated with the certificate
CertificateAnd this certificate has issued by the Amazon Root CA.
And there are IoT Policy - TestPolicy asccociate with this certificate. TestPolicy { "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "iot:Publish", "Resource": [ "arn:aws:iot:us-east-1:AWS_ACCOUNT:topic/$aws/things/THING_NAME/shadow/get", "arn:aws:iot:us-east-1:AWS_ACCOUNT:topic/$aws/things/THING_NAME/shadow/update" ] }, { "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "iot:Receive", "Resource": [ "arn:aws:iot:us-east-1:AWS_ACCOUNT:topic/$aws/things/THING_NAME/shadow/get/accepted", "arn:aws:iot:us-east-1:AWS_ACCOUNT:topic/$aws/things/THING_NAME/shadow/get/rejected", "arn:aws:iot:us-east-1:AWS_ACCOUNT:topic/$aws/things/THING_NAME/shadow/update/accepted", "arn:aws:iot:us-east-1:AWS_ACCOUNT:topic/$aws/things/THING_NAME/shadow/update/rejected", "arn:aws:iot:us-east-1:AWS_ACCOUNT:topic/$aws/things/THING_NAME/shadow/update/delta" ] }, { "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "iot:Subscribe", "Resource": [ "arn:aws:iot:us-east-1:AWS_ACCOUNT:topicfilter/$aws/things/THING_NAME/shadow/get/accepted", "arn:aws:iot:rus-east-1:AWS_ACCOUNT:topicfilter/$aws/things/THING_NAME/shadow/get/rejected", "arn:aws:iot:us-east-1:AWS_ACCOUNT:topicfilter/$aws/things/THING_NAME/shadow/update/accepted", "arn:aws:iot:us-east-1:AWS_ACCOUNT:topicfilter/$aws/things/THING_NAME/shadow/update/rejected", "arn:aws:iot:us-east-1:AWS_ACCOUNT:topicfilter/$aws/things/THING_NAME/shadow/update/delta" ] }, { "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "iot:Connect", "Resource": "*" } ]} Remember, this policy must have adequate permissions for CONNECT, SUBSCRIBE, Publish and Publishto the Shadow topic. Once you have setup these stuff, now I need to convey the certificate to the EC2 instance.
scp -i <SSH KEY> TestDeviceShadow/* ubuntu@ec2-<EC2 Public Address>.compute-1.amazonaws.com:/home/ubuntu/certs
Apart from the device certificate, it is necessary to provide the CA certificate in the device.
Download the CA Cert in the device
cd certs/curl -o ~/certs/Amazon-root-CA-1.pem \ https://www.amazontrust.com/repository/AmazonRootCA1.pem
Now there all credential we need to test the IoT Device Shadows Install the IoT Core Python Device SDKgit clone https://github.com/aws/aws-iot-device-sdk-python-v2.git
sed -i "s/__version__ = '1.0.0-dev'/__version__ = '<SDK_VERSION>'/" \ aws-iot-device-sdk-python-v2/awsiot/__init__.py
python3 -m pip install ./aws-iot-device-sdk-python-v2
cd ~/aws-iot-device-sdk-python-v2/samples
Execute the shadow.pypython3 shadow.py --ca_file ~/certs/Amazon-root-CA-1.pem --cert ~/certs/device.pem.crt --key ~/certs/private.pem.key --endpoint your-iot-endpoint --thing_name your-iot-thing-name
You can derive the iot endpoint by checking the AWS IoT ConsoleFind the Connect > Connect One Device in the left paneScroll down and you will see the IoT endpoint
Back to the script, after you execute the shadow.py, you will see the prompt in your terminal
You will need to enter the desired value. So I enter “yellow”.
Then you can observe that the state changed to “yellow”. This results may also observe from the AWS IoT Console
Go to Things, and select your thing object, on the bottem of the target thing page, you can navigate to the Device Shadow tab, then select the Classic Shadow, then you can see the Device Shadow State below
For testing, I enter “green” as the input of shadow.py. And the state change show in both terminal and IoT Console
Test the Shadow DocumentNow you can try to edit the Shadow Document directly. For example, I change the desired state from red to green. Then you will notice that the change will reflect to the Delta report.
Test with AWS IoT Test MQTT ClientFirst, it is necessary to subscribe to the shadow topic in the MQTT client, for receiving the state change events.
The client can subscribe to the topic $aws/things/ESP32/shadow/update/# The wildcard symbol “#” indicates that it wants to subscribe all topic under the update/ prefix. And you can re-run the program with new color value. You can find the MQTT client will receive the state change events. At first, the color was “red”.
The message published to $aws/things/ESP32/shadow/update/document topic
Then it changed to “green”.
The message published to $aws/things/ESP32/shadow/update/accepted topicNoted that any unsuccessful messages were received on the topic $aws/things/ESP32/shadow/update/rejected
Edit the shadow document againI change the desired stat value “blue” to “black”.
The first received event will be on the delta topic, it means that there are differences between desired state and reported state. At the same time, the message will published to the topic $aws/things/ESP32/shadow/update/accepted for notifying the device to update the state
And also published to the shadow document topic for recording.
{ "previous": { "state": { "desired": { "color": "blue" }, "reported": { "color": "blue" } }, "metadata": { "desired": { "color": { "timestamp": 1699430576 } }, "reported": { "color": { "timestamp": 1699430576 } } }, "version": 20 }, "current": { "state": { "desired": { "color": "black" }, "reported": { "color": "blue" } }, "metadata": { "desired": { "color": { "timestamp": 1699431256 } }, "reported": { "color": { "timestamp": 1699431256 } } }, "version": 21 }, "timestamp": 1699431256}
But the reported state is not “Black”. you can see the event published to the accepted topic.
Meanwhile, the message published to the document topic
ConclusionsYou will found the state change from (Desired: “Blue”, Reported: “Blue”) to (Desired: “Black”, Reported: “Blue”) and the final state is (Desired: “Black”, Reported: “Black”). References[+] Create a virtual device with Amazon EC2 - https://docs.aws.amazon.com/iot/latest/developerguide/creating-a-virtual-thing.html[+] Tutorial: Provisioning your device in AWS IoT - https://docs.aws.amazon.com/iot/latest/developerguide/shadow-provision-cloud.html[+] Tutorial: Installing the Device SDK and running the sample application for Device Shadows - https://docs.aws.amazon.com/iot/latest/developerguide/lightbulb-shadow-application.html[+] Tutorial: Interacting with Device Shadow using the sample app and the MQTT test client - https://docs.aws.amazon.com/iot/latest/developerguide/interact-lights-device-shadows.html[+] Reserved topics - Shadow topics - https://docs.aws.amazon.com/iot/latest/developerguide/reserved-topics.html#reserved-topics-shadow

entry.title: Getting to Know Lambda, feat. a Small Container-Reuse Experiment
entry.content:
🌐 中文版：繁體中文
PrefaceFirst off, why does serverless always come up alongside Lambda? Let me introduce this service. FaaS (Function as a Service)Once you talk about serverless computing, its core concept comes up: Function as a Service (FaaS). Here’s Wikipedia’s explanation of FaaS:
FaaS is a cloud computing model. Built on Platform as a Service (PaaS), serverless computing provides a micro-architecture where the end customer doesn’t need to deploy, configure, or manage server services; the server services needed to run the code are all provided by the cloud platform.
Right, the core of this concept is letting users focus on designing products or business logic without worrying about deploying, configuring, or setting up servers. The first to put this concept into practice and launch a service was AWS’s Lambda, released in 2014. (Microsoft’s Azure Functions followed, of course.) Lambda functions Lambda runs your code on high-availability compute infrastructure and performs all administration of the compute resources, including server and operating system maintenance, capacity provisioning and automatic scaling, and logging. With Lambda, all you need to do is supply your code in one of the language runtimes that Lambda supports [1]. [name=AWS Documents]
Behaviorally it’s basically the figure below. There’s some upstream trigger, usually a service that invokes the Lambda function, or a manual invocation via the AWS CLI. After Lambda finishes running the function, it returns the result to the original service and can forward to a downstream destination, which is usually another service.
Now suppose you’re a beginner just getting into Lambda. You might be eager to open the Console, use the sample code (or, for some people, delete the sample without reading it and just paste in your local code), test the Lambda function with the default event, and then find it doesn’t work. Don’t rush. Before diving in, it’s best to have a concept of the Lambda runtime and Lambda program model. Basic specs RAM Storage
Configuration, RAMRAM is proportional to CPU processing power, so raising RAM also raises CPU processing speed.128MB to 3008MB
Reference:https://koding.work/aws-lambda-performance-is-related-to-memory-size/
Lambda RuntimesLambda supports development in multiple programming languages via runtimes. Each major programming language version has its own runtime. These runtimes provide the basic language libraries and execution environment. Mainstream languages have officially-supported runtimes, like NodeJS, Python, Java, Go, Ruby, and so on, and you can also define a custom runtime. For example a C++ runtime; the official docs provide a GitHub repo and a post on how to use such custom runtimes [3].
I’ve defined a Perl runtime myself, but you’ll need to write your own images. :(
Also, Lambda runtimes are all developed on Amazon Linux. So if you need a custom runtime, it’s generally recommended to spin up a t2.micro EC2 (choosing an Amazon Linux AMI) and build the runtime there. Lambda programming modelThe programming model Lambda provides is common across all runtimes. It defines a handler to process incoming events. This approach essentially tells Lambda the function’s entry point. The runtime passes an object containing the invocation event and context into the handler, such as the function name and request ID. If you create functions with different runtimes, you should see handlers in different languages in the console’s code block. Handler (Python) [4] def handler_name(event, context): ... return some_value Handler (Java17) package example;import com.amazonaws.services.lambda.runtime.Context;import com.amazonaws.services.lambda.runtime.LambdaLogger;import com.amazonaws.services.lambda.runtime.RequestHandler;// Handler value: example.HandlerIntegerpublic class HandlerIntegerJava17 implements RequestHandler<IntegerRecord, Integer>{ @Override /* * Takes in an InputRecord, which contains two integers and a String. * Logs the String, then returns the sum of the two Integers. */ public Integer handleRequest(IntegerRecord event, Context context) { LambdaLogger logger = context.getLogger(); logger.log("String found: " + event.message()); return event.x() + event.y(); }}record IntegerRecord(int x, int y, String message) {}
Handler (Go) package mainimport ( "fmt" "context" "github.com/aws/aws-lambda-go/lambda")type MyEvent struct { Name string `json:"name"`}func HandleRequest(ctx context.Context, name MyEvent) (string, error) { return fmt.Sprintf("Hello %s!", name.Name ), nil}func main() { lambda.Start(HandleRequest)}
And so on. Also, although a freshly-created Lambda only has the single Lambda-Handler file, you can actually access the /tmp directory in the Lambda execution environment. Each execution environment provides 512 MB to 10,240 MB of disk space in /tmp, in 1 MB increments [5]. I’ll get into the specifics when I cover the Lambda execution environment lifecycle. PermissionsIn Lambda, operations are performed on behalf of the source service mainly through an execution role. So what is a Lambda execution role?
A Lambda function’s execution role is an AWS IAM role that grants the function permission to access AWS services and resources. For example, you can create an execution role that has permission to send logs to Amazon CloudWatch and upload trace data to AWS X-Ray. This page provides information on how to create, view, and manage a Lambda function’s execution role [6].
The biggest difference between an execution role and a regular role is that when the function is invoked, Lambda automatically provides your function with temporary credentials by assuming this role. The developer doesn’t have to call sts:AssumeRole in the function code. The necessary setup for this is the role’s trust policy, which must specify the Lambda service as a trusted principal: { "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Effect": "Allow", "Principal": { "Service": "lambda.amazonaws.com" }, "Action": "sts:AssumeRole" } ]}
Once you have the execution role, you can attach policies to it, either AWS-managed policies or your own.
Of course, if you choose “Create a new role with basic Lambda permissions” when creating the Lambda, it creates a role with the LambdaBasicExecutionRole policy.
{ "Version" : "2012-10-17", "Statement" : [ { "Effect" : "Allow", "Action" : [ "logs:CreateLogGroup", "logs:CreateLogStream", "logs:PutLogEvents" ], "Resource" : "*" } ]} This policy basically grants the Lambda function the ability to create a log group, create log streams within it, and write logs. When the Lambda is invoked, a log group containing the Lambda name is created in CloudWatch. If my Lambda is named TestInvocations, the log group name is /aws/lambda/TestInvocations.
And underneath will be the corresponding log stream.
There’s something interesting here: each time you change the function or make a configuration adjustment (e.g. changing the timeout), the next invocation produces a new log stream. That’s because each new configuration needs to be applied to a new sandbox, which reinitializes a new Lambda execution environment. If you open a log stream, you’ll find every invocation comes with different messages:
START (Print Output, if there are any) END REPORT
The span from Start to End is when Lambda is executing, and the timestamp difference for this span is bounded by your Lambda timeout setting. Let’s do a small experiment on this.
Experiment 1: Lambda timeoutCreate a Lambda function named TestInvocation, choosing Python3.11 for the runtime and keeping default permissions. Then edit the code under the Code section of the Lambda console.
After creation, you get an empty Lambda handler. Here we import time and add a 3-second delay inside the handler. Then click Test; there’s a test JSON event you can use directly. After testing, go to the Monitor page and click “View CloudWatch logs”.
This jumps to the corresponding log group in CloudWatch. Click the newest log stream by timestamp to observe the result.
You can see there’s a 3-second gap between Start and End, with “sleep for 3 seconds” printed. Sharp eyes will notice one log entry shows “Task timed out after 3 seconds”. That’s because a freshly-created Lambda function has a default timeout of 3 seconds. You can change this under “Configuration” in the Lambda console. The maximum timeout is 15 minutes. So let’s set 15 minutes and change the handler’s delay to about 14 minutes to test.
This is a hard limit, meaning you can’t open a support case to raise the quota [8].
After waiting 14 minutes, the logs confirm it did run for 14 minutes. One thing not mentioned in the earlier log screenshots is INIT_START, the initialization phase that occurs every time an execution environment is initialized. The initialization phase includes Extension Init, Runtime Init, and Function Init [7]. image from AWS official docs The first two init phases are more about building the execution environment, starting the runtime, downloading the deployment package into the environment, and so on. But at the Function Init phase, one more thing happens: it runs code outside the Lambda handler.
Here, outside the handler:
That’s a bit vague. Suppose you declare a global variable outside the handler, or initialize a DB connection outside the handler. These are well-suited to doing outside the handler, run during the span from Init-Start to Start, and as long as the same execution environment keeps being used, whatever Function Init does runs only once. This brings us to a Lambda characteristic called container reuse. Experiment 2: a Lambda characteristic, container reuseFirst, container reuse requires noting that a Lambda execution environment is a container. An ordinary Docker-like container environment tears the container down once execution finishes, but in Lambda’s use case it isn’t suitable to shut the environment down after every execution. Instead it keeps waiting for the next invocation request. You can observe this characteristic in the logs. If you invoke the Lambda three times in a row on the Lambda page, you’ll see the subsequent invocation requests all appear in the same log stream, following after the previous invocation’s logs.
In other words, for the same Lambda execution environment, Lambda finishes one execution and goes straight on to the next request, meaning the same Lambda sandbox can be reused. If you’re interested in Lambda container reuse, check out this official blog:
Understanding Container Reuse in AWS Lambdahttps://aws.amazon.com/blogs/compute/container-reuse-in-lambda/
Here’s another interesting point: if you invoke using the Lambda console’s Test button, it waits for execution to finish before letting you click Test again. What happens if we use the AWS CLI to invoke the function, opening three terminal tabs to invoke our Lambda at the same time? Other key concepts Lambda execution environment Cold start Lambda deployment package Lambda synchronous / asynchronous invocation Lambda networking
References[1] https://docs.aws.amazon.com/zh_tw/lambda/latest/dg/welcome.html[2] https://docs.aws.amazon.com/zh_tw/lambda/latest/dg/lambda-runtimes.html[3] https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/compute/introducing-the-c-lambda-runtime/[4] https://docs.aws.amazon.com/zh_tw/lambda/latest/dg/python-handler.html[5] https://docs.aws.amazon.com/zh_tw/lambda/latest/dg/lambda-runtime-environment.html[6] https://docs.aws.amazon.com/zh_tw/lambda/latest/dg/lambda-intro-execution-role.html[7] https://docs.aws.amazon.com/zh_tw/lambda/latest/dg/lambda-runtime-environment.html#runtimes-lifecycle[8] https://docs.aws.amazon.com/zh_tw/lambda/latest/dg/gettingstarted-limits.html#function-configuration-deployment-and-execution

entry.title: Lambda Layers: Concept and Hands-On
entry.content:
🌐 中文版：繁體中文
PrefaceWhen configuring Lambda, the vast majority of people have hit ImportModuleError. So you can follow the scenario below, spin up the same Lambda environment, and work through it step by step. Scenario Region: IAD(us-east-1) Runtime: Python3.11 Lambda Name: “ITHomeLambdaFunction” Lambda codeimport json requestsdef lambda_handler(event, context): # TODO implement x = requests.get('https://www.ntust.edu.tw/') print(x.text) return { 'statusCode': 200, 'body': json.dumps('Hello from Lambda!') }
[Error]: Runtime.ImportModuleErrorIf you deploy the scenario above and run a test, you may get an error like this: { "errorMessage": "Unable to import module 'lambda_function': No module named 'requests'", "errorType": "Runtime.ImportModuleError", "requestId": ".......", "stackTrace": []}
The cause is that from AWS Lambda Python 3.8 runtime onward, the requests module is no longer natively supported, so you need to add a layer yourself. What is a Lambda layer?In Lambda, a layer is a zip archive for storing dependencies or modules. Different Lambda functions can also share data through a layer. Once you add a layer to your Lambda function, Lambda places the layer’s contents into the /opt directory in the Lambda execution environment.
Note: each function can include at most 5 layers.
Packaging a module into a layerDepending on the runtime you use, modules in each layer need to follow a different file structure when zipping [1]. For Python, the file structure can be:
/opt/python /opt/python/lib/python3.x/site-packages
And all runtimes support these two additional directories:
/bin (PATH) /lib (LD_LIBRARY_PATH)
Now let’s package requests into an archive.
Package the layer contents locally with the command below (if your package installer is pip3, replace the command’s prefix with pip3):
pip install requests --target=./python This creates a python/ directory locally and downloads the needed modules into it. Note that the directory name here must match the language used by the runtime.
Package the directory: zip -r layer.zip python/ to package all files under the python directory into a single zip.
In the Lambda console, there’s a layer item in the left navigation; clicking it jumps to the layers page, where you can choose to add a new layer.
Name the layer, upload the layer.zip you just built, then choose the runtime and architecture to create the layer.
Once done, go back to the Lambda main page to add the layer.
On the add-layer page, choose Custom Layer and you’ll see the layer you just created.
TestingNow run the test from the console again and it won’t error.
Or invoke via the AWS CLI: aws lambda invoke \ --cli-binary-format raw-in-base64-out \ --function-name ITHomeLambdaFunction \ --payload '{ "Test": "ITHome" }' \ response.json
Checking CloudWatch, the data comes through too.
Though splitting the returned content into separate log entries is a bit weird, lol.
References[1] Layer paths for each Lambda runtime

entry.title: ⚙️Configuring Error Retries on Lambda
entry.content:
🌐 中文版：繁體中文
PrefaceThis is another problem I ran into while solving a case, but I’d never actually configured retries on Lambda, so in the spirit of experimentation I tried it out in my own environment. Error retries in Lambda are usually for re-sending an invocation request after an asynchronous invocation fails. For asynchronous invocations, Lambda places the event in a queue and returns a success response containing no other information. A separate process reads events from the queue and delivers them to your function.
The diagram was made with ZenUMLhttps://app.zenuml.com/https://mermaid.js.org/syntax/zenuml.html
Creating the LambdaCreating the Lambda is simple: create a function named TestInvocations using the NodeJS.14.x runtime. Modifying the Lambda handler codeEdit the code under the Code section of the Lambda console main page, changing index.js: let outside = 0;exports.handler = (event, context, callback) => { console.log(JSON.stringify({ 'RequestId': context.awsRequestId, 'outside': outside++ })); return callback('Error', 'retry test')};
Once edited, click deploy to upload the modified code.
Configuring retriesIn the Lambda console main page, go to the Configuration tab, select Asynchronous Invocation, then Edit.
Retry attempts can be set to at most 2. When your Lambda function errors after receiving an asynchronous invocation, it retries twice and then the event is discarded. You can additionally configure a Dead Letter Queue (DLQ) to store the discarded events for later processing.
For details, see the official docs: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/zh_tw/lambda/latest/dg/invocation-async.html#invocation-dlq
Triggering the LambdaWe can invoke the Lambda function via the AWS CLI.
If you haven’t set up the AWS CLI, see this doc to configure it >> https://aws.amazon.com/cli/
aws lambda invoke --function-name TestInvocations --invocation-type Event test.txt
Here --invocation-type is set to Event, meaning you’re invoking the Lambda asynchronously. It then returns status code 202, meaning your request has been accepted by Lambda but won’t be processed immediately (since it’s asynchronous).
Reference:https://docs.aws.amazon.com/zh_tw/lambda/latest/dg/API_Invoke.html
For Lambda synchronous and asynchronous invocation, see the corresponding official docs:https://docs.aws.amazon.com/zh_tw/lambda/latest/dg/invocation-async.htmlhttps://docs.aws.amazon.com/zh_tw/lambda/latest/dg/invocation-sync.htmlAs for their architectural differences, I can write a separate post to organize that later!
Observing the resultsGo to the Monitor tab in the Lambda console and click View CloudWatch logs, which opens the CloudWatch Logs main page.
Each time you create a Lambda, its execution role is given a policy named AWSBasicExecutionRole by default, which includes permission to create CloudWatch log groups and CloudWatch logs, and creates a log group named /aws/lambda/<your Lambda name>. Under this log group are many log streams, and a new log stream is created each time you change your Lambda function and re-trigger it.
Select the newest log stream and you’ll find three invocations: the first is the one we triggered, and the second and third are the retries we configured. Trigger request 1Retry 1Retry 2 Here you can observe that the logs after invocation show the error message, with the first retry one minute after the first failed request, and the second retry two minutes after the first retry fails, after which it doesn’t retry again. You can also see that the request ID on retry is the same as the original, which you could probably use to judge whether an invocation is a retry and whether the event has already been processed. ConclusionWhen developing Lambda code and doing related configuration, always pay attention to the invocation type and its corresponding settings, so you don’t mix them up unknowingly. Referenceshttps://azole.medium.com/aws-lambda-reuse-and-retry-behavior-ffaac616d869https://docs.aws.amazon.com/zh_tw/lambda/latest/dg/invocation-retries.html

entry.title: Combination Sum | Medium | LeetCode#39. Combination Sum
entry.content:
🌐 中文版：繁體中文
Problem statement
Difficulty: Medium Statement: given an integer array candidates and a target integer target, return all unique combinations of candidates where the numbers in each combination sum to target. You may return the combinations in any order.
In this problem, each number in candidates can be chosen an unlimited number of times. Two combinations are unique if at least one number is chosen a different number of times.E.g. [2,2,3] != [2,2,2,2,3]The test cases guarantee that the total number of unique combinations summing to the target is fewer than 150 for the given input.
SolutionInitial ideaSince it’s a combination problem, backtracking comes to mind immediately. Unlike 77. Combinations, this one doesn’t limit the depth, because the problem says numbers in candidates can be reused an unlimited number of times, so the termination condition isn’t limited by depth as usual. We may need a variable to store the value at each choice, pass it to the next level to accumulate, and finally check whether it equals target. If not, keep choosing numbers. Also, unlike usual, since the same number can be reused, when entering each level we don’t skip the current number and can reselect it. My solutionclass Solution {public: vector<vector<int>> result; void combinationHelper(int currentVal, vector<int> &candidate, int target, vector<int> &subResults, int start){ if(currentVal == target){ result.push_back(subResults); return; } else if(currentVal < target){ for(int i=start; i< candidate.size();i++){ subResults.push_back(candidate[i]); //currentVal += candidate[i]; combinationHelper(currentVal + candidate[i], candidate, target,subResults, i); subResults.pop_back(); } } } vector<vector<int>> combinationSum(vector<int>& candidates, int target){ vector<int> sub; combinationHelper(0,candidates, target, sub, 0); return result; }};
Here we again define a helper function to handle the main backtracking. Parameter explanation:
currentVal: the current combination’s running sum candidate: the list of numbers given target: the target value given subResults: the array holding the current combination start: controls the starting position of numbers
if(currentVal == target) is the recursion’s termination condition, meaning we found a valid sum. If the current sum currentVal is less than target, keep choosing numbers from candidate to combine. A for loop iterates candidate starting from index start, to ensure no duplicate combinations appear. combinationHelper(currentVal + candidate[i], candidate, target, subResults, i) After choosing a number candidate[i] each time, add it to the running sum currentVal and recurse to search the next number. Here i is passed to the recursive function, meaning the same number can be chosen multiple times.
I made a mistake before this: writing currentVal += candidate[i] and passing currentVal. But this accumulates the change to currentVal and can’t correctly restore its value after the recursion returns, affecting the whole search.
subResults.pop_back()
Backtrack to the previous choice. Once target is found, the array is added to result, and finally we return the result. Execution result ComplexityTime complexityAt each recursion level, we can choose any candidate number, letting each number be chosen multiple times and forming a large number of combinations. Each choice to recurse produces two options: choose this number or not.So considering all possible combinations, the time complexity can approach $O(2^n)$. Space complexity Recursive callIn the worst case, the recursion depth depends on the target value target. Each choice recurses, and as the sum keeps accumulating, the deepest recursion level can reach $O(target)$.Each recursion stack level saves the current state (including parameters), so the worst-case stack space complexity is $O(target)$. Result storageresult stores all qualifying combinations. If the number of combinations found is k and each combination’s average length is m, the space for result storage is $O(k * m)$.In the worst case, the number of combinations k can approach $O(2^n)$, since each candidate can be chosen multiple times. Each combination’s length m can also approach target in the worst case.
So the overall space complexity can be written as: $O(target+k⋅m)$

entry.title: Problem-Solving Notes | Graphs
entry.content:
🌐 中文版：繁體中文
IntroWhen we stored data before, common data structures were arrays, hash tables, linked lists, and so on. Imagine you’ve just started university and have a course schedule listing various courses in a table, but you don’t know which courses are prerequisites, which might be taken later, or which might block others. In this case, using a graph to represent the relationships between courses is very convenient. So one of the key points of a graph is preserving the relationships between pieces of data.
This blog post mainly references the explanation in this article
Definition of a GraphContinuing the course graph above, each course represents a node, which can hold data, the data being the course name. And courses are connected by arrows, representing the relationships between courses. vertex: each node in the graph is called a vertex, or node, and the set of all vertices is defined as $V$ or $V(G)$edge: each line segment is called an edge. In a graph an edge is usually represented by a pair of vertices, $(V_{i}, V_{j})$ representing the edge between $V_{i}$ and $V_{j}$, and the set of all edges is usually defined as $E$ or $E(G)$
With $V$ and $E$ we can define what a graph is: the set of relationships between nodes, $G(V, E)$
Classification of graphsGraphs are mainly divided into Directed Graphs and Undirected Graphs based on whether the edges have direction Directed Graph: the relationship between vertex(A) and vertex(B) is one-way, so the edge has direction; the set formed by all vertices and directional edges is a directed graphUndirected Graph: the relationship between vertex(A) and vertex(B) is two-way, so the edge between them has no direction, and the set of vertices and edges formed is an undirected graph
Graph representationsSo how do we represent a graph with a data structure? Common representations are the Adjacency Matrix and the Adjacency List. Adjacency Matrix Let’s first look at the adjacency-matrix representation in an undirected graph: if there’s an edge between vertex(A) and vertex(B), then the positions corresponding to (A,B) and (B,A) are 1, and if there’s no edge between any two vertices, the matrix value is 0. For a directed graph, if there’s an edge from vertex(A) to vertex(B) but no edge from vertex(B) to vertex(A), then (A,B) is 1 but (B,A) is 0. From the adjacency-matrix representation above you can also see that the adjacency matrix of an undirected graph is symmetric, while a directed graph’s is not. This also lets us deduce that transposing a directed graph’s matrix and overlaying it on the original matrix gives the undirected-graph representation. Directed graph: $A[i][j]=1$ means there’s an edge from node i to node jUndirected graph: $A[i][j]= A[j][i] = 1$ means there’s an undirected edge between node i and node j With $A^T = A^{T}[i][j] = A[j][i]$ meaning there’s an edge from node j to node i. So $A_{undirected}[i][j] = A[i][j] V A[j][i]$ Adjacency List The adjacency-list representation first uses a one-dimensional array to represent all vertices, and for each array entry uses a linked list to represent the other vertices connected to it. Here, the order in which the linked list is connected doesn’t matter, because a graph is defined as a set. In the undirected graph above, taking vertex(D) as an example, it connects to vertex(C), vertex(B), vertex(E), so [3], i.e. vertex(D), can build a linked list connecting to vertex(C), vertex(B), vertex(E) (not necessarily in order). For a directed graph, vertex(D)’s linked list can only include nodes departing from vertex(D), i.e. vertex(B) and vertex(E). Differences
Adjacency Matrix Adjacency List
Space complexity $O(\lvert V \rvert^{2})$ $O( \lvert V \rvert + \lvert E \rvert)$
Notes Good for dense graphs (many vertices and edges) Good for sparse graphs (few edges)
Access Contiguous memory is faster Dynamic memory is slower
Add edge Adding an edge just sets the corresponding position from 0 to 1, so $O(1)$ Adding a vertex to the front of the linked list is $O(1)$, but worst case is $O( \lvert E \rvert )$
Delete edge Deleting an edge just changes the corresponding position from 1 to 0, so $O(1)$ Like deleting data in a linked list, $O( \lvert E \rvert)$
Explanation of related conceptsAdjacent: as long as there’s an edge between vertex(A) and vertex(B), they count as adjacentSubgraph: for a $G’$, if the sets of edges and vertices composing it satisfy $V(G’)\subseteq V(G)$, $E(G’) \subseteq E(G)$, then $G’$ is a subgraph of $G$Path: the series of consecutively connected edges passed through from vertex(V1) to vertex(V2) is called the path from vertex(v1) to vertex(v2)Length/Distance: the number of edges in a pathSimple path: if in a path, except for the start vertex and end vertex, all other vertices are passed through only once, then this path is a simple pathCycle: if a simple path’s start vertex and end vertex are the same, this path is called a cycle. If the edges in the cycle are undirected, it’s an undirected cycle; if the cycle is traversed in order by direction, then the cycle is directed (directed cycle)Acyclic graph: if there’s no cycle in a graph, the graph is called an acyclic graph. A tree is usually a kind of graph too, however if no simple path can be found in a tree whose start vertex and end vertex are the same, then the tree must be an acyclic graph Weight: the weight, which can usually represent the distance or cost between two geographic locations. You can add a weight to an edge, and a graph with weights is called a weighted graph Connected: what counts as two vertices being connected to each other? That’s being able to walk from vertex(A) to vertex(B) and from vertex(B) to vertex(A). So for an undirected graph, that’s vertex(A) and vertex(B) being connected by an edge, and for a directed graph, that’s the existence of edge(A→B) as well as edge(B→A) Connected in undirected graph: for an undirected graph, if any vertex has a path connecting to the others, then this undirected graph is called connected Connected components: in an undirected graph, there’s some subgraph that is connected, and if adding other vertices or edges would break this connected property, then this subgraph is called a connected component. Both subgraphs at the bottom of the figure above satisfy this property. Strongly connected in directed graph: in a directed graph, for any two vertices vertex(A) and vertex(B), there exist both (1) a path from vertex(A) to vertex(B) and (2) a path from vertex(B) to vertex(A). Then this directed graph is called strongly connected
Strongly connected component: in a directed graph, there’s some subgraph that is strongly connected, and if adding other vertices or edges would break this strongly connected property, then this subgraph is called a strongly connected component. (The maximal set that maintains being connected.) Self-loop: if there’s an edge from vertex(A) to vertex(A), it’s a self-loop Graph application scenariosGraphs are mainly used in scenarios like the Minimum Spanning Tree (MST), network flow, and shortest-path problems. Before applying them to a scenario, you first need to know the methods for searching vertices in a graph. Reference https://hackmd.io/@meyr543/SJJ47oWoY https://ithelp.ithome.com.tw/articles/10336847 https://ithelp.ithome.com.tw/articles/10268666?sc=rss.iron https://hackmd.io/@bangyewu/BknWuaVlT https://alrightchiu.github.io/SecondRound/graph-introjian-jie.html

entry.title: Steps to Create a Lambda Function URL
entry.content:
🌐 中文版：繁體中文
What is a Lambda URL? Official definition: A function URL is a dedicated HTTP(S) endpoint for a Lambda function. You can create and configure a function URL through the Lambda console or the Lambda API. When you create a function URL, Lambda automatically generates a unique URL endpoint for you. Once created, the URL endpoint never changes.
The function URL endpoint format is: https://<url-id>.lambda-url.<region>.on.aws
Note that some regions don’t support function URLs, in which case you may need the old approach: API Gateway + Lambda Integration. Access controlWhen creating a function URL, the AuthType parameter determines how Lambda authenticates or authorizes requests to the function URL. AuthType options:
AWS_IAM: If you want authenticated users or roles to call your function through the function URL, choose AWS_IAM. NONE: Lambda doesn’t perform any authentication before invoking the function, but the Lambda function’s resource policy is always in effect, so you must still grant access for the function URL to receive requests.
For details, see here.
How to create a Lambda URL?Create an execution role Create a role with the AWSLambdaBasicExecutionRole permissions.
{ "Version" : "2012-10-17", "Statement" : [ { "Effect" : "Allow", "Action" : [ "logs:CreateLogGroup", "logs:CreateLogStream", "logs:PutLogEvents" ], "Resource" : "*" } ]}
Note the role ARN:Role ARN: arn:aws:iam::1XXXXXXXXXXX:role/Lambda-URL_Role
Create a Lambda function with a function URL (.zip archive) Write Function Code
exports.handler = async (event) => { let body = JSON.parse(event.body); const product = body.num1 * body.num2; const response = { statusCode: 200, body: "The product of " + body.num1 + " and " + body.num2 + " is " + product, }; return response;};
Create deployment packages
zip function.zip index.js
Create a Lambda function with the create-function command.
aws lambda create-function \ --function-name my-url-function \ --runtime nodejs18.x \ --zip-file fileb://function.zip \ --handler index.handler \ --role arn:aws:iam::1XXXXXXXXXXX:role/Lambda-URL_Role
Add a resource policy to the function granting permission, to allow public access to the function URL.
aws lambda add-permission \ --function-name my-url-function \ --action lambda:InvokeFunctionUrl \ --principal "*" \ --function-url-auth-type "NONE" \ --statement-id url
I chose NONE for convenient testing, but it’s better to provide AWS_IAM authentication.
Return policy
Create a URL endpoint for the function with the create-function-url-config command.
aws lambda create-function-url-config \ --function-name my-url-function \ --auth-type NONE
Return Endpoint
Endpoint: https://xxxxxxxxxxuxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx.lambda-url.us-east-1.on.aws/ Testing the endpointcurl 'https://abcdefg.lambda-url.us-east-1.on.aws/' \-H 'Content-Type: application/json' \-d '{"num1": "10", "num2": "10"}'
CloudFormation for creating a function URLBelow is the CFN YAML for creating a function URL, which makes it easy to create the corresponding resources: Resources: MyUrlFunction: Type: AWS::Lambda::Function Properties: Handler: index.handler Runtime: nodejs18.x Role: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/lambda-url-role Code: ZipFile: | exports.handler = async (event) => { let body = JSON.parse(event.body); const product = body.num1 * body.num2; const response = { statusCode: 200, body: "The product of " + body.num1 + " and " + body.num2 + " is " + product, }; return response; }; Description: Create a function with a URL. MyUrlFunctionPermissions: Type: AWS::Lambda::Permission Properties: FunctionName: !Ref MyUrlFunction Action: lambda:InvokeFunctionUrl Principal: "*" FunctionUrlAuthType: NONE MyFunctionUrl: Type: AWS::Lambda::Url Properties: TargetFunctionArn: !Ref MyUrlFunction AuthType: NONE Create a Lambda function with a function URL (AWS SAM)And this is the YAML to create the resources via SAM: ProductFunction: Type: AWS::Serverless::Function Properties: CodeUri: function/. Handler: index.handler Runtime: nodejs18.x AutoPublishAlias: live FunctionUrlConfig: AuthType: NONE
Reference[1] https://docs.aws.amazon.com/zh_tw/lambda/latest/dg/lambda-urls.html[2] https://docs.aws.amazon.com/zh_tw/lambda/latest/dg/urls-tutorial.html

entry.title: Linux Process Deep Dive-1: Knowledge of PID 0
Unboxing + Basic Setup | Getting Into the Meshtastic Open-Source Project | Meshtastic Series
entry.content:
🌐 中文版：繁體中文
🔋 Basic intro: https://hackmd.io/@BASHCAT/S1m_x-AOA/%2FUAmGpkIzQy-Fc5xKmcyBtQ🔋 Official Web Page: https://meshtastic.org/docs/about/🔋 Useful Videos:
https://youtu.be/6hW40yaj3x4?si=rGFPADhNIWfiZnL8 https://youtu.be/x99R78fkSg0?si=cU1XbtR8HUWploHr
🔋 FB - Taiwan Mesh Network https://www.facebook.com/groups/meshtastictw/about🔋 Reddit thread https://www.reddit.com/r/meshtastic/
What is Meshtastic?An open-source project based on LoRa wireless communication technology. Using LoRa-related devices, it does low-power, long-range wireless signal transmission over the LoRa protocol, without relying on existing mobile-communication infrastructure. It suits things like an emergency-backup communication system, or mountain rescue communication. With Meshtastic nodes, a message is sent out by a device, and as long as it reaches another node, the message can be forwarded on to other nodes. Also, as of this writing (2025/07/13) many nodes in Taiwan have already been set up privately. It’s low-cost and the barrier isn’t high, and unlike a handheld radio you don’t even need a license.
Buying the deviceI observed that, whether on the Taiwan mesh network or on Reddit, most people start with the Heltec v3. But power consumption seems to be a commonly-criticized point, so I ended up buying what “seems to be” the more power-efficient Heltec T1114v2 as my starter board (still not sure this choice was right). I bought it directly from Heltec’s official store; here’s the store link. Some people buy from Taobao instead, so it’s up to you.
https://www.reddit.com/r/meshtastic/comments/1ewbtgy/heltec_mesh_node_t114_first_look/
Unboxing the Heltec T114I bought the board + antenna + adapter cable all at once (though later reading around, most people swap in a better antenna and SMA adapter cable), plus a GPS module (though I hear they’re really not that expensive on Taobao?).
After admiring it, before flashing the firmware, get into the good habit of always plugging the antenna into the board first. RF devices can damage components if powered on or operating without an antenna. After plugging the adapter cable and the included antenna into the Heltec T1114, you can plug in power and flash the firmware. Flashing the firmwareChoose a USB Type-C cable with data-transfer capability, not a charge-only cable.
Each board’s firmware differs; here you can use the Meshtastic Web Flasher to get different firmware versions based on the board model.
Web Flasher: https://flasher.meshtastic.org/
After plugging in the T114 and entering the Flasher page, you first need to choose your board; I chose Heltec Mesh Node T114. For firmware, I recommend the latest release in the stable (Beta) channel; Alpha firmware is mostly still in development and testing. Then you can click Flash. A screen appears asking you to click Enter DFU mode, which puts your Heltec T114 into flashing mode; you can also manually double-press the T114’s RST button. A new drive will also appear on your local computer. A T114 in DFU mode looks like the image below. Now click Download UF2 in the Web Flasher, and the firmware file downloads to your local Downloads directory. Then simply copy the firmware file directly into the Heltec drive directory, either by dragging it or with the Linux cp command. But on every platform I tried, near the end of copying the drive ejects, and Windows/Linux may show an error message. Don’t rush to troubleshoot yet; first confirm whether the firmware was flashed successfully!
At this point, connecting to the Heltec T114 with the Meshtastic app succeeded, so the firmware was actually flashed successfully; the end-of-flash handling just may not be done well. Basic setupHere I downloaded the Android version of the Meshtastic App, and the app setup afterward basically follows these two resources:
https://hackmd.io/@BASHCAT/S1m_x-AOA/%2F5Vy7EE6dQL2v_XHPkbSKtwhttps://youtu.be/6hW40yaj3x4?si=-UTeOGxNK6JHDrnQ
On the first Bluetooth connection, you need to enter the PIN shown on the Heltec T114’s panel on your phone to pair. After pairing succeeds, you can configure the board remotely via the app. New folks probably don’t need to tune much. First set your Region by country; here I set it to “TW.” Taiwan’s usable frequency can be set at the very bottom under frequency assignment, choosing the region’s 923.875Mhz. Then you can start scanning the Taiwan mesh network community’s QR code to join a channel, and test sending/receiving in the community’s SignalTest channel. But before that, if you can’t receive or send any messages, first check the antenna and adapter cable. I recommend not using the included adapter cable and antenna; go buy a better adapter cable and antenna yourself. Reading around, the community almost universally recommends the TX915 antenna; you can also refer to the official antenna support list.https://meshtastic.org/zh-TW/docs/hardware/antennas/ Also, if you test other antennas, you can contribute to this GitHub repo: https://github.com/meshtastic/antenna-reports
For the adapter cable, you can buy from Jin-Hua Electronics: IPEX-SMA female-to-female connector cable
The next post will cover app setup in detail!!
Once set up, you can send messages on a channel like this. Meshtastic App screenshots

entry.title: Climbing Mt. Fuji | Pre-Trip Preparation and Planning Log | Mountain Hut Reservations
entry.content:
🌐 中文版：繁體中文
The Mt. Fuji tripSince the date I managed to book at Goraikokan was 7/16, I chose 7/16–7/17 of this year (2024) for this Mt. Fuji climb. For climbing Mt. Fuji, the general advice is to book a mountain hut and not do an overnight single push (bullet climbing), so this time I prioritized the hut reservation date and then arranged the climbing schedule around it. Also, Mt. Fuji is an active volcano, so always watch for volcanic-activity alerts; you can check this on Mt. Fuji’s official site.
Climbing routesYoshida routeStarting from Mt. Fuji 5th Station at 2300 meters elevation, the route is 5.8 km, taking about 5–7 hours. It has the most huts of any route, with huts from the 7th to 9th stations, making it a popular beginner route. It’s also our route this time.
Source: https://www.fujisan-climb.jp/trails/yoshida/index.html
Besides the Yoshida route, Mt. Fuji has other climbing routes. Subashiri routeThe Yoshida and Subashiri routes merge after the Original 8th Station, so the crowds grow from there. This route’s biggest fun is experiencing the sunabashiri (sand run) on the way down, i.e. sliding through the sand; in fact the Yoshida route’s descent path also starts on the Subashiri route, splitting off again around the 8th station.
Source: https://www.fujisan-climb.jp/trails/subashiri/index.html
If you want to read about the Subashiri route experience, this post is pretty complete: https://manyujp.com/fujisan-1/
Fujinomiya routeThe shortest route, but a steep climb all the way; recommended for those with plenty of hiking experience.
Source: https://www.fujisan-climb.jp/trails/fujinomiya/index.html
Gotemba routeThe gentlest grade, also with a sand run, but fewer huts and toilets. It also has the fewest climbers.
Source: https://www.fujisan-climb.jp/trails/gotenba/index.html
Entry applicationSince July 1, 2024, Yamanashi Prefecture charges climbers on the Yoshida route a 2000-yen-per-person entry fee, and only allows 4000 people per day to climb Mt. Fuji.
Source: https://www.fujisan-climb.jp/info/20240220_2024anzentaisaku.html
Mountain hut reservations Different routes on Mt. Fuji have different huts. The Yoshida route has the most, with huts from the 7th station to the Original 8th station. Below is a list of huts on the Yoshida route.
Station Hut name Website
8th Station 御来光館 (Goraikokan) https://www.goraikoukan.jp
八合目トモエ館 (Tomoekan) https://tomoekan.com
富士山ホテル (Fujisan Hotel) https://www.fujisanhotel.com/
元祖室 (Gansomuro) https://www.ganso-muro.jp/
白雲荘 (Hakuunso) http://fujisan-hakuun.com/en/
蓬莱館 (Horaikan) https://www.horaikan.jp/
太子舘 (Taishikan) https://www.mfi.or.jp/~taisikan/
7th Station 東洋館 (Toyokan) https://www.fuji-toyokan.jp/
鳥居荘 (Toriiso) http://toriiso.com/
富士一館 (Fuji-ichikan) https://www.fuji-ichikan.jp/
鎌岩館 (Kamaiwakan) https://kamaiwakan.jpn.org/
七合目トモエ館 (Tomoekan 7th) https://kamaiwakan.jpn.org/
From experience, many huts open reservations early!!! For example, if the site says reservations open 5/20 23:00, since that’s Japan time it should be 22:00 Taiwan time. But when the four of us split up to grab huts this time, we found some huts opened reservations as early as 21:00!!! Some huts that should only be reservable a few days later also quietly opened early!!! So be sure to prepare for the hut grab earlier than early.
Reserving GoraikokanGoraikokan opened reservations at noon on 5/7 this year, and I used my company’s network speed to frantically grab a four-person room with my companions. Truly lucky, and near the opening time the site times out like crazy. Usually after reservations open, you click ご予約／ご宿泊 on the side of the site and the available dates pop up; a circle means there are spots. But it’s really hard to grab, so keep refreshing to see if spots appear. Once inside, you choose the number of beds and fill in things like a contact address in Japan and some basic personal info, so I recommend preparing all of it before the grab.
We also chose one night with two meals, i.e. dinner and breakfast the next day. You can choose Western or Japanese meals when booking.
Dinner starts being served from 5:00 PM. Breakfast is prepared as early as 1:30 AM the next day. Check-in time: after 14:00Check-out time: 0:00 ~ 6:00Cancellation policy: if you cancel for personal reasons, a cancellation fee is chargedNo-show: 100%Same day: 100%Day before: 80%9 days before: 50%20 days before: 30% If the Yoshida route is closed on the day of your stay, or if Yamanashi or Shizuoka Prefecture instructs you that climbing is prohibited, the cancellation fee is waived.
Transportation arrangementsThis time we chose to arrive at Lake Kawaguchi to stay overnight first, then depart from Lake Kawaguchi to the 5th Station the next morning. Narita Airport → ShinjukuI took the Keisei Skyliner NEX; you can buy it in advance on Klook or KKday, get a QR code, and redeem it at the NEX machine at the airport.
Shinjuku → Lake KawaguchiThen take a highway bus to Kawaguchiko Station to stay overnight; I reserved the Shinjuku-to-Kawaguchiko ticket on the highway bus site in advance. A mobile ticket looks like the one below; just hand it to the attendant to scan and you can board.
Highway bus site: https://highway-buses.jp/chi/
Lake Kawaguchi → 5th StationYou can reserve tickets online for the first bus. When using the ticket, you click to activate it; I recommend activating it only when the bus arrives, since after activation a 2-hour countdown starts and the ticket becomes void after 2 hours.
The boarding spot at Kawaguchiko Station is at platform 7.
Shuttle bus ticket reservation: https://fujikyubus.quicktrip.jp/bought
If you want to go to Mt. Fuji 5th Station, definitely watch the time. We rushed for the first bus at 6:40, but the bus was a bit late and we arrived at the 5th Station around 7:45.
Fuji bus timetable: https://www.fujikyubus.co.jp/mycar/timetablefares/
As an aside, on the first day from the start up to Goraikokan there was heavy fog and a downpour, a very miserable day. Be sure to prepare a rain jacket, rain pants, and cold-weather clothing; on the way up I saw many foreigners in short sleeves and shorts freezing to death… I’ll organize the climbing write-up later lol. Also, you can buy the round-trip tickets at once, but I recommend buying the return bus to Lake Kawaguchi after you finish climbing, unless you’re very good at controlling your up/down timing. After descending you can also wander the shrine or the nearby souvenir shops. ReferenceFull Mt. Fuji route map (PDF) - https://www.fujisan-climb.jp/tc/b2rg1t00000018zh-att/map_tc.pdf

entry.title: PVE VM Live Migration Based on CPU Power Consumption | PVE Series 2
entry.content:
🌐 中文版：繁體中文
PrefaceIn the previous post we covered how to do live migration of VMs in Proxmox VE. Now we’ll add a condition to trigger migration. Since my need here is power consumption, I need to know how to get CPU power consumption info. Getting CPU power consumption infoThere are several ways to get CPU or other hardware power consumption. The simplest is powerstat to view CPU power in a Linux/Unix environment. Also, if the host has a BMC and supports IPMI, you can use ipmitool to get the host’s power-consumption info.
Aside: Proxmox VE itself actually supports an IPMI watchdog. You can uncomment it in /etc/default/pve-ha-manager to use the IPMI watchdog, since the default is the OS-level softdog. But if the motherboard doesn’t support it, just use the default.
Here are a few commands to check whether your host supports IPMI:sudo apt-get install ipmitoolCheck whether the BMC (Board Management Controller) exists and is running properly; if it returns no info or shows an error, the server may not support IPMI:sudo ipmitool mc info Or check with dmidecode:sudo dmidecode | grep -i ipmiIf the server returns no IPMI/BMC-related info, the hardware may not support it.
Let’s try getting the info with powerstat: sudo powerstat -R
This command takes at least 60 samples, one CPU power reading per second, and finally outputs the average consumption. You can use this result in a script as a condition for migration. Migration scenarioAfter getting CPU power simply, next let’s introduce the migration scenario. Continuing the two-node architecture from the previous post, when node A judges its power consumption exceeds a threshold, it migrates; and if the target node is powered off, it wakes it up to migrate. We can implement this with a bash script. Before
After
#!/bin/bashPOWER_THRESHOLD=6.0NODE="pve2"VM_ID="100"BACKUP_NODE="pve"BACKUP_NODE_IP="172.25.166.68"BACKUP_NODE_MAC="0c:9d:92:86:bb:63"POWER_CONSUMPTION=$(powerstat -R 1 60 | grep -oP 'CPU:\s+\K[0-9.]+')if (( $(echo "$POWER_CONSUMPTION > $POWER_THRESHOLD" | bc -l) )); then echo "Power consumption too high ($POWER_CONSUMPTION W) on $NODE. Migrating VM $VM_ID to $BACKUP_NODE..." wakeonlan $BACKUP_NODE_MAC # VM Live Migration qm migrate $VM_ID $BACKUP_NODE --online echo "Complete VM $VM_ID migrated to backup node $BACKUP_NODE ($BACKUP_NODE_IP) | ($BACKUP_NODE_MAC)..."else echo "Power consumption is normal ($POWER_CONSUMPTION W) on $NODE."fi
This simple bash script first sets a low threshold of 6 watts, for experimental convenience, basically ensuring the node always migrates. Here I’m actually migrating the VM on node pve2 to node pve. The POWER_CONSUMPTION=$(powerstat -R 1 60 | grep -oP 'CPU:\s+\K[0-9.]+') gets the average CPU power over 60 samples via powerstat, taking one minute (a limitation of the command). Then wakeonlan wakes the remote host, and qm performs the PVE node migration. QMqm migrate
qm is the QEMU/KVM Virtual Machine Manager, a handy command-line tool PVE provides. Its migrate option migrates the VM with the given VM ID to another node, and if the VM is running you need to add --online for live migration. If you’re interested in the qm command, see its manual.
Wake On LAN (WOL) Wake On LAN (WOL), also called “network wake-up,” lets a computer on the same LAN send a command to a powered-off or sleeping host to boot it back to operation. To use this, first confirm the motherboard supports WOL; if it does, you need to enable the PCI/PCIe wake-up feature in the UEFI/BIOS.
How it worksWhen I first looked up WOL, I was curious how a powered-off computer can still receive a packet to wake it. The secret is that when a computer is off or sleeping, there’s still a trickle of power to give the NIC or host minimal operating capability, so it can listen to other packets on the LAN, continuously receiving and checking broadcast info from the same LAN. The host responsible for waking a node broadcasts a Magic Packet on the LAN. This Magic Packet usually starts with 6 consecutive FFs: FF FF FF FF FF FF, followed by the MAC address, and sometimes a 4-to-6-byte password. This Magic Packet is broadcast on the LAN, and once the sleeping/powered-off host parses the content with its minimally-operating NIC and finds the info in the Magic Packet matches the local host, it starts the boot process. That’s also why the bash script above appends the MAC address after wakeonlan. Enabling WOL in the BIOSEnter the BIOS on each of the two nodes to enable it, then save changes and reboot.
