Command testHere I first power off node B and try to wake it from node A. wakeonlan 04:42:1a:e7:5a:a0
From the history you can also see node 2 successfully booted from a powered-off state.
The experiment But the command test showed that the boot wait time also needs to be considered, so we can change the script to the following.
#!/bin/bashPOWER_THRESHOLD=6.0NODE="pve2"VM_ID="100"BACKUP_NODE="pve"BACKUP_NODE_IP="172.25.166.68"BACKUP_NODE_MAC="0c:9d:92:86:bb:63"MAX_RETRIES=12 SLEEP_INTERVAL=10POWER_CONSUMPTION=$(powerstat -R 1 60 | grep -oP 'CPU:\s+\K[0-9.]+')if (( $(echo "$POWER_CONSUMPTION > $POWER_THRESHOLD" | bc -l) )); then echo "Power consumption too high ($POWER_CONSUMPTION W) on $NODE. Migrating VM $VM_ID to $BACKUP_NODE..." wakeonlan $BACKUP_NODE_MAC echo "Waiting for $BACKUP_NODE ($BACKUP_NODE_IP) to be reachable..." RETRY_COUNT=0 while ! ping -c 1 $BACKUP_NODE_IP &> /dev/null; do RETRY_COUNT=$((RETRY_COUNT + 1)) if [ "$RETRY_COUNT" -ge "$MAX_RETRIES" ]; then echo "Error: $BACKUP_NODE did not respond after $((MAX_RETRIES * SLEEP_INTERVAL)) seconds. Exiting." exit 1 fi echo "Waiting for $BACKUP_NODE to come online... ($RETRY_COUNT/$MAX_RETRIES)" sleep $SLEEP_INTERVAL done echo "Backup node $BACKUP_NODE is online. Starting migration..." qm migrate $VM_ID $BACKUP_NODE --online echo "VM $VM_ID successfully migrated to backup node $BACKUP_NODE ($BACKUP_NODE_IP)."else echo "Power consumption is normal ($POWER_CONSUMPTION W) on $NODE."fi
This adds a retry mechanism: after sending the Magic Packet, it tries to ping the host to check whether it’s alive. Of course I confirmed I’m not blocking ICMP packets, so after boot it should definitely be pingable. The max retry count is 12, with a 10-second wait between retries, so it waits at most 2 minutes.
These numbers are just for experimental convenience; whether to change it to backoff retry in real operation is up to you.
Here I wanted to reverse the experiment, first powering off node 1 PVE.
Then on node 2 PVE2 I run the script above. As expected, it first checks whether the average CPU power over one minute exceeds the threshold (6 watts), which it definitely will, so it then wakes the pve node, keeps pinging node 1, and after two retries, node pve is available and migration starts, completing successfully.
If you observe the Ubuntu VM’s memory metric, you’ll see a gap, which is the expected downtime during migration. When I handled MQ issues at AWS, I’d also see such gaps in some instances’ memory or CPU metrics during maintenance windows, which usually indicates an underlying instance replacement or restart, possibly for maintenance or a security patch.
ClosingThis post did a simple little experiment: from one node in the PVE cluster, we woke another PVE node on the same LAN and did a live migration. If I later have another host available, I’ll cover using the HA (High Availability) cluster in PVE. ReferenceIPMI watchdoghttps://blog.jason.tools/2019/02/pve-ipmi-watchdog.html qmhttps://pve.proxmox.com/pve-docs/qm.1.html

entry.title: Hands-On Proxmox VE VM Live Migration | PVE Series 1
entry.content:
🌐 中文版：繁體中文
Introducing Proxmox VEProxmox VE (PVE) is an open-source virtualization environment that can support both LXC (Linux Container) based containers and kernel-based VMs, i.e. KVM, the virtualization technology that uses the Linux kernel as a hypervisor.
Proxmox also handles the guest’s hardware requests through QEMU, which sits between host and guest, translating them to the real hardware. Running together with KVM brings a boost in instruction-processing performance, so virtualization can run at near-local speed. Physical node setupFlashing the Proxmox VE image Prepare a USB and put the Proxmox VE ISO image on it. I chose the Proxmox VE 7.4 ISO Installer.
PVE image official download
Then prepare the nodes and adjust the boot order on each host; enter the BIOS and set USB as the first priority. While you’re there, check whether KVM is enabled in the BIOS; you must enable it first. In my environment, it’s under Intel Virtualization Technology in the BIOS’s Advanced settings; enable it.
After booting normally, the installation wizard appears; just follow it through. Once installed, log into the node you set up via the web, and you can start building the cluster. Building the clusterConfirm node infoThere are two nodes now; before building the cluster, confirm /etc/hosts: Node 1172.25.166.68 pve.oplab.io pveNode 2172.25.166.42 pve2.oplab.io pve2
StartingFirst go to node 1’s Datacenter, find Cluster, and choose Create Cluster.
Name the cluster (here it’s LabCluster), choose your cluster network, then click Create.
After creation, the screen looks like this; you can see node 1 pve added to the cluster.
Next we need to join the other nodes to this cluster. Find Join Information under Cluster and copy the info it shows.
Then go to the second node pve2 (a separate host in my case) to join the cluster. Find Join Information under Cluster and paste in the join info you just copied. Once joined, both nodes can see each other.
If you now hastily create a VM and think you can migrate it, you’d be wrong. Your backup node will error because it can’t find the VM’s config file, like this:
Right, migration still needs two conditions:
The VM config file must be shared between nodes, or more completely, the VM disk must be shared Also, the ISO image used to create the VM must be shared
To achieve both, you need a shared-storage solution.
Migration flow Let me add some context on our migration flow. In this post we’ll migrate manually through the PVE interface: two PVE nodes, a pre-built shared-storage architecture, a VM created on that architecture, then migrating that VM from one node to another.
So next we’ll build the storage architecture with Ceph.
Introducing Ceph The Ceph Storage Cluster, also called RADOS (Reliable, Autonomic Distributed Object Store), provides a reliable, self-managing distributed object store. Developed in C++, this cluster is the software storage system at the bottom of the Ceph architecture, where all the environment’s data lives. It has self-healing and self-management capabilities, and is composed of automatically-operating OSD storage nodes and lightweight monitor programs.
Ceph components Ceph OSDs Ceph’s daemon (ceph-osd) Stores data, handles data replication, recovery, etc. Provides monitoring info to the Ceph Monitor by checking ceph-osd heartbeats For high availability (HA) and redundancy: at least 3 Ceph OSDs are needed
Monitors ceph-mon Maintains maps showing cluster state, including the monitor map and OSD map Responsible for managing authentication between daemons and clients For high availability (HA) and redundancy: at least 3 Ceph Monitors are needed
Managers ceph-mgr Tracks runtime metrics and the Ceph cluster’s current state, e.g. storage utilization, current system load For high availability (HA) and redundancy: at least 2 Ceph Managers are needed
MDSs: The Ceph Metadata Server (Ceph MDS) stores metadata for the Ceph filesystem That is, a Ceph block device or Ceph object storage doesn’t use MDS
If you want to create a Ceph Filesystem (CephFS), you also need to create an MDS beforehand Ceph MDS lets POSIX filesystem users run commands like ls or find without burdening the Ceph storage cluster
Ceph is a distributed storage system, supported at the bottom by a cluster of multiple servers (the PVE cluster we just set up). If you need to expand storage or scale the system, just add more servers to the cluster, which makes scaling very simple. In this architecture, Ceph is highly reliable, with the system automatically healing and managing itself. When data is written, it’s automatically replicated to multiple nodes, so even if a node fails, the whole system keeps working and the data isn’t corrupted. This design lets Ceph provide a stable and secure storage solution.
Installing CephFirst install Ceph on every node; there are two nodes here, so both need it.
Click Start quincy installation (I didn’t specify a version, just used the one offered).
During download, it asks whether to continue; type Y.
After it finishes, it asks you to specify a network interface.
After a successful install, it prompts the next steps, which we’ll follow:
Install Ceph on every node Add additional Ceph Monitors Create a Ceph OSD on each node Create a Ceph Pool
Repeat the install flow above on the other nodes. Once every node is installed, checking Health should show a warning OSD count 0 < osd_pool_default_size 3, which is normal because no OSD has been created yet.
Creating a Ceph OSDTo create a Ceph OSD, you first need idle disk space. So first find a disk on each node to configure. Enter Disk on the pve node and format an idle disk; if you have no idle disk, you can use a USB external drive.
Then under PVE > Ceph > OSD, click Create: OSD, choose the disk you just formatted, and click Create.
Do the same steps on the other nodes to install OSDs.
Once installed, you can see the OSD type and status in the OSD view on both nodes.
Also, for redundancy and high availability, you can create two additional Ceph Managers (active-standby).
Per the suggestions in this article:
The ceph-osd process consumes CPU during operation, so each ceph-osd process is usually bound to a CPU core. The ceph-mon process isn’t very CPU-intensive, so you don’t need to reserve too much CPU for it. ceph-mds is also very CPU-intensive, so it needs more CPU resources. ceph-mon and ceph-mds need 2G of memory, and each ceph-osd process needs 1G (2G is better).
Creating a Ceph PoolA Ceph Pool combines OSDs across nodes, and it’s where our VM disks will later be stored. On the pve node, go to Ceph > Pools and choose Create: Ceph Pool. Give the pool a name, here syncbricks-ceph. You also need to specify the pool size; normally Min.Size is at least 2 and Size defaults to 3, but since I only have two hosts, I set size to 2 for now, letting both OSDs join the Ceph Pool.
After creation it should show a warning, because PVE defaults to wanting 3 OSDs but there are only two.
There are two OSDs currently online, so this is normal for now. Also, after the Ceph Pool is created, you’ll find syncbricks-ceph appear under both nodes. Now the two nodes can share the VM disk, enabling the later VM migration.
Creating a Ceph File System
Ceph File System (CephFS) is a POSIX-compliant filesystem built on top of the Ceph distributed object store RADOS. CephFS aims to provide a highly-available, high-performance file-storage solution for various applications, usable as scratch space for high-performance computing (HPC) and shared storage for distributed workflows.
In CephFS’s architecture, file metadata is stored in a RADOS pool separate from file data, and served through an elastically-scalable MDS cluster, which supports higher-throughput workloads. Clients can directly access RADOS to read and write file data blocks, so workloads can scale linearly with the underlying RADOS object store, without any gateway or agent mediating data I/O.
Data access is coordinated by the MDS cluster, which manages a distributed metadata cache, with clients and MDSs jointly maintaining metadata state. The MDS consolidates metadata changes and efficiently writes them to the RADOS journal, storing no metadata locally. This design lets clients collaborate quickly and consistently under a POSIX filesystem.
With the intro done, let’s continue. So far we’ve handled sharing the VM disk; next we’ll share the VM ISO image. If it isn’t shared, a later migration will throw the error Can't migrate VM with local CD/DVD, meaning it must be done the shared way.
Per this thread, sharing an ISO image requires at least these steps:
Create Ceph File System: Ensure CephFS is created with at least two MDS on standby
Add Ceph FS: Mount CephFS on the nodes so all nodes can share the same ISO image
Creating MDSSo we create an MDS on each of the two nodes.
Then on node 1 do Create: Ceph FS, naming it cephfs.
After creation, cephfs appears on both nodes, and you can upload an ISO image to the shared filesystem. Here I uploaded the Ubuntu 22.04 Desktop image.
Creating a VM to testThis time I create the Ubuntu VM on the pve node. During creation, when setting the OS, choose Use CD/DVD disc image file(iso), set Storage to the Ceph filesystem cephfs just created, then choose the image you want from the filesystem.
When the creation flow reaches the Disks part, remember to set Storage to the syncbricks-ceph just created.
Then create the VM.
After it’s created, you need to enter the VM to install Ubuntu, which I won’t detail here.
Manually testing migrationOnce the VM is created, select it under pve, right-click, and a Migration option should appear, letting us migrate manually.
We migrate VM 100 from node pve1 to node pve2. Afterward you can see the VM’s position on the left has appeared under pve2, meaning the migration succeeded.
So far so good. For the next step, I want to use a script to auto-migrate based on conditions like CPU usage or CPU power consumption. This process will also need node 1 to power on a shut-down node 2, which uses the interesting Wake On Lan (WOL) feature; I’ll leave that for the next post.
ReferenceProxmox VEhttps://ithelp.ithome.com.tw/articles/10338613https://kawsing.gitbook.io/opensystem/andoid-shou-ji/pomoxve/jian-li-cong-jihttps://www.linuxyes.com/blog/linuxyes-3/post/proxmox-ve-replication-ha-9https://blog.tenyi.com/2020/01/proxmox-ve-two-nodes-ha-cluster.htmlhttps://medium.com/彼得潘的-swift-ios-app-開發教室/工控機安裝proxmox-ve-pve-94a09647d95f Cephhttps://www.linuxtek.ca/2023/01/27/ceph-clustering-with-proxmox/https://kawsing.gitbook.io/opensystem/andoid-shou-ji/pomoxve/ceph-object-storagehttps://kawsing.gitbook.io/opensystem/andoid-shou-ji/pomoxve/ceph-object-storage/ceph-xu-yao-da-liang-ji-yi-tihttps://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7BcSnUz_2zQhttps://forum.proxmox.com/threads/ceph-mount-a-pg-pool-for-images-isos.134367/

entry.title: Other Ways to Do Manual Migration | PVE Series 3
entry.content:
🌐 中文版：繁體中文
PrefaceIn the first post of the PVE series, I demonstrated migration from the PVE console. Here I record another way to do migration. Manual migrationYou can first enter a node’s shell, then go to the /etc/pve/nodes directory, where you’ll find all the nodes in the same cluster. root@pve:/etc/pve/nodes# ls -ltotal 0drwxr-xr-x 2 root www-data 0 Sep 10 11:06 pvedrwxr-xr-x 2 root www-data 0 Sep 10 14:21 pve2 Then enter the target node pve2, where you’ll find many directories. The ones related to migration are lxc and qemu-server, depending on whether you’re migrating a container or a VM. To migrate a container, move the config file under lxc to the same path on the target node, e.g. /etc/pve/nodes/pve/lxc/. Likewise for a VM: move the config file under qemu-server to /etc/pve/nodes/pve/qemu-server/. root@pve:/etc/pve/nodes/pve2# ls -ltotal 2-rw-r----- 1 root www-data 102 Sep 11 14:09 config-rw-r----- 1 root www-data 83 Sep 22 14:40 lrm_statusdrwxr-xr-x 2 root www-data 0 Sep 10 11:06 lxcdrwxr-xr-x 2 root www-data 0 Sep 10 11:06 openvzdrwx------ 2 root www-data 0 Sep 10 11:06 priv-rw-r----- 1 root www-data 1675 Sep 10 11:06 pve-ssl.key-rw-r----- 1 root www-data 1688 Sep 10 11:06 pve-ssl.pemdrwxr-xr-x 2 root www-data 0 Sep 10 11:06 qemu-server
Since we’re migrating a VM, enter qemu-server/, where you’ll find two VMs. root@pve2:/etc/pve/nodes/pve2/qemu-server# ls -ltotal 1-rw-r----- 1 root www-data 451 Sep 22 14:47 101.conf-rw-r----- 1 root www-data 456 Sep 22 14:11 102.conf
We choose to migrate VM 101, so move 101.conf to the corresponding directory on the other node pve. mv 101.conf ../../pve/qemu-server/
Then check on the pve node. root@pve:/etc/pve/nodes/pve/qemu-server# ls -ltotal 1-rw-r----- 1 root www-data 452 Sep 22 14:11 100.conf-rw-r----- 1 root www-data 451 Sep 22 14:51 101.conf
After confirming the move is done, check the VM’s status. qm list You’ll find VM 101 is stopped; then start it with a command. qm start 101
The VM has moved and started successfully, running smoothly. Migration with local storageIn PVE, you can also use a ready-made command to online-migrate a VM with a local disk: qm migrate <vmid> <targetnode> --with-local-disks --online But actual measurement showed it took nearly 40 minutes to migrate, and that’s just a 256GB Ubuntu VM.
Closing This post just records that migration can be done by moving the config file.

entry.title: 【Study Notes】OTA Update -1
entry.content:
🌐 中文版：繁體中文
What is an OTA Update (Over-The-Air Update)?Updating a device’s software/firmware over wireless communication. The OTA flow Notify The device is notified of a pending OTA update The device can choose to ignore the update or accept it to trigger the download
Download The device downloads the update via various supported protocols The update package downloads to a pre-configured storage area E.g. an S3 bucket
The update may be a brand-new firmware image or a patch to existing firmware
Verify Verify the validity of the update package
Install The device starts updating via the update package (usually through a bootloader) to the latest firmware After installation, checks can run to verify functionality The device reports the successful firmware update to the OTA update provider
These are the four main steps. Modular OTA update A modular OTA consists of several small libraries and an orchestrator. Each library handles a specific sub-task, such as notifying of a pending OTA update or downloading a file via MQTT The orchestrator synchronizes all the small libraries with the bootloader and memory pool to perform the OTA update.
The modular OTA approach lets you swap or change different parts of the OTA as requirements change. For example:
If you want to trigger OTA from AWS IoT, you can use the IoT Job library to check for new OTA updates or send notifications about OTA job status. Alternatively, you can replace it with any other library. You can use the OTA Job Parser in the IoT Job library to parse the received OTA Job Document. Alternatively, you can use your own custom Job Document Parser based on the OTA Job Document.
Modular OTA update flowBelow is the modular OTA update flow from the FreeRTOS official site.
Orchestrator The orchestrator is the core component that specifies how to coordinate an OTA update The orchestrator is provided by the user and contains as many custom components as needed to accomplish the desired OTA update method A typical update includes the “Notify,” “Download,” “Verify,” and “Install” phases. The orchestrator provides these phases by stitching together component libraries and other external libraries A description of each component library can be found below
IoT Job Libraries The IoT Job Handler is the first component used in the entire OTA flow This library provides the ability to start pending IoT jobs and update job status When the job handler learns of a new OTA update (via an IoT Job), the handler starts the job and passes the job and its metadata into the parser chain If a parser is configured to handle the job, it forwards the information that the job started successfully back to the Job Handler This successful-start notification is forwarded back to the OTA update provider (i.e. IoT Jobs) to mark the update as started. If no parser can understand the job, the failure to start the OTA update is forwarded to the provider
OTA Job ParserThe parser validates whether the IoT job is an OTA update and parses the fields into a usable format before calling the downloader. MQTT file streaming library The file downloader provides the ability to download OTA files. The file downloader handles downloading the update via a CBOR- or JSON-format MQTT stream The download itself is performed in chunks, more easily thought of as blocks of the whole OTA update file. This is done to improve download reliability and to allow larger firmware updates than might be possible in a single download “block.”
Bootloader and Signature Verifier The bootloader exists to verify new firmware and install it onto the device Modular OTA deliberately avoids implementing a bootloader, since multiple industry-wide bootloaders already exist for a large number of supported microcontrollers Modular OTA leaves the choice of bootloader and signature-verification mechanism to the user.
Difference between AWS IoT Jobs and AWS IoT OTA Update AWS IoT Jobs Defines a set of remote operations that can be sent to and run on one or more devices Most commonly, jobs are used to perform software or firmware updates, but can also be used for any arbitrary operation, such as reboot, credential rotation, etc.
AWS IoT OTA Update A feature built on AWS IoT Jobs, specifically implementing software/firmware update operations, and only that operation An OTA update is a job, but with a predefined Job Document. It bundles common software-update functionality (like code signing) to build a software-update solution faster
Comparison table
AWS IoT Jobs AWS IoT OTA Updates
Purpose Any custom behavior FreeRTOS OTA update
Job Document Customizable Predefined
Create API CreateJob CreateOTAUpdate
Code signing User must implement Integrated
HTTP/MQTT User chooses Integrated
AWS IoT Device SDK support C, C++, Python, Java, Javascript C only
Platform Abstraction Layer (PAL) None Yes [3]
Max file limit HTTP: 5GB (Amazon S3 limit), MQTT: 24MB (MQTT file stream limit) 16MB (OTA update limit)[4]
AWS IoT Over-The-Air (OTA) Library https://github.com/aws/ota-for-aws-iot-embedded-sdk
This AWS library includes both FreeRTOS and the AWS IoT Device SDK for Embedded-C. This library also includes the OTA Platform Abstraction Layer (PAL) [3] to simplify the difficulty of porting the library to specific hardware [5]. There’s also an OTA Operating System (OS) Functional Interface to simplify porting to RTOSes other than FreeRTOS, or even bare metal.
Since AWS IoT OTA is for resource-constrained devices, the native Device SDK doesn’t integrate FreeRTOS. For the same reason, the OTA file size is limited to 16MB.
References[1] https://www.freertos.org/freertos-core/over-the-air-updates/index.html[2] https://repost.aws/articles/ARDHNhV0bnRGau0kmdhTSZZA/comparing-aws-iot-jobs-and-aws-iot-over-the-air-ota-updates[3] https://www.freertos.org/Documentation/api-ref/ota-for-aws-iot-embedded-sdk/docs/doxygen/output/html/ota_pal_interface.html[4] https://docs.aws.amazon.com/general/latest/gr/amazon-freertos.html#limits-ota-manager[5] Porting Guide - https://www.freertos.org/Documentation/api-ref/ota-for-aws-iot-embedded-sdk/docs/doxygen/output/html/ota_porting.html

entry.title: Hands-On Practice: S3 Gateway Endpoints
entry.content:
What is S3 Gateway Endpoints? Let’s consider a scenario
How could your Lambda function access the content in the S3 bucket?
If you want a service to access the content in the S3 bucket, it usually go through VPC endpoint. S3 supports two types of VPC endpoint,each of which is Gateway endpoint and Interface endpoint
The diffeences between two types of VPC endpoints are listed below
S3 Gateway Endpoints S3 Interface Endpoints
Use S3 Public IP Address Use Private IP Address in VPC to access S3
Use the same S3 DNS Name Name must include VPC Endpoint ID [3]
cannot access internally can access internally
cannot access from other AWS region can access from other AWS region by using VPC peering or AWS Transit gateway
Free In chrarge
So if your scenario is that a Lambda function want to access the content in S3 bucket in the same region, it is great to utilize the Gateway Endpoint
Consideration of S3 Gateway EndpointIt is worth to mestion that there are several things you need to consider before choosing S3 Gateway Endpoints, make sure you go through the section in the official documentation
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/privatelink/vpc-endpoints-s3.html#gateway-endpoint-considerations-s3
Private DNSWhen you are trying yo create Gateway Endpoint or Interface Endpoint for your S3, you can decide creating private DNS for cost down.
This is implement by Route53 ResolverFor detail you can check：https://docs.aws.amazon.com/zh_tw/Route53/latest/DeveloperGuide/resolver.html
Steps for building Gateway Endpoint Go to AWS Console to create the endpoint
VPC / Endpoints / Create Endpoint
Choose AWS services , and com.amaazonaws.us-east-1.s3
Then, press create endpoints
Associate Route Table Make sure the route table that assoicate to the gateway endpoint is clean. If you don’t have on, then make one.
Configure policy For testing purposes, I choose Full Access
Then, press create endpoint
Check the routingAfter establishing the endpoint, you can check if the default route of route table is well configured
Next, we must configure a Lambda function for accessing S3 bucket. Configure Lambda FunctionIf you put a Lambda funciton into a VPC, it will attach to 2 subnets by defaults. Make sure two subnet have default route to S3 Gateway Endpoints.
Create Lambda function, and enable the VPC
Lambda Code
import jsonimport boto3def lambda_handler(event, context): print("CREATE CLIENT") s3 = boto3.client("s3") print("START REQUEST") resp = s3.list_objects(Bucket="testbucket4-s3gateway-endpoint") print(resp) return { 'statusCode': 200, 'body': json.dumps('Hello from Lambda!') }
In this Lambda code, Lambda will try to list the objects in the bucket, can print out the information of response object in the log.
Configure policy of Lambda execution role
I simply attach AWS Managed Policy AmazonS3FullAccess to the execution role for testing
Notice, you should not give full access to your Lambda function in production mode, make sure giving adequient permssion to the role.
Check invocations Press test button in the Lambda console, you’ll noticee the lambda get invoked successfully
Then you need to check the invocation logs in CloudWatch
You can see that the object information were listed and printed out in the invocation logs. Reference[1] https://docs.aws.amazon.com/zh_tw/vpc/latest/privatelink/vpc-endpoints-s3.html#create-gateway-endpoint-s3[2] https://docs.aws.amazon.com/zh_tw/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/privatelink-interface-endpoints.html#types-of-vpc-endpoints-for-s3[3] https://docs.aws.amazon.com/zh_tw/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/privatelink-interface-endpoints.html#accessing-s3-interface-endpoints

entry.title: Hands-On Practice: Amazon SNS Fan out to Amazon SQS
entry.content:
IntroductionAmazon SNS offen works well with Amazon SQS, by subscribing SQS to SNS, the SNS service can push messages to SQS. This may eliminating the need to periodically check or “poll” for updates. What is Amazon SQS?By official definition
Amazon SQS is a message queue service used by distributed applications to exchange messages through a polling model, and can be used to decouple sending and receiving components—without requiring each component to be concurrently available.
Scenario The Fanout scenario is when a message published to an SNS topic is replicated and pushed to multiple endpoints, such as Kinesis Data Firehose delivery streams, Amazon SQS queues, HTTP(S) endpoints, and Lambda functions. This allows for parallel asynchronous processing.For example, you can develop an application that publishes a message to an SNS topic whenever an order is placed for a product. Then, SQS queues that are subscribed to the SNS topic receive identical notifications for the new order. An Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) server instance attached to one of the SQS queues can handle the processing or fulfillment of the order. And you can attach another Amazon EC2 server instance to a data warehouse for analysis of all orders received.[1]
StepsHere we will go through each step of fan out to Amazon SQS. The initial step is to remember both SNS arn and SQS arn. Create SQS QueueFirst, you’ll need to create a standard queue in SQS console
After creating the standard queue, it will shows the arn. Make sure noted this arn, you’ll need to provide this arn when creating the subscriptions Create SNS TopicSecond, you need to create a SNS topic in the SNS console..
And again, you’ll need to note the topic arn. Provide Permission to SNS to send messages to SQSBy default, SNS will not have permission to send messages to SQS, so you need to provide permission to SNS for sending messages.
Go to SQS Console Press “Edit” in the top corner Scroll down to the “Access Policy”
Append new statement in the Access Policy
{ "Effect": "Allow", "Principal": { "Service": "sns.amazonaws.com" }, "Action": [ "sqs:DeleteMessage", "sqs:ReceiveMessage", "sqs:SendMessage" ], "Resource": "arn:aws:sqs:us-east-1:xxxxxxxxxxxx:QueueforSNS", "Condition": { "ArnEquals": { "aws:SourceArn": "arn:aws:sns:us-east-1:xxxxxxxxxxxx:StandardTopicforSQS" } }}
Subscribe SQS queue to SNS topicNow you’ll need to subscribe the SQS queue to the SNS topic.
Go to SNS console Scroll down and choose “Create Subscription”
Choose your topic arn Set the protocal to SQS Choose the SQS arn
Once complete, you will notice that the subscripe confirmation also completes. If you create a SQS type subscription by using console, you don’t need confirm the subscription manually.
But if you create a cross-account subscription, you will receive the confirmation url in the SQS queue, and you will need to click the confirmation URL. [3]
Provide Permission to User for topic/queue operationsYou can add permissions to an IAM User to publish SNS messages to a topic. { "Statement": [ { "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "sns:Publish", "Resource": "arn:aws:sns:us-east-2:XXXXXXXXXXXX:MyTopic" } ]}
And you also need to provide permissions to SQS queue to recieve and delete messages { "Statement": [ { "Effect": "Allow", "Action": [ "sqs:ReceiveMessage", "sqs:DeleteMessage" ], "Resource": [ "arn:aws:sqs:us-east-2:XXXXXXXXXXXX:MyQueue1", "arn:aws:sqs:us-east-2:XXXXXXXXXXXX:MyQueue2" ] } ]}
However,if you want to perform cross-account operations, you will need to provide permissions to the other account. For example, if you want to let acount: 111122223333 to publish messages to SNS topic in your account, here is an example policy. { "Statement": [ { "Effect": "Allow", "Principal": { "AWS": "111122223333" }, "Action": "sns:Publish", "Resource": "arn:aws:sns:us-east-2:XXXXXXXXXXXXX:MyTopic" } ]} if you want to let acount: 111122223333 to perform receive abd delete messages to queue in your account, here is an example policy. { "Statement": [ { "Effect": "Allow", "Principal": { "AWS": "111122223333" }, "Action": [ "sqs:DeleteMessage", "sqs:ReceiveMessage" ], "Resource": [ "arn:aws:sqs:us-east-2:XXXXXXXXXXXX:MyQueue" ] } ]}
Test subscriptionNow we can test the message delivery to the queue.
Go to the SNS console Press “Push Message” in the top right corner Enter the message subject and meesage body
Go to the SQS console Press “Send and Receive Message” in the top right corner Scroll down , and press the “Poll for all messages” And you’ll find the messages are in polling progress.
Then the test meesages showed in the console
ConclusionsWe successfully fan out the message from the Amazon SNS to the Amazon SQS. Reference[1] https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sns/latest/dg/sns-common-scenarios.html#SNSFanoutScenario[2] https://docs.aws.amazon.com/zh_tw/sns/latest/dg/sns-sqs-as-subscriber.html[3]https://docs.aws.amazon.com/zh_tw/sns/latest/dg/sns-send-message-to-sqs-cross-account.html

entry.title: Must-Know Problem-Solving Knowledge | Queue | LeetCode Notes
Must-Know Problem-Solving Knowledge | Stack | LeetCode Notes
entry.content:
🌐 中文版：繁體中文
What is a Stack?A Stack is a data structure with the Last-In-First-Out (LIFO) property.
Stack implementation (C++)Here I want to implement a complete Stack in C++, realizing the common operations like push, pop, isEmpty, and so on. Implementing a Stack with an ArrayWhen implementing a Stack in C++, note that some variables shouldn’t be accessible from outside, like
top: used to point to the top of the stack, i.e. the topmost index capacity: the stack’s memory size *stack: a pointer to the stack
So the variables related to the above need to be private member variables. Also, when implementing a Stack with an array, you sometimes run out of memory, so you can solve this by creating a function that automatically expands the capacity. Also, when implementing Pop, you don’t actually need to remove the data; instead you subtract 1 from top, as if we really deleted the data from the stack, but we actually didn’t, and we just overwrite the existing data on a future Push. This approach saves memory-operation cost.
Note: before a Pop or a Top operation (returning the current topmost data value of the stack), you need to first check whether the stack is empty, st.empty()
Full code# include <iostream>using namespace std;class StackArray{ private: int top; //Index of top element of Stack int capacity; // Allocated memory int *stack; void DoubleCapacity(); public: // Define constructor with initial state: top=-1, capacity=1 StackArray():top(-1),capacity(1) { //Init a int array with capacity=1 stack = new int[capacity]; } void Push(int x); void Pop(); bool isEmpty(); int Top(); int getSize(); };void StackArray::DoubleCapacity() { // Double capacity capacity = capacity *2; // Reallocate memory int *new_stack = new int[capacity]; //copy elements to new stack for(int i = 0; i < capacity/2;i++){ new_stack[i] = stack[i]; } // free memory, this is used to free memory that allocated by new[] delete[] stack; // redrect new_stack to stack stack = new_stack;}void StackArray::Push(int x) { if (top == capacity-1){ DoubleCapacity(); } stack[++top] = x;}void StackArray::Pop() { if (isEmpty()) { cout << "Empty Stack, nothing to pop!" << endl; return; } //update top top--;}bool StackArray::isEmpty(){ if(top == -1){ return true; } else { return false; }}// Return top element of stackint StackArray::Top(){ if(isEmpty()) { cout << "Empty Stack, nothing on the top!" << endl; return -1; } return stack[top];}int StackArray::getSize(){ return top+1;}int main(){ StackArray sk; sk.Pop(); sk.Push(14); sk.Push(9); cout << "\n top: " << sk.Top() << "\nsize: " << sk.getSize() << endl; sk.Push(7); cout << "\n top: " << sk.Top() << "\nsize: " << sk.getSize() << endl; sk.Pop(); sk.Pop(); cout << "\n top: " << sk.Top() << "\nsize: " << sk.getSize() << endl; sk.Pop(); cout << "\n top: " << sk.Top() << "\nsize: " << sk.getSize() << endl; return 0;}
Output: Empty Stack, nothing to pop!top: 9size: 2top: 7size: 3top: 14size: 1Empty Stack, nothing on the top!top: -1size: 0
Code explanationclass StackArray{ private: int top; //Index of top element of Stack int capacity; // Allocated memory int *stack; void DoubleCapacity(); public: // Define constructor with initial state: top=-1, capacity=1 StackArray():top(-1),capacity(1) { //Init a int array with capacity=1 stack = new int[capacity]; } void Push(int x); void Pop(); bool isEmpty(); int Top(); int getSize(); };
We define the Stack itself and the corresponding operations by creating a StackArray class. For initialization, we use the constructor StackArray (the constructor has the same name as the class) to initialize the private member variables top=-1, capacity=1, and declare a new memory space, an integer array of size capacity, with the pointer stack* pointing to it. Then in the public section we declare the various operations we’ll later perform on the Stack. void StackArray::DoubleCapacity() { // Double capacity capacity = capacity *2; // Reallocate memory int *new_stack = new int[capacity]; //copy elements to new stack for(int i = 0; i < capacity/2;i++){ new_stack[i] = stack[i]; } // free memory, this is used to free memory that allocated by new[] delete[] stack; // redrect new_stack to stack stack = new_stack;} The DoubleCapacity function mainly multiplies capacity by 2, then defines a new stack with double the capacity, copies all the old stack’s data over, then frees the old stack’s array memory and updates the pointer. void StackArray::Push(int x) { if (top == capacity-1){ DoubleCapacity(); } stack[++top] = x;}void StackArray::Pop() { if (isEmpty()) { cout << "Empty Stack, nothing to pop!" << endl; return; } //update top top--;}
For Push, first make sure the Stack is full or not. The way to check is whether top‘s value equals capacity-1 (subtract 1 because it’s an array); if equal, it’s full and needs more space, so just call the DoubleCapacity function we defined earlier. Then push data into the Stack. Here, to reduce line count, ++top and stack[top] =x are merged into one line. For Pop, you first need to check whether the Stack is empty, so call the isEmpty() function to confirm. If empty, print a message and return to the main function; if not empty, just decrement the top value by 1. bool StackArray::isEmpty(){ if(top == -1){ return true; } else { return false; }}// Return top element of stackint StackArray::Top(){ if(isEmpty()) { cout << "Empty Stack, nothing on the top!" << endl; return -1; } return stack[top];}int StackArray::getSize(){ return top+1;}
For isEmpty(), compare whether top is the initial value; if so it’s empty, if not it’s not empty. For Top(), likewise first check whether the stack is empty; if empty return to main func, if not empty return the content value at the top of the stack getSize(): just return top+1 (because of array index arithmetic, it’s declared as -1 at first, so you add it back)
Implementing a Stack with a Linked List If you implement a Stack with a Linked List, the first or head in the Linked List, i.e. the first element of the chain, is the top of the Stack, so pushing onto the Stack is equivalent to using the push_front() function in the Linked List. The code below mainly implements it with two classes, StackNode and StackList. StackNode defines the Linked List’s node, while StackList defines the head node, i.e. *top.
What’s the difference between defining a node with a struct vs a class?
Member variables defined with a struct are always public, accessible by anyone, but with a class you can put the stack’s entry top in private, which restricts access to the node, so main() can’t change each node’s data. This could be a security consideration.
Full code# include <iostream>using namespace std;class StackList;// Define node structureclass StackNode{ private: int data; StackNode *next; public: //Define constructor StackNode(): data(0),next(0){ //next = 0; } //Define constructor with initial data StackNode(int x):data(x), next(0){} //Define constructor with initial data and next node address StackNode(int x, StackNode *nextNode):data(x), next(nextNode){}; friend class StackList;};// Define first node, and stack-related functionsclass StackList{ private: StackNode *top; int size; public: StackList():top(0),size(0){}; void Push(int x); void Pop(); bool isEmpty(); int Top(); int getSize();};void StackList::Push(int x){ if(isEmpty()){ top = new StackNode(x); size++; return; } //push_front() in linked list StackNode *newNode = new StackNode(x); //Link the new node to the origin top node newNode->next = top; //update top pointer top = newNode; size++;}void StackList::Pop(){ if(isEmpty()){ cout << "Empty stack, nothing to pop out!" << endl; return; } StackNode *tempNode = top; top = top->next; delete tempNode; // set tempNode to a null pointer, to prevent dangling pointer // The constructor will set the *next to 0 (NULL) tempNode =0; size--;}bool StackList::isEmpty(){ if( size == 0) return true; else return false;}int StackList::Top(){ if(isEmpty()){ cout << "Empty stack, nothing to return" << endl; return -1; } return top->data;}int StackList::getSize(){ return size;}int main(){ StackList sk; sk.Pop(); sk.Push(32); sk.Push(4); std::cout << "\ntop: " << sk.Top() << "\nsize: " << sk.getSize() << std::endl; sk.Push(15); std::cout << "\ntop: " << sk.Top() << "\nsize: " << sk.getSize() << std::endl; sk.Pop(); sk.Pop(); std::cout << "\ntop: " << sk.Top() << "\nsize: " << sk.getSize() << std::endl; sk.Pop(); std::cout << "\ntop: " << sk.Top() << "\nsize: " << sk.getSize() << std::endl; return 0;}
Output Empty stack, nothing to pop out!top: 4size: 2top: 15size: 3top: 32size: 1Empty stack, nothing to returntop: -1size: 0
Code explanationclass StackList;class StackNode{private: int data; StackNode *next;public: StackNode():data(0){ next = 0; } StackNode(int x):data(x){ next = 0; } StackNode(int x, StackNode *nextNode):data(x),next(nextNode){}; friend class StackList;};class StackList{private: StackNode *top; // remember the address of top element int size; // number of elements in Stackpublic: StackList():size(0),top(0){}; void Push(int x); void Pop(); bool IsEmpty(); int Top(); int getSize();};
StackNode part:
First, declare class StackList at the beginning, because in class StackNode we’ll make StackList a friend class Then define class StackNode. Here three constructors are defined, corresponding to three cases: No argument given: initialize the node’s data and pointer to 0, meaning a single node with data 0 Given argument x: initialize the node’s data to x and next to 0, meaning a single node with data x Given argument x and the next node’s address next: meaning a node is added to a non-empty stack
Then make StackList a friend class of StackNode
StackList part:
First declare the private members *top, size, representing the stack’s top node and the stack’s size Then the public members. First, likewise use the constructor to initialize size=0, top=0 (nullptr) Define functions like Push(int x), Pop(), IsEmpty(), Top(), getSize()
void StackList::Push(int x){ if(isEmpty()){ top = new StackNode(x); size++; return; } //push_front() in linked list StackNode *newNode = new StackNode(x); //Link the new node to the origin top node newNode->next = top; //update top pointer top = newNode; size++;}
For the Push function, first likewise confirm whether it’s an empty stack, because this affects which constructor we use. If empty, create a new node new StackNode(x), i.e. a new node with data=x, and point top at that node; at this point the stack size needs +1, then return to the main function. If the stack isn’t empty, we need to realize push_front, so again add a new node. There are two ways to write this: the one above defines the node via the second constructor, manually points it at the original top node, then updates the top pointer. This can also be rewritten as stackNode *newNode = new StackNode(x, top), then just update the top pointer.
void StackList::Pop(){ if(isEmpty()){ cout << "Empty stack, nothing to pop out!" << endl; return; } StackNode *tempNode = top; top = top->next; delete tempNode; // set tempNode to a null pointer, to prevent dangling pointer // The constructor will set the *next to 0 (NULL) tempNode =0; size--;}
For the Pop function, likewise first confirm whether it’s empty; if the stack is empty, return to main() If not empty, follow the same steps as deleting a node in a regular Linked List: define a temporary node, temporarily keep the top node, then update top to the next node, then delete the temporary node’s data The most important step is to set the temporary node to 0, i.e. nullptr (because next is set to 0), to prevent a dangling pointer, since the pointer variable still exists. Remember stack size needs -1
bool StackList::isEmpty(){ if( size == 0) return true; else return false;}int StackList::Top(){ if(isEmpty()){ cout << "Empty stack, nothing to return" << endl; return -1; } return top->data;}int StackList::getSize(){ return size;}
isEmpty just checks the size value Top() likewise first checks whether it’s an empty stack; if not, just return the top node’s data value getSize() returns size
Stack-related STLYou need to include the stack template library # include <stack>stack<int> sk; The <int> inside the angle brackets means this stack holds integers.If you want to hold other types of data in the stack,you can also declare it like this stack<float> sk;stack<string> sk;stack<char> sk;
Using the STL you don’t need to implement push() and pop() yourself sk.push(123); // | -78 |sk.push(666); // | 666 | sk.push(-78); // | 123 | // |_____|
int a = sk.pop(); // -78
sk.top(); //666, since -78 is poped from stack
sk.empty(); //return true or false
Time complexity of Stack operationsAccording to the summary in [5], the average time complexities of regular stack operations are:
Access: $O(N)$ Search: $O(N)$ Insertion: $O(1)$ Deletion: $O(1)$
$N$ is the number of data items in the stack Classic Stack LeetCode problemsEasy
20. Valid Parentheses 1614. Maximum Nesting Depth of the Parentheses 232. Implement Queue using Stacks
Medium
71. Simplify Path 155. Min Stack 150. Evaluate Reverse Polish Notation
Hard
224. Basic Calculator
Reference[1] https://hackmd.io/@meyr543/SksrPAEIt[2] https://hackmd.io/@Greenleaf/advanced_cpp#%F0%9F%8E%A0-stack-%E5%A0%86%E7%96%8A[3] https://alrightchiu.github.io/SecondRound/stack-yi-arrayyu-linked-listshi-zuo.html[4] https://hackmd.io/@CLKO/BkZaF56Cm?type=view[5] https://www.bigocheatsheet.com/

entry.title: Deploying Prometheus and Grafana on a Proxmox VE Cluster
entry.content:
🌐 中文版：繁體中文
PrefaceOn the Proxmox VE cluster I built earlier, I needed to periodically collect GPU power-consumption info as the basis for a script’s decisions, so I needed Prometheus to collect the info. Node background infoIP CIDR: 172.25.166.139/24CPU(s) 4 x Intel(R) Core(TM) i3-8100 CPU @ 3.60GHz (1 Socket)Kernel Version Linux 6.8.4-2-pve (2024-04-10T17:36Z)
Installing PrometheusCreate the Prometheus user sudo groupadd --system prometheussudo useradd -s /sbin/nologin --system -g prometheus prometheus
Create the directories Prometheus needs mkdir /var/lib/prometheusfor i in rules rules.d files_sd; do mkdir -p /etc/prometheus/${i}; done
Create a temporary prometheus directory under tmp for downloading, and download the latest Prometheus mkdir -p /tmp/prometheus && cd /tmp/prometheuscurl -s https://api.github.com/repos/prometheus/prometheus/releases/latest \ | grep browser_download_url \ | grep linux-amd64 \ | cut -d '"' -f 4 \ | wget -qi -
Extract the file, move the config files, and delete the temporary directory when done tar xvf prometheus*.tar.gzcd prometheus*/mv prometheus promtool /usr/local/bin/mv prometheus.yml /etc/prometheus/prometheus.ymlmv consoles/ console_libraries/ /etc/prometheus/cd ~/rm -rf /tmp/prometheus
Create the systemd config file sudo tee /etc/systemd/system/prometheus.service<<EOF[Unit]Description=PrometheusDocumentation=https://prometheus.io/docs/introduction/overview/Wants=network-online.targetAfter=network-online.target[Service]Type=simpleUser=prometheusGroup=prometheusExecReload=/bin/kill -HUP $MAINPIDExecStart=/usr/local/bin/prometheus \ --config.file=/etc/prometheus/prometheus.yml \ --storage.tsdb.path=/var/lib/prometheus \ --web.console.templates=/etc/prometheus/consoles \ --web.console.libraries=/etc/prometheus/console_libraries \ --web.listen-address=0.0.0.0:9090 \ --web.external-url=SyslogIdentifier=prometheusRestart=always[Install]WantedBy=multi-user.targetEOF
Use chown to set the owner of all the directories just created to prometheus for i in rules rules.d files_sd; do sudo chown -R prometheus:prometheus /etc/prometheus/${i}; donefor i in rules rules.d files_sd; do sudo chmod -R 775 /etc/prometheus/${i}; donesudo chown -R prometheus:prometheus /var/lib/prometheus/
Then load the Prometheus config and start the Prometheus service plus the boot-time service sudo systemctl daemon-reloadsudo systemctl start prometheussudo systemctl enable prometheus
At this point, accessing the node’s port 9090 via a browser should reach the Prometheus page.
Installing the Prometheus Exporter A Prometheus Exporter mainly runs on a node to actively export the node’s info to a specific service for Prometheus to access. So the need here is to install it on every node in the cluster.
apt install python3 python3-pippip3 install prometheus-pve-exporter --break-system-packages
The reason for --break-system-packages is that PVE enables PEP 668 by default, which restricts installing Python packages with pip3 in the global environment, since it means this Python environment is system-managed. This parameter bypasses that restriction. Next create an auth file so prometheus-pve-exporter can log into PVE. The auth method here uses a Proxmox VE API Token; create one in advance if you haven’t. sudo tee /etc/prometheus/pve.yml<<EOFdefault: user: "root@pam" token_name: "<YOUR TOKEN NAME>" token_value: "<YOUR TOKEN VALUE>" verify_ssl: false port: 8006EOF
You can visit http://<Service IP>:9221/pve to confirm you can retrieve system info, and also check target health on Prometheus’s dashboard.
Creating an API Token In the Proxmox web interface, create an API Token.
Go to user management (Datacenter → Permissions → API Token). Create a token for a user and assign appropriate permissions (e.g. Read-Only) Record the Token-ID and Token-Secret.
Then create the systemd config file for easy service management sudo tee /etc/systemd/system/prometheus-pve-exporter.service<<EOF[Unit]Description=Prometheus exporter for Proxmox VEDocumentation=https://github.com/znerol/prometheus-pve-exporter[Service]Restart=alwaysUser=prometheusExecStart=/usr/local/bin/pve_exporter --config.file=/etc/prometheus/pve.yml[Install]WantedBy=multi-user.targetEOF
Enable the prometheus-pve-exporter service systemctl daemon-reloadsystemctl start prometheus-pve-exportersystemctl enable prometheus-pve-exporter
Once all the exporters in the cluster are installed, be sure to go to /etc/prometheus/prometheus.yml on the control node (the one with Prometheus) and add the worker nodes’ ip addr to targets.
...- job_name: 'proxmox' metrics_path: /pve static_configs: - targets: - <WorkerNode IP Address>:9221
Installing GrafanaAdd the official repo sudo apt-get install -y software-properties-commonsudo add-apt-repository "deb https://packages.grafana.com/oss/deb stable main"wget -q -O - https://packages.grafana.com/gpg.key | sudo apt-key add -
Install Grafana sudo apt-get updatesudo apt-get install grafana -y
Enable Grafana sudo systemctl start grafana-serversudo systemctl enable grafana-server
Open http://<Controller Node IP>:3000 in a browser; the credentials are admin/admin (you’ll be prompted to change them on first login).
Next, to connect Grafana to Prometheus, go to /home/connections/data sources/ and choose Add Data Source, then choose Prometheus, and on the page specify the service name and Prometheus URL.
Then find a good dashboard. Based on my needs I found a few nice ones:
NVIDIA GPU: https://grafana.com/grafana/dashboards/6387-gpus/https://www.leadergpu.com/articles/524-collecting-gpu-metrics-with-grafanaPower Monitoring: https://grafana.com/grafana/dashboards/20173-poweropen/
I chose the NVIDIA GPU Metrics dashboard and clicked Download JSON.
Then in Grafana’s Dashboard, choose New, then Import Dashboard, specify the source, and finally click import.
At this point the dashboard still shows No Data, because we haven’t installed an important component yet: the Nvidia GPU Exporter. Installing the NVIDIA GPU Exporterwget https://github.com/utkuozdemir/nvidia_gpu_exporter/releases/download/v1.2.1/nvidia-gpu-exporter_1.2.1_linux_amd64.debsudo dpkg -i nvidia-gpu-exporter_1.2.1_linux_amd64.deb
Then modify /etc/prometheus/prometheus.yml ... - job_name: 'nvidia' scrape_interval: 5s static_configs: - targets: - 'WORKERNODE_1_IP:9835' - ....
Then restart the prometheus service systemctl restart prometheus
Checking Prometheus, you’ll find all the nodes with the NVIDIA GPU Exporter installed are now visible from Prometheus.
And you’ll find Grafana successfully pulling GPU data.
Note: each node must have the graphics-card driver installed first to correctly pull data.
The next issue to solve is GPU passthrough, letting VMs on PVE access the graphics card.
Referenceshttps://codychen.me/2021/38/proxmox-%E9%80%8F%E9%81%8E-prometheus-%E5%91%88%E7%8F%BE%E5%9C%A8-grafana/https://samynitsche.de/3-monitoring-proxmox-with-prometheus-and-grafana

entry.title: Must-Know Problem-Solving Knowledge | Tree | Basics | LeetCode Notes
entry.content:
🌐 中文版：繁體中文
What is a Tree? A Tree is a common data structure. Intuitively, a tree structure represents a hierarchical structure, like a family tree or a lineage chart of different languages and language families, which are often represented with trees. Basic introduction Node: the basic unit of a tree Root: the initial node of the tree structure Branch: the branch between nodes Child: a node other than the root Leaf: a node not connected to any other child node, i.e. an end node of the tree structure
Definition of a TreeDefinition of a Tree: a finite set made up of one or several nodes, and
there exists a specific node that is the root the remaining nodes can be partitioned into $n >= 0$ disjoint sets $T_{1},T_{2},…,T_{n}$, which are the subtrees of this root
This is a recursive definition. For node A (the root) in the figure above, there are two subtrees whose roots are node B and node C. Every node in the tree is the root of some subtree. For example, node C contains two subtrees whose roots are node E and node F, and nodes E and F are roots of two trees that have no subtrees.
A’s subtrees: $T_{1}(B,D)$, $T_{2}(C,E,F)$ B’s subtrees: $T_{1}(D)$ C’s subtrees: $T_{1}(E)$, $T_{2}(F)$
Properties of a Tree
The degree is the number of subtrees of a node. Using the figure above, the degrees of the different nodes are: A’s degree = 2 B’s degree = 1 C’s degree = 2
Leaves of the tree The leaves of this tree are D, E, F
Children of the tree B, C are A’s child nodes D is B’s child node E, F are C’s child nodes
Parents of the tree A is the parent node of B, C B is the parent node of D C is the parent node of E, F
Siblings of the tree B, C are siblings of each other E and F are siblings of each other It’s easy to understand if you think of a family tree or lineage chart
Descendant nodes of the tree: all nodes in the subtree of a given node A’s descendant nodes are all nodes of the whole tree C’s descendant nodes are E and F; if new nodes grow under E and F, they’d also be C’s descendant nodes
Level of the tree: the level is defined starting from the root, and the root’s level is level 1 A: Level 1 B, C: Level 2 D, E, F: Level 3
Depth: the level difference from a node to the root B, C’s depth is 1 D, E, F’s depth is 2
Pros and cons of a TreeHere we can summarize the pros and cons of the data structures learned earlier.
Structure Pros Cons
Array Fast access Inefficient insertion/deletion of elements
Linked list Efficient insertion/deletion and similar operations Inefficient access to a specific node’s value, needs to traverse the list
A tree structure can improve storage and retrieval efficiency. For example, a Binary Sort Tree can guarantee search speed while also guaranteeing the speed of insertion, deletion, and modification. Tree representation The Left Child-Right Sibling Representation is a way to express a tree structure. Its principle is that each node has at most one left child, and to the right of a node there is at most one nearest sibling. With this representation we can draw the tree above as the tree below.
The benefit of this representation is that you can easily get a tree with degree 2 (degree = 2), just by rotating the left-child right-sibling tree 45 degrees clockwise.
The root of this tree has an empty right child, which is guaranteed, because the root of the tree before conversion must have no sibling.
And the above tree with degree at most 2 means each node has at most two subtrees. This kind of tree is also called a Binary Tree.
Binary TreeA Binary Tree and a Tree are two different things. A binary tree is defined as follows:
A finite set made up of nodes (which can be the empty set), where each node has at most two subtrees, and the left subtree and right subtree are ordered (unlike a Tree, where left and right are unordered).
From the definition you can see the difference between a Binary Tree and a Tree: a Tree can’t be empty, while a Binary Tree can be empty; a Binary Tree cares about the order of the left and right subtrees, while a Tree doesn’t care about order. Types of Binary TreeSkewed Tree Left skewed tree: all nodes have only a left subtree Right skewed tree: all nodes have only a right subtree
Full Binary Tree Except for the leaves, all nodes have two children, meaning every node has both a left and right subtree All leaf nodes are at the same level The levels aren’t necessarily all filled
Perfect Binary Tree A Full Binary Tree whose levels are all filled
Complete Binary TreeNumbering a binary tree’s nodes top to bottom and left to right, if the numbered nodes are exactly the same as a full binary tree’s nodes, it’s called a complete binary tree. The numbered nodes above match a Full Binary Tree’s nodes, so it’s a Complete Binary Tree. The node numbering above doesn’t match a Full Binary Tree’s node numbering, so it’s not a Complete Binary Tree. A full / perfect binary tree is a complete binary tree, but a complete binary tree isn’t necessarily a full / perfect binary tree.
Summarizing the properties of a Complete Binary Tree: the nodes of each level are all filled except the last level, and the last level’s nodes are all aligned to the left.
Representing a Tree with a Linked ListA node structure looks like this: struct Node{ Node* parent; Node* left; Node* right; int data;};Node* root = 0;
Representing a Tree with an ArrayAccording to this article, you can also implement a tree with an array. That is, access nodes by array index, and judge left or right subtree by the odd/even index. Build an array and get a node by array index: the root’s index is one, twice the index is the left child, twice the index plus one is the right child, and the index divided by two is the parent. int tree[1024]; // tree[0] do nothingint parent(int index) {return index / 2;}int left(int index) {return index * 2;}int right(int index) {return index * 2 + 1;}void binary_tree(){ cout << "Root: " << tree[1]; cout << "The left child of the root: " << tree[left(1)]; cout << "The right child of the root: " << tree[right(1)];}
But the downside of this is obvious: the tree’s size is fixed, and if it isn’t a perfect binary tree, the array will have a lot of empty slots, wasting a lot of memory. Taking an array size of 1024 as an example, the tree’s height is only 10 ($2^{10}$). Binary Tree Traversal What counts as traversal?It depends on the implementation. If the tree is implemented with a linked list, being at node(A) you can move from A to B via the pointer to node(B), which can be considered traversal.
Operations you can perform on the current node:
V: visiting, which can be an operation like printing the node’s data L: move to the left child R: move to the right child
If the current node is now node A, adding a constraint that “L always comes before R” produces three traversal methods: preorder traversal, inorder traversal, postorder traversal, and level-order traversal.
Pre-Order TraversalThe traversal order is: Root, Left subtree, Right subtree Applicable to Depth-First Search (DFS)
The traversal order is illustrated above. At first CurrentNode enters the Root node, i.e. node A, then checks in VLR order: first Visiting node A (possibly printing the node’s value), then checks whether left-child B(L) is null; if not, CurrentNode moves to B(L), then with currentNode as scope visits B and continues checking its left-child, moving to node D(L) and Visiting D(L). Since node D is a leaf (both left and right children are null), it returns to B as currentNode and visits its right child E(R). Once done, all nodes within B’s scope have been visited, so it returns to B’s parent node as currentNode’s scope, which is A(V), and continues visiting its right child, which is C(R). After visiting C it visits its left child F(L), and after that, trying to visit C’s right child finds it null. All nodes have been visited, completing this traversal, printing A B D E C F. In-Order TraversalThe traversal order is: Left subtree, Root, Right subtreeIt actually uses depth-first search, just changing the order in which nodes are output.
The traversal order is illustrated above. At first CurrentNode enters the Root node, i.e. node A, then checks in LVR order: first check whether left-child B is NULL; if not, CurrentNode moves to B(L), then with currentNode as scope checks its children in order, first checking whether B’s left-child D is NULL; if not, move CurrentNode to D(L), then do another in-order check with D as currentNode. At this point D’s left and right children are both NULL, so it returns to D itself for visiting (possibly printing D’s value, etc.). All nodes in the current scope have been visited, so it returns to D’s parent as the current CurrentNode’s scope, and currentNode moves back to B. Then it visits B’s right child E(R), and after that, all of B’s scope has been visited, so it returns to B’s parent A(V) for Visiting, then moves to C(R), checks the current currentNode’s left child F(L) and visits it, then moves back to C(V) to visit, and after confirming there’s no right child, this traversal ends, printing D B E A F C. Post-Order TraversalThe traversal order is: Left subtree, Right subtree, Root
The traversal order is illustrated above. At first CurrentNode enters the Root node, i.e. node A, then checks in LRV order: first check whether left-child B is NULL; if not, CurrentNode moves to B(L), then with currentNode as scope checks its children in order, first checking whether B’s left-child D is NULL; if not, move CurrentNode to D(L), then do another post-order check with D as currentNode. At this point D’s left and right children are both NULL, so it returns to D itself for visiting (possibly printing D’s value, etc.). All nodes in the current scope have been visited, so it returns to D’s parent as the current CurrentNode’s scope, and currentNode moves back to B.
Returning to B means the loop or function with D as CurrentNode has ended.
With B as CurrentNode, in post-order terms the left child has now been visited, so next we visit the right child, moving to E(R). But since E, like D, is a leaf, it won’t move toward null, so it returns to node B(v) for visiting. This completes the visiting of all nodes with B as scope. Then it returns to A(V), and with A as CurrentNode it checks, now moving toward the right child C(R). At this point currentNode is C(R); checking in post-order it finds F is a leaf node, so it visits F, and then finds C’s right child is null, so it skips the right child and returns to C(V) to visit C, after which currentNode returns to A(V) for visiting, completing this traversal, printing D E B F C A. Level-order TraversalThis is breadth-first search (BFS), which mainly visits each node top to bottom by level order, and within the same level visits from left to right.
It’s usually implemented with a Queue.
The output order is: A B C D E F G H I Implementing different traversals of a Binary TreeBrute-force implementation of a Binary Tree# include <iostream># include <string># include <queue>using namespace std;class BinaryTree;class TreeNode{ public: TreeNode *leftchild; TreeNode *rightchild; TreeNode *parent; string str; //constructor TreeNode(): leftchild(0), rightchild(0),parent(0), str(""){}; TreeNode(string s): leftchild(0), rightchild(0), parent(0), str(s){}; friend class BinaryTree;};class BinaryTree{ public: // the root is the starting node ot the tree TreeNode *root; BinaryTree(): root(0){}; BinaryTree(TreeNode *node): root(node){}; void Preorder(TreeNode *current); void Inorder(TreeNode *current); void Postorder(TreeNode *current); void Levelorder();};
In main() we create and link the nodes in order, forming a Binary Tree. int main(){ // Instanitate all tree nodes TreeNode *nodeA = new TreeNode("A"); TreeNode *nodeB = new TreeNode("B"); TreeNode *nodeC = new TreeNode("C"); TreeNode *nodeD = new TreeNode("D"); TreeNode *nodeE = new TreeNode("E"); TreeNode *nodeF = new TreeNode("F"); TreeNode *nodeG = new TreeNode("G"); TreeNode *nodeH = new TreeNode("H"); TreeNode *nodeI = new TreeNode("I"); //Construct a binary tree nodeA -> leftchild = nodeB; nodeA -> rightchild = nodeC; nodeB -> leftchild = nodeD; nodeB -> rightchild = nodeE; nodeE -> leftchild = nodeG; nodeE -> rightchild = nodeH; nodeC -> leftchild = nodeF; nodeF -> rightchild = nodeI; // Given a root node BinaryTree T(nodeA); //Traversal T.Preorder(T.root); cout << endl; T.Inorder(T.root); cout << endl; T.Postorder(T.root); cout << endl; T.Levelorder(); cout << endl; return 0;} The tree built here looks like this
Next we define the traversal methods, mainly implemented recursively, because this lets us return to a child’s parent after visiting the child. Pre-Order// V-> L-> Rvoid BinaryTree::Preorder(TreeNode *current){ if(current){ // visiting the current node cout << current->str << " " ; // if leftchild exists, moving currentNode to the left child Preorder(current->leftchild); Preorder(current->rightchild); }}
In-Order// L -> V -> Rvoid BinaryTree::Inorder(TreeNode *current){ if(current){ Inorder(current->leftchild); cout << current->str << " " ; Inorder(current->rightchild); }}
Post-Order// L -> R -> Vvoid BinaryTree::Postorder(TreeNode *current){ if(current){ Postorder(current->leftchild); Postorder(current->rightchild); cout << current->str << " " ; }}
Level-OrderThe characteristic of Level-Order is accessing left to right within the same level and top to bottom across different levels. Since what’s accessed first is visited first, this property resembles a Queue, so we choose a Queue to implement it. // Using Queuevoid BinaryTree::Levelorder(){ queue<TreeNode*> q; q.push(this->root); while(!q.empty()){ TreeNode *current = q.front(); q.pop(); cout << current->str << " " ; if(current->leftchild != NULL){ q.push(current->leftchild); } if(current->rightchild != NULL){ q.push(current->rightchild); } }}
First we define a Queue and push the root node into the queue. When traversal begins, current is defined as the Queue’s front and that node is removed from the Queue, then the current node’s value is printed. After that, first check the left child; if not NULL, push it into the queue. Within the same level, check whether the right child is empty; if not, push it into the queue too. Then, since the Queue isn’t empty, the front at this point is the left child from before, so update current to the front and print its value, then check whether its left and right subtrees are empty, pushing into the queue if not. The next iteration handles the right child just pushed into the queue, likewise printing its value and checking whether its descendants are empty, pushing into the queue if not. This completes the visiting of the second level, and afterward it processes the next level (the elements now in the Queue). OutputA B D E G H C F I // PreorderD B G E H A F I C // InorderD G H E B I F C A // PostorderA B C D E F G H I // Levelorder
ConclusionThis post introduced what a Tree is, its definition and properties, the Binary Tree, and the different traversal methods and code. Later I’ll go further into extended code implementations, and introduce the BST (Binary Search Tree) along with the implementation of BFS and DFS. Reference[1] https://hackmd.io/@meyr543/r1lbVkb-K[2] https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/difference-between-bfs-and-dfs/[3] https://alrightchiu.github.io/SecondRound/binary-tree-jian-li-yi-ke-binary-tree.html[4] https://web.ntnu.edu.tw/~algo/BinaryTree.html[5] https://alrightchiu.github.io/SecondRound/binary-tree-traversalxun-fang.html?source=post_page-----a02fedbc51a8--------------------------------#in[6] https://it5606.medium.com/%E5%BB%BA%E7%AB%8Bbinary-tree-a02fedbc51a8[7] https://hackmd.io/@Aquamay/HyCgHXfid[8] https://jimmyswebnote.com/tree/

entry.title: VNF Deployment and Flow Scheduling in Geo-distributed Data Centers
entry.content:
🌐 中文版：繁體中文
AbstractNFV can reduce the equipment procurement and maintenance costs of network operations. Through NFV, network functions can be decoupled from the physical infrastructure and run as virtual network functions (VNFs) on commodity hardware. NFV makes networks more flexible and controllable, but various technical challenges remain, such as how to effectively deploy VNFs across different geographic locations and how to schedule network traffic among geo-distributed data centers. This paper studies this topic and tries to minimize deployment and communication costs. The problem is converted into a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) problem, and the paper proposes a relaxation-based algorithm to handle its computational complexity. Finally, experimental results show the algorithm effectively reduces deployment and communication costs. Ch1-IntroductionTraditional data-center or cloud-computing network architectures rely on specific hardware to provide specific network services, such as firewalls and intrusion detection systems. These make hardware costs too high. NFV’s emergence replaces this hardware-dependent network architecture. With NFV, network functions can be virtualized into software-based VNFs running on ordinary COTS servers. And to provide a network service, a network flow needs to pass through a set of ordered network functions. However, to actually apply NFV technology, you must consider how VNFs are chained into service chains to reduce costs. Past research in this area focused only on deployment cost, aiming to reduce data-center resource consumption like CPU, memory, and storage, or focused solely on communication cost, like minimizing point-to-point latency. But it rarely considered the communication cost of VNF deployment. On a service chain, the network functions on each link are ordered, each link has its own flow rate, and deploying different VNFs across geo-distributed data centers leads to different communication costs. This means the relationship between deployment cost and communication cost can’t be ignored. Furthermore, prior work rarely considered the traffic-balancing problem in NFV services; prior research usually assumed a VNF flow couldn’t be distributed to multiple VNF instances of the same type, or that its distributed flow rate was predefined, which is unrealistic and inefficient for private NFV services in large-scale networks. This paper argues that the number of VNF instances and the corresponding network traffic should be adjusted according to the current network state. This paper considers the trade-off between deployment cost and communication cost for ordered service chains across geo-distributed data centers, and allows one network function to have multiple VNF instances. Main contributions:
This paper jointly considers network topology, the number and deployment of VNFs, and flow scheduling, converting the VNF deployment and flow scheduling problem into a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) problem, to reduce deployment cost and communication cost. Based on this MILP formulation, it designs a low-complexity relaxation-based algorithm and runs extensive experiments to illustrate the algorithm’s advantages over existing ones; the results show the proposed algorithm effectively reduces deployment and communication costs.
Ch2-System ModelA. DCs TopologySince data centers are distributed worldwide, the network traffic transmitted between different data centers has different costs. Here an undirected graph represents the data centers’ network topology $G_{d}=(D,E_{d})$.$D$ is the data centers and $E_{d}$ is the network edges.$H_{dp}$ is the weight of edge $e_{dp} \in E_{d}$ where $d,p \in D$.(This means D and P are data centers, and H is the weight of the network link between D and P, representing the transmission cost between these two data centers.)Note that there’s no transmission cost from a data center to itself, $H_{dd}=0$. B. Chain SetA set of chains $C={c1,c2,…}$ is deployed to the data centers. For a service chain $c_{i} \in C$, the source node and destination node are denoted $o_{i}$ and $t_{i}$ respectively.Each service chain $c_{i}$ has a set of ordered network functions $c_{i}={s_{i,1},s_{i,2},….s_{i,j},…}$ processing traffic at rate $R_{i}$.We define $|c_{i}|$ as the length of service chain $c_{i}$, and define $n(s_{i,j})$ to denote the network-function type of $s_{i,j}$.For example, as in the figureThe three service chains have lengths 2, 3, 3 (note: different service chains may need one network function). For example, $c1$, $c2$, $c3$ may all commonly contain network function $f1$, i.e. $n(s_{1,1})=n(s_{2,2})=n(s_{3,2})=f_{1}$. C. NFs GraphBased on the chain set above, we can construct the network-function graph $G_{n}$.This graph is a directed acyclic graph (DAG).$G_{n}=(V_{n},E_{n})$, and $V_{n}$ can be categorized into three kinds:
sources $O$ network function $N$ destinations $T$Each edge $e_{m,n} \in E_{n}$ represents the network traffic between network functions $m$ and $n$.For each service pair $(s_{i,j},s_{i,j+1})$ in chain $c_{i}$, there’s a network function pair $(m,n)$ in $G_{n}$ with a directed link from $m$ to $n$, where $n(s_{i,j})=m$, $n(s_{i,j+1})=n$.
As mentioned, different network functions may be shared by different service chains at different flow rates.For each edge $e_{m,n} \in E_{n}$, we define a set $U_{m,n} = { i : c_{i} \in C, n(s_{i,j})=m,n(s_{i,j+1})=n}$ to record the service chains with the network-function pair ($m$,$n$). Different network flows with different flow requirements are transmitted on edge $e_{m,n}$, denoted $R_{i}$, $\forall i \in U_{m,n}$.For example, the network flows from service chains $c1$ and $c2$ are transmitted on edge $e_{f_{1},f_{2}}$, as shown below.The rates are 2 and 1 respectively. D. VNFs GraphOur goal is to deploy all network functions in graph $G_{n}$ in the form of VNF instances.Each network function $n$ in $G_{n}$ may have multiple VNF instances in different data centers.For example, as shown belowNetwork function $f1$ may have two VNF instances located in data centers $d1$ and $d2$. Note that each network function $n$ may have at most $|D|$ possible instances across all $|D|$ data centers, and each pair $(m,n)$ in $G_{n}$ may correspondingly have at most $|D|^{2}$ links between them. So in the VNF graph $G_{v}=(V_{v},E_{v})$, the node set $V_{v}$ includes $|V_{n}| \cdot |D|$ instances denoted as set $V$, the sources set $O$, and the destination set $T$, and $E_{v}$ denotes the links between them.For each edge $e_{u,v} \in E_{v}$, let $f^{i}{uv}$ denote the flow rate between instances $u$, $v$ in service chain $C{i}$. For example, consider two network functions $(f1,f2)$ in graph $G_{n}$ and edge $e_{f_{1},f_{2}}$; the corresponding $G_{v}$ is shown below, with 2 data centers.
The instances of $f1,f2$ are $v1$ $v2$ and $v3$ $v4$, and we can observe that network functions $f1$, $f2$ have 4 edges total, and the network traffic between $f1$ and $f2$ can be freely distributed among these four edges. For any instance $v \in V$, we use $d(v)$ and $n(v)$ to denote its data-center location and network-function type respectively. For example, $d(v_{1})=d1$, $n(v_{1})=f1$. Let $N(n)$ denote the set of VNFs providing network function $n$; for example, in the figure above, $v1$ and $v2$ provide network function $f1$, i.e. $N(f1)={ v1,v2 }$. For each VNF instance pair $(u,v)$, the flow rate through the edge can be denoted $f_{uv}^{i}$, where for chain $c_{i}$ the edge satisfies $e_{u,v}\in E_{v}$ and in graph $G_{v}$, $\forall i\in U_{n(u),n(v)}$.
Ch3-Problem FormulationBased on the system model in the previous chapter, we can formulate the VNF deployment and flow scheduling problem as a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) problem, with the objective of minimizing the total deployment and communication cost between all VNF pairs. VNF Instance PlacementAs shown in $G_{v}$, each network function can be hosted by all data centers, and each data center can host all types of network functions. So we define a binary variable $x_{v}$ to denote whether the VNF instance providing network function $n(v)$ in data center $d(v)$ is actually deployed.
Flow requirement constraintsThe traffic needed for each service chain $c_{i}$ can be distributed to all its VNF instances.For example, the flow rate $R_{i}$ between network-function pair $m$, $n$ in chain $c_{i}$ is distributed to all edges between instances $v$, $u$ in $G_{v}$, where $n(u)=m$, $n(v)=n$.
For the source node and destination node, the following equations can be listed. VNF flow constraintFor each VNF instance, the input traffic originates from the input instance $i(v)$ to be processed, then distributed to the output instance $o(v)$.
where $\alpha_{n(v)}$ is a scaling factor determined by the network function. The relationship between $x_{v}$ and $f^{i}_{uv}$As long as there’s traffic through VNF instance $v$, the binary variable should be set to 1 to provide network function $n(v)$, and this VNF instance should be deployed in $d(v)$. This can be described as
A Joint MILP Formulation Summarizing the above, we get the following Cost-min problem. Cost-Min The coefficients $\gamma$ and $\delta$ are user-defined to balance deployment cost and communication cost, and can be adjusted for different QoS requirements. Ch4-Relaxation-Based AlgorithmBecause of the integer variable $x_{v}$, solving the Cost-Min problem computationally is prohibitive, especially in large-scale networks. In this chapter we propose a relaxation-based approach to solve the Cost-min problem. First we relax $x_{v}$ to a real number in the range [0,1] to reduce computational complexity. After relaxation, our model is simplified to a linear programming (LP) problem, as in line 1 of the algorithm, which can be easily solved with Matlab.
We sort $x_{v}$ in ascending order, as in line 2 of the algorithm table, and set each non-zero $x_{v}$ value to 1, as in line 5 of the algorithm table. In this case, we obtain a new VNF deployment solution in the form of integer $x_{v}^{*}$, and record the number of VNF instances per network function as $count_{n(v)}$, as in line 6 of the algorithm table. We take the integer solution $ x_{v}^{*} $ as input and compute the flow scheduling solution $ f_{uv}^{*j} $ and the total cost $cost’$. We take the integer solution $x_{v}^{*}$ as input and compute the flow scheduling solution $f_{uv}^{*j}$ and total cost $cost’$ by solving the Cost-Min-LP problem again in line 11. Note that relaxation may lead to more VNF instances, so our next step tries to further reduce the number of instances and the deployment cost, while keeping the communication cost close to optimal, from line 12 to line 22. We start from instance $v$ within the minimum value of non-zero $x_{v}$.Note that if $v$ is the only VNF instance providing network function $n(v)$ in the network, i.e. $count_{n(v)}$ == 1, then $v$ must be deployed, and we skip to the next instance.Otherwise, if there’s a VNF instance providing the same network function $n(v)$ in the network (see line 14), we set $x_{v}^{*}$ to 0 and recompute the flow scheduling solution $f_{uv}^{*i}$ and the new total cost $cost’$. Only when the new cost is lower than the current $minCost$ do we update the NFV deployment solution $x_{v}^{*}$, the flow scheduling solution $f_{uv}^{*j}$, and the total cost $minCost$, then update the instance count of network function $n(v)$ (see lines 18, 19). On the other hand, if the total cost doesn’t decrease, we set $x_{v}^{*}$ back to 1 and move to the next instance, until we traverse all VNF instances in $V$ (line 25). Finally we return the NFV deployment solution $x_{v}^{*}$, the flow scheduling solution $f_{uv}^{*j}$, and the total cost $minCost$ as the algorithm’s output. Ch5-Performance EvaluationIn this section, we evaluate the relaxation-based algorithm (“RLX”) by comparing it with Cost-Min’s optimal result (“OPT”) and a shortest-path algorithm (“SP”).Experiment setup:
