The network has $|D|$ = 20 data centers. $H_{dp}$ is randomly set in the range [1,20], representing the hop count between DCs There are 20 service chains in total, with multiple chains sharing 15 different types of network functions The service chains’ traffic is set in the range [1, 10] The coefficient $\gamma$ is set to 10 and $\delta$ to 1 We use the commercial solver Gurobi to solve our Cost-Min and Cost-Min-LP problemsThis study provides extensive experiments by varying parameters in different scenarios.
The value of 𝛾First, we investigate the effect of 𝛾 and 𝛿. We set 𝛿 = 1 and vary 𝛾 from 5 to 50. The results are in Figure 4.The results in Figure 4 show that all three algorithms’ costs grow as 𝛾 increases. The reason is that increasing 𝛾 leads to higher VNF deployment cost.Notably, SP’s growth rate is much larger than the other two, because SP mainly focuses on communication cost by reducing each network flow’s path length, ignoring deployment cost.So when deployment cost becomes the dominant part, SP shows less advantage.For example, when 𝛾 = 10, the deployment cost’s share of the total cost is 57% for RLX, 35% for OPT, and 82% for SP. The effect of number of hopsWe study the total cost of OPT, RLX, and SP for different network topologies by varying the hop upper bound from 2 to 20.As Figure 5 shows, OPT’s and RLX’s costs grow slightly as the hop count increases, since more hops may increase communication cost. However, SP shows a downward trend. The main reason is that when the hop count between different data centers is small, SP can find many shortest paths and deploy VNF instances on them, and some network functions may have multiple instances, leading to higher deployment cost.When the hop count increases, SP finds fewer shortest paths, resulting in fewer VNF instances and lower deployment cost. So the total cost decreases. The effect of rateSimilarly, we change the rate-requirement upper bound of the 20 chains from 3 to 30 to show the effect of flow requirements.Figure 6 shows that as the rate upper bound increases, all three algorithms’ total costs increase too.This is because more traffic leads to higher communication cost and total cost. The effect of the number of chainsIn this part, we discuss the effect of the chain count from 5 to 50 and compare the three algorithms’ results.An upward trend for all three can be observed in Figure 7.The reason is that more service chains bring more network functions deployed in data centers and more network flows distributed to VNF instances.This leads to higher deployment and communication cost, so all three algorithms’ total costs rise. The effect of the number of NFsFinally, Figure 8 shows all three algorithms’ results with the network-function count ranging from 10 to 55.We can conclude the cost also rises. This is because all algorithms need to place more VNF instances in data centers, leading to higher deployment cost. Meanwhile, more network traffic between network functions in different data centers also leads to higher communication cost. So the total cost trends upward.Nonetheless, our RLX’s advantage can always be observed under any setting, since it outperforms SP and approaches OPT. ConclusionIn this paper, we studied the VNF deployment and network-flow scheduling problem in geo-distributed data centers. We further formulated this problem as mixed-integer linear programming, with the objective of minimizing total deployment and communication cost. We then proposed a low-complexity relaxation-based algorithm to handle the computational complexity. Extensive simulation-based performance-evaluation results show our algorithm has better performance and effectively reduces total cost in various scenarios. Sourcehttps://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/8422334

entry.title: 🔋 AWS Certified Cloud Practitioner Study Notes
entry.content:
🌐 中文版：繁體中文
CCP preparation Exam guide: https://d1.awsstatic.com/zh_TW/training-and-certification/docs-cloud-practitioner/AWS-Certified-Cloud-Practitioner_Exam-Guide.pdf
Exam domain weightings
Related resources
https://terahake.in/post/aws-ccp-certified-exp/ https://awslc.medium.com/aws-cloud-practitioner%E8%AD%89%E7%85%A7%E6%BA%96%E5%82%99-6b8bacc6a490 https://jayendrapatil.com/aws-certified-cloud-practitioner-exam-learning-path/?fbclid=IwAR3eiyroyZ_jTn2pA5ut_ophP8JNCzgspERnug_luC_HGltA-OkLwRwrhAU https://d1.awsstatic.com/whitepapers/AWS_Cloud_Best_Practices.pdf?fbclid=IwAR1xXOBkWwESyy_9Srngna7rAbP_g1ddYMl2KO3moKJbzz1YDgrNOrv_z08 https://d0.awsstatic.com/whitepapers/aws_pricing_overview.pdf?fbclid=IwAR2mDUgA-IDHrqrQFGn3XL1kA0O1XojD6d6rdxwLWmvuL4D4mi4DKeDNonQ http://yhhuang1966.blogspot.com/2020/03/aws-aws-certified-cloud-practitioner.html
Practice exams
https://www.examtopics.com/exams/amazon/aws-certified-cloud-practitioner/
The five pillars of Well-Architected Operational Excellence The ability to run and monitor systems to deliver business value, and to continually improve supporting processes and procedures.
Security The ability to protect information, systems, and assets while delivering business value through risk assessments and mitigation strategies.
Reliability Recover from infrastructure or service disruptions Dynamically acquire computing resources to meet demand Reduce disruptions such as misconfigurations or transient network issues
Performance Efficiency The ability to use computing resources to meet system requirements, and to maintain that efficiency as demand changes and technologies evolve
Cost Optimization The ability to run systems to deliver business value at the lowest price point.
AnalyticsAmazon Athena Analyze data in S3 with interactive standard-SQL queries Serverless You can define a schema and analyze data in S3 with SQL
Amazon Kinesis Makes it easy to collect, process, and analyze real-time streaming data Things like video/audio streams, application logs, web clickstream analytics, IoT telemetry, and so on Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose Amazon Kinesis Data Analytics Amazon Kinesis Data Streams Amazon Kinesis Video Streams
Amazon QuickSight A powerful BI (Business Intelligence) service You can build interactive dashboards
Application integrationAmazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) A publish/subscribe service. With an Amazon SNS topic, publishers can push messages to subscribers. It works like a coffee shop, where the cashier passes coffee orders to the barista making the drinks. In Amazon SNS, a subscriber can be a web server, an email address, an AWS Lambda function, or several other options
Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) is a message queue service In Amazon SQS, an application sends messages into a queue. A user or service retrieves a message from the queue, processes it, and then deletes it from the queue
Compute and serverlessAWS BatchAmazon EC2 Instance types General purpose Compute, memory, and networking resource needs are roughly balanced across the application
Compute optimized For compute-intensive applications Also useful when you need to handle batch workloads that process many transactions in a single group
Memory optimized Deliver fast performance for workloads that process large datasets in memory. In computing, memory is temporary storage. It holds all the data and instructions the CPU needs to complete its work. Workloads that need to preload a large amount of data before running the application. This could be a high-performance database, or a workload that performs real-time processing of a large amount of unstructured data
Accelerated computing Use hardware accelerators or coprocessors to perform certain functions more efficiently than is feasible running software on a CPU Use hardware accelerators or coprocessors to perform certain functions more efficiently than is feasible running software on a CPU
Storage optimized Designed for workloads that require high sequential read and write access to very large datasets on local storage. Good fits include distributed file systems, data warehousing applications, and high-frequency online transaction processing (OLTP) systems Designed to deliver tens of thousands of low-latency random I/O operations per second (IOPS) to applications For applications with high IOPS requirements
EC2 pricing On-Demand Suitable for non-interruptible short-term workloads No contract required
Savings Plan Commit to a certain amount of compute usage over one or three years Cheaper than On-Demand
Reserved Instances Purchase instances for a one-year or three-year term Usage can be matched against the On-Demand instances in the account
Spot Instances Good for applications that can tolerate interruptions Such as batch jobs
Dedicated Hosts Physical EC2 servers
AWS Elastic Beanstalk After you provide your code and configuration settings, Elastic Beanstalk takes care of deploying the resources needed to perform the following Adjusting capacity Load balancing Automatic scaling Application health monitoring
AWS Lambda Amazon Lightsail Amazon Lightsail provides easy-to-use virtual private server (VPS) instances, containers, storage, databases, and more at a cost-effective monthly price.
Amazon WorkSpaces Amazon WorkSpaces is a fully managed desktop virtualization service for Windows and Linux that lets you access resources from any supported device.
ContainersAmazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) A highly scalable, high-performance container management system that makes it easy to run and scale containerized applications on AWS Supports Docker
Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) Lets you run Kubernetes on AWS
AWS Fargate A serverless compute engine for containers, usable with both Amazon ECS and Amazon EKS.
DatabasesAmazon Aurora An enterprise-grade relational database, up to 5x faster than standard MySQL and 3x faster than standard PostgreSQL Supports two database options: MySQL, PostgreSQL Very low cost Data is replicated across facilities (six copies at any time, up to 15 read replicas) Continuous backup to Amazon S3 Point-in-time recovery
Amazon DynamoDB A serverless database with no underlying instances or infrastructure to manage You create tables to store and look up data Data is divided into items, and items have attributes Attributes represent different features of the data Stores disk mirrors across multiple availability zones to improve availability High performance and highly scalable, with millisecond response times A NoSQL database Can’t be queried with SQL; queried by key attributes, which is highly flexible Use case: Amazon Prime Day handling a huge volume of user order requests
Amazon ElastiCache Provides a caching layer for databases to increase read/write speed Memcached Redis
Amazon DAX (DynamoDB Accelerator) Provides a native caching layer for DynamoDB, improving NoSQL read times
Amazon Relational Database Service (RDS) A relational database management service (data is stored in a way that establishes relationships with other data)
Supports most database engines
Amazon Aurora MySQL PostgreSQL MariaDB Oracle Microsoft SQL Server
Advantages
Automatic vulnerability patching Backups Redundancy Failover Disaster recovery
They can also be deployed further to Amazon Aurora
Amazon Redshift A database purpose-built for high-speed, real-time ingestion and querying, for data-analytics workloads Most relational databases have a capacity ceiling, so they aren’t suited to historical data analysis And the data types are varied, which a typical relational database struggles with, so this is where a Data Warehouse comes in A data warehouse handles big data and is suited to historical analysis rather than operational analysis For example, “what were our sales an hour ago?” is a number that won’t change anymore Operational analysis, by contrast, is like “how much coffee inventory do we have right now?”, data that is constantly changing Redshift can achieve 10x the performance of a traditional database
AWS Database Migration Service (Amazon DMS) Migrate customer databases to AWS The database stays fully operational during the migration Downtime for applications that rely on the database is kept to a minimum The source and target databases don’t have to be the same type Oracle -> RDS for Oracle MySQL -> RDS for MySQL
Heterogeneous migration When the source and target databases differ in schema structure, data types, and database code, you need a heterogeneous migration It takes two steps
Convert with the AWS Schema Conversion Tool
Use DMS to migrate the database
Development and test database migrations You can use the DMS service to migrate a copy of a database to a production or test environment
Database consolidation Continuous database replication Can be used for disaster recovery
AWS DocumentDB Used for full document storage Good for content management, catalogs, and user profiles
Amazon Neptune A graph database used for designing social networks and recommendation engines Also good for fraud detection Or supply-chain tracking and management
Amazon QLDB (Quantum Ledger Database) An immutable system of record Entries can’t be deleted from the audit trail
AWS Auto Scaling
Dynamic scaling Predictive scaling
AWS CloudFormation You can treat infrastructure as code (IaC). That is, you can build environments by writing lines of code instead of provisioning resources individually through the AWS Management Console. It lets you create infrastructure and applications repeatedly without performing manual actions or writing custom scripts. It determines the correct operations to perform when managing a stack, and automatically rolls back changes when it detects errors.
AWS CloudTrail A comprehensive API auditing tool Every API request made to AWS is logged in CloudTrail It records who made the request, when it was made, the source IP, the response, and so on You can store these logs indefinitely in an S3 bucket CloudTrail events are typically updated within 15 minutes of the API call
Amazon CloudWatch CloudWatch lets customers monitor their AWS infrastructure and the applications running on it It works by tracking and monitoring metrics (resource-related variables) CPU utilization RAM usage
CloudWatch alarms When a metric crosses a threshold, it can trigger an alarm Integrated with SNS, it can send alert text messages
CloudWatch dashboards List metrics in near real time
Advantages of CloudWatch: Access all metrics from one central place for system-wide visibility View applications, infrastructure, and services Reduce MTTR (mean time to resolution) and improve total cost of ownership (TCO) Analyze applications in depth and help optimize customer applications
AWS Trusted Advisor An automated advisor It evaluates resources against the five pillars Cost optimization Performance Security Fault tolerance Service Limits
It runs a series of checks for each pillar and compiles categorized items for review Some checks are free Example check: whether MFA is enabled
Networking and content deliveryAWS Elastic Load Balancing An AWS service that automatically distributes incoming application traffic across multiple resources (such as Amazon EC2 instances)
ELB acts as the single point of contact for all web traffic coming into an Auto Scaling group. That is, when you add or remove Amazon EC2 instances in response to incoming traffic, the requests are first routed to the load balancer and then spread across the multiple resources that will handle them.
Security, identity, and complianceShared Responsibility Model
Customers remember to patch their own OS The relationship between AWS and the customer is like that between a homeowner and the builder
AWS Artifact Provides access to compliance reports, which are themselves verified by third parties AWS Artifact Agreements A company may need to sign agreements with AWS regarding your use of certain types of information across AWS services You can review, accept, and manage agreements for an individual account and for all accounts in AWS Organizations. Different types of agreements are available
AWS Artifact Reports You can review, accept, and manage agreements for an individual account and for all accounts in AWS Organizations. Different types of agreements are available, and this information can be accessed in AWS Artifact Reports Access this information in AWS Artifact Reports
Amazon GuardDuty An AWS threat-detection service Analyzes a continuous stream of metadata generated by your account, such as data from CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs, and DNS logs Runs separately from your existing AWS services and won’t affect the performance of your existing infrastructure
AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) IAM lets you control permissions in a fine-grained way You can create IAM users in IAM When first created, an IAM user has no permissions by default (can’t create EC2, S3, etc.) Principle of least privilege IAM policies JSON documents describing which API operations a user can and can’t perform You can attach policies to users or groups Effect: Allow Deny Action: which actions can be taken on a resource Resource: which AWS resource the API call applies to
IAM groups
Roles Roles are switched between for different jobs You can also create roles in AWS A role has associated permissions that can allow or deny specific actions A user can temporarily assume a role, with no username or password They only get temporary permissions
Amazon Inspector Runs automated security assessments against infrastructure to improve the security and compliance of applications deployed on AWS Can be used to spot deviations from best practice Vulnerability checks The service has three parts: Network configuration reachability The Amazon agent The security assessment service
AWS Shield A service that protects applications against DDoS attacks AWS Shield Standard Protects all AWS customers automatically, for free Uses analytics to detect in real time and automatically mitigate malicious traffic
AWS Shield Advanced Provides detailed attack diagnostics and detection/mitigation of sophisticated DDoS attacks.
AWS WAF Use a Web Application Firewall (WAF) to filter incoming traffic Machine learning helps identify new threats Proactive defense You can set up a Web ACL
AWS Organizations A central place to manage multiple AWS accounts Manage billing, control access, compliance, and security Lets all AWS accounts share resources Features: Centralized management of AWS accounts All accounts can consolidate billing (with discounts) Implement hierarchical grouping of accounts (e.g. BU (business unit), OU (organizational unit)) Control which AWS services each account can access and which API actions it can perform Service Control Policies (SCPs) can be used to specify the maximum permissions for member accounts
Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) If you don’t want your database deleted every time you finish using an EC2 instance, you can use the EBS service You can create a virtual disk (an EBS volume) and attach it to an EC2 instance EBS isn’t directly bound to EC2, so it can persist data independently of EC2’s lifecycle You need to define: size, type, configuration Use case: persistent storage that EC2 writes to, so backing up the data is important EBS allows incremental backups of data (called snapshots) Take snapshots of EBS regularly to back up important data Instance store: the temporary block storage provided within EC2; when the EC2 instance terminates, the data in the store is also lost
EBS snapshots: the first backup copies all the data in the volume, and subsequent ones only store the data blocks that changed since the most recent snapshot, which is an incremental backup
Amazon S3 Data is stored as objects, not in a file directory but in a bucket Maximum upload object size: 5TB You can enable Object Versioning to prevent accidental deletion You can create multiple buckets to hold different data categories or storage tiers You can set permissions to restrict who can access an object Amazon S3 Standard: 99.999999999% durability, meaning the probability that a file stays intact after a year How data is stored: data is stored in at least three facilities, with copies in different locations Static website hosting: host HTML files or other static file assets on S3
Amazon S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (IA): for data accessed infrequently but that must be retrieved quickly when needed Good for backups, disaster recovery, and long-term data storage Amazon S3 Glacier: can be used for long-term storage of audit data You can create a vault and use a Vault Lock policy to meet local regulatory requirements for how long audit data must be retained You can use a control in the Vault Lock policy: a Write Once Read Many (WORM) model to prevent future writes
Lifecycle policies: automatically move data between different tiers For example, you need to keep an object in S3 Standard for 90 days, then move it to S3-IA for 30 days, then move it to S3 Glacier after 120 days. In cases like this you can create a lifecycle policy to automate these actions
Amazon S3 One Zone-IA Data is stored in a single zone Cheaper than S3 Standard-IA Choose this storage class if you want to save on storage costs
Amazon S3 Intelligent-Tiering Good for data with unknown or changing access patterns A small monthly monitoring and automation fee per object
Objects:
Amazon S3 Glacier Designed specifically for data archiving Can retrieve data in minutes or hours Can be used to store archived customer data or old photo/video files
Amazon S3 Glacier Deep Archive The lowest-cost object storage class, suited to archiving Can retrieve objects within 12 hours
Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) Allows multiple instances to access the data in EFS at the same time Can scale up or down on demand
EBS vs S3
EBS S3
Storage capacity 16TB Unlimited, individual objects up to 5TB
Feature Survives when the EC2 instance terminates Write Once Read Many (WORM)
Storage type Solid-state
Durability
99.999999999%
Use case An 80GB video file being edited: you can enable object versioning and don’t have to re-upload a whole new object each time; uses block storage Static website hosting, geographically distributed storage, data backups, serverless
Summary Complex write/read/modify functionality Complete objects, occasionally-modified data
EBS vs EFS An EBS volume attaches to an EC2 instance, and EBS is an availability-zone-level resource. To attach EC2 to EBS, both must be in the same availability zone EBS is a disk that can hold file data, databases, or applications. Once the disk is full it won’t automatically expand EFS isn’t a blank disk, it’s a real Linux file system EFS is a regional resource, so any EC2 in the region can write to the EFS file system As more data is written, EFS expands automatically
RDS vs DynamoDB
RDS DynamoDB
Automatic high availability, provides recovery Key-value pairs, no schema required
Customer owns the data Massive throughput capacity
Customer owns the schema PB-scale expansion potential
Customer has control over the network Fine-grained API access control
Use cases:
A sales/supply-chain management system: if you need business analytics with complex relational joins, RDS is a good fit For cases other than the above, DynamoDB works almost everywhere. Most cases don’t need complex relational joins, like an employee contact table, which a single table can handle. DynamoDB eliminates the complex features and management overhead of RDS while letting you build a fast, high-performance database
Pricing Free tier: Always free AWS Lambda allows one million free calls per month
Free for 12 months S3 offers up to 5GB of free storage for 12 months
Some services offer short-term trials Lightsail offers a one-month trial, with up to 750 hours during the trial period
Pricing models Pay-as-you-go: pay for what you use, no long-term contracts Reserved capacity Volume-based discounts: some services offer tiered pricing, where the per-unit cost decreases as usage increases E.g. the more S3 storage you use, the less you pay per GB
Pricing calculator Billing dashboard Access Cost Explorer and create budgets Compare your month-to-date balance with the previous month and get a forecast for next month based on current usage View free-tier usage for each service Publish AWS Cost and Usage Reports
Consolidated billing One of the features of AWS Organizations You can consolidate the bills of individual AWS accounts, but still view line items per account You can aggregate AWS resource usage at the organization level Even if an individual account’s bill is small, consolidating bills across the organization may qualify for volume discounts Simplifies the billing process A free feature The default limit on the number of accounts allowed in an organization is 4
Budgets service You can set budget amount thresholds and send alert reminders to an email address Information in Budgets updates three times a day
Cost Explorer A console-based service that lets you view and analyze your AWS spending visually Shows which service you spent the most money on Provides 12 months of historical data so you can track cost over time Provides powerful reports, and you can also customize report content
Support plans Basic Support (free) 24-hour customer service Documentation, whitepapers, forums AWS Trusted Advisor AWS Personal Health Dashboard
Developer plan Basic Support Customer support via email (12-hour response)
Business Support Basic and Developer support AWS Trusted Advisor full best-practice checks Direct phone contact with cloud support engineers (4-hour response SLA) 1-hour SLA for impaired production systems Infrastructure Event Management (e.g. large events, global launches, etc.)
Enterprise Support (for companies running mission-critical workloads) Basic, Developer, and Business support (plus a 15-minute SLA for business-critical workloads) Access to a Technical Account Manager (TAM) The TAM reviews your enterprise architecture with you against the Well-Architected Framework
AWS Marketplace A digital catalog containing thousands of software products from independent software vendors, simplifying the steps to find, deploy, and manage third-party software running in your AWS architecture You can use AWS Marketplace to find, test, and buy software that runs on AWS When a customer uses a third-party application from Marketplace, there’s no need to build, install, or maintain the infrastructure those programs require One-click deployment Also pay-as-you-go Many vendors offer free trials Enterprise-focused features Custom terms and pricing, and management of custom license agreements Private marketplace, where you can build a catalog of pre-approved software solutions that meet local regulatory or security requirements Integrated procurement systems AWS cost-management tools
AWS Cloud Adoption Framework (AWS CAF) Provides recommendations to a customer company, offering guidance to help manage the process of migrating to the cloud AWS CAF perspectives (different people bring different perspectives and will have different migration strategies) Business: focuses on business capabilities People: focuses on business capabilities Governance: focuses on business capabilities Platform: technical capabilities Security: technical capabilities Operations: technical capabilities
Migration strategies The 6 R’s Rehosting Pick an application and move it almost as-is to AWS Rehosting alone can save up to 30% of the total cost
Replatforming / lift-tinker-and-shift Some cloud optimizations are made, but no changes to the core code are needed
Retiring Some enterprises have applications in their IT portfolio that are no longer used
Retaining Some applications need to be replaced, but the timing isn’t right and they may keep running for several more months These applications can be migrated to AWS
Repurchasing Drop legacy licensed software and move to cloud-native products, etc. High upfront cost, but large potential benefits
Refactoring Rewrite the code Some features may not have been possible on-premises before
AWS Snow FamilyAll are tamper-resistant and all encrypt data with the customer’s own 256-bit key AWS Snowcone Holds up to 8TB of data and includes edge computing (with EC2 and AWS IoT Greengrass) You can order the device through the AWS console The customer installs the device, copies data onto it, then ships it back to AWS AWS then copies the data to an S3 bucket in the customer’s AWS account 8TB, 4G RAM, 2 CPU
AWS Snowball Edge Two options Compute Optimized: Good for large-scale data migrations and periodic transfer jobs 80TB
Storage Optimized: Good for machine learning, full-motion video analysis, and a local compute stack 80TB
Fits into an existing server rack You can use EC2 or IoT Greengrass for compute Use cases IoT device streaming Video transcoding Industrial signal processing
AWS Snowmobile The device sits in a giant 45-foot container Shipped by truck Holds 100PB (100,000TB) of data The device is tamper-resistant, waterproof, fire-suppressing, and temperature-controlled A security team monitors the escort team via video
Availability ZoneAn AZ is a data center, or a group of data centers, within a region. Availability zones each sit tens of miles apart from one another. This distance is close enough to maintain low latency (the time between a request for content and its receipt) between availability zones. Yet if a disaster strikes one part of the region, they are also far enough apart to reduce the chance of multiple availability zones being affected. Edge locationsThese use CloudFront to store cached copies of your content at sites closer to the customer’s location, in order to speed up delivery

entry.title: AWS for DevOps Notes |【DevOps Skill Tree】
entry.content:
🌐 中文版：繁體中文
Regions & AZsRegion: a group of data centers spanning multiple geographic locations, e.g. us-east-1 Availability Zone (AZ): each region has multiple mutually-isolated locations called AZs. An AZ may contain one or more data centers with independent networking and power. us-east-1a, us-east-1b, etc. Local Zone: no physical data center of its own, usually connected to an AZ. For example, Taiwan’s Local Zone connects to ap-northeast-1, aiming to serve edge locations to reduce latency. AWS Outposts: physical servers deployed on the customer’s premises, providing local access to AWS services IAMThe service used for access control in the AWS environment. It manages which users have permission to access which resources. Security Best Practices: don’t use the root user for daily business; create corresponding users with appropriate permissions and do business with those.
Below are common IAM terms and their relationship diagram: IAM User, IAM Group, IAM Role, Permission policy, Identity-provider object. Their relationships are as follows.
Whichever IAM entity (IAM User, IAM Role) it is, it needs a corresponding policy to grant it permissions. Here’s the structure of a policy. IAM Policyexample policy { "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "S3ConsoleAccess", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": [ "s3:GetAccountPublicAccessBlock", "s3:GetBucketAcl", "s3:GetBucketLocation", "s3:GetBucketPolicyStatus", "s3:GetBucketPublicAccessBlock", "s3:ListAccessPoints", "s3:ListAllMyBuckets" ], "Resource": "*" }, { "Sid": "ListObjectsInBucket", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "s3:ListBucket", "Resource": ["arn:aws:s3:::amzn-s3-demo-bucket"] }, { "Sid": "AllObjectActions", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "s3:*Object", "Resource": ["arn:aws:s3:::amzn-s3-demo-bucket/*"] } ]}
Version 2012-10-17: the default policy language version 2008-10-17: an older policy language version
Statement contains multiple policies, which can be custom or AWS-managed policies
Sid the ID of an individual policy statement, which can describe the policy’s behavior
Effect Allow: allow the listed action on the listed resource Deny: deny the listed action on the listed resource
Action its format is [service name]:[API operation on that service] the action here is the permission
Resource usually the resource’s ARN can also use the wildcard * Example "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::amzn-s3-demo-bucket/*"
Condition specifies the condition under which the policy takes effect Example. "Condition" : { "StringEquals" : { "aws:username" : "johndoe" }}
List of Actions, Resources, and Conditions for AWS servicesAWS managed policies; some handy policies can be used directly
How IAM works https://docs.aws.amazon.com/zh_tw/IAM/latest/UserGuide/intro-structure.html
Source: AWS Developer Guide A user or application authenticates to AWS using credentials (AWS or third-party). IAM compares the credentials with trusted principals, and if they match, authorizes access to AWS resources. IAM then requests to grant the principal access to the resource, and decides to Allow or Deny the principal’s access based on the policy’s rules. VPCWhat is a VPC?
A regional resource; you can create a network domain for deploying AWS services. E.g. CIDR: 10.0.0.0/16 SubnetA VPC can be divided into subnets, which are AZ-level resources. CIDR: 10.0.0.0/24 They’re usually split into Public Subnet and Private Subnet. Normally without special configuration it’s a Private Subnet, unless the default route in the route table is set to an Internet Gateway. Also, to let resources in a Private Subnet access the external network, you need to set up a NAT Gateway.
Amazon VPC Quotas:VPCs per region: 5 (Can limit increase)Subnets per region: 200 (Can limit increase)IPv4 CIDR blocks per VPC: 5 (up to 50) (Can limit increase)
Which IPs are reserved in the AWS environment? x.x.x.0: the subnet’s first IP, used to identify the subnetx.x.x.1: VPC Routerx.x.x.2: DNS Serverx.x.x.3: reserved for future usex.x.x.255: Broadcast (though broadcast isn’t supported in a VPC) Network ACL & Security GroupsWhat is a Network ACL?
A stateless firewall that can control whether source-IP traffic can enter and leave a subnet Allow / Deny rules Inbound / Outbound An ACL can be attached at the subnet level Rules contain only IP rules
What is a Security Group?
A stateful firewall that can control traffic into an ENI or EC2 instance Allow rules Can specify IP address, port, protocol Can include other security groups
VPC Flow LogsWhat is a VPC Flow Log? Mainly used to determine which source IPs’ packets flow into each interface. Users can create flow logs for a VPC, subnet, or network interface. It can also be used to monitor and troubleshoot connectivity issues, including:
Subnets to Internet Subnets to Subnets Internet to Subnets
VPC PeeringVPC Peering establishes a private connection between different VPCs, provided the two VPCs’ CIDRs don’t overlap. Note that VPC Peering isn’t transitive. For example, if VPC_A peers with VPC_B and VPC_B peers with VPC_C, that doesn’t mean VPC_A and VPC_C can access each other. VPC_A <---> VPC_BVPC_B <---> VPC_CVPC_A <-x-> VPC_C
VPC EndpointsA VPC endpoint mainly lets different services access each other without going through the public network. What’s the difference between a Gateway Endpoint and an Interface Endpoint? First, back to the VPC-endpoint principle: without one, requests may have to flow over the public network. If an EC2 in a Public Subnet wants to access an S3 bucket, the request would go through the Internet Gateway and flow over the external network to S3.
Alternatively, you access it via a VPC endpoint. The VPC endpoint for accessing S3 and DynamoDB is a Gateway Endpoint, whose feature is letting services in a subnet access S3 or DynamoDB via routing.
During creation, you select the subnet’s route table, and this entry is automatically added to the selected route table.
Destination Target
prefix_list_id gateway_endpoint_id
Unlike a Gateway Endpoint, a VPC Interface Endpoint can be used for most services. The main difference is that an Interface Endpoint can integrate with a security group and supports custom DNS resolution (private DNS name), but it’s more expensive.
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/privatelink/gateway-endpoints.html
EC2ELBAuto-Scaling GroupS3DNSRoute53Lambda
What is Lambda?
Lambda is an event-driven serverless service with custom business-logic code that triggers invocations of other services based on different conditions. It supports both synchronous and asynchronous requests and is highly scalable. You can set reserved concurrency to reserve a certain number of Lambda functions to handle large volumes of API requests, and on top of reserved concurrency, provisioned concurrency to warm up Lambda functions, pre-running the Lambda environment initialization to reduce cold starts and further lower latency. Lambda supports many runtimes, such as Python 3.11, Nodejs20, Java 17, Java8, Ruby, etc. You can also define a custom runtime. For Python, you define the behavior after the function is triggered in the handler. def handler_name(event, context): ... return some_value
See this doc for which runtimes will be deprecated. A deprecated runtime can still be triggered, but AWS won’t do security patches or maintenance for it, and if a deprecated runtime is attacked and affects AWS infrastructure, under the shared responsibility model AWS has the right to freeze the user’s function. So in short: proceed at your own risk.
What are the ways to create a Lambda function?
You can upload a zip file, use a blueprint, or create it via a container image. Note that if you package an image, it’s best to package it on an Amazon Linux environment, since if the app involves certain low-level system calls, errors may occur, because Lambda itself runs on Amazon Linux EC2.
Since Lambda’s own VPC is managed by AWS, how do you connect it to another custom VPC?
First, be sure the Lambda’s execution role has the AWSLambdaVPCAccessExecutionRole permission; only with it can a Hyperplane ENI be created when the Lambda is created, serving as the network interface between the Lambda function and the target resource.
What’s the main difference between synchronous and asynchronous invocation of a Lambda function?
The main difference is whether it responds immediately. On synchronous invocation, you get a response immediately on success, while on asynchronous invocation the request waits in an event queue for Lambda’s poller to consume it, so the client may receive StatusCode: 202 on asynchronous invocation. Here’s a simple synchronous invocation via the AWS CLI: aws lambda invoke --function-name my-function \ --cli-binary-format raw-in-base64-out \ --payload '{ "key": "value" }' response.json
On a successful invocation, the response may look like: { "ExecutedVersion": "$LATEST", "StatusCode": 200}
And this is an asynchronous invocation via the CLI: aws lambda invoke \ --function-name my-function \ --invocation-type Event \ --cli-binary-format raw-in-base64-out \ --payload '{ "key": "value" }' response.json
A successful output would be: { "StatusCode": 202}
How do you handle errors in asynchronous Lambda invocation?
Normally if an error occurs, Lambda retries twice first, which you can also observe in the logs. If the error cause is throttling, Lambda returns the event to the event queue and still retries, but with exponential backoff up to 6 hours. You can also set up a Dead-Letter Queue, usually to keep records of asynchronous invocations, which also helps further troubleshooting. A DLQ can typically be an Amazon SQS or Amazon SNS topic.
https://aws.amazon.com/tw/blogs/architecture/understanding-the-different-ways-to-invoke-lambda-functions/
Reserved Concurrency && Provisioned ConcurrencyTo let a Lambda function auto-scale, it’s generally recommended to set reserved concurrency so the function always keeps a certain number of instances to handle requests.
The max reserved concurrency is: the account’s unreserved concurrency - 100In short, at least 100 concurrency is kept on the account.
Provisioned concurrency specifies how many of these reserved functions need to be pre-warmed. Warming here means initializing the Lambda execution environment, like loading the runtime and initializing variables, and also running the initialization of variables outside the handler. This means the initialization happens once, and then the execution environment is kept to respond quickly to later requests.
As the figure in the AWS docs above explains in detail, without provisioned concurrency, every new request after the Lambda terminates has to go through the Lambda Init phase again.
Ref:
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/zh_tw/lambda/latest/dg/provisioned-concurrency.html#optimizing-latency https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/lambda-concurrency.html#reserved-and-provisioned
How do you compute the needed concurrency? $Concurrency = (average requests per second) \times (average request duration in seconds)$ Average requests per second times average request duration gives a rough estimate of how much concurrency you need. For a concrete measurement, look at Lambda Invocation Metrics for the average requests per second, then estimate the average request duration via the Duration metric. API GatewaySNS / PinpointSQSMQCloudformationAWS CDKECSEKSFargate

entry.title: Problem-Solving Notes | Backtracking & Recursion
💻 Common Windows Commands
The One Line That Got Rewritten | Channel Hop | GaianSpace CTF 2026
entry.content:
🌐 中文版：繁體中文 This is the opening post of my favourite storyline in GaianSpace CTF 2026. The whole series is built around one idea: you hand-build a LoRa demodulator yourself, and then keep growing it: from a single fixed parameter set, to implicit headers, to Doppler drift, and finally to frequency hopping. This first post doesn’t touch IQ yet; it’s a warm-up at the packet layer. The real IQ work starts in the next post, True Color Is a Lie. Rest of the series: Isodata Seven、Subsidy Claim、Two Voices、No Name on the Door、Hopscotch
What the challenge is about Every morning, Babb’s corn farm receives a GaianSpace AgriLink satellite tile through a LoRa mast. This particular morning the tractor shows map integrity: unverified and refuses to use the tile. Support won’t open a ticket without the tile’s delivery stamp, but the farmer can’t find it anywhere on the tablet. Luckily, the mast kept a log of what it received. Goal: find the delivery stamp. The files given are mast_rx_0540.log (the receive log, 641 lines of hex packets) and agrilink_welcome.txt (the sign-up welcome letter, “some of it may be out of date”). Flag format: GAIANSPACE{...} Read the log, rebuild the tileThe first packet in the log decodes to a chunk of text metadata: tile=0704 site=BABB-N date=2025-07-04 src=S2 L2A gsd=10m px=128x128 ch=B02,B03,B04,B08,B11 scale=refl*400
That one line tells us everything:
The data comes from Sentinel-2, 128×128 pixels, 10 m resolution. And there are 5 channels: B02 (blue) B03 (green) B04 (red) B08 (near-infrared) B11 (short-wave infrared)
But the welcome letter only mentions 4 channels (blue/green/red + NIR). It quietly left one out.
The remaining packets follow the format AL 02 04 07 'D' <channel 0–4> <row 0–127> <128 pixel bytes>. 5 channels × 128 rows = 640 data packets, plus one trailing packet. Drop them back into five 128×128 grayscale images and the whole tile comes back. Compose blue/green/red (B04/B03/B02) into a true-colour image and you get exactly what the farmer sees on the tablet: circular pivot-irrigation fields, roads, solar panels. Everything looks normal, and there’s no stamp in sight:
The stamp is hiding in a channel the tablet never showsThe tablet only builds true colour from blue/green/red, so if the stamp lives in another channel, the farmer will never see it. I ran a high-pass filter on each channel (subtract a Gaussian blur, then boost the contrast) to amplify the tiny brightness variations: hp = a - gaussian_filter(a, 1.5)v = clip(128 + hp * 6, 0, 255)
Line the five high-pass images up side by side and the answer jumps right out. Only B08 (near-infrared) has three lines of text written across the fields:
The brightness difference in the raw image is tiny and completely invisible to the eye, and the true-colour composite doesn’t use B08 at all. That’s the whole trick: the stamp was written into a channel the tablet simply never renders. FlagGAIANSPACE{AL-STAMP-Q9VRR9}
Takeaways When something is “invisible,” first list what data isn’t being displayed. The way in here: the metadata lists 5 channels, the welcome letter claims 4, and the tablet only uses 3. The stamp is hiding in the channel everyone ignores. For image stego, a per-channel high-pass or contrast stretch makes hidden watermarks pop. Especially with multispectral satellite imagery, where different bands carry wildly different amounts of information, so don’t just stare at the visible light. Don’t rush to chase the noise in the log (dropped packets, RSSI, SNR). I spent a while hunting missing packets and looking for patterns in RSSI, and they were all red herrings. Reconstruct the actual data and look at it first; that beats drilling into details. The challenge name channel-hop means “search across different channels (bands),” not LoRa frequency hopping. Real hopping doesn’t show up until the final post in the series, Hopscotch.

entry.title: Integrating a Lambda Function into Amazon Connect from Scratch
entry.content:
🌐 中文版：繁體中文
PrefaceIn today’s business environment, providing high-quality, efficient customer service is one of the keys to success. Amazon Connect is a powerful cloud contact center that helps businesses easily build highly reliable contact centers and interact seamlessly with customers. This post will walk you step by step through integrating a Lambda function into Amazon Connect to achieve more custom functionality. We’ll follow these steps to do the integration: Step 1: Create a Connect instanceFirst, we’ll create a Connect instance in the Amazon Connect console. In the Amazon Connect console, choose Add Instance. This step requires setting your instance-alias, which creates a unique access URL for your Connect instance.
This step adds an admin; you’ll need to set a username and password.
For the remaining steps just click Next, and finally create the instance. Creation takes a while, so you can create the Lambda function in the meantime.
Step 2: Create a Lambda functionGo to the Lambda console and choose to create a Lambda function. Our Lambda’s region is the same as the Connect instance’s region, both us-east-1.
Choose Author from Scratch, name the function TestConnect, and choose Python 3.11 for the runtime. Keep everything else default, then create the function. After creation, modify the Lambda code, adding a line in your handler. print("Invoke Success!")
Then click deploy. Step 3: Add Flows to Amazon Connect In this step, we’ll add Flows to the Connect instance. We’ll use the Lambda function just created, letting Amazon Connect invoke it in certain situations.
Go to the Connect instance you just created and click Flows in the left navigation.
Scroll down to AWS Lambda, choose the Lambda name you just created, then click Add Lambda Function.
Step 4: Configure contact flows In this step, we’ll configure contact flows so Amazon Connect triggers the Lambda function and performs custom actions in certain situations. We’ll set a voice prompt and the action taken when the Lambda function is triggered.
Open the access URL of the Connect instance you just created.
A screen like this appears.
In the left panel, find Routing and choose Flows.
Open it and choose Create Flow. The first step is to enter a name for your flow; here I called it TestConnect-LambdaFlow. At first only an Entry appears on the canvas. Search for Lambda Invoke in the left search bar, and an Invoke AWS Lambda function block appears; drag it onto the center canvas. Click the dots in the top-right of Invoke AWS Lambda function and choose edit setting; an edit window appears on the right, where you enter the ARN of the Lambda function you created, then click Save.
Then search for Play Prompt in the left search bar and drag it onto the center canvas, again clicking the top-right dots and choosing edit setting.
Choose the Text-to-speech or chat text option, and below enter the message shown when the customer first joins the chat. Here I entered: Hi there, this flow section will try to invoke Lambda function. Click Save when done. Then search for Disconnect under Terminate in the left search bar and drag it onto the center canvas. Finally connect all the block arrows; the overall flow looks like the figure below.
The Lambda function is invoked whether it succeeds or not, but the prompt is only triggered on success; on failure it disconnects directly, and a failed Lambda invocation also disconnects directly. Finally click Save, then Publish.
Be sure to click Publish; if you don’t, your configured flow won’t appear on the dashboard.
Step 5: Test the chat Once everything is configured, we’ll test. Through a simulated chat interface, we’ll check whether the Lambda function is triggered successfully and verify the integration works as expected.
Click the icon that looks a bit like the Windows logo at the top of the left panel, choose Dashboard, and return to the main screen.
Click Test Chat, and the Test Chat page appears; click Test Settings in the top left.
A settings menu appears; under Contact Flow choose the flow you just created, then click Apply.
After clicking Apply, a simulated chat interface appears showing the customer joining the chat. Since our setting always disconnects regardless, we can go back to the Lambda page to check whether the function was triggered.
Step 6: Check the logs Finally, we’ll check the Lambda function’s logs to confirm it was invoked correctly and ensure the integration’s reliability.
Back in the Lambda console, click View CloudWatch logs.
Open the newest log stream and you’ll find the string Invoke Success!, confirming our Lambda was invoked successfully.
ConclusionThrough this post, you’ve learned how to integrate the customer-service flow using Amazon Connect and a Lambda function, and achieve custom customer interactions. Let’s take this integration journey together!

entry.title: A Stray Drone Writing in the Sky with Its Flight Path | Connect the Dots | STARPWN 2026
entry.content:
🌐 中文版：繁體中文 In the same Prismantir drone-swarm world, this is the challenge with the shortest story but the most memorable payoff. 150 million bytes of raw telemetry, and at the very end you open an image to find a drone writing letters in the sky with its own flight path.
What the challenge is about While known for their big eye in the sky, Prismantir huge drone fleet is also a behemoth to keep in control. Every night, each drone patrols its assigned block, following its route with clockwork precision. But tonight, one unit broke the formation. Can you trace where did it go?
In plain terms: Prismantir’s huge drone fleet patrols its assigned city blocks every night, following routes with clockwork precision. But tonight one unit broke formation, and the task is to find where it went. You get a single file: PRISM_S03_B10-30_20260830.raw, about 149.7 MB. First, confirm the file formatLooking at the header with xxd: 00000000: fd1d 0000 7a01 01fd 0000 0641 7264 7543 ....z......ArduC00000010: 6f70 7465 7220 5634 2e36 2e31 2028 3537 opter V4.6.1 (5700000020: 3539 3163 6238 299c 1cfd 2100 007b 0101 591cb8)...!..{..
Two things jump out immediately: the plaintext string ArduCopter V4.6.1, which is the ArduPilot drone firmware’s version string. And every record starts with 0xFD, the MAVLink v2 frame start marker. Manually peeling the first packet by the MAVLink v2 header format matches perfectly: payload length, sysid=1, compid=1, msgid=253 (STATUSTEXT), content "ArduCopter V4.6.1 (57591cb8)". So this file is a raw MAVLink v2 stream with no extra wrapping. Unlike a typical .tlog, there’s no per-packet timestamp outer layer here, just MAVLink packets written one right after another. pymavlink is too slow, so hand-roll a parser againFirst I tried pymavlink: from pymavlink import mavutilm = mavutil.mavlink_connection('PRISM_S03_B10-30_20260830.raw', dialect='ardupilotmega')while True: msg = m.recv_match(blocking=False) ...
It technically works, but parsing a 150 MB file this way, with pure Python walking the full ardupilotmega dialect lookup table, is slow enough to make you question your life choices. Since MAVLink v2’s wrapping is itself simple (each field is at a fixed position, and the payload length is in the second byte), I just wrote a minimal parser: import structdata = open("PRISM_S03_B10-30_20260830.raw", "rb").read()n = len(data)pos = 0while pos < n: if data[pos] != 0xFD: nxt = data.find(b'\xfd', pos + 1) if nxt == -1: break pos = nxt continue plen = data[pos+1] incompat = data[pos+2] sysid = data[pos+5] compid = data[pos+6] msgid = data[pos+7] | (data[pos+8] << 8) | (data[pos+9] << 16) header_len = 10 sig_len = 13 if (incompat & 0x1) else 0 total_len = header_len + plen + 2 + sig_len # header + payload + CRC (+ signature) payload = data[pos+header_len : pos+header_len+plen] # ... handle payload by msgid ... pos += total_len
Because this capture is a clean, uninterrupted stream, walking it linearly needs no resync at all, and all 4,158,449 messages parse in about 3 seconds, more than an order of magnitude faster than the general library. The rule of thumb here: if the standard library becomes the bottleneck and the protocol format is simple, it’s worth hand-rolling a dedicated parser. Find the fleetTallying sysid (MAVLink’s marker for which vehicle sent a message) reveals 10 different drones (sysid 1–10). Each sends roughly the same proportion of message types (HEARTBEAT, GPS_RAW_INT, GLOBAL_POSITION_INT, ATTITUDE, STATUSTEXT), perfectly matching the “a huge fleet patrolling simultaneously” scenario. The STATUSTEXT contents are all just standard ArduPilot auto-mission logs (disarm, takeoff, fly to waypoint…), and no drone’s text log hides anything unique, so the information must be in the coordinates. Plot each drone’s coordinatesParse GLOBAL_POSITION_INT (msgid 33) to get each drone’s coordinates: if msgid == 33 and len(payload) >= 28: time_boot_ms, lat, lon, alt, rel_alt = struct.unpack_from('<Iiiii', payload, 0) positions[sysid].append((time_boot_ms, lat/1e7, lon/1e7, alt/1000.0))
(MAVLink stores lat/lon as int32 scaled by 1e7, so divide back.) The coordinates fall around latitude 36.11–36.16, longitude -115.19 to -115.32, which is Las Vegas on the map, and makes sense since this CTF is tied to DEF CON. Overlay all 10 drones’ tracks (longitude, latitude; one colour per drone) on a single plot and the answer jumps out:
Nine drones’ tracks are tight, boxy street-grid patterns, each confined to its assigned rectangular block, matching the challenge’s “patrol your block precisely every night.” Only the red one (sysid 4) completely ignores block boundaries, sweeping across others’ turf in big loops, its shape clearly different from the other 9. That’s the one that broke formation. It should be obvious by now: sysid 4 spells out BVLOS:
But those four letters aren’t the flag themselves. FlagBVLOS is a very common acronym in drone regulation: Beyond Visual Line Of Sight, meaning flying a drone beyond the operator’s unaided visual range. It fits the scenario well:
a drone that flew off to where no one could see it. Assembling the flag per the given example format (each word capitalized, underscore-separated):
starpwn{Beyond_Visual_Line_Of_Sight} Takeaways Judge a file’s format by more than its extension. An undocumented .raw file can be identified and worked on just from the leading 0xFD magic byte and the plaintext firmware version string. When a general library hits a wall on large data, hand-rolling the protocol parse is often well worth it. MAVLink v2’s header is fixed-length and self-describing (the payload length is in the second byte), so a linear walk with struct.unpack_from is more than an order of magnitude faster than the full dialect library. sysid is the most natural way to split multiple vehicles mixed into one stream. When a capture might contain more than one vehicle, tally sysid first. The challenge name “Connect the dots” is literal. Spelling text with a flight path is a real-world amateur stunt (like Strava art), and taking the name as a “how to solve” hint rather than just flavour points straight at the solution: plot the ordered coordinate points and read them with your eyes.

entry.title: Three Drones Lose GPS at Once | Deadly Parade | STARPWN 2026
entry.content:
🌐 中文版：繁體中文 This challenge is a sequel to the previous one, One to Rule Them All, in the same Prismantir drone-swarm world. But the gameplay is completely different: the last one was protocol security, while this one is a pure signal-localization problem. And honestly, I submitted two wrong answers and had to take the long way around before remembering how to compute a circumcenter from middle-school geometry.
What the challenge is about Prismantir was assigned to protect a VIP during DynaCon’s parade, and their team already had their hands full. They stopped the attacker before he even got out of bed, but his devices were already in place and active. The sky above the Glittercity was tuned to a dead channel. No one realized what was happening until Prismantir’s drones began falling from the sky like ducks. Your mission is to find where these deadly toys could have been hiding.
In plain terms: the Prismantir team was protecting a VIP at DynaCon’s parade and was already stretched thin on manpower. They caught the attacker before he even got out of bed, but his jamming devices were already running, and the radio channel above Glittercity had been tuned to dead silence, and nobody realized something was wrong until Prismantir’s drones started falling from the sky one after another like ducks. The goal: find where these jamming devices were hiding. The challenge gives just one thing: PRISM_S05_DNCN_20260831.pcap, a roughly 198 MB packet capture with over two million packets. First, confirm what kind of packets these arefile PRISM_S05_DNCN_20260831.pcapcapinfos PRISM_S05_DNCN_20260831.pcap
The result shows a Linux cooked-mode capture v2 (linktype 276) capture, totaling 2.079 million packets over 3159 seconds. Looking with tshark: frame -> sll -> ip -> udp -> data (100% of packets)
Every packet is 127.0.0.1:14550 <-> 127.0.0.1:45177, the standard MAVLink UDP port on loopback. Same as the previous challenge, One to Rule Them All, it’s the MAVLink v2 protocol (the 0xFD magic at the start), just wrapped in a full pcap (Linux SLL2 cooked capture + IPv4 + UDP) this time, rather than a bare byte stream. Another performance problem, so hand-roll a parser againtshark/pymavlink are far too slow for two million packets. Same as my experience in Connect the Dots, I just hand-rolled a parser, manually peeling apart the pcap record format, SLL2 header, IP header, UDP header, and MAVLink v2 header: import structf = open("PRISM_S05_DNCN_20260831.pcap", 'rb')gh = f.read(24)magic, vmaj, vmin, tz, sigfigs, snaplen, network = struct.unpack('<IHHiIII', gh)assert network == 276 # LINKTYPE_LINUX_SLL2while True: rec_hdr = f.read(16) if len(rec_hdr) < 16: break ts_sec, ts_usec, incl_len, orig_len = struct.unpack('<IIII', rec_hdr) data = f.read(incl_len) ts = ts_sec + ts_usec/1e6 proto_type = struct.unpack('>H', data[0:2])[0] # SLL2 EtherType if proto_type != 0x0800: continue ip_start = 20 # SLL2 header is a fixed 20 bytes ihl = (data[ip_start] & 0x0F) * 4 if data[ip_start+9] != 17: # 17 = UDP continue udp_start = ip_start + ihl udp_len = struct.unpack('>H', data[udp_start+4:udp_start+6])[0] payload = data[udp_start+8 : udp_start+udp_len] if len(payload) < 10 or payload[0] != 0xFD: continue plen = payload[1] sysid = payload[5] msgid = payload[7] | (payload[8] << 8) | (payload[9] << 16) mpayload = payload[10:10+plen] # ... handle by msgid ...
Written this way, two million messages parse in about three seconds, more than an order of magnitude faster. The parsed result shows a full patrol fleet of 10 drones (sysid 1–10) plus one ground station (sysid 255), the same fleet setup as in Connect the Dots. Find the incident: filter warning-level system messagesMAVLink has a STATUSTEXT (msgid 253) message type dedicated to text status messages, with a severity field. Filtering for severity ≤ 4 (warning and above), the attack scene immediately appears: 1026.66s sysid=2 sev=2 EKF variance1026.66s sysid=2 sev=2 EKF Failsafe: changed to LAND Mode1038.44s sysid=2 sev=4 EKF3 IMU1 stopped aiding1051.32s sysid=2 sev=4 SmartRTL deactivated: bad position1438.29s sysid=5 sev=2 EKF variance / EKF Failsafe: changed to LAND Mode1458.55s sysid=5 sev=4 SmartRTL deactivated: bad position1775.77s sysid=3 sev=2 EKF variance / EKF Failsafe: changed to LAND Mode1802.33s sysid=3 sev=4 SmartRTL deactivated: bad position2805.08s sysid=9 sev=4 SmartRTL deactivated: buffer full <- unrelated
Three drones (sysid 2, 5, 3) show an identical GPS-jamming signature: the EKF (Extended Kalman Filter, the algorithm a drone uses to fuse sensor data and figure out “where am I now”) variance spiking, the EKF downgrading into LAND protection mode, both IMUs (inertial measurement units) stopping GPS aiding, and SmartRTL (smart return-to-launch) aborting due to an unreliable position. sysid 9’s failure is a separate unrelated issue (telemetry buffer full), so rule it out. Pinpoint the exact moment GPS was lostSTATUSTEXT timestamps actually lag; a more accurate approach is to look directly at GPS_RAW_INT (msgid 24)’s fix_type field, the first-hand signal of GPS fix status. An easily-overlooked detail here: MAVLink fields are stored sorted by type size from largest to smallest, not in declaration order. If you build the struct format in the documented field order, mixed field sizes will misalign everything after. The safe approach is to check the message type’s real wire order with pymavlink: from pymavlink.dialects.v20 import ardupilotmega as mavcls = mav.mavlink_map[24]print(cls.fieldnames, cls.orders)# real order: time_usec, lat, lon, alt, eph, epv, vel, cog, fix_type, sats_visible, ...
time_usec, lat, lon, alt, eph, epv, vel, cog, fix_type, sats_vis = \ struct.unpack_from('<QiiiHHHHBB', mpayload, 0)
In fact fix_type only ever takes two values: 1 (no fix) and 6 (RTK precision fix), with no gradual signal degradation in between, just a clean binary switch. That’s a clue in itself: it means a sharply-bounded jamming area, not the gradient of a naturally weakening signal. Here I grab the moment each affected drone first shows fix_type=1, the coordinate where it truly crossed the death-zone boundary (10 to 14 seconds before the EKF actually declared failsafe):
sysid lat lon
2 36.0924468 -115.2422644
5 36.0997050 -115.2479014
3 36.0778960 -115.2440574
I also cross-validated with SIMSTATE (msgid 164, the true coordinates reported by ArduPilot’s SITL simulator, bypassing EKF/GPS entirely) to confirm each drone really did end up near these coordinates. But I guessed wrong twiceFirst: just averaging the three points. Reverse-geocoding (Nominatim) landed in a Spring Valley area community called Spanish Trail. I submitted starpwn{Spanish_Trail} and starpwn{Spanish_Trail_Country_Club}, both wrong. Second: all three points’ addresses pointed to the same larger-area community name, Spring Valley. I submitted starpwn{Spring_Valley}, still wrong. Where was the problem? The three points roughly form a near-collinear line, and taking a simple average of such a distribution corresponds to no meaningful geometric property. It’s not triangulation, just forcing an answer. The correct approach: circumcenter triangulationIf the jammer’s effective range is roughly circular, then each drone’s “first crossing into the death zone” coordinate is, in theory, a point on this circle’s boundary, and should be roughly equidistant from the center. And the point equidistant from three known points is the circumcenter of the triangle they form, the very thing taught in middle-school geometry. import mathP1 = (36.0924468, -115.2422644) # sysid 2P2 = (36.0997050, -115.2479014) # sysid 5P3 = (36.0778960, -115.2440574) # sysid 3lat0 = (P1[0] + P2[0] + P3[0]) / 3R = 6371000def to_xy(lat, lon): x = math.radians(lon) * R * math.cos(math.radians(lat0)) y = math.radians(lat) * R return x, ydef from_xy(x, y): lon = math.degrees(x / (R * math.cos(math.radians(lat0)))) lat = math.degrees(y / R) return lat, lonax, ay = to_xy(*P1); bx, by = to_xy(*P2); cx, cy = to_xy(*P3)d = 2 * (ax*(by-cy) + bx*(cy-ay) + cx*(ay-by))ux = ((ax**2+ay**2)*(by-cy) + (bx**2+by**2)*(cy-ay) + (cx**2+cy**2)*(ay-by)) / duy = ((ax**2+ay**2)*(cx-bx) + (bx**2+by**2)*(ax-cx) + (cx**2+cy**2)*(bx-ax)) / dlat_c, lon_c = from_xy(ux, uy)r = math.hypot(ux-ax, uy-ay)print(lat_c, lon_c, 'radius_m=', r)# -> 36.086798, -115.263377 radius ≈ 1998 m
Here I first project lat/lon into meter-unit planar coordinates with a simple local planar projection (to_xy / from_xy), because the circumcenter formula is planar geometry and applying it directly to lat/lon would distort due to Earth’s curvature; after computing the circumcenter I convert back to lat/lon. The result is a clean circle with a radius of nearly 2 km:
Dropping this coordinate on a map: https://www.openstreetmap.org/?mlat=36.086798&mlon=-115.263377#map=15/36.086798/-115.263377
The marker lands precisely on a clearly-named park, Echo Trail Park, right next to the Spanish Trail golf course and the Flamingo Wash detention basin, open but with tree cover, a very plausible place to actually hide a jammer. Flagstarpwn{Echo_Trail_Park}
Takeaways MAVLink fields are laid out by type size, not the declaration order in the docs. Before hand-rolling a parser for a new message type, check the real wire order with pymavlink‘s mavlink_map[id].orders or the official XML definition. Don’t build the struct format from the docs’ field list order. A clean binary signal is more notable than a gradual noisy one. fix_type switching only between 1 and 6 with no intermediate values hints that this is a deliberately designed, discoverable event worth investigating specifically, rather than assuming real-world GPS naturally fades like that. Averaging is not triangulation. Taking the centroid of three roughly-collinear “boundary entry points” corresponds to no real geometric meaning; when those points represent “the boundary of entering a circular effective range,” the correct estimate is their circumcenter, and here that solution was clearly more accurate, landing directly on a named park rather than the vague result of a centroid landing on some random residential street. Cross-validate when you have ground truth. ArduPilot SITL’s SIMSTATE message reports the simulator’s true coordinates, bypassing the whole EKF/GPS judgment chain. Using it to confirm the jamming-entry coordinates ruled out “the drone actually drifted elsewhere,” letting debugging focus on the localization method itself rather than suspecting the data. When stuck on wrong answers, look at the map itself, not just the geocoder’s text. Reverse-geocoding APIs usually return the nearest street name, not necessarily the most prominent named landmark nearby (a park or golf course may be marked on OSM but not surfaced by a reverse-address query). Actually opening the map to see what’s around that coordinate is what made the named POI Echo Trail Park emerge.

entry.title: A Sentence Hidden in Sensor Drift | Degradift | GaianSpace CTF 2026
entry.content:
The final post of the GaianSpace CTF 2026 “05-rad-hard-rampage” series. 🌐 中文版：繁體中文
This chapter has four radiation faults; the first three posts covered Single Event Upset (SEU), Single Event Latch-up (SEL), and Total Ionizing Dose (TID). This one wraps up with the fourth: Displacement Damage (DDD): not a single high-energy particle strike, nor burning out the circuit, but the lattice being knocked askew hit after hit, so the readings slowly creep and slowly drift. And this challenge has a little twist: the recovered numbers look like perfectly reasonable CO₂ readings, but they aren’t actually CO₂ at all.
What the challenge is about
Displacement damage builds up: the lattice takes hit after hit, the readings creep, and by the end of the run the numbers have wandered far from the truth. We logged the whole decline. The characterization team worked out exactly how fast it drifts.
In plain terms: Foundation One’s CO₂ sensor didn’t break in a day. Displacement damage is cumulative: the lattice takes hit after hit and the readings slowly climb, until by the end of the run the numbers are far from the truth. We logged the whole decline, and the characterization team worked out the exact drift rate. Subtract the drift from each reading and what’s left is what the sensor really saw at the time. The on-call operator will tell you the recovered values are just cleaner CO₂ readings, but look again, they’re not CO₂. Files given:
sensor_log.csv: sample index and the degraded readings (30 records). ddd_characterization.md: the measured drift model.
The model is written right in the file: drift(n) = round( 1.7 * n + 0.013 * n^2 ) [ppm], n = sample index
logged reading = actual in-flight value + this drift The recorder also has a fixed CO₂ baseline, and the gas team will only say “somewhere around three hundred thirty ppm,” refusing to be more precise. First, subtract the driftMatching the hint “Creep, not jump.” Displacement Damage Dose (DDD) is yet another distinct radiation effect: high-energy particles knock atoms in the semiconductor lattice out of position, creating permanent lattice defects. These defects slowly change the sensor’s response, showing up as readings that creep upward over time, a cumulative drift rather than a one-off jump, which is why the challenge stresses “creep, not jump.” And this drift is quadratic (0.013 * n^2), so it drifts faster the later it gets. The subtraction is simple: def drift(n): return round(1.7 * n + 0.013 * n * n)as_flown = [reading - drift(n) for n, reading in rows]
The resulting in-flight values fall between 385 and 458, which still looks like reasonable CO₂ ppm numbers.
But that’s exactly the trap the challenge means by “the operator will tell you these are just cleaner readings.”
Look again: they’re not CO₂Matching the second hint, “Not parts per million.” The challenge says the baseline is “around three hundred thirty” and deliberately won’t give an exact number. So what if these numbers are actually character codes (in-flight value = baseline + ASCII code)? Then the baseline is the unknown to solve for. For each candidate baseline between 300 and 360, decode “in-flight value − baseline” as ASCII and see which baseline makes all 30 bytes land in the printable range and spell out GAIANSPACE{...}: for base in range(300, 360): vals = [x - base for x in as_flown] if all(32 <= v < 127 for v in vals): print(base, bytes(vals).decode())
The left panel shows the curves before and after subtracting the drift (the blue line clearly climbs, the orange line is flattened but the numbers still look mundane); the right panel is the baseline scan, where 333 ppm is the only baseline that spells out the flag:
One detail here: nearby baselines (332, 334…) also decode to “all printable” characters, so “is it printable” alone can’t be your filter. 332 decodes to HBJBOTQBDF|ejtqm5..., jumbled symbols that aren’t text at all. You have to tighten the criterion to “does it actually spell a meaningful flag” to uniquely pin down 333. The final result: FlagGAIANSPACE{displ4cement_drift}
Takeaways When a key constant is described vaguely, enumerate it. For a deliberately imprecise “around three hundred thirty,” rather than overanalyzing the wording, just enumerate nearby integers and filter by “does it decode to a valid result”. A baseline is exactly the kind of thing you sweep. Numbers that look normal don’t mean they’re the data’s actual intent. The post-drift values look like mundane CO₂ ppm, which is precisely the trap. “Look again” usually means reinterpret from a different angle (here, “as character codes minus a baseline”). Your filter criterion has to be precise enough. “Is it printable” isn’t strong enough here (several baselines are all-printable); you must tighten to “does it spell meaningful text” to anchor uniquely. (Series wrap-up) One “radiation” theme can produce four challenges with completely different solutions. SEU is brute-forcing a key, SEL is using CRC to find the stuck bit, TID is reconstructing logic, DDD is subtracting drift then shifting perspective. Those are four real space-radiation failure mechanisms (upset, latch-up, ionizing dose, displacement damage), each mapping to its own solving mindset. This chapter was genuinely thoughtfully designed.

entry.title: 📑 DMS Troubleshooting Notes
entry.content:
🌐 中文版：繁體中文
Network Debug If you can’t SSH to a server, what would you do? First ping the server to see if it’s reachable If it’s still failing, troubleshoot based on the error message the SSH connection prints Unable to open connection to example.com Host does not exist Check whether the target server’s domain name can be resolved via ping If you used the hostname, try the IP instead (alternate between the two)
Connection timed out: the client tried to establish a network socket with the SSH server, but the server didn’t respond in time Check whether you’re connecting on port 22, or on a custom port $ netstat -all
Check whether firewall rules are blocking inbound traffic from a specific IP or on port 22 $ iptables --list See whether a Drop method is configured Or whether port 22 hasn’t been added to the allowed connections
Connection Refused: the request is being routed to the host, but the host didn’t receive it Check whether you’re connecting on port 22, or on a custom port Check whether firewall rules are blocking inbound traffic from a specific IP or on port 22 See whether a Drop method is configured Or whether port 22 hasn’t been added to the allowed connections Check whether the service is currently running and bound to the expected port
How do you check the firewall? iptable -nL ufw status
Check SSH status Older OS versions can use service service ssh status If the result correctly shows a process id, it’s running correctly If it isn’t running it’ll show a message like ssh stop/waiting You can start the service with service ssh start
Newer OS versions can use systemctl systemctl status sshd If it’s running correctly it’ll show active or running If it isn’t running it’ll show inactive You can start the service with systemctl start sshd
Check the SSH service port There are two ways to check which port SSH is running on First, look at the ssh config file grep Port /etc/ssh/sshd_config
If you know the ssh service is running, you can use ss to check whether it’s on the expected port ss -plnt // queries socket info from the kernel netstat -plnt
What are some causes of a failed SSH connection? The SSH public key hasn’t been injected onto the server We generate an ssh key pair locally, and may protect the private key with a passphrase Inject the ssh public key onto the remote server at ~/.ssh/authorized_keys Sometimes you’ll often get the error Permission denied (publickey) Cause 1: that private key doesn’t have permission to log in Cause 2: the public key wasn’t placed in the path correctly, or the public key is lost Cause 3: the local ssh public and private keys aren’t correctly paired Before connecting, ssh checks whether our public and private keys pair correctly
Default paths $ ssh-keygen The public key goes by default to /home/username/.ssh/id_rsa.pub The private key goes by default to /home/username/.ssh/id_rsa
How do you inject the public key into the server’s path? ssh-copy-id USER@HOST By default it goes to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys
The firewall is blocking the connection Check the policy
Host Key Check Fails You get an error message like this. Every server has a fingerprint; a different server, or a reconfigured server, has a different fingerprint. On a successful login, your computer saves the fingerprint to compare against the next connection. If the fingerprint doesn’t match, you get this kind of warning. If you’re certain you reconfigured the server, you can ignore this warning You can delete the entry in ~/.ssh/known_hosts, or empty the file, which turns off all key checking
Your SSH Key File Mode Issues To protect the SSH key file, its permissions should be 0600 (owner R+W) or 0400 (owner R)
How do you enable passwordless authentication in SSH? Edit the settings in /etc/ssh/sshd_config PasswordAuthentication noPubkeyAuthentication yes
Explain how the Ping and Tracert commands work. Ping: sends an ICMP Echo Request to a specific target to confirm the communication status with the destination From the TTL value in the ping reply you can infer the OS the other side is using and the number of routers the packet passed through
Tracert: makes clever use of timeout errors to discover the path to the destination
How do you change the MTU value under Linux? What is a Jumbo Frame? A frame larger than the standard Ethernet frame, bigger than 1518/1522 bits Can only run on full-duplex Ethernet The standard Ethernet IP message size is 1500 bits, or 1518 bits including the Ethernet header and FCS (6+6+2+4) A jumbo frame refers to a Layer-2-encapsulated, Layer-3 IP message whose value is larger than 9000 bits If you use normal 1500-bit frames, the smaller the frame, the larger the number of transmitted packets and the more computation, so: It increases the host’s computation and consumes CPU resources It affects network throughput So enlarging the frame can reduce CPU computation and speed up transmission
How do you change the frame size (how do you create a jumbo frame)? Change the MTU (Maximum Transmission Unit) value
ifconfig ${Interface} mtu ${SIZE} up
e.g. ifconfig eth1 mtu 9000 up But this needs to be reset after a reboot
Edit the config file
On Ubuntu/Debian it’s under /etc/network/interfaces Add mtu 9000 Restart the service /etc/init.d/network-manager restart When going through a switched network, changing the MTU value on the host alone isn’t enough; you still need to check whether the network devices have jumbo frames enabled
Testing MTU ping -l 9000 -f <domain> The -f flag tells the OS it can’t change the packet size on its own
Explain how email communication works. When you type an email address, the part after “@” is the domain name http://linux.vbird.org/linux_server/0380mail.php#whatmail_dnshttps://weils.net/blog/2017/04/19/how-email-works-dkim-all-in-one/https://docs.digitalocean.com/support/how-to-troubleshoot-ssh-connectivity-issues/https://www.linux.com/topic/networking/4-reasons-why-ssh-connection-fails/https://help.skysilk.com/support/solutions/articles/9000150151-how-to-troubleshoot-ssh-connection-issues-using-vnc-console
How would you resolve a DNS configuration failure? https://www.digitalocean.com/community/tutorial_series/an-introduction-to-managing-dns
Can you explain how the HTTP protocol works? Usually a user makes a request to the server via a browser or a crawler We call this client a User Agent, a proxy program The requested server may also have resources like HTML files or images When the HTTP client makes a request, it establishes a TCP connection to the server’s designated port (80 by default) The HTTP server then listens for the client’s request on that port Once it receives the request, the server returns a status to the client, e.g. “HTTP/1.1 200 OK”, along with the returned content or an error message HTTP 1.1 added a keep-alive mechanism, so one connection can be reused across multiple request/response exchanges This can reduce waiting time
And HTTPS? It just performs a TLS/SSL handshake before the HTTP connection
What HTTP status codes do you know? 2xx 3xx 400 - Bad Request: the syntax of the HTTP request sent to the server is wrong or invalid Check:
An error in the URL
