Cookies for the site may be corrupted; clear the browser’s cookies and cache
Try opening the same page in a different web browser
401 - Unauthorized: the user tried to access a resource without being authenticated; the user must provide credentials to view the protected resource Check:
Check the URL for errors; if the URL is valid, go to the homepage and log in, enter your info, then retry
The browser may have cached invalid info, so clear the cache
403 - Forbidden: happens when the user makes a valid request but the server refuses service because it lacks permission to access the resource Check:
Make sure the access permissions for the /www data on the server are correct
Check the .htaccess settings (the .htaccess file controls access to resources)
This can also happen if the site has no index file, in which case you need to rename the homepage to index.html/index.php
Contact the site administrator to get access (permissions should be set to read)
If other users can access it, you need to contact your ISP to resolve the issue
404 - Not Found: the user can communicate with the server but can’t locate the requested resource Check:
Again, check whether the URL is wrong
Press F5 to refresh the page
Clear the browser cache
Change the DNS server settings
500 - Internal Server Error: this means something is wrong on the website server; the server can’t detect the exact problem, but the client can still try the following Check:
High network traffic: press F5 to reload the page
Clear the web browser’s cache and cookies
Check that the site’s .htaccess file was created correctly
Check whether any files and folders have incorrect permissions
502 - Bad Gateway: the server, acting as a gateway or proxy, couldn’t get a valid response from the upstream server; this can also be caused by a DNS issue Check:
Press F5 to reload the page
Close all open browsers and start a new browser session
Clear the browser cache
Temporarily disable the CDN (Content Delivery Network)
Restart network devices (modem, router, etc.)
503 - Service Unavailable: the server is overloaded or under maintenance Check:
Press F5 to reload the page
Restart network devices (modem, router, etc.)
504 - Gateway Timeout: the server, acting as a gateway or proxy, couldn’t get a response from the backend server within the allowed time Check:
Press F5 to reload the page
Restart network devices (modem, router, etc.)
Change the DNS server (if all devices on your network get the same error)
If there’s still an error, you may need to contact your network admin or ISP
Can you explain how SMTP works? Can you explain how DNS works? There are two kinds: authoritative DNS, and recursive servers Authoritative servers receive and respond to DNS queries, finding their way layer by layer up to the root DNS server A recursive server doesn’t have DNS records itself, but passes the request along to authoritative DNS servers to get the IP address How it works: When you type www.ntust.edu.tw, the DNS server receives a request to look up the IP address The DNS server begins resolving the IP address for www.example.com And checks whether a DNS record is in the local DNS server’s cache It looks in /etc/resolv.conf and turns the domain into an FQDN
If not, it goes to the root DNS server to look it up The root DNS server tells the DNS server the IP address of “the DNS server that manages tw” Once the local DNS server gets that IP, it sends a DNS request dig tw ns +short
The DNS server managing tw tells the local DNS server the IP address of “the DNS server that manages edu.tw” dig @nameserver edu.tw ns dig @a.dns.tw edu.tw ns +short
Once the local DNS server gets that IP, it sends a DNS request The DNS server managing edu.tw tells the local DNS server the IP address of “the DNS server that manages ntust.edu.tw” dig @nameserver ntust.edu.tw ns +short
Then the local DNS server makes a request to that IP address dig @RealAuthorieServer ntust.edu.tw a +short
The DNS server managing ntust.edu.tw returns the IP address of www.ntust.edu.tw
Can you walk through the TLS/SSL handshake process? https://www.cloudflare.com/zh-tw/learning/ssl/what-happens-in-a-tls-handshake/ It runs at the Session layer, mainly exchanging information between the two parties and authenticating each other, and through the encryption algorithms they use, producing a consistent working key When does the TLS handshake happen? When a user navigates to a site that uses HTTPS, the browser first begins querying the site’s origin server, and that’s when the TLS handshake happens. It also happens whenever other communication uses HTTPS (including API calls and DNS over HTTPS queries). After opening a TCP connection via the TCP handshake, the TLS handshake takes place
What happens during the TLS handshake? The following takes place between client and server: Specify the TLS version (TLS 1.0, 1.2, 1.3) Decide which cipher suite to use Verify the server’s identity via the server’s public key and the SSL certificate authority’s digital signature Generate a session key to use symmetric encryption after the handshake completes
What are the steps of the TLS handshake? The specific steps vary depending on the key-exchange algorithm used The most commonly used is the RSA key-exchange algorithm Client Hello: The client sends a hello message to the server to begin the handshake, including the TLS versions the client supports, the cipher suites it supports, and a client random number
Server Hello: Replying to the client hello, the server returns a message containing: An SSL certificate where does this come from? how is it generated? The server’s chosen cipher suite A server random number
Authentication The client verifies the server’s SSL certificate with the certificate authority that issued it This confirms the server is who it claims to be, and that the client is interacting with the actual owner of the domain
premaster secret The client then sends another string of random bytes, the premaster secret The premaster secret is encrypted with the public key (the client takes the public key from the SSL certificate to encrypt it) It can only be decrypted with the server’s secret key
The secret key is used The server decrypts the premaster secret with its private key
Generate the session key Both client and server use the client random, the server random, and the premaster secret to generate the session key
Client ready The client sends a finished message
Server ready The server sends a finished message
All TLS handshakes use asymmetric encryption (public and private keys), but not all TLS handshakes use the private key in the process of generating the session key. For example, an ephemeral Diffie-Hellman handshake has the following steps: Client Hello Contains the protocol version, client random, and a list of cipher suites
Server Hello Contains the SSL certificate, the selected cipher suite, and the server random
The server’s digital signature The server encrypts the client random, the server random, and the DH parameters with its private key The encrypted data serves as the server’s digital signature This confirms the server has the private key matching the public key in the SSL certificate
Server and client compute the premaster secret Client and server each use the exchanged DH parameters to compute a matching premaster secret Unlike the RSA handshake, where the client generates the premaster secret and sends it to the server
Establish the session key Client and server compute the session key from the premaster secret, the client random, and the server random
Client ready The client sends a finished message
Server ready The server sends a finished message
What might cause a TLS handshake to fail? Common error message: SSL Handshake Failed error Common causes: Protocol mismatch server-side error Cipher suite mismatch server-side error → the server doesn’t support the cipher suite the client requested Inaccurate system clock (but the process just now didn’t use any time info :| ) Misconfigured browser Certificate error server-side error The domain name in the certificate doesn’t match the domain name in the URL The certificate expired Or the certificate chain is broken Using a self-signed certificate
The server is SNI-Enabled server-side error
Protocol mismatch Collect info on the client or server with tcpdump -i any -s 0 host IP address -w File name Analyze the collected packets with Wireshark Find the TLS version used in the client hello Look at the error info in the server’s subsequent processing https://docs.apigee.com/api-platform/troubleshoot/runtime/ssl-handshake-failures
What do you do if a site’s certificate expires? Renew the certificate
Can you explain what SSL is? Its full name is Secure Sockets Layer, used to ensure the sensitive data passed between two systems isn’t tampered with or read TLS is a more secure version of SSL
Linux Admin This feels more about command usage or how to configure things
How do you manage users and groups in Linux? And how would you do it in Windows? View users with cat /etc/passwd Add a user with useradd Add a group with groupadd Then use gpasswd to add or remove a user from the root (sudo) permission group
Can you explain how the curl command works? A command-line tool that can send data to a server
How would you use the curl command for troubleshooting? $ curl protocol://IP/host:port Troubleshooting web servers curl http://example.com -I uses the -I flag to return the header
Troubleshooting SMTP servers curl smtp://example.com uses port 25 as the SMTP port by default But some ISPs block the standard SMTP port to prevent spam You can also use port 2525 or 587
Troubleshooting FTP curl ftp://example.com uses port 21 by default
How do you use the curl command to connect through a proxy? curl --proxy yourproxy:port https://yoururl.com
How do you use curl to skip validating a self-signed SSL certificate? curl -k https://localhost/ curl --insecure https://localhost/
Various curl usages:$ curl [protocol://domain:port/]$ curl -o <filename to save as> [protocol://domain:port/] download a specific file$ curl -O [protocol://domain:port/file] directly download the file in the URL$ curl -C - -O [protocol://domain:port/file] resume downloading from where it was interrupted$ curl -L [protocol://domain:port/] follow the URL's 301/302 redirect$ curl --trace-ascii debugdump.txt [protocol://domain:port/] trace the whole curl process and save the result to debugdump.txt curl making HTTP requests-X/--request [GET|POST|PUT|DELETE|PATCH] use the specified http method to make the http request-H/--header set the headers carried in the request-i/--include show the response headers in the output-d/--data carry HTTP POST data-v/--verbose output more info for easier debugging-u/--user carry a username and password-b/--cookie carry a cookie (either as an argument or a file path) POST data to an HTML form with curl Suppose the form’s HTML looks like this <form method="POST" action="form.php"> <input type=text name="email"> <input type=submit name=press value=" OK "> </form> curl -X POST --data "email=test@example.com&press=%20OK%20" http://www.example.com/form.php
Upload a file with curl Suppose the form’s HTML is <form method="POST" enctype='multipart/form-data' action="upload.php"> <input type=file name=upload> <input type=submit name=press value="OK"></form> curl -X POST -F 'file=@./upload.txt' http://www.example.com/upload.php
Common RESTful CRUD commands with curl: GET a single or all resources $ curl -X GET "http://www.example.com/api/resources"$ curl -X GET "http://www.example.com/api/resources/1" POST JSON data $ curl -X POST -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"status":false,"name":"Jack"}' "http://www.example.com/api/resources" PUT JSON data $ curl -X PUT -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"status":false}' "http://www.example.com/api/resources" DELETE a resource $ curl -X DELETE "http://www.example.com/api/resources/1"
Carry a cookie with curl Pass the cookie in the command $ curl --cookie "name=Jack" http://www.example.com Read the cookie from a file $ curl --cookie stored_cookies_file_path http://www.example.com
Specify a User Agent with curl $ curl --user-agent "Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64)" http://www.example.com
Basic Authentication: if the page uses basic authentication, you can carry --user username:password to pass it $ curl -i --user secret:vary_secret http://www.example.com/api/resources
Use a proxy to connect with the curl command$ curl --proxy yourproxy:port https://youurl.com Limit the download speed with curl$ curl --limit-rate 2000B [URL] Inject a specific Content-Type into the request to handle a particular issue$ curl --header 'Content-Type: application/json' http://yoururl.com Show only the headers in the response$ curl --head http://yoururl.com Connect to an HTTPS/SSL URL and ignore any SSL certificate errors When trying to access a secure URL with an SSL/TLS certificate, if there’s a certificate error or a CN mismatch, you’ll get the following error curl: (51) Unable to communicate securely with peer: requested domain name does not match the server's certificate.$ curl --insecure https://yoururl.com
Connect using a specific protocol (SSL/TLS)$ curl --sslv3 https://yoururl.com$ curl --tlsv1 https://example.com$ curl --tlsv1.0 https://example.com$ curl --tlsv1.1 https://example.com$ curl --tlsv1.2 https://example.com$ curl --tlsv1.3 https://example.com Download a file from an FTP server$ curl -u user:password -O ftp://ftpurl/style.css Can you explain how to use the MTR command? MTR How it works: MTR first uses traceroute against the specified host to find each network node along the way (gateways, routers, bridges, etc.), then uses ping to check the connection status of each node, updating the output report in real time so the administrator can see everything at a glance. mtr www.google.com.tw mtr -n www.google.com.tw // show everything by IP addressmtr -b www.google.com.tw // show both IP address and domain namemtr -c 5 www.google.com.tw // specify the ping limit (ICMP ECHO limit)mtr -c 5 -r www.google.com.tw > output.txt // output the report
L (Loss): packet loss rate S (Snt, Sent Packet): number of packets sent Avg (Average RTT): Best (Best RTT): Worst (Worst RTT):
So what can you discover with this tool?????
Can you explain how to use the iperf command? iperf3 is a network bandwidth testing tool that can test a client’s upload speed It uses TCP to measure bandwidth, determine link quality and latency, plus jitter and packet loss To test bandwidth, you need to run an iperf3 process on both the server and the client so they can send data to each other for the test # server side iperf3 -s // open a listening socket, default port 5201, start a server thread # client sideiperf3 -c SERVER_IP/HOSTNAME iperf3 also supports use on Android and iOS (there’s an app) Specify the test duration iperf3 -c SERVER_IP -t 20 -i 4 // test for 20 seconds, output data every 4 seconds Save the test results iperf3 -c SERVER_IP --logfile output.txt Specify a port # server sideiperf3 -s -p 12345# client sideiperf3 -c SERVER_IP -p 12345 Multiple connections # test with two connections at onceiperf3 -c SERVER_IP -P 2 To test UDP performance, use the -u flag iperf3 -c SERVER_IP -u Reverse transfer: test download speed (server sends, client receives) Default data flow: client $\rightarrow$ server iperf3 -c SERVER_IP -R
IPv4, IPv6 iperf3 -c SERVER_IP -fiperf3 -c SERVER_IP -6 Send a custom file iperf3 -c SERVER_ip -F YOUR_FILE
Can you explain how to use the tracert command? In what situations would you use it?It’s mainly used for real-time network troubleshooting, to find the routing path a packet takes as it travels through the network to its destination address.It achieves traceroute mainly by sending ICMP packets and setting the TTL field in the IP header.Each time it sends three 40-byte packets, including the source address, destination address, and the timestamp the packet was sent, to the destination. The first is a probe, then it uses UDP; since we don’t want the destination host to process them, the destination port is set to an unlikely value.$ tracert -d -h maximum_hops -j host_list -w timeout target_host-w specifies the number of milliseconds to wait for a timeout What does an asterisk in the tracert output mean? If tracert shows an asterisk (*), it means that node may have some defensive measure causing our packets to be dropped Possibly iptables set to Drop, or similar
Can you explain how the tracert command works? Property 1: it achieves its function mainly through the TTL (Time To Live) value; every time a packet passes a node, the router decrements the TTL by 1 Property 2: the caller sends a packet with TTL=1; the first router decrements the TTL by 1 to get 0 and stops forwarding the packet It then returns an ICMP Time Exceeded response, and the computer extracts the address of the first gateway the packet passed through from that response Next it sends an ICMP packet with TTL=2 to get the second gateway’s address So by incrementing the TTL value step by step, it obtains all the gateway addresses along the way
If the tracert response isn’t an ICMP Time Exceeded, what does that mean? Most firewalls, or routers with firewall features enabled, won’t return various ICMP packets by default Other routers or switches can be set by the admin not to return ICMP responses So the traceroute program can’t necessarily get all the gateway addresses along the way When a packet with a certain TTL gets no reply, this doesn’t stop the trace; the program still increments the TTL and sends the next packet, up to the preset trace limit (maximum_hops) specified by a parameter
If it can’t get an ICMP response, how does it know the packet arrived? When traceroute sends UDP datagrams to the destination, it chooses a port number that a normal application wouldn’t use (above 30000) So when the UDP datagram reaches the destination, that host sends back an “ICMP port unreachable“ message, and when traceroute receives it, it knows the destination has been reached.
Why does traceroute use ports above 30000? It’s related to the UDP convention that port numbers must be below 30000 With UDP, the host might simply drop the packet because it doesn’t offer a UDP service, and not return any info So using a port above 30000, the most the destination host can do is return a port unreachable response
What is an FQDN (fully qualified domain name)? In /etc/resolv.conf, any hostname that doesn’t end with “.” has a domain name automatically appended by the system The search entry in the file tells the system what domain names it can append domain rsync.twnameserver 168.95.1.1 (cache server)nameserver 8.8.8.8 (cache server)search hdns.com.tw example.com In the example above, just type blog and the system automatically turns it into blog.rsync.tw and sends it to 168.95.1.1 for DNS resolution. If that fails it tries blog.hdns.com.tw instead, and so on If the DNS service at 168.95.1.1 can’t be reached, the system automatically falls to the second entry, the 8.8.8.8 server
How do you set up a DNS cache server? Change the nameserver in /etc/resolv.conf
What’s the difference between an authoritative DNS server and a DNS cache server? DNS Authoritative Server: takes DNS records from its own database and responds to requests A cache server asks other hosts for DNS data
What is an NS (nameserver) record in DNS? The root server records the location of each subdomain’s authoritative host via NS records NS records have two uses: downward delegation, and parallel delegation Downward delegation: create a subdomain (e.g. create a .tw subdomain with the server) and delegate it to TWNIC’s hosts Parallel delegation: all nameservers for the same domain name must have identical NS records Above, ntpu.edu.tw has been delegated to six nameservers, and the ntpu.edu.tw NS records on all six must be exactly the same
How do you find out which hosts your DNS is currently officially delegated to? The nameservers you filled in when you bought the domain; the registrar, based on the registered domain name sends your nameservers to the registry, and once the registry confirms, it puts your host data into their records which produces a set of NS data $ dig [domain] ns Use the command above to confirm whether the current nameserver data matches what you filled in at registration
What is an SOA record? An SOA record is the system administration record for a domain name If you use managed DNS you don’t need to handle it (CloudFlare, Gandi LiveDNS) A self-hosted DNS server needs it configured It mainly represents the domain’s administrator, the admin host, the zone file serial number, and the global TTL data
What are A/AAAA records? When you need to map a domain name to a server’s IP address, you use an A record An A record points to an IPv4 address An AAAA record points to an IPv6 address $ dig +short blog.rsync.tw a$ dig +short blog.rsync.tw aaaa
What is an MX record? The mail server record for the domain If someone emails you, the mail host first checks whether the domain has an MX record If it does, it connects to that mail host; if no MX record is specifically configured the sending host tries to resolve the domain’s A record and if there’s an A record, it tries to connect to that host’s mail server. When the domain has an MX record, the mail host tries to connect to mg.ntust.edu.tw You can set mail server priority in MX records; the smaller the number, the higher the priority So mail to ntust.edu.tw is delivered first to mg.ntust.edu.tw If there’s no MX record, it’s delivered to the domain name’s A record, i.e. 140.118.31.99
What is a CNAME record? A kind of alias for a hostname, used when your destination address is a hostname rather than an IP address In that case you need to use a CNAME to map it Limitation: if a CNAME record is set under a given record, you can’t set other records Why?
E.g. if you set a CNAME for a domain, you can’t set A, MX, TXT, etc. records for it
If someone sets a CNAME for a domain name: say I register HelloWorld.tw and want to point web visitors to the same site as blog.HelloWorld.tw, so I set HelloWorld.tw CNAME blog.HelloWorld.tw
But HelloWorld.tw must carry SOA and NS records, which conflict with the CNAME and cause the domain to operate unstably. So to achieve the same effect, you can use a web redirect
Can you explain how to use the dig command? In what situations would you use it? It’s a DNS debugging tool that can simulate ordinary computer queries, recursive queries, non-recursive queries, DNS cache server queries, DNSSEC queries, TCP queries, and so on. The sections of a dig response Header ID: a plain number, the identifier for the DNS query QR: 0 query, 1 response Opcode: 0 QUERY, 1 IQUERY, 2 STATUS AA: authoritative server response TC: truncated RD: whether the client requested a recursive query RA: whether the server’s response supports recursive queries Z: reserved RCODE: 0 no error, 1-5 error codes QDCOUNT: number of entries in the Question section ANCOUNT: number of entries in the Answer section NSCOUNT: number of entries in the Authority section ARCOUNT: number of entries in the Additional section
Question Answer Authority Additional
dig options @server specify the server: which server to send the DNS query to; if unspecified, use the system default +short brief output, showing only the ANSWER section, or blank if there’s no response -4 use only an IPv4 address to connect to the server -6 use only an IPv6 address to connect to the server +tcp connect to the DNS server over TCP DNS natively uses UDP/53, and if someone forgot to open the firewall on the host or router you can use +tcp to switch the DNS query to a TCP connection if the normal query gets no response but +tcp goes through, it means the firewall isn’t open
cdflag used to turn off DNSSEC in the query DNSSEC is an extended security protocol for DNS that ensures DNS records can’t be forged (via digital signatures) If DNSSEC is managed poorly it causes DNSSEC validation to fail leading to unstable DNS resolution In that case you can turn it off with this flag if the normal query gets no response but adding +cdflag gives a correct response, it means DNSSEC is broken
Command examples # query a cache server's A record$ dig @8.8.8.8 blog.rsync.tw. a# query the domain's MX$ dig rsync.tw mx# query the domain's owner$ dig rsync.tw soa# trace mode$ dig +trace blog.rsync.tw a# tcp query mode$ dig +tcp blog.rsync.tw a# reverse IP lookup = nslookup <IP>$ dig -x 8.8.8.8 ptr# turn off DNSSEC in the query$ dig +cdflag @8.8.8.8 blog.rsync.tw a
DNS Troubleshooting Step 1: query the NS address Before you start debugging with dig, first confirm the domain’s nameserver address, because every response must come from a nameserver. If you use a domain registry or a service like Cloudflare, the nameservers belong to those providers; they can also be whatever you filled into the nameserver field at registration $ dig +short rsync.tw ns You can see which nameservers there are (which servers are responsible for the DNS records) Or work from the top down, from a higher-level DNS server $ dig +short tw ns $ dig +short @a.dns.tw edu.tw ns $ dig +short @moestar.edu.tw [target domain name] ns Why not just dig +short ntust.edu.tw? Because that would query the DNS NS record via the system’s cache server
Possible situations: Empty, no response If you get an error when querying NS, or you get a response but no data Possible situation 1: the nameserver was filled in wrong; ask the domain registry to check Possible situation 2: the domain expired and wasn’t paid for, or something is wrong with its status (check with the whois command)
The nameserver is a public DNS Some people mistake a public DNS for a nameserver and fill 8.8.8.8 into the nameserver field, but that’s wrong
Different from what you filled in The domain registry didn’t update your name to the domain authority, or you just happened to change nameservers
Step 2: query the nameserver’s data directly After confirming the NS address, send a query to the nameserver Query the domain you want to resolve. The nameserver’s response should be the newest and most complete, so whether you want to know if a record has been updated or whether the resolution is correct, you get your answers by querying the nameserver directly.
Possible problems (2): Nameservers out of sync Make sure every nameserver’s response data is correct
Nameserver not responding Means there’s a problem with the nameserver’s DNS service The DNS service may not be running, or the machine has a problem You can ping the nameserver; if it responds, it’s a DNS service problem Then you can use dig +tcp to check whether it’s a firewall problem If it responds, work toward solving the firewall problem # query the nameserver's response; you can query SOA because that record must exist$ dig @(NS IP) (domain) soa# if there's no response, ping to see whether it's a host or network problem$ ping (NS IP)# if ping responds, use +tcp to check whether it's a firewall problem$ dig +tcp @(NS IP) (domain) soa
Step 3: check the authoritative server’s answer Nameservers are usually delegated from the top down e.g. rsync.tw’s nameserver is delegated from .tw down to the ns[1-3].gandi.net nameservers
Delegation isn’t necessarily correct (the user fills it in themselves and may fill it in wrong); the upper level directly becomes the nameserver based on the user’s input Correct delegation:
Correct top-down delegation
The server gives an authoritative-server answer $ dig @ns1.gandi.net rsync# response; <<>> DiG 9.10.3-P4-Ubuntu <<>> @ns1.gandi.net rsync.tw a; (2 servers found);; global options: +cmd;; Got answer:;; ->>HEADER<<- opcode: QUERY, status: NOERROR, id: 45858;; flags: qr aa rd; QUERY: 1, ANSWER: 1, AUTHORITY: 0, ADDITIONAL: 1;; WARNING: recursion requested but not available...omit...
Without the +short flag, you can see the header section, and you can look at the AA flag in it In the response there’s “flags: qr aa rd;”, and aa = AA means an authoritative-server answer It means this server knows it manages this domain, so it responds from its zone-file data A query to a public DNS won’t have this AA flag And if a query to a nameserver has no AA, it means the admin didn’t configure the server correctly
Step 4: query the cache server (public DNS) The last step is to query the cache server’s response and see whether it’s correct. Normally all user computers get DNS data through a cache server (such as 8.8.8.8, 168.95.1.1), so we test whether it’s correct: $ dig @8.8.8.8 www.rsync.tw a
Possible problems (4) Getting stale data DNS has a TTL caching time Within the caching time, data is kept until the TTL (seconds) elapses Here you need to confirm whether every authoritative server’s query returns the newest data
Resolution fails with NXDOMAIN If everything in the query process above is fine, but these public DNS cache servers don’t respond DNSSEC may be broken In that case you need to ask your domain’s registrar to cancel your DNSKEY
What happens when DNSSEC breaks? How do you fix it? Symptoms: Possibly only the authoritative DNS server delegated to your domain can look up your A record But if you query your domain’s A record from a public DNS server (e.g. 8.8.8.8) it may return an error
Check: You can add the +cdflag option to make the DNS cache server turn off DNSSEC validation cdflag tells 8.8.8.8 that this DNS query doesn’t need DNSSEC validation
Possible cause: If you used a domain managed-DNS service and enabled DNSSEC but then changed the nameserver, this causes the DNSSEC chain validation to fail because the DNSKEY wasn’t migrated (the new nameserver doesn’t have the DNSKEY), which causes validation to fail
Fixes: Either use the interface the domain registrar provides and turn off DNSSEC Or re-sign DNSSEC on the new nameserver, then update the DNSKEY
How do you enable DNSSEC in Linux? You can edit the DNSSEC setting value in /etc/systemd/resolv.conf
What do you do if the nameserver set in /etc/resolv.conf keeps getting reset? Point it with a symbolic link to /etc/systemd/resolv.conf $ cd /etc$ rm resolv.conf$ ln -s /run/systemd/resolve/resolv.conf resolv.conf Or directly edit the DNS address in /etc/systemd/resolv.conf
How would you handle an OOM problem with a Linux process? What is the OOM Killer? In Linux, it’s responsible for watching processes that use too much memory, especially ones that consume a lot of memory very quickly To prevent memory from being exhausted, the kernel kills that process Sometimes you can’t SSH to a machine but can ping it, meaning it’s not a network failure; often the reason is that the sshd process was killed by the OOM killer The kernel uses a specific algorithm to compute a score for each process to decide which one to kill Each process’s OOM score can be found in “/proc/PID/oom_score“ After rebooting the machine, checking the system log “/var/log/messages“ you’ll find an error like “Out of Memory: Kill process 1865 (sshd)” echo -17 /proc/PID/oom_adj resolves this issue Adjustable range: 15 to -16 -17 disables it
Or change kernel parameters: sysctl -w vm.panic_on_oom=1 (default is 0)sysctl -p
What’s the difference between kill -9 and kill -15? What signal does each send? $ kill PID# signal: SIGKILL$ kill -9 PID // immediately force the program to stop# signal: SIGTERM$ kill -15 PID // notify the program to stop normally, the default signal$ kill -l lists all available signals
How do you find which signal corresponds to which number in the kill command? $ kill -l <number>
Can you explain when to use the ss command? It can output all established TCP connections The ss command lets you specify your own filter to filter out the socket info you need: # list all connections from this machine to host 192.168.0.1:$ ss -o state established dst 192.168.0.1# list all connections from this machine to port 80 on host 192.168.0.1$ ss -o state established dst 192.168.0.1:80# list all connections from host 192.168.0.2:$ ss -o state established src 192.168.0.2# list all ssh connections, including outbound ssh from this machine and inbound ssh from outside:$ ss -o state established '( dport = :ssh or sport = :ssh )'
How do you list services in Linux? Look in /etc/init.d Or systemctl list-units --type service -all sudo systemctl | grep running service --status-all
How do you view established sockets? systemctl list-sockets netstat ss

RESTful API What’s your understanding of RESTful web services? A RESTful web service is a web service architecture that follows the REST style REST (Representational State Transfer), implemented using HTTP
What is a REST resource? Everything under the REST architecture counts as a kind of resource, somewhat like an object in OOP A resource can be a text file, an HTML page, an image, or other dynamic resources A REST server provides access to these resources and lets clients use them Each resource is identified by a URI
What is a URI? A Uniform Resource Identifier, used to identify a resource in the REST architecture <protocol>://<service-name>/<ResourceType>/<ResourceID> Two kinds of URI: URN, URL URN: Uniform Resource Name Identifies a resource by a unique, persistent name
URL: Uniform Resource Locator Carries information about the resource’s location
What’s your understanding of JAX-RS? JAX-RS = Java API for RESTful Web Services
Can you name some common HTTP status codes you know? 1xx - informational response (what’s this?) 2xx - success response 3xx - redirection 4xx - client error 5xx - server error 200 OK 201 - CREATED, used with PUT or POST 304 - NOT MODIFIED, used for conditional GET requests to reduce bandwidth use; this response’s body should be empty 400 - BAD REQUEST, validation error or missing data 401 - UNAUTHORIZED, the request doesn’t contain valid authentication info 403 - FORBIDDEN, no permission to access the resource, or access is forbidden 404 - NOT FOUND, the resource method is unavailable 500 - INTERNAL SERVER ERROR, some exception thrown while the server was running 502 - BAD GATEWAY, the server couldn’t get a response from another server
Can you name some common HTTP methods you know? GET: retrieve information from the server, a read-only operation POST: used to create a resource on the server PUT: used to update or replace an existing resource on the server DELETE: used to delete a resource on the server OPTIONS: get the list of supported options for an existing resource on the server HEAD: same as GET, but sends only the status line and the header section
What’s the difference between SOAP and REST?
SOAP REST
Simple Object Access Protocol Representational State Transfer
A protocol for implementing web services An architectural design style for the web
SOAP can’t use REST REST can use SOAP as part of its implementation
Has strict standards No strict compliance required
Client and server are more tightly coupled REST clients are flexible and don’t depend on how the server is developed
Supports only XML Supports XML, JSON, MIME, text, etc.
SOAP exposes resources through service interfaces Uses URIs to expose resources
As a protocol, it defines its own security measures Inherits security measures only from the protocol it’s implemented over
What are the best practices for developing RESTful web services? Develop the REST API using the JSON data format as much as possible for receiving and returning data, because most clients and servers have built-in ways to easily read and parse JSON objects An application responding in JSON should set Content-Type to application/json Some HTTP clients look at the value of the response’s Content-Type header to parse it The request header’s Content-Type should also be set to application/json
When naming resource endpoints, use plural nouns rather than verbs; API endpoints should be short and easy to understand Verbs aren’t used because the HTTP method already describes the request’s action Common HTTP verbs/methods: GET, POST, PUT, DELETE
Use nesting to represent the hierarchy of resources e.g. GET for URI: /authors/:id/address Don’t nest too deeply
Error handling should return the application’s appropriate error code; REST also defines appropriate HTTP status codes that can be sent along for different scenarios Error codes should come with appropriate error messages to help developers take corrective action, but not too detailed, to keep attackers from learning too much 400 - Bad Request 401 - Unauthorized 403 - Forbidden 404 - Not Found 500 - Internal Server Error 502 - Bad Gateway 503 - Service Unavailable
What distributed system architectures do you know? I know of a technology used to maintain and run distributed systems, namely Kubernetes
So what is a Software Stack? It’s a collection of independent components that work together to run an application These components may include: OS, protocols, runtime environment, libraries, DB, and function calls Depending on the application you need to run, at minimum it’s the OS, DB, programming support tools, and the application
And what is a Solution Stack? To develop a web application, you need to define the target OS, web server, DB, and language Or define the OS, middleware, DB, and application, and sometimes hardware is included too Examples: BCHS OpenBSD C httpd SQLite

Apache Troubleshootinghttpd.conf misconfiguration Syntax Error On Linux, use apachectl -configtest to detect syntax errors On Windows, go to Apache’s bin directory first, then run httpd.exe -t After fixing the problem, restart Apache and recheck with the command above
Vulnerabilities Use the latest version of Apache Use a vulnerability scanner to check Keep an eye on the latest CVEs and apply patches
Apache HTTP Server LogsYou should analyze the error logs in Apache HTTP Server. They provide detailed information about any errors occurring on the web server. Paths: /var/log/apache2/error.log, /etc/apache2/apache2.conf, /etc/httpd/conf/httpd.conf By default they go into the error_log file in the log directory within the Apache install directory.You can also set in httpd.conf which types of errors to log; httpd.conf has 8 log levels of information.Besides the error log, there’s also an access log that records all requests the server has processed.These logs can also offer additional explanation of what might be causing a problem, and can supplement the information in the error log. Using the Mod_log_forensic moduleThe mod_log_forensic module is used to provide a forensic log of client requests.This includes the request before and after processing, and uses the same ID to reference the same request, so you can easily identify any problem triggered by a specific request.It can be used to analyze which requests cause the web server to crash.To enable this module, configure the following in the Apache httpd.conf file: LoadModule log_forensic_module_forensic.soLoadModule uniques_id_module modules/mod_unique_id.soForensicLog logs/forensic_log You can also use the check_forensic bash script together with the mod_log_forensic module to list any incomplete requests found in the forensic logcheck_forensic <log_file> Using the mod_whatkilledus moduleWhen things go really wrong and the Apache server crashes, the mod_whatkilledus module can be used to log detailed technical information about the crash, along with the original client request that caused it. Also, if the mod_backtrace module is enabled, this will include a backtrace showing the point of failure, which is useful for annotating the error log with a backtrace once certain conditions are met On Unix systems, these modules only work if the --enable-exception-hook flag was enabled in the httpd build. On Windows there’s no special requirement
Documentation for mod_whatkilledus and mod_backtrace: https://emptyhammock.com/projects/httpd/diag/quick-start.html
Using third-party modulesUsing third-party modules can cause problems when installing Apache HTTP ServerSo you should disable third-party modules and check whether the problem can be reproduced; if disabling the modules resolves it, re-enable each module one by one to identify which one is the cause Running Apache HTTP Server as a single process and using a debugging toolA typical Apache HTTP Server install runs multiple processesBut for troubleshooting it’s best to run as a single processYou can use the X option when starting Apache$ httpd -X makes Apache start in single-process mode, meaning Apache won’t fork new children or detach from the terminalThis way all traffic and communication go through a single process, so you can run apache httpd under a debugger (e.g. gdb), get the backtrace from the crash, and force the server to dump a core $ gdb httpd Then with gdb you first set breakpoints, then single-step through to see line by line where the error might be Script execution problemsDynamic content is usually served by scripts that Apache HTTP Server runs via the mod_cgi moduleThis module has its own logging mechanism to record any errors that occur during script execution Once the ScriptLog directive is enabled, mod_cgi logs the output of any script that doesn’t run as expected, includingthe server response code, the request received, and any response made to the client To enable this, edit the httpd.conf file and specify the ScriptLog directive and the location to save the logScriptLog logs/cgi_log IIS TroubleshootingServer-side security What security recommendations are there for the server side? Remove unnecessary services A default install sometimes installs many unnecessary features, e.g. remote registry, print server, etc. The more services, the more open ports, so more risk is exposed Turn off non-essential services on the server
Ensure protection for remote access If a web admin needs to log in to the web server remotely, use tunneling and encryption protocols to ensure the remote connection is properly protected Use a security token on the device or software Remote access should be limited to a specific number of IPs and accounts
Separate development/test/production environments Because it’s easier and faster for developers to develop newer versions of a web app on the production server, it’s common for web app development and testing to be done directly on the production server itself. You might find an updated version of a specific site on the web, or find content under /test/, /new/, or other similar subdirectories that shouldn’t be known to the public So if you develop, test, and run production on the same server, and permissions aren’t set well and security is easily overlooked in early development, the site is easy to break into
Web app content and server script security Web app or site files should sit on a separate partition or drive from the OS system files and log files because if an attacker gains access to the web directory, they might use other vulnerabilities to escalate privileges and access data across the whole disk
Ensure proper permissions and privileges Always assign the least privilege needed to run a particular network service
Install all patches on time Monitor or audit the server You should regularly monitor and review all network service logs, website access logs, DB server logs (e.g. Microsoft SQL Server, MySQL, Oracle), and OS logs If you find strange activity in the logs, resolve it immediately
User account management Disable unused default accounts the userdel command
Set the correct permissions for each account
Remove unused modules and applications Apache installs many predefined modules by default A typical web server won’t use these modules, so you need to turn them off to prevent attacks targeting such modules
Use the security tools provided by the network server software Microsoft publishes many tools to help admins secure their IIS web server install Apache also provides the mod_security module
Use an external scanner nessus nikto or other vulnerability scanners
Log filesSystem error information - /var/logs/syslog or /var/logs/messagesLogs related to login credentials - /var/logs/secure or /var/logs/auth.log (Debian)Which service’s logs go where? - /etc/rsyslog.conf, placed under /etc/rsyslog.d Syslog levels SyscallC/C++ What happens if a program uses malloc but doesn’t free? The heap memory stays occupied until the program ends; it isn’t released automatically

entry.title: Single Event Upset and 128 Candidate Keys | Cosmic Bit Blunder | GaianSpace CTF 2026
entry.content:
🌐 中文版：繁體中文 This is the first post of the GaianSpace CTF 2026 chapter “05-rad-hard-rampage.” The whole series is beautifully designed: four challenges, each mapping exactly to one of the four real failure mechanisms that space radiation causes in electronics: Single Event Upset (SEU), Single Event Latch-up (SEL), Total Ionizing Dose (TID), and Displacement Damage (DDD). I’m writing one post per challenge.
The other three posts: Single Event Latch-up / Lunar Latch-up、A Logic Gate Shorted by Radiation / Ionized Transistangle、Sensor Drift / Degradift The backdrop here: a high-energy proton passed through the flight computer and flipped exactly one bit in the key. This is very common in space, where high-energy particles and radiation easily cause bit flips or errors in electronics and signals.
What the challenge is about
High in the Foundation One orbit, a single cosmic-ray proton punched through the flight computer and flipped exactly one bit in the key that protects the mission log. The log still decrypts to garbage. The reliability team wants the log back, and they are sure the rest of the key survived intact.
In plain terms: high in orbit, a cosmic-ray proton punched through Foundation One’s flight computer and flipped exactly one bit in the key that protects the mission log. The log now decrypts to garbage. The reliability team wants it back, and they’re sure the rest of the key is intact. The on-call engineer’s instinct is: “the whole key is toast, just rewrite a fresh one”, but the challenge warns that doing so would lose the log along with it (change the key and the already-encrypted ciphertext can never be decrypted again). Only two files are given:
cipher.bin: 32 bytes, the encrypted mission log (AES, single-block scheme). corrupted.key: 16 bytes, the damaged 128-bit key.
Flag format: GAIANSPACE{...}
First, figure out what a “Single Event Upset” actually changedSingle Event Upset (SEU) is the most classic radiation effect in space electronics: a high-energy particle passes through a memory cell and, in that instant, knocks over the stored charge, flipping one bit from 0 to 1 or 1 to 0. The data is changed, but the circuit itself isn’t damaged, so rewrite it and it recovers. For this challenge, the key inference is: since only one bit is wrong, there are only 128 possible correct keys. A 128-bit key has only 128 bit positions. The correct key must be corrupted.key with one of its bits flipped back, and that search space is small enough to brute-force directly, which matches the challenge’s blunt hint, “try them all.” Flip each bit back and see which one decodes to readable textThe challenge says “AES, single-block scheme,” i.e. ECB mode with no IV needed. The approach is direct: for each of the 128 candidate keys, flip one bit back, AES-128-ECB decrypt cipher.bin, then count how many of the resulting bytes are printable ASCII. import subprocesskey = open('corrupted.key','rb').read()results = []for i in range(128): k = bytearray(key) k[i // 8] ^= (1 << (i % 8)) # flip bit i back out = subprocess.run( ["openssl","enc","-d","-aes-128-ecb","-K",bytes(k).hex(), "-nopad","-in","cipher.bin"], capture_output=True).stdout printable = sum(32 <= c < 127 for c in out) results.append((printable, i, bytes(k), out))results.sort(reverse=True)
Of the 128 candidates, 127 decode to random noise (printable count drifting between 5 and 19), and only flipping bit 50 (byte 6, bit 2, d2 → d6) decodes a full 30 consecutive printable characters, standing out from the noise on its own:
Why is this signal so clean and easy to spot? Because AES has an avalanche effect: if the key is right, the whole block reverts to correct plaintext, and if even one key bit is wrong, the whole block is unrecognizable. So you don’t even need to know what the flag looks like. The printable-character count alone is enough to pick out the right answer. The decoded contentDecrypting with the repaired key gives: GAIANSPACE{s1ngle_event_upset}\x02\x02
That trailing \x02\x02 is PKCS#7 padding (padding length 2). Strip it and you get exactly a 30-character flag; add the 2 padding bytes and it’s exactly 32 bytes, matching the ciphertext length perfectly. That’s effectively a second layer of validation, since only the correct key yields valid PKCS#7 padding, confirming once more that bit 50 was the one that got flipped. FlagGAIANSPACE{s1ngle_event_upset}
Takeaways The challenge’s physical constraint directly determines the solution. “Only one bit is wrong” compresses “guess the whole key” ($2^{128}$, impossible) down to “128 possibilities” (runs in a second). When reading a challenge, first convert the conditions into a search-space size, then decide whether to write a brute-forcer. Many crypto challenges that look brutal are really just a tiny enumeration. AES’s avalanche effect makes filtering extremely reliable. Right key → whole block correct, wrong key → whole block garbage, with no grey zone in between. So a crude metric like “printable-character count” is enough to uniquely pick the answer, without knowing anything about the plaintext first. PKCS#7 padding is free secondary validation. The end of the decryption is exactly a valid padding pattern, giving near-certainty you picked the right key. With block-cipher challenges, glance at the padding after decrypting.

entry.title: Dissecting NASA's HDTN Architecture: How Does Space DTN Actually Work?
entry.content:
🌐 中文版：繁體中文
Preface: from the concept of DTN to a space network that actually worksIn the previous post, Why Space Networking Needs DTN: From TCP/IP’s Limits to Deep-Space Networks, I laid out the most fundamental differences between space networks and the terrestrial Internet. On Earth, we usually expect a complete, immediately-usable path between source and destination. Even if a packet is occasionally lost along the way, TCP can handle it through a whole set of mechanisms like ACK, timeout, and retransmission. But in space, a disconnection doesn’t necessarily mean a fault. For example, the situation might be: a satellite flying out of a ground station’s visible range, a lunar rover entering a crater, or a spacecraft temporarily shutting off its comms module to save energy. Connections between nodes can also be affected by orbital position, celestial occlusion, antenna direction, and communication schedules. So a space network can’t only look at is there a path to the destination right now? It must further consider: when is the next opportunity to forward data?, until then, which node should hold the data?, and if the contact window suddenly vanishes, how is transmission resumed? These are the problems Delay/Disruption-Tolerant Networking (DTN) tries to solve. My previous post already introduced DTN’s most core operating model: Store → Carry → Forward
But that’s still a relatively abstract concept. Because if we really want to deploy DTN on the ISS, satellites, lunar relay stations, or even future deep-space networks, what software components are needed behind the scenes? And there are many questions:
After data enters a node, how does the system decide whether to send immediately or temporarily write to disk?When a contact window appears, who’s responsible for telling the system to release the data again?When a path suddenly drops, how does the system recompute the next hop?
High-rate Delay Tolerant Networking (HDTN), developed by NASA Glenn Research Center, is exactly an implementation that turns DTN from an old abstract concept into an engineering system. Let’s keep reading. [1][2] What is HDTN?HDTN stands for High-rate Delay Tolerant Networking. It isn’t a new protocol unrelated to DTN, but a DTN implementation designed for high-bandwidth needs. Recall that DTN solves the reliable-transport problem in space networks:
Nodes aren’t always connected Communication delays can be very long The network topology changes over time Data may have to stay at a relay node for a while The communication path may suddenly drop mid-transfer
But as laser comms, high-resolution imagery, scientific instrument data, and large file transfers increase, the system faces another problem:
Even if DTN can tolerate disconnection, can it transfer large amounts of data quickly when a contact window appears?
Early DTN implementations mostly ran in resource-constrained environments, prioritizing stability and mission needs over extremely high throughput. However, future space missions need not just the ability to transmit, but to transmit as much data as possible within a limited contact window. So NASA developed HDTN to improve DTN’s processing efficiency through modern hardware, parallel processing, and a modular architecture. [1][2] Why does NASA need High-rate DTN?In a Technical Memorandum released in 2022, NASA Glenn Research Center used the International Space Station (ISS) as the test and integration scenario for HDTN. The ISS does have computers, but not just computers; it’s a complex environment with many subsystems (an onboard computer usually has a great many subsystems), science payloads, radio equipment, and ground networks. [1] When science data is sent from the ISS back to a research team, it may pass through multiple nodes: Science instrument on the ISS ↓Joint Station LAN (JSL) ↓ Comms equipment ↓Tracking and Data Relay Satellite (TDRS) ↓ Ground station ↓ Ground network ↓ Research team
The above is just one possible delivery path. Also, different data has different needs. Some may be software updates, some telemetry, some large science files, and some may include imagery and streaming content. Each kind of data differs in size, priority, and bandwidth need. And the ISS keeps moving in orbit, so the comms links won’t stay permanently stable. Some links may be temporarily available, and may suddenly drop. This means the ISS network needs to simultaneously have:
High throughput Local storage capability Routing management Disconnection recovery Interoperability between different DTN implementations Support for different underlying transports
HDTN’s goal is to build a high-speed DTN system that can automatically manage data flow in such environments. [1][2] Understanding HDTN through a logistics systemLet’s return to the logistics analogy from the previous post, which compared DTN to an international logistics system (like DHL). The traditional Internet is more like a real-time phone call: Dial → Establish connection → Real-time call
DTN is more like logistics delivery: Ship → Consolidate → Store → Transport → Transfer → Final delivery
When shipping a package, the sender and recipient don’t need to be online at the same time. The trucks, planes, ports, and distribution centers don’t need to form a complete transport line at the same second; the package can stay at a logistics center and wait for the next truck or plane. HDTN can be understood as the automated warehousing and dispatch platform behind this logistics system:
Logistics system HDTN
Package Bundle
Consolidation center entrance Ingress
Warehouse Storage
Flight and truck schedule Contact Plan
Dispatch and route planning Scheduler / Router
Shipping dock Egress
Next logistics center Next Hop
The actual truck, plane, or ship used Convergence Layer
This analogy should resonate, and you can probably see that HDTN doesn’t just send data out. What it really does is decide, based on future usable communication opportunities, whether data should be forwarded immediately now, held temporarily, or rerouted another way. HDTN’s core architectureI personally feel that text descriptions alone aren’t as clear as looking directly at Fig. 1 in the original paper. The figure below is the HDTN modules interaction, an overview of how all the internal modules interact. [1]
Fig. 1. HDTN modules interaction. Source: [1]
From this figure you can intuitively see that HDTN’s core components roughly include Ingress, Storage, Scheduler, Router, and Egress, with BPGen, BPSink, a Web Interface, the Contact Plan, and a CGR Client coordinating externally. [1] This separation of responsibilities is quite similar to the mainstream microservices or event-driven architecture in modern cloud systems, where each component focuses on a specific task and exchanges state through events. BundleIn an ordinary IP network, we often use the packet as the basic data unit. But in DTN, the main data unit is the bundle. A bundle can be understood as a standard shipping container in the DTN world. It contains not just application data, but also the source, destination, creation time, lifetime, and other metadata. Bundle├── Source Endpoint├── Destination Endpoint├── Creation Timestamp├── Lifetime├── Payload└── Additional Metadata
In a traditional network, a packet is usually expected to be forwarded immediately, but a bundle is different. From the start, it’s designed to be held at a node, wait, re-forward, and even cross multiple non-continuous contact windows. It’s also specifically noted that a bundle’s size isn’t fixed. Besides measuring how many bits can be transferred per second, you must also consider how many bundles the system can process per second. [1] In other words, the challenge of achieving high-speed DTN isn’t just network-card speed, because even with sufficient bandwidth, if every bundle requires heavy parsing, memory allocation, and state management, the CPU can still become the bottleneck. IngressIngress is the first stop after a bundle enters an HDTN node. It receives the bundle, parses the header, confirms the data’s source and destination, and decides the next step based on the current link state. The simplest logic is: Receive Bundle │ ▼Parse source and destination │ ▼Is the next hop usable right now? │ ├── Yes ──▶ Hand directly to Egress │ └── No ──▶ Send to Storage to hold
If the link is currently usable, Ingress can use a cut-through forwarding style, handing the bundle directly to Egress, reducing unnecessary disk I/O and I/O wait. If the link is currently unusable, the bundle first enters Storage. This is the first key decision in Store-Carry-Forward:
Can I forward now, or must I store first?
StorageIn an ordinary network, a router usually doesn’t hold packets for long; ideally a packet is forwarded immediately after reaching the router. If the queue fills up, packets may simply be dropped and left for the upper-layer protocol to handle again. But in DTN, waiting may be a normal state. Suppose a lunar probe needs to send data via a relay satellite, but the next contact window won’t appear for two hours. In that case, the system can’t simply drop the data, nor retry infinitely. Storage‘s job is to let the bundle safely stay on the node, waiting for the next transmission opportunity. Bundle arrives at node │ ▼No usable link right now │ ▼Write to Storage │ ▼Wait for LinkUp event │ ▼Release Bundle from Storage │ ▼Send to Egress
HDTN’s Storage uses a multi-threaded implementation and can spread data across multiple disks. [1] The reason is intuitive: when large amounts of data enter a node at once, disk I/O and data management itself can become a performance bottleneck, so the Storage module is quite important. Unlike a backup component on terrestrial networks that can always be scaled out, it’s a core part of the space DTN architecture. Contact PlanOn an ordinary terrestrial network, a router usually chooses a path based on the current network state (SDN), but a space network adds a very special dimension: time. The position changes of satellites, space stations, lunar relay stations, and ground stations are often predictable. A given link may not exist now, but appear ten minutes later, and disappear again five minutes after that. So DTN needs to handle a special piece of data: the Contact Plan. The Contact Plan can be understood as a timetable of future contact windows. [ { "source": 1, "destination": 2, "startTime": 100, "endTime": 300, "dataRate": 1000000 }]
This means: Node 1 → Node 2can transfer data between times 100 and 300with a usable rate of 1 Mbps
In a real mission, the Contact Plan may contain more nodes, more windows, and different link rates. The biggest difference from terrestrial networks is: space routing isn’t judged only by “spatial topology,” but must also consider temporal topology. Scheduler and RouterWith a Contact Plan, the system also needs components to manage data flow according to the schedule. In this HDTN architecture, the Scheduler reads the Contact Plan and emits events based on link state: [1] linkUplinkDown
When Ingress receives a linkUp event, it knows a destination is currently usable and can hand the bundle directly to Egress. When Storage receives a linkUp event, it can also start releasing previously-held bundles to Egress. Conversely, if a link drops, the system stops transmitting and reevaluates subsequent paths. On the other hand, the Router‘s job is to compute the next hop. The Router decides which node a bundle should go to next based on the Contact Plan and destination, then notifies Egress to update the Outduct. Contact Plan │ ▼Compute feasible paths │ ▼Choose Next Hop │ ▼Emit RouteUpdate │ ▼Egress updates Outduct
HDTN’s routing mindset isn’t quite the same as ordinary shortest-path algorithms. An ordinary BFS or Dijkstra might only ask:
Which path is shortest right now?
But space DTN must also ask:
Which path will appear at the right time?How long can this window last?Is the usable bandwidth enough for this batch of bundles?If this window is missed, how long until the next opportunity?
This is also the core concept of Contact Graph Routing (CGR); see the previous post too. Version differences: the division of responsibilities between Scheduler and RouterA version difference should be added here. The Technical Memorandum describes Scheduler and Router separately: [1]
The Scheduler reads the Contact Plan The Scheduler emits linkUp and linkDown The Router communicates with the CGR Client The Router passes RouteUpdate to Egress
But in NASA’s currently-public HDTN GitHub README, the Router’s responsibilities have been adjusted. The README currently mentions: [3]
The Router manages link-availability state based on the Contact Plan The Router uses Dijkstra’s algorithm to compute the next hop The Router recomputes paths after a link suddenly drops or the Contact Plan updates The Router passes RouteUpdate to Egress
So when reading the HDTN architecture, note the paper’s publication time and the code version. But regardless of how the module boundaries shift, the overall design spirit hasn’t changed:
Manage link state based on the Contact Plan, and recompute a bundle’s next hop when network events occur.
EgressEgress is a bundle’s last stop before leaving an HDTN node. It receives bundles from Ingress or Storage, and sends them to the appropriate Outduct and next hop based on the Router’s computed result. Ingress ─────┐ │ ▼ Egress ─────▶ Outduct ─────▶ Next Hop ▲ │Storage ─────┘
In HDTN, two terms describe the direction of data in and out:
Name Purpose
Induct Entry point for receiving external data
Outduct Exit for sending data to the next hop
You can think of the Induct as a logistics center’s unloading dock and the Outduct as its shipping dock. The same node may have multiple Outducts, each leading to a different next hop. The Router’s job is to tell Egress which exit to use now. Event-Driven Architecture: what to do when a link suddenly drops?Space networks don’t always run according to the ideal schedule; there are too many influencing factors. Even if the Contact Plan predicts a link should be usable, the real environment can still have:
Sudden signal-quality degradation Antenna-tracking failure Temporary comms-equipment anomaly A link dropping early A Contact Plan update A next-hop node not responding
So HDTN can’t rely only on static scheduling; it also needs an event-driven architecture to notify other modules when state changes. HDTN uses ZeroMQ pub-sub sockets to pass events. [1] What’s that? For example, when Egress finds a link has suddenly vanished, it can emit a LinkStatus change notification: Egress detects link drop │ ▼Emit LinkStatus Change │ ▼Scheduler updates link state │ ├──▶ Send linkDown to Ingress │ ├──▶ Send linkDown to Storage │ └──▶ Notify Router to recompute path
After the Router recomputes the next hop, it notifies Egress to update the Outduct. Notice this flow is a lot like the event-driven architecture in modern distributed systems: Event occurs ↓Publish state change ↓Subscribers receive notification ↓Each module updates its behavior
This design means HDTN doesn’t have to cram all logic into one large program, and lets different modules keep relatively clear responsibility boundaries. Convergence LayerAs the previous post said, the Bundle Protocol isn’t meant to completely replace TCP, UDP, or other underlying protocols; it’s more like an overlay network, handling cross-node, cross-time data-forwarding logic. But when a bundle actually has to move from one node to another, it still needs to ride on some actual transport. That’s the purpose of the Convergence Layer. Application Data ↓Bundle Protocol ↓Convergence Layer ↓Underlying Transport / Link
Using the logistics system again:
Network concept Logistics analogy
Bundle Standard shipping container
Bundle Protocol International logistics rules
Convergence Layer The actual truck, plane, or ship used
Physical Link Roads, air routes, or shipping routes
HDTN supports several Convergence Layers, including: [1][3]
UDP Convergence Layer Simplified TCP (STCP) TCP Convergence Layer Version 3 (TCPCLv3) TCP Convergence Layer Version 4 (TCPCLv4) Licklider Transmission Protocol (LTP)
Each Convergence Layer suits different scenarios:
Convergence Layer Characteristic
UDP Simple structure, but doesn’t guarantee reliable transport on its own
STCP Relatively lean, suited to efficient data sending
TCPCL Sends bundles over TCP, supporting fuller DTN node connection management
LTP Designed for high-delay and intermittent links, suited to space comms
LTPAmong the Convergence Layers HDTN supports, LTP is particularly worth noting. LTP stands for Licklider Transmission Protocol, a transport protocol designed for long-delay environments, especially suited to scenarios like deep-space comms where ordinary low-delay assumptions don’t hold. [6] Suppose a link’s one-way delay is two seconds, so the round-trip time (RTT) can reach four seconds. In that case, if the system stops and waits for a response after every small chunk, overall throughput will be terrible. So HDTN’s LTP implementation needs to maintain many sessions simultaneously to keep the link continuously transmitting. Session 1 ─────▶ Wait for ACKSession 2 ─────▶ Wait for ACKSession 3 ─────▶ Wait for ACKSession 4 ─────▶ Wait for ACK...
While an earlier session is still waiting for a response, later sessions can keep sending data. Test results indicate that once link delay exceeds one second, increasing the number of concurrent LTP sessions is an important factor in achieving gigabit-level data rates. [1] This is a lot like the pipeline concept in ordinary high-bandwidth networks: don’t let the whole link sit idle waiting for a single response. How is HDTN different from an ordinary message queue?If you’ve used Amazon SQS, RabbitMQ, Kafka, or other message queues, HDTN’s architecture may feel somewhat familiar. They do share some things in common:
Message Queue HDTN
Message Bundle
Queue Storage
Producer Bundle Source
Consumer Destination Node
Broker DTN Node
Retry Retransmission
Routing Rule Contact Plan / Router
Durable Storage Bundle Storage
But the problems HDTN faces are more special. An ordinary message queue usually assumes the underlying network is roughly available. Even with a brief disconnection, the service is expected to recover in a relatively short time. HDTN, however, must accept:
The network may not exist for a long time The next connection may be minutes or hours away Nodes keep moving Contact windows are predictable but very limited Bandwidth, delay, and error rate are highly asymmetric A relay node itself may also be temporarily offline
So HDTN isn’t just moving a message queue into space; it redesigns how data is stored, routed, scheduled, and transmitted in an extreme network environment. HDTN’s complete data flowStringing the earlier components together, a bundle’s lifecycle in an HDTN node is roughly as follows. Scenario 1: the link is currently usableBundle arrives at Induct │ ▼Ingress parses header │ ▼Confirm next-hop link usable │ ▼Hand directly to Egress │ ▼Egress chooses Outduct │ ▼Bundle sent to Next Hop
This reduces unnecessary Storage I/O and suits data that can be forwarded immediately. Scenario 2: the link is currently unusableBundle arrives at Induct │ ▼Ingress parses header │ ▼Confirm next-hop link unusable │ ▼Write to Storage │ ▼Wait for linkUp event │ ▼Storage releases Bundle │ ▼Egress sends to Next Hop
This is the most typical Store-Carry-Forward flow in DTN. Scenario 3: a sudden drop mid-transferEgress detects link drop │ ▼Publish LinkStatus Change │ ▼Update link state │ ▼Stop releasing Bundle │ ▼Router recomputes path │ ▼Egress updates Outduct │ ▼Wait for the next usable transmission opportunity
For HDTN, a disconnection isn’t a system crash, but another event to handle. Viewing it through a distributed-systems lensFrom a software-engineering standpoint, the most interesting thing about HDTN isn’t just space comms, but that it’s essentially an event-driven distributed system. It needs to handle:
Asynchronous events Durable storage Pipelining Route updates Backpressure Retry State synchronization Fault recovery Multiple underlying transports Interoperability between different DTN implementations
These problems aren’t rare in existing cloud architectures, but space networks push the conditions to a more extreme direction. A ground system might treat a few seconds of timeout as a service anomaly, while a space system may have to incorporate several minutes of waiting into its normal flow. Another difference is that a ground system may require a service to recover connectivity as fast as possible, but a space system must accept that no usable path exists at all right now. One last observation: time in terrestrial networks is usually just a performance metric, while in space DTN, time itself is part of the routing topology. ISS testing: HDTN is more than a theoretical architectureThe Technical Memorandum also compiles interoperability and performance tests between HDTN and other DTN implementations, including: [1]
Interoperability tests between HDTN and DTN Marshall Enterprise (DTNME) Bundle Protocol Version 6 (BPv6) and Version 7 (BPv7) tests Transmission tests of different Convergence Layers Simulated delay and packet loss Using HDTN as a gateway node Simulations with the ISS network topology LTP long-delay link tests
One point worth mentioning is that, to find the cause of the low data rate in the SDIL tests, they later ran a series of “4-box” tests locally at GRC to simulate the data flow between ISS payload, ISS onboard gateway, ground gateway, and ground node. [1] These tests compared not only protocols but also different deployment environments: including a fully KVM-based virtual machine, an LXC container, native hardware (bare metal), and a ZBook + KVM image combination close to the actual ISS onboard gateway. [1] The result is interesting: although iperf3 showed these environments all theoretically had decent baseline bandwidth, when actually running end-to-end DTN tests, the KVM VM environment showed significant performance loss; in contrast, LXC performed closer to native hardware, and native hardware could reach near line rate. [1] Also, once they included the ZBook + KVM gateway image the ISS actually uses, performance dropped noticeably again; even after trying to adjust the VM’s core and memory configuration, the improvement was slight. [1] In other words, an important takeaway from this experiment isn’t just that HDTN can run, but that the virtualization layer itself can become a bottleneck. The authors explicitly note at the end that these local tests made them suspect the low data rate in the earlier SDIL tests might not have been solely a VPN or DTNME-version issue, and that KVM itself may also affect performance more significantly than originally expected. [1] Another notable test simulated a link with about two seconds of one-way delay and four seconds of RTT. The results show that simply increasing bandwidth isn’t enough. The system also needs to tune LTP sessions, pipeline limit, buffer, and other parameters to maintain higher throughput under high-delay conditions. [1] This illustrates one thing:
Space network performance isn’t a single-NIC or single-protocol problem, but a systems-engineering problem for the whole data-processing pipeline.
HDTN project statusNASA has made the HDTN source code public on GitHub: [3] GitHub: nasa/HDTN The currently-public project is written in C++ and built with CMake. It appears to support multiple operating systems and hardware platforms, including Linux, Windows, macOS, FreeBSD, OpenBSD, Raspbian, and ARM64. [3] Main dependencies include: CMakeBoostZeroMQOpenSSLC++ Compiler
The main modules currently in the code include: IngressStorageRouterEgressTelemetry Command Interface
A test method is also provided; you can observe HDTN’s data flow with tcpdump and Wireshark: sudo tcpdump -i lo -vv -s0 port 4558 -w hdtn-traffic.pcap
Next Hop: does HDTN have to run on a large server?Having understood HDTN’s basic architecture, a natural question arises:
Since HDTN is already split into Ingress, Storage, Router, and Egress modules, does it have to run fully on a high-end x86 server?
This doubt is reasonable; deep-space exploration intuitively seems to pair with high-end servers. But future space missions can’t rely only on large servers. Future lunar bases, satellites, probes, ground stations, and edge nodes may have different:
CPU architectures Memory capacities Storage space Energy constraints Thermal conditions Bandwidth needs Mission roles
So the paper’s future work mentions some directions worth researching:
Can HDTN be ported to the ARM platform? Can it run on a Raspberry Pi? Can different modules be split across multiple devices? Can an edge device become a space DTN node? How much does performance drop under limited hardware resources?
NASA has since also researched the Raspberry Pi and ARM platforms. [3] I’ll leave this for the next post to explore:
How to run NASA HDTN on a Raspberry Pi?From ARM porting and CMake build modifications to distributed deployment
ClosingThe previous post introduced why DTN suits the space environment. This one further breaks down NASA HDTN’s software architecture, explaining that Store-Carry-Forward isn’t an abstract term but an engineering flow completed by multiple components together. HDTN’s core components include:
Component Function
Bundle A data unit that can be passed across time and nodes
Ingress Receives bundles and decides whether to forward immediately
Storage Holds bundles when a link is down
Contact Plan Describes future usable contact windows
Scheduler / Router Manages link state and computes the next hop
Egress Hands bundles to the correct Outduct
Convergence Layer Lets bundles ride on actual transport protocols
ZeroMQ Events Synchronizes state when a link fails or the schedule changes
To summarize HDTN’s design spirit in one sentence:
HDTN doesn’t assume the network always exists; it lets data wait safely when the network doesn’t exist, and keep moving forward when the next communication opportunity appears.
This architecture isn’t only applicable to the ISS; it may also become an important underlying capability for future lunar, Mars, and deep-space infrastructure.
References Daniel Raible, Rachel Dudukovich, Brian Tomko, Nadia Kortas, Blake LaFuente, Dennis Iannicca, et al., Developing High Performance Space Networking Capabilities for the International Space Station and Beyond, NASA/TM-20220011407, 2022.NASA Technical Reports Server
NASA Glenn Research Center, High-Rate Delay Tolerant Networking (HDTN).NASA Official Website
NASA, High-rate Delay Tolerant Network (HDTN) Software.GitHub: nasa/HDTN
IETF, RFC 9171: Bundle Protocol Version 7.RFC 9171
IETF, RFC 9174: Delay-Tolerant Networking TCP Convergence-Layer Protocol Version 4.RFC 9174
IETF, RFC 5326: Licklider Transmission Protocol, Specification.RFC 5326

entry.title: Problem-Solving Notes | Dynamic Programming (DP)
entry.content:
🌐 中文版：繁體中文
IntroEven before I started grinding LeetCode, I’d heard how terrifying DP problems are, so before actually starting on problems like these I wanted to organize my DP knowledge.
While reading material online I found this article explains it really well, so I highly recommend reading this article first. The author mentions that to understand DP, patience matters, and you also need to be comfortable with recursion, because DP problems are usually solved with recursion.
What is Dynamic Programming (DP)?Here I have to mention the conclusion from that article: Dynamic Programming is a tool to help make recursive code more efficient. So the author also believes you shouldn’t, when facing a problem, first try to identify whether it’s a DP problem. Instead, first judge whether recursion is needed, and on top of that recursion you then think about how the recursive code might be very wasteful, so there should be room to improve the answer, and the way to improve it is through Dynamic Programming.
DP is a way to improve an existing solution!
Next I’ll introduce the steps for using this tool. There are 4 steps, and I’ll explain them step by step using one problem. Problem: LeetCode 62. Unique Paths
This problem gives an m x n grid with a robot at the top-left corner. Each move the robot can go down or right by one cell, and the robot tries to reach the Finish cell at the bottom-right. We need to find how many unique path combinations are possible. Step 1: RecursionThis step is usually the most important and the key to laying out the whole solving plan. What you need to do is return to the purest central idea: recursion, which is essentially proposing a brute-force solution first.
At the same time this convinces the interviewer that you know what recursive relation this problem uses, meaning you have to find the recursive relation first before there’s room for later improvement.
First, this problem asks how many paths can ultimately reach the end. So what do we need to know first? We need to know how many paths there are from the start to any given cell. Looking at the figure above, we can see that from the start grid[0][0] to its bottom-right cell grid[1][1] you can come from the right or from below (the problem restricts moves to right or down), two routes total, while going straight right from the start or straight down each has only one route. The example above should also show that for any cell [i][j], its previous step could be:
moving down from the cell above, i.e. [i-1][j] moving over from the cell to the left, i.e. [i][j-1]
And moving one cell from above or from the left are on the same path, so the count doesn’t change. So we know that for any cell [i][j], the number of paths from the start to it is [i-1][j] + [i][j-1].
One more example also verifies this: if we want to move to grid[2][2], the total number of paths must be grid[1][2] + grid[2][1].
