If we write the above idea as a recursion like below, the recursion’s termination condition occurs when it reaches the row right next to the start or the column below it, where it stops. class Solution {public: int uniquePaths(int m, int n) { if(m==1 || n==1) return 1; return uniquePaths(m-1,n) + uniquePaths(m,n-1); }};
But running this you’ll find an error: Time Limit Exceeded! That means there’s something that needs improving, so on to step two.
Step 2: Recursion + MemoizationThis step is where DP actually begins, but not every inefficient problem needs DP, so first weigh whether this problem is worth solving with DP. Based on the result of step one, you only need to use DP if the following conditions both hold:
Overlapping subproblems: you solve the same subproblem multiple times An optimal substructure: by obtaining the optimal solution of each subproblem, you can get the optimal solution of the whole problem
If during an interview or while solving you find these two can’t be fully satisfied, then you shouldn’t use DP (or the approach introduced in this article). You might be able to use other techniques like backtracking instead.
So how do we confirm this problem satisfies these two conditions?
I drew the recursion tree of Step 1 below. You can see that not all subproblems actually overlap, but you can still see a lot of repeated computation, like uniquePaths(2, 6) and uniquePaths(2, 5), so it can still be seen as having overlapping subproblems. Recursion tree of the Step 1 solutionYou can zoom in to look
The second condition is also satisfied, because we can use [m-1][n] and [m][n-1] to get the optimal solution of [m][n].
So the goal of this step is simple: make the repeated computation happen only once, and find a way to safely store it (memoization).
The purpose of storing is to let subsequent repeated computations be conveniently looked up, reducing the amount of computation. So for the later lookups in storage, we also want to get as close to $O(1)$ complexity as possible, using an array or a hash table depending on the situation. class Solution {public: vector<vector<int>> dp; int helper(int m, int n){ if(dp[m][n]){ return dp[m][n]; } else if(m==1 || n==1) { dp[m][n]=1; return dp[m][n]; } dp[m][n] = helper(m-1,n) + helper(m,n-1); return dp[m][n]; } int uniquePaths(int m, int n) { dp = vector<vector<int>>(m + 1, vector<int>(n + 1, 0)); return helper(m,n); }};
This is the corrected result. It mainly uses a 2D vector to store the computed path counts, and since we need to initialize the array size to m+1 x n+1 (to avoid out-of-bounds access here), we split it into two functions. For this problem there aren’t many changes needed; compared to the original logic we only change two places:
store the result of a recursive call when a recursive call already exists in the array, return the stored value (i.e. the result of helper(m,n) is already stored in dp[m][n])
Running it again now, you’ll find Submit Accepted.
And the time complexity of this run is $O(M \times N)$, which is a big efficiency boost compared to step one’s $O(2^{M+N})$ (because each level of the recursion decomposes the problem into two subproblems). Although the time complexity dropped, the space complexity used went up, but this also shows that DP is an approach that trades space for time. This is actually very worthwhile, because the space complexity of doing so is mostly linear growth, yet it can improve time complexity exponentially.
So the progress so far is: first being able to propose a brute-force recursive approach, then improving the earlier approach with extra memory! (For an interview, getting to this step is already great.)So is there anywhere we can optimize further? That’s step three.
Step 3: Iteration + TabulationNormally, if there’s no obvious performance improvement in the previous step (or the interviewer wants you to improve your answer further), you’ll need step three. This step uses Tabulation rather than Memoization, and implements it with Iteration rather than Recursion.
But whether it’s Tabulation or Memoization, their goal is the same: store earlier computation results and retrieve them when they’re recomputed later.
The difference between the two is mainly in how the data is stored. Tabulation mainly stores via arrays (usually 2D arrays), while Memoization usually stores via sets, hash tables, etc. So Tabulation iterates over each array through iteration, while Memoization relies on recursive calls. This change won’t necessarily improve time or space complexity, but the key point is: using the iterative array approach can accommodate a larger input size without being limited by the maximum call stack depth of recursive calls (too deep a call stack risks a stack overflow).
So looking back at the original Unique Paths problem, if we want to use iteration, we can iterate in reverse via a loop.
Look at the right side of this figure. In principle it walks from the bottom-right to the top-left. The reason the author chooses to start from the second-to-last row and second-to-last column cell and work backward is that the bottom row and the rightmost column all have a walkable path count of 1. So for grid[1][5], the number of steps to reach it from the new start equals grid[2][5] plus grid[1][6], giving us the relation $F(m,n) = F(m+1, n) + F(m, n+1)$. After rewriting the program it looks like this: class Solution {public: int uniquePaths(int m, int n) { // init a m x n 2D vector with value 1 vector<vector<int>> dp(m, vector<int>(n, 1)); for(int i=m-2; i>=0; i--){ for(int j=n-2; j>=0; j--){ // do it backwardly dp[i][j] = dp[i+1][j] + dp[i][j+1]; } } return dp[0][0]; }};
Here’s a detailed explanation of the code changes:
Declare a 2D vector of size m x n with value 1 (representing a whole grid, where the default path count is 1) Set up loops, using the second-to-last row and second-to-last column cell ([m-2][n-2]) as the loop’s start, decrementing the index by 1 each iteration Traverse each cell, with the rule being the relation we just derived Iterate all the way back from the bottom-right to [0][0]; once we reach [0][0], its stored value is the total of all paths
Visualizing the traversal looks like the figure below.
The execution result and complexity are the same as step two, and both are 100% Runtime!The author also mentions this approach is well suited to “go from A to B” type problems, where all you have to do is fill in a table.
Step 4: Iteration + Tabulation [Optimized] You don’t necessarily need to reach this step every time; if an interview gets through the first three steps, that’s already very good.
The goal of this step is to reduce space complexity. After the previous steps, the time complexity should already be optimized. The reason there’s still a chance to keep optimizing space complexity is that even though we earlier built an m x n grid to iteratively store the path counts, we don’t actually have to keep accessing the entire table at once. If you observe the recursive relation we’ve built so far (look at the traversal figure above), for any cell, the only cells needed are the one directly below it and the one directly to its right. So when declaring the array we only need a 2 x n array with m=2 (for Unique Paths, that’s all the space needed). So how do we store the path values this way? The start here is still [m-2][n-2], i.e. step three’s second-to-last row and second-to-last column cell. You can think of it as taking the bottom two rows from the original m x n table and iterating as before. The iteration rule, as just mentioned, is that for any cell we only need the cell directly below and directly to its right. So for the first row (i=0) the rule is $F(m, n) = F(m+1, n) + F(m,n+1)$. Once the first row is computed, the second row used to compute it (which will all be 1 at first) has no further use, so we copy all the first row’s values into the second row to compute the new first row, following the same iteration rule. The final $F(0, 0)$ is then the overall path count.
class Solution {public: int uniquePaths(int m, int n) { // init a m x n 2D vector with value 1 vector<vector<int>> dp(2, vector<int>(n, 1)); for(int i=m-2; i>=0; i--){ for(int j=n-2; j>=0; j--){ // Handloe first row // (m+n) = (cell below) + (cell on the right) dp[0][j] = dp[1][j] + dp[0][j+1]; } // Move to second row dp[1] = dp[0]; } return dp[0][0]; }};
Here we can compare the space complexity difference between step three and step four. Step three has to store the whole table, so its space complexity is $O(n \times m)$, while step four only stores $2*n$ cells, so its space complexity is $O(2 \times n) = O(n)$. We can also observe the difference in the results: Step three Step four Referencehttps://medium.com/@al.eks/the-ultimate-guide-to-dynamic-programming-65865ef7ec5bhttps://shannonhung.github.io/posts/lecture-dp/

entry.title: Why Space Networking Needs DTN: From TCP/IP's Limits to Deep-Space Networks
entry.content:
🌐 中文版：繁體中文
Preface: can we still get online smoothly in space? I recently watched the livestream of NASA’s Artemis II lunar flyby mission. Watching the rocket lift off, I felt I’d witnessed another milestone for humanity.In recent years, progress from NASA, the Commercial Lunar Payload Services (CLPS), SpaceX’s Starship, and various countries’ investment in lunar and deep-space missions has made space infrastructure no longer just a sci-fi concept but increasingly a matter of engineering practice. But as an engineer, a very practical question came to mind: “If we want to develop technology in space, or even build bases, can we take our existing terrestrial network architecture and use it directly in space?” To answer this, I dug into some related papers and technical documents. This post is my study notes and summary.
Intuitively, we might think: “Just make the antennas bigger, push up the signal power, and launch a few more relay satellites, and we can extend the Earth’s Internet into space, right?” But in reality, the challenges space networks face are absolutely not simply insufficient bandwidth or weak signals. The most fundamental problem is that the basic assumptions of the entire network environment completely change in space. The Internet on Earth usually assumes that an end-to-end path is clear most of the time, and packets reach their destination in a very short time. A disconnection is usually treated as an “abnormal condition.” But in space networks, extremely long delays, intermittent connectivity, and communication interruptions are the norm. NASA’s introduction to DTN (Delay/Disruption-Tolerant Networking) also notes that DTN aims to provide a more reliable, standardized way of transferring data in long-delay, interruption-prone environments like space communications (NASA). DTN’s core isn’t to find a way to make the speed of light faster, but to frankly accept that “delay and interruption are unavoidable,” and redesign network transport as a system that can store, wait, hand off, and recover.
Why isn’t the Earth’s Internet suitable for the space environment?Every day we scroll our phones, call APIs, and log into remote servers, all of which silently rely on a set of TCP/IP assumptions we take for granted:
There’s definitely a connected path between source and destination at this moment Round-trip latency (RTT) is extremely low, usually milliseconds to a few hundred milliseconds If a packet is lost, it usually means congestion, equipment failure, or transient interference A disconnection is an exception, not the norm The routing topology changes, but never dramatically at the scale and speed of celestial motion
On Earth these assumptions are very reasonable. Even for intercontinental connections, latency usually stays within what TCP can tolerate; and even if some router in the middle fails, the underlying routing protocols quickly find an alternate route. But the space environment is an entirely different story. In space, the Earth, Moon, Mars, satellites, probes, and ground stations are all in relative motion. The contact window between communication nodes may only appear at specific times. On top of that, different antenna angles, individual equipment energy limits, different orbital positions, and even celestial occlusion all directly determine whether a given link is up at that moment. NASA’s ION-DTN teaching materials also note: extreme distances, extremely high data loss rates, topology changes from orbital motion, and spacecraft operating discontinuously to save power all make space communication several dimensions more complex than terrestrial networks (ion-dtn.readthedocs.io). We can use a table to quickly contrast the two:
Dimension Terrestrial network assumption Space network reality
Path connectivity An end-to-end path usually exists An end-to-end path may temporarily not exist
Network latency (RTT) Usually extremely short (milliseconds) Can be seconds, minutes, or even longer
View of disconnection An anomaly or error A normal state
Topology stability Relatively stable Constantly changing with orbits and contact windows
Retransmission cost Relatively cheap Very expensive, and can miss the contact window
Node state Equipment mostly online 24/7 Spacecraft often in low-power, offline, or occluded states
On terrestrial networks, a disconnection usually means something is broken, but in space networks, a disconnection is very likely just an everyday part of the network topology.
Three fatal flaws of TCP/IP in the space environment1. The scale of delay: from milliseconds to “minutes”If you took intro to computer science in college, you know TCP’s design relies heavily on ACKs, timeouts, retransmission, and congestion control. These mechanisms work great on Earth because RTT is short. But in space, distance amplifies delay mercilessly:
Between low-orbit satellites and ground stations, it might barely stay in the milliseconds-to-tens-of-milliseconds range Earth-to-Moon one-way light travel is about 1.3 seconds, so RTT reaches 2.6 seconds For Earth-to-Mars, delay varies with the two bodies’ orbital positions and can reach from several minutes to over twenty minutes
This means that if we insist on establishing a traditional TCP session between Earth and Mars, the connection might time out just during the handshake and waiting for a single ACK. Worse, TCP would misinterpret this physically long delay or occlusion-based disconnection as network congestion, triggering rate reduction and retransmission that utterly cripple throughput. 2. Intermittent connectivity: the other side isn’t always thereSpace nodes aren’t always mutually visible. Imagine these scenarios:
A lunar rover drives into a crater and may not have line of sight to Earth A probe on the far side of the Moon must wait for a relay satellite to fly over before it can send data to Earth A satellite may temporarily shut off its comms module to save its energy budget The rotation and revolution of the Sun, planets, and satellites themselves constantly cause signal occlusion
The space version of the networking problem may not be “is there a complete path to take right now?”but rather: since there’s no path right now, when is the next available communication opportunity? Until then, who should hold onto this piece of data?
3. Treating interruption as the norm: disruption as topologyAs mentioned, a disconnection on Earth means a fault or anomaly, but an interruption in space is often just because a satellite flew out of visible range or an antenna is slewing. So space networks need not a simple, aggressive retry mechanism, but a network architecture that incorporates “interruption” itself into its normal operating model. And that’s exactly the impetus for DTN’s birth.
DTN: Store-Carry-ForwardDTN stands for Delay/Disruption-Tolerant Networking. It’s a network architecture designed specifically to handle long delays, intermittent connectivity, unstable links, and high error rates. IETF RFC 9171 explicitly states that DTN is an architecture suited to highly stressed environments (IETF Datatracker). Traditional networking’s logic is straightforward: Send -> Route -> Deliver immediately
DTN’s logic is: Store -> Carry (while disconnected) -> Forward (when a connection opportunity arises)
The aerospace industry usually calls this pattern Store-Carry-Forward. When a DTN node receives data, it doesn’t need to forward it immediately. If the next hop isn’t currently in visible range, it can safely “store” the data on local disk or memory, and then “forward” it when the next contact window appears. DTN’s mindset is no longer about finding a path that’s connected right now, but about planning how data should traverse a series of “future” communication opportunities to finally relay to its destination.
A real-world analogy for DTNHere’s an analogy: if TCP/IP is like a real-time phone call, then DTN is more like an international logistics system. When you ship a package, the sender and recipient don’t need to be online at the same time, and the trucks, planes, and logistics centers don’t need to be connected into one line at the same second. Your package first reaches a consolidation center (Store), flies across the Pacific with a plane (Carry), and once it reaches the destination country’s sorting center, is handed to a local driver for delivery (Forward). That’s also how DTN works:
Property Traditional Internet Space DTN
Analogy Real-time phone call Postal / logistics system
Data unit Packet (forwarded immediately) Bundle (can be held)
Path dependency Needs a continuous end-to-end path Relies on a series of future communication opportunities (contacts)
Time tolerance Extremely sensitive to timeouts Can tolerate long waits
Communication model Session-oriented Message/object-oriented
View of disconnection A failure A normal state
Routing consideration Based on the current topology state Based on a dynamic topology with a “time axis”
In other words: in space, waiting itself is part of what the network protocol must handle.
Bundle ProtocolIn the DTN world, the most central protocol is the Bundle Protocol (BP). If the basic data unit of a traditional IP network is the packet, then DTN’s basic data unit is the bundle.You can think of a bundle as a standard shipping container in the DTN world: it doesn’t just carry data, but also includes the source, destination, creation time, lifetime, and the metadata needed for subsequent routing, security, and status tracking. This is also the biggest difference between a bundle and an ordinary packet. A packet usually assumes it will be forwarded immediately by the network; a bundle is designed to be held by a node, sent later, handed off across nodes, and continue waiting for the next transmission opportunity after an interruption. The most modern Bundle Protocol version is BPv7, defined in IETF RFC 9171. CCSDS (the Consultative Committee for Space Data Systems) also published a BPv7-based experimental space-communication specification in 2025. This means BPv7 is no longer just an academic concept, but is increasingly being incorporated into the standardization foundation for future space data systems and mission interoperability (ccsds.org). The point of the Bundle Protocol isn’t to slice data smaller, but to turn data into mission-level message units that can be “stored, waited on, handed off, and tracked.”
What’s actually inside a bundle?To aid understanding, we can simplify a bundle into this structure: Bundle├── Primary Block│ ├── Source Endpoint│ ├── Destination Endpoint│ ├── Creation Timestamp│ └── Lifetime├── Extension Blocks│ ├── Routing Metadata│ ├── Security Metadata, e.g. BPSec│ └── Other mission- or protocol-related info└── Payload Block └── The actual mission data, e.g. science data or telemetry
The most important are the Primary Block and the Payload Block. The Primary Block provides the basic information needed for this bundle to be identified and processed in the DTN network, such as source, destination, and lifetime. The Payload Block carries the actual mission data to be sent. Extension Blocks provide extra capabilities such as security, routing-assist info, or other metadata. In other words, a bundle isn’t just the data itself, but a data container with context. It knows where it came from, where it’s going, and how long it can live, and it can carry extra information so relay nodes can still make forwarding decisions without an end-to-end connection. The internal structure of a Bundle NodeHaving understood bundles, the next question is: who’s responsible for handling these bundles? In the BPv7 architecture, the conceptual node responsible for sending, receiving, and processing bundles is called a Bundle Node, a DTN node composed of several functional components. The CCSDS BPv7 Experimental Specification describes a Bundle Node as any entity that can send and/or receive bundles. Architecturally, it mainly consists of three conceptual components:
Application Agent (AA) Bundle Protocol Agent (BPA) Convergence Layer Adapter (CLA)
Ref: Graphical Representation of a Bundle Node. Source: CCSDS 734.20-O-1, “Bundle Protocol Specification, Experimental Specification,” Figure 1-1 4
This figure can be understood as follows:
Component Function
Application Agent (AA) Interacts with upper-layer applications, including handling application data and administrative records
Administrative Element (AE) Generates and processes administrative records, e.g. bundle status reports
Application-Specific Element (ASE) Handles the actual application data, e.g. science data, telemetry, or mission payload
Bundle Protocol Agent (BPA) Executes the Bundle Protocol’s own procedures: receiving, processing, storing, and forwarding bundles
Convergence Layer Adapter (CLA) Sends bundles over different underlying networks, e.g. TCP, UDP, LTP, or CCSDS link protocols
In short, the AA handles application-layer data, the BPA handles the Bundle Protocol’s core logic, and the CLA handles actually sending the bundle over some underlying network segment.
This layered design suits space networks well, because the same Bundle Node may face several different links at once. For example, it interacts with ground systems over TCP/UDP on one side, and communicates with spacecraft over LTP or a CCSDS space link on the other. The upper-layer application only needs to hand data to BP; whether a given segment goes over the terrestrial IP network, a lunar-surface local network, or a deep-space link is handled by different CLAs. Convergence LayerSo BP isn’t meant to replace TCP, UDP, RF, optical comms, or the CCSDS link layer. More precisely, BP is an overlay layer responsible for DTN-level data-delivery semantics, not the actual transport details of each underlying link segment. BP uses the so-called Convergence Layer (CLA) to decide how this container should be transported over the current segment. On Earth it might go over TCP/UDP; in space it switches to LTP (Licklider Transmission Protocol) or the CCSDS link layer. What actually sends a bundle over a given link is the CLA, which you can think of as the different modes of transport in a logistics system:
DTN architecture Logistics analogy
Bundle Standard shipping container
BPA Logistics dispatch center
CLA Truck, ship, plane, or rail
Underlying network Actual roads, routes, or rail network
In the ground segment, a bundle might be transported over a TCP/UDP convergence layer, while over long-distance or interruption-prone space links it might switch to LTP or CCSDS-related link protocols. In short: BP coordinates the long-term strategy from departure to arrival, while the Convergence Layer only handles the short haul from this stop to the next.
Having understood bundles, Bundle Nodes, and the Convergence Layer, DTN’s basic operating logic becomes clear: data is first encapsulated into a bundle, stored and processed by Bundle Nodes, and handed off stop by stop across various underlying networks via different CLAs. But the next question arises:
If nodes in space aren’t always connected to each other, how does a Bundle Node know when it can hand off data? And which next hop should it choose?
This brings us to a crucial concept in DTN routing: the Contact Plan. Contact PlanHaving understood the Bundle Protocol, the next question is: how does a space network do routing? On terrestrial networks, routers usually decide a packet’s next hop based on the current network topology. But in a space network, a link being down now doesn’t mean it’s down forever; it may just be waiting for the next orbital position, the next ground-station contact window, or the next time a satellite enters comms range. So in DTN, we first need an important concept: the contact, a communication opportunity. In DTN, a contact means: “an opportunity for two nodes to send data to each other during a specific time window.” It’s not just a connection; it carries time and capacity attributes, for example: contact: from: LunarRelay-1 to: EarthGroundStation-Madrid start: 2026-05-05T10:00:00Z end: 2026-05-05T10:12:00Z data_rate: 50Mbps latency: 1.3s
Collect all known future contacts and you get a Contact Plan.
If a terrestrial network’s routing table is a flat map of the current network, then a space network’s Contact Plan is a three-dimensional timetable with a fourth dimension (time). It’s a bit sci-fi, and the following helps illustrate it:
So you can think of a Contact Plan as a space topology map with its own time axis.
Contact Graph Routing (CGR)With a timetable, we need an algorithm to plan the route. Traditional network AS protocols like OSPF or BGP only care about where a path exists right now, but in space the decision logic must become:
When does this path become available? How long is the contact window? Is it enough to transfer all the data? Is the next relay node’s disk full yet? Is there a route that departs later but arrives earlier?
To solve this, Contact Graph Routing (CGR) was born. CGR doesn’t find a path on ordinary network nodes, but on a graph built from future communication opportunities (contacts), using a modified Dijkstra algorithm to find the optimal solution (NASA technical report).
So compared to a traditional graph problem, in the CGR world, spatial distance isn’t the only consideration; the timing opportunity is the key that decides whether data can arrive.
NASA LunaNetDTN is absolutely not a concept that only lives in papers or simulators; it’s already core to NASA’s plans for the future lunar network architecture. To support future lunar missions, NASA proposed LunaNet. It isn’t a single satellite, but a standardized network framework. The goal is to let different countries’ probes, different vendors’ relay satellites, and even lunar-surface bases all interconnect, forming a Lunar Network of Networks (NASA). In this architecture, DTN is the cornerstone of LunaNet’s reliable data transport.
Even if a probe can never talk directly to Earth, as long as there’s a solid Contact Plan and the DTN protocol, scientific data can still be sent back to Earth steadily, relay by relay, like a relay race. An extreme distributed system!?If you’re like me, an engineer with more of a cloud-infra background, you can actually think of DTN as a distributed system operating in an extreme environment. Because space networking isn’t just an underlying comms protocol; it actually covers a large and complex set of systems-engineering topics:
Distributed systems concept Space DTN’s corresponding implementation
Queueing Bundle queue / priority scheduling
Scheduling Contact-aware forwarding
Replication Custody transfer (handing off custody and backup)
Fault Tolerance Disruption-tolerant delivery
Resource Allocation Allocating node storage (buffer) and energy
Observability Bundle status reports / trajectory tracing
Security BPSec / node identity authentication
In ground systems, we mostly pursue speed, that millisecond-level real-time consistency, but in space networks we can only rely on eventual delivery, because in space, reliability isn’t defined as delivering immediately, but as the data never being lost no matter how many disconnections and waits it goes through. These data may be key metrics from exploration equipment or expensive spacecraft, or scientific observation data; either way, they’re worth waiting for. Advanced topics and future challengesAlthough DTN standards are gradually maturing, in practice there are many hardcore pits left to fill: 1. Capacity-aware RoutingCGR is great at finding paths, but what if a relay node’s buffer is about to overflow? What if multiple high-priority science missions are all competing for the same contact window? Perfectly integrating a node’s storage capacity and link bandwidth into routing decisions is a major hot area right now. 2. ML-assisted vs Deterministic RoutingSome propose bringing machine learning into DTN to predict the best route. But in expensive space missions, explainability and determinism are often preferred over black-box AI. That is, how to make a routing algorithm both adapt to dynamic changes and let the ground control center precisely track and override decisions is, I think, one of the directions for deeper research into future space networks. 3. Security-aware RoutingWhen a space network becomes a multi-national, multi-institution shared network, security becomes paramount. How do you prevent malicious nodes from attacking, jamming or tampering with the Contact Plan, or even paralyzing other nodes’ buffers by sending junk bundles? These all need tighter trust mechanisms to guard against, and security is an issue in every field. A simple Space DTN labThis sounds like tech only NASA is qualified to play with, but we can actually set up a minimal proof-of-concept (PoC) environment with an ordinary computer and Docker, because it’s essentially a distributed system with extreme properties. We only need to carve out three nodes: Node A (lunar rover) -> Node B (orbital relay satellite) -> Node C (Earth ground station)
You can deliberately set the connection between A and B to only 60 seconds, and observe how Node B buffers the data, waits for the contact window with Node C to arrive, and finally forwards the data.
You can use tc netem to simulate tens of seconds of extreme delay, or use the open-source ION-DTN or HDTN to test a BPv7 implementation. Going a bit further, you can hook up Prometheus and Grafana to observe DTN’s core behavior under disconnection, delay, and contact-window constraints. Without actually launching a rocket, you can experience the design logic of deep-space communication architecture right on your laptop. ClosingThe Earth’s Internet is so great probably because it’s built on a stable, low-latency environment where everyone is almost always online. Fixed servers, data centers, networking equipment, and undersea cables weave all of this together. But in space, distance itself brings unavoidable delay, and orbital motion brings relentless disconnection. None of this can obviously be brute-forced away by adding bandwidth. The fascinating thing about DTN is that it completely breaks our craving for real-time connectivity: data hitches rides through the universe, relaying step by step toward its destination.
References NASA, Delay/Disruption Tolerant Networking. (Link) ION-DTN Documentation, Introduction to Delay/Disruption Tolerant Networking. (Link) IETF, RFC 9171: Bundle Protocol Version 7. (Link) CCSDS, Bundle Protocol Version 7 (BPv7) Experimental Specification, 2025. (Link) NASA, LunaNet Interoperability Specification Document Version 5, 2025. (Link) NASA NTRS, Multigraph-based Routing in Delay Tolerant Networks, 2023. (Link) T. Alhajj and V. Corlay, Improved Contact Graph Routing in Delay Tolerant Networks with Capacity and Buffer Constraints, arXiv, 2024/2025. (Link) NASA NTRS, Delay Tolerant Network Routing as a Machine Learning Classification Problem, 2018. (Link) NASA, DTN Resources for Mission Developers. (Link) NASA, Delay/Disruption Tolerant Networking Overview. (Link) NASA NTRS, Contact Multigraph Routing: Overview and Implementation, 2023. (Link) NASA NTRS, Dynamic Routing for Delay-Tolerant Networking in Space Flight Operations, 2008. (Link)

entry.title: Passing Functions in C/C++: A Deep Look at Function Pointer Address Changes
📑GitHub Actions Study Notes
entry.content:
🌐 中文版：繁體中文
I didn’t actually have CI/CD experience before, so I wasn’t too familiar with the common CI/CD platforms out there. But recently, due to a project need, I had to use GitHub Actions to build a CI/CD pipeline for a BreakSentence API in Azure Cognitive Services. With the delivered requirements still vague 😭, I figured I’d first understand this feature and make a record. Basic introductionGitHub Actions is a CI/CD platform that can automate building, testing, and deployment. Users can create workflows to build and test every pull request to a repository, or deploy merged pull requests to a production environment. ComponentsThe component terms that make up GitHub Actions are:
Workflow Event Jobs Runner Steps Action
First, how these components work together: when some event occurs in a repository, the GitHub Actions workflows you configured are triggered. An event here could be, for example, a pull request or an issue being created, and so on.
The workflow you define contains one or more jobs, which can be processed in parallel or sequentially. Each job runs on its own virtual-machine runner or inside a container. Each job contains one or more steps that run a script you define or some action. An action is the smallest unit in GitHub Actions, a reusable extension, usually some common command (?😥). 🔀Workflows A workflow is one or more jobs configured to automate a process. You define a workflow by writing a YAML file, and it’s triggered when an event occurs, or can be triggered manually. Workflows are defined under the .github/workflows path in the repo. A repo can have multiple workflows responsible for various tasks. For example, one workflow for building and testing And another for deploying the app to production after a release
✴️EventsAn event represents a specific activity in a repository, such as:
pull request open issues pushes a commit to repo, etc.
For the events that can trigger workflows, see this doc:https://docs.github.com/en/actions/using-workflows/events-that-trigger-workflows 🗂️JobsA set of steps is called a job, and it runs on a runner. Each step may be a shell script or an action that runs. Steps run in order, and since each step runs on the same runner, data can be shared between steps. For example: one step builds the app, then another tests it. You can also set job dependencies; once one job depends on another, it waits for the other to finish before starting its own task.https://docs.github.com/en/actions/using-jobs 📑ActionsAn action is a program designed specifically for the GitHub Actions platform to perform complex, frequent, and repetitive tasks.Using actions reduces the amount of repetitive code in workflow files.An action can do things like pull a repository from GitHub, set up the correct toolset for the build environment, and configure authentication with your cloud provider. Creating actions: https://docs.github.com/en/actions/creating-actions 📦RunnersA runner is a server that runs a workflow, and each runner runs one job at a time.GitHub provides Ubuntu, Windows, and macOS runners to run workflows.There are also solutions for those needing large runners: https://docs.github.com/en/actions/using-github-hosted-runners/using-larger-runnersIf the needed environment requires a different OS or special hardware configuration, you can host your own runner: https://docs.github.com/en/actions/hosting-your-own-runners Creating a workflowGitHub Actions uses YAML to create workflows. Each workflow is stored in its own YAML file placed under the .github/workflows path. Creating an example workflow Create the path: .github/workflows Create learn-github-action.yml inside .github/workflowsname: learn-github-actionsrun-name: ${{ github.actor }} is learning GitHub Actionson: [push]jobs: check-bats-version: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v3 - uses: actions/setup-node@v3 with: node-version: '14' - run: npm install -g bats - run: bats -v Commit the change and push it to the repository
Workflow file explained line by lineReference: Workflow Syntax
name: specifies the workflow name, which appears in the repository’s Actions tab run-name: the text message shown each time the workflow runs; here it’s the repo username + “is learning GitHub Actions”
on: specifies the activity that triggers the workflow; here it uses the push event, so the workflow runs whenever someone pushes a change to the repository jobs: groups the jobs in the workflow together check-bats-version: a custom job name runs-on: sets the job to run on a runner with the latest Ubuntu Linux OS; this specification triggers creation of a hosted virtual machine steps: groups all the steps under the check-bats-version job uses: specifies a step’s command or action actions/checkout@v3: runs the v3 version of the actions/checkout action. This step checks out your repo onto the runner and lets you operate on your code. Whenever your workflow runs against the repository’s code, you should use the checkout action. actions/setup-node@v3: installs the specified version of Node.js (version 14 in this example)
run: the run command tells the job to execute a specific command on the runner. In this example it tells the job to run npm install bats on the runner, and the next step checks the bats version
Finding and customizing actionsAn action can be defined in:
The same repository as your workflow file Any public repository A published container image on DockerHub
GitHub Actions MarketplaceMarketplace link
The Marketplace has many actions provided by other contributors that you can download.
Each action provides the corresponding YAML syntax you can copy and paste into your own workflow file. If an action requires input, you need to configure the workflow additionally; see this doc:https://docs.github.com/en/actions/learn-github-actions/finding-and-customizing-actions#using-inputs-and-outputs-with-an-action Adding an action in the same repositoryExample file structure |-- hello-world (repository)| |__ .github| └── workflows| └── my-first-workflow.yml| └── actions| |__ hello-world-action| └── action.yml Example workflow file jobs: build: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: # This step checks out a copy of your repository. - uses: actions/checkout@v3 # This step references the directory that contains the action. - uses: ./.github/actions/hello-world-action syntax: ./path/to/dir And action.yml is for providing metadata for the action. Adding an action from a different repositoryIn this case, under uses in your workflow file you specify {owner}/{repo}@{ref} to indicate the referenced action’s repo, e.g. actions/setup-node@v3. Referencing a container on DockerHubHere the syntax changes to: docker://{image}:{tag} Hands-on: Azure Break Sentence CI/CD PipelineOverall architecture diagram Event requirementsRunner environment package setup OS: Ubuntu Linux Python 3.8.10 Environment Variables AZURE_API_KEY AZURE_LOCATION
Seems like custom actions could work here
Break Sentence 🧪Goal: When a user uploads a file, extract the article inside, call BreakSentence.py to segment sentences, and save to a specific output folder. Task Azure API key disabled -> change email to re-register, or pay to renew Test accessing secrets via environment variables in the YML file Change the secret values stored in the repository BreakSentence.py -> needs file-reading added May need to open both text files and Excel files
BreakSentence.py -> wrap it as a command-line tool
Currently errors at Setup Python ✅Resolved No module specified, need pip to install the specific module ✅Resolved Can’t access the secret value as an environment variable ✅ResolvedNeed to put the env section under the step that runs breaksentence.py Ran successfully
Currently the script only prints the API call response and saves the segmented sentences in a list.The next step is to change the input/output method. References[1]https://ithelp.ithome.com.tw/articles/10266827[2]https://docs.github.com/en/actions/learn-github-actions/understanding-github-actions[3]https://docs.github.com/en/actions/learn-github-actions/finding-and-customizing-actions[4] GitHub Actions Push to Azure Cloud

entry.title: Git for DevOps Notes |【DevOps Skill Tree】
entry.content:
🌐 中文版：繁體中文
Basic Q: How do you confirm a directory is a git repository?
Check whether there’s a .git directory.
Q: Explain git directory, working directory, and staging area
Git directory:Where the project history is stored. It contains all commit history, branches, labels, etc., stored in the .git folder in the project directory. The git directory is the main data store responsible for version management; you can view info with the git log command. Working directoryThe project directory you’re currently operating on. In the working directory, git extracts a specific version (usually the latest) from the git directory and checks out the files, so you can edit and modify them directly. Changes to the working directory aren’t automatically detected by git; you need to manually add and commit to update. Staging AreaA temporary space where you can add working-directory changes, waiting for further commit. When you run git add, the file moves from the working directory to the staging area. Finally, when you run git commit, Git commits the staging area’s contents into the git directory (.git), forming a new commit.
Q: What’s the difference between git pull and git fetch?
In short, git pull = git fetch + git merge. git fetch simply downloads the latest changes from the remote repository to local and updates the local remote-branch record (origin/main), but doesn’t merge these changes into the current working branch, so after git fetch you need to manually use git merge or git rebase. git pull is the combined command of git fetch and git merge. If both the remote and local have modifications during git pull, you can hit a merge conflict.
Q: How do you determine whether a file is tracked? If not, track it
Check whether the file is tracked
Use git status to check the current file status. If a file appears under Untracked files, it’s not tracked; if it’s under Changes not staged for commit, it’s tracked but the modification isn’t committed. Taking this blog as an example: On branch enYour branch is up to date with 'origin/en'.Changes not staged for commit: (use "git add <file>..." to update what will be committed) (use "git restore <file>..." to discard changes in working directory) modified: source/_posts/k8s-devops.mdUntracked files: (use "git add <file>..." to include in what will be committed) source/_posts/git-dveops.md
Add the untracked file to tracking
git add <file>
Q: Explain the purpose of gitignore
It ensures certain files aren’t tracked by Git. When you add or modify .gitignore to ignore certain files or folders but find they’re already tracked, you can first use git rm --cached to remove them from tracking, and then Git will ignore them per .gitignore. Example git rm --cached -r node_modules/
Q: Before committing, what methods can you use to know what changes were made?
git diff To see the difference between the latest commit and the staging area, add the cached parameter: git diff --cached
To see the difference between the working directory and the latest commit: git diff HEAD
Scenario questions Q: You have a file in the remote repository, but you don’t want Git to track it. What do you do so Git no longer tracks it going forward?
Add the file to .gitignore so it won’t be added to the staging area.
Q: In your organization, a dev team uses a monolithic remote repo that’s huge, with thousands of files. The team finds normal git operations, like git status, have become very slow. What causes this, and how do you help them?
Problem analysis:
A large number of files and a complex directory structure increase the burden when operations like git diff and git status do comparisons A large amount of history reduces read performance If the files themselves are large, modifying them also becomes slow
Solutions:
Restructure: use git submodule or git subtree to split the monolith into multiple smaller repos, moving different parts into their own independent repos. For cloning, if developers only need the latest version without the full history, use the --depth parameter for a shallow clone If developers only need certain folders or files in the project, use Sparse Checkout to check out the needed parts
git sparse-checkout init --conegit sparse-checkout set <PATH_TO_FOLDER>
Use Git LFS to manage large files
git lfs installgit lfs track "*.c" # track all big .c files
BranchesA branch is a parallel line of development for code in git, letting developers make changes without affecting the main line.
What is a branch strategy (flow)? Give some examples of branch strategies
Git Flow Image Source: https://medium.com/@sreekanth.thummala Suited to projects with long release cycles that need stable versions.
main branch: the main branch, storing stable, released versions develop branch: the development branch, where all new features are merged feature branch: for developing new features; each new feature should be created from develop, and merged back into develop after development release branch: when develop reaches a releasable stage, a release branch is created from develop for final testing and fixes hotfix branch: for urgently fixing issues in a released version; created from main, and merged back into both main and develop after the fix
Downside: frequently creating and merging branches can increase git-history complexity
GitHub Flow
GitHub Flow is more lightweight, suited to projects with rapid iteration and continuous deployment. It has only two main branches and usually suits small teams.
main branch: the main branch, containing stable, always-deployable code feature branches: developers create a new branch from main to develop a feature or fix a bug. After the feature is done and tested, a Pull Request (PR) is opened and merged back into main
Downside: not suited to long-lived projects
GitLab Flow
Combines features of Git Flow and GitHub Flow, suited to projects of intermediate complexity, allowing testing and deployment in different environments. Suited to projects with multiple test environments that need stable releases.
main branch: the main branch, storing stable versions feature branch: for developing features and fixing bugs; created from main and merged back into main when done environment branches: e.g. pre-production, staging. Correspond to different deployment environments for testing and validation release branch: for release management of specific versions
Downside: complexity still rises when managing multiple versions
Trunk Based Development
This flow is more extreme, emphasizing rapid development and continuous integration.
main branch: the only main branch, so all development activity merges directly into main short-lived feature branches: feature branches exist very briefly, usually completed within a few days and merged back into main, or development happens directly on main
Downside: highly dependent on automated testing and CI/CD systems. High requirements on team skill and collaboration
You now have two branches, main and dev. How do you ensure they’re in sync?
git checkout maingit pullgit checkout devgit merge main
When you run the git branch command, how does it work, and what actually happens?
Behind the scenes Git does the following. 1. It creates a new branch pointer: git creates a new file in the .git/refs/heads folder, with the filename being the branch name you set. Then it points to the current commit: the new file’s content is the SHA-1 hash pointing to the current commit, meaning the new branch starts from the current commit.
When you run git branch, how does Git know the latest commit’s SHA-1?
It finds the corresponding branch name in .git/refs/heads and outputs the corresponding SHA-1 value. ~/leozzmc.github.io/.git/refs/heads❯ cat en fc58a8885d29bc422d8089e08eaf826d41a2b5c8
When you check out another branch, Git also updates .git/HEAD to refs/heads/<Branch Name>. Merge You have two branches, main and dev. How do you merge dev into main?
git checkout maingit merge devgit push origin main
How do you resolve merge conflicts?
First confirm which files have conflicts. You can check with git status; these files are unmerged. Then open the conflicting file, and git should mark the conflicting regions, like: <<<<<<< HEAD// changes from the current branch (HEAD)======= // changes from the branch being merged>>>>>>> branch-name
Then you may need to communicate with other developers or the team to decide which parts to keep. After editing and saving the file, mark the conflict resolved with git add <filename>. Then you can commit.
What merge strategies are you familiar with?
Git has several common merge strategies, such as: Fast-Forward If the branch being merged and main have no new commits, you can use a fast-forward merge. Git fast-forwards main’s pointer directly to the branch’s latest commit, without creating a new merge commit. This suits linear development and keeps git history clean. git merge <branch_name> --ff
RecursiveThis is Git’s default merge strategy. When merging branches with a common ancestor, it computes the differences between the two branches from the common base commit, then automatically generates a merge commit. git merge <branch-name>
Squash A squash commit compresses all commits into a single commit and merges it into the target branch, so only one commit record appears on the main branch. This suits packaging scattered commits into a clean commit after feature development. git merge --squash <branch-name>
Octopus Suited to merging multiple branches at once, usually merging multiple feature branches into main. Git merges changes from multiple branches into a single commit. git merge <branch1> <branch2> <branch3>
Ours Merge A special merge strategy. Use Ours Merge when merge conflicts can’t be resolved or you don’t want to keep the other branch’s changes. Even with conflicts, Git keeps the current branch’s content and discards the merged branch’s changes. This is usually for temporary emergency merges or irreconcilable conflicts. git merge -s ours <branch_name>
What’s the difference between git reset and git revert?
git revert creates a new commit to undo a previous commit. Say you have commit A, commit B, commit C, and you want to undo the changes in B. You can use git revert B to create a new commit D whose content is the opposite of B, so the final commit history is A->B->C->D. git reset resets the current branch’s pointer (HEAD) to a specified commit, and you can choose whether to keep working-directory changes. This means git reset can change a branch’s commit history. git reset --soft <commit-hash> # only moves HEADgit reset --mixed <commit-hash>git reset --hard <commit-hash>
Rebase In what situations do you use git rebase?
When a team is developing a feature on a feature branch created from main, and development is done, and the team wants to merge the feature into main without keeping any commits from the feature branch, you can use git rebase. (But a better approach is git merge --squash, first compressing all commits on the feature branch into one commit.)
How do you revert a specific file to a previous commit?
git checkout HEAD~1 -- /path/to/the/file
Or git restore --source-<commit-hash> -- <filename> git restore is a newer command, similar to checkout, restoring a file to a specified commit’s content.
How do you squash the last two commits?
If these two commits haven’t been pushed, you can reset back the previous two commits and commit again. git reset --soft HEAD~2git commit -m "new combined commit message"
But if the two commits are already pushed to the repo, use: git rebase -i HEAD~2
This opens an editor showing the commit history, something like: pick <commit-hash-1> Commit message for the second-to-last commitpick <commit-hash-2> Commit message for the last commit
Just change the second line’s pick to squash, which compresses the last commit into the second-to-last one. pick <commit-hash-1> Commit message for the second-to-last commitsquash <commit-hash-2> Commit message for the last commit
After saving and exiting, and editing a new commit message, you’ll see the two commits merged into one.
How do you delete a remote branch?
git push origin --delete <branch>
After deleting a remote branch, other collaborators can no longer pull that branch from the remote repository!
What is gitattributes?
.gitattributes is a Git config file used to set file attributes and how files are handled, letting you process files during Git operations (e.g. merge, commit). Main uses include:
Managing line endings: one of the most common uses. Different OSes use different line-ending characters (Windows: CRLF, Linux: LF), which can cause unnecessary change conflicts. You can set .gitattributes to unify how line endings are handled.
* text=auto
The command above lets Git set line endings automatically based on the system, converting them to LF (Unix/Linux) on commit.
How do you discard local changes before committing?
git checkout -- <filename>
And how do you discard a local commit?
git reset HEAD~1
This removes the most recent local commit; if you also need to discard local changes, add --hard. git reset --hard HEAD~1
Git Diff What does git diff do?
It shows the changes between the working directory and the staging area, displaying all modified files not yet added to the staging area. To see changes between the staging area and the latest commit: git diff --cached
To see changes between the working directory and the latest commit: git diff HEAD
You can also view the difference for any file, between two commits, or between two branches: git diff <commit1> <commit2>git diff <filename>git diff <branch1> <branch2>
Which is faster, git diff-index HEAD or git diff HEAD?
git diff-index HEAD > git diff HEAD git diff-index HEAD directly compares the index (staging area) with a specific commit (HEAD), so it doesn’t need to scan the entire working directory, making it faster. git diff HEAD, however, compares the entire working directory with a specific commit, so it scans the whole working directory and computes file differences, which slows down when there are many files. Git Internal Explain how git status works
git status does a series of checks and comparisons:
First it checks the difference between the working directory and the staging area, to see which files are modified but not staged
Git computes a SHA-1 hash for each file and checks whether that hash exists in the staging area; if the record doesn’t match, it’s considered not staged.
Then it compares the staging area with the latest commit (HEAD) to determine which files are staged but not yet committed
Git checks whether the hash in the staging area matches the hash committed in HEAD.
Check untracked files
Git scans all files in the working directory not in the staging area and marks them as untracked files, while also checking the .gitignore settings to filter out files that shouldn’t be tracked.
Update working state
When running git status on a large repository, Git uses incremental scanning and caching to speed it up:
Git sometimes enables core.untrackedCache to record the state of untracked files, avoiding a full rescan each time If core.preloadIndex is enabled, Git preloads the index, reducing disk I/O and thus speeding up file-status checks
Both settings can be enabled via git config.
Ref: https://deepinout.com/git/git-questions/218_git_why_is_git_corepreloadindex_default_value_false.html
Output the result

entry.title: Fleet Provisioning - Provisioning Devices to AWS IoT in Advance
entry.content:
IntroductionWhat is Fleet Provisioning?Fleet Provisioning can be divided into Provisioning by Claim and Provisioning by Trusted User. Provisioning by ClaimDevices can use embedded provisioning claim certificates (special-purpose certificates) and private keys for manufacturing. If these certificates are registered with AWS IoT, the service can exchange them for a unique device certificate that the device can use for general operations. Provisioning by Trusted UserIn many cases, when trusted users such as end-users or installation technicians set up devices at their deployment locations using a mobile application for the first time, the devices connect to AWS IoT.
This article mainly focuses on the Provisioning by Claim method for fleet provisioning.
Provisioning by Claim Process Configuration - AWS IoT CoreCreate Certificates and Public/Private Key PairsGenerate certificates for provisioning
You can do this on the AWS IoT Console under Secure >> Certificates >> Add Certificates >> Create Certificates
Next, a corresponding screen will appear, and you need to download the certificate and private key to your local machine. Additionally, for convenience, please download the Root CA certificate to your local machine.
Create Provisioning Template and Attach Policy Create Provisioning Template
Choose Provisioning devices with claim certificates, and then click Next
Create an IoT service role by clicking Create Role After entering the Role Name, click View
Attach policy Search and attach the AWS managed policy AWSIoTThingsRegistration
Claim certificate policy, click Create IoT Policy
Enter the Policy Name and paste the sample JSON
Sample IoT Policy { "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Effect": "Allow", "Action": ["iot:Connect"], "Resource": "*" }, { "Effect": "Allow", "Action": ["iot:Publish","iot:Receive"], "Resource": [ "arn:aws:iot:aws-region:aws-account-id:topic/$aws/certificates/create/*", "arn:aws:iot:aws-region:aws-account-id:topic/$aws/provisioning-templates/templateName/provision/*" ] }, { "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "iot:Subscribe", "Resource": [ "arn:aws:iot:aws-region:aws-account-id:topicfilter/$aws/certificates/create/*", "arn:aws:iot:aws-region:aws-account-id:topicfilter/$aws/provisioning-templates/templateName/provision/*" ] } ]}
Check the certificate
Once completed, you can proceed to set up provisioning in advance. Configure Pre-provisioningThe template example for fleet provisioning can be found at:
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/iot/latest/developerguide/provision-template.html#fleet-provisioning-example
{ "Parameters" : { "ThingName" : { "Type" : "String" }, "SerialNumber": { "Type": "String" }, "DeviceLocation": { "Type": "String" } }, "Mappings": { "LocationTable": { "Seattle": { "LocationUrl": "https://example.aws" } } }, "Resources" : { "thing" : { "Type" : "AWS::IoT::Thing", "Properties" : { "AttributePayload" : { "version" : "v1", "serialNumber" : "serialNumber" }, "ThingName" : {"Ref" : "ThingName"}, "ThingTypeName" : {"Fn::Join":["",["ThingPrefix_",{"Ref":"SerialNumber"}]]}, "ThingGroups" : ["v1-lightbulbs", "WA"], "BillingGroup": "LightBulbBillingGroup" }, "OverrideSettings" : { "AttributePayload" : "MERGE", "ThingTypeName" : "REPLACE", "ThingGroups" : "DO_NOTHING" } }, "certificate" : { "Type" : "AWS::IoT::Certificate", "Properties" : { "CertificateId": {"Ref": "AWS::IoT::Certificate::Id"}, "Status" : "Active" } }, "policy" : { "Type" : "AWS::IoT::Policy", "Properties" : { "PolicyDocument" : { "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [{ "Effect": "Allow", "Action":["iot:Publish"], "Resource": ["arn:aws:iot:us-east-1:123456789012:topic/foo/bar"] }] } } } }, "DeviceConfiguration": { "FallbackUrl": "https://www.example.com/test-site", "LocationUrl": { "Fn::FindInMap": ["LocationTable",{"Ref": "DeviceLocation"}, "LocationUrl"]} }}
The pre-provisioning hook is a Lambda function that validates the parameters passed from the device before provisioning. This Lambda function must exist in your account to provision devices. This part is set up to perform actions before configuring devices. For example, check devices against a known device database to prevent unauthorized devices from connecting to your account.
Choose Create a Lambda function
Sample provisioning hook where you validate the request before activating a certificate Github: https://github.com/aws-samples/aws-iot-fleet-provisioning#sample-provisioning-hook-where-you-validate-the-request-before-activating-a-certificate
import jsonfrom datetime import dateprovision_response = { 'allowProvisioning': False, "parameterOverrides": {"CertDate": date.today().strftime("%m/%d/%y")}}def handler(event, context): ######################## ## Stringent validation against internal API's/DB etc to validate the request before proceeding ## ## if event['parameters']['SerialNumber'] = "approved by company CSO": ## provision_response["allowProvisioning"] = True ##################### return provision_response
Hook Input https://docs.aws.amazon.com/zh_tw/iot/latest/developerguide/pre-provisioning-hook.html#pre-provisioning-hook-input
{ "claimCertificateId" : "string", "certificateId" : "string", "certificatePem" : "string", "templateArn" : "arn:aws:iot:us-east-1:XXXXXXXXXXXX:provisioningtemplate/MyTemplate", "clientId" : "221a6d10-9c7f-42f1-9153-e52e6fc869c1", "parameters" : { "string" : "string", ... }}
When registering a device with AWS IoT, this object is sent to the Lambda function by AWS IoT. The parameters object passed to the Lambda function contains attributes from the parameters argument passed in the RegisterThing request payload. Configuration - Device SideThe downloaded Claim certificate and private key need to be moved to the device. You can use commands like scp to copy files from your local machine to your device via SSH. Additionally, you will need to install the desired IoT Device SDK on the device.
AWS IoT Device SDKs, Mobile SDKs, and AWS IoT Device Client - - https://docs.aws.amazon.com/zh_tw/iot/latest/developerguide/iot-sdks.html
Currently, Device SDK supports writing code in C++, javascript, Java, Python, Embedded-C languages, depending on your requirements and scenarios. Using AWS IoT Device SDK https://github.com/aws/aws-iot-device-sdk-python-v2
This article mainly uses the Python IoT Device SDKv2. To install the SDK on the device, first ensure that the device has git, Python3, and Python3-pip packages. git clone https://github.com/aws/aws-iot-device-sdk-python-v2.git
Initialize the package # (Optional) Setup the version number of your local build. The default version # for awsiotsdk is set to "1.0.0-dev", you can set the version number of the# local build in "aws-iot-device-sdk-python-v2/awsiot/__init__.py"sed -i "s/__version__ = '1.0.0-dev'/__version__ = '<SDK_VERSION>'/" \ aws-iot-device-sdk-python-v2/awsiot/__init__.py# Install using Pip (use 'python' instead of 'python3' on Windows)python3 -m pip install ./aws-iot-device-sdk-python-v2
In aws-iot-device-sdk-python-v2/samples/fleetprovisioning.py , you can set up the Provisioning Template. Afterwards, you need to specify on your device: AWS IoT EndpointClaim CertificatePrivate Keyto connect to AWS IoT Core.You can find the script’s operating steps here:
https://github.com/aws/aws-iot-device-sdk-python-v2/blob/main/samples/fleetprovisioning.md
python3 fleetprovisioning.py --endpoint <endpoint> --cert <file> --key <file> --template_name <name> --template_parameters '{\"SerialNumber\":\"1\",\"DeviceLocation\":\"Seattle\"}' --csr <path to csr file>
Reference Documents[+] https://github.com/aws-samples/aws-iot-fleet-provisioning[+] https://docs.aws.amazon.com/zh_tw/iot/latest/developerguide/iot-provision.html[+] https://docs.aws.amazon.com/zh_tw/iot/latest/developerguide/provision-wo-cert.html#claim-based[+] https://aws.amazon.com/tw/blogs/iot/how-to-automate-onboarding-of-iot-devices-to-aws-iot-core-at-scale-with-fleet-provisioning/

entry.title: Problem-Solving Notes | Graphs-2
entry.content:
🌐 中文版：繁體中文
IntroThis continues from the previous post on the basic introduction to graphs. Next we need to understand how to search for a specific vertex in a graph, i.e. how to traverse a graph. There are three basic algorithms:
Breadth-First Search (BFS): for traversing directed and undirected graphs Depth-First Search (DFS): for traversing directed and undirected graphs Topological Search: for detecting a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG).
BFSI introduced Tree BFS (Level-Order Traversal) before. Level-Order visits nodes of different levels in order, and the level actually corresponds to the distance between nodes in the graph concept, representing the distance between the root and a node. So what’s different about graph BFS? If we want to traverse a connected undirected graph, we can start from any node (say vertex(A)). And since it’s connected, we can traverse all the nodes in the same connected component as vertex(A), and obtain the shortest distance from vertex(A) and the walkable paths. Algorithm introductionBefore running bfs() we need several data structures to store the data gathered during traversal:
queue: same as Tree BFS, used to record the nodes of each level in order label: records each node’s search status; needs to record found, not found, removed distance array: records each node’s distance from the start point predecessor array: records which node each node was found from, usable to trace back paths
Step1 Initialize data structures
First we need to initialize:
all vertices are not found all vertices’ distances are set to infinity clear all vertices’ predecessors (NULL or -1) create an empty queue
Step2 Push the start point
Then (1) Push the start point into the queue; here we choose vertex(A) as the start(2) Mark vertex(A) as found (shown in gray here)(3) Set distance[A] to 0. Setting it to 0 means this vertex is the start point of this connected component(4) predecessor[A] stays unchanged, so after BFS ends, any node whose predecessor value is null is a start point Step3 Search Neighbors
Next we use the queue’s front as the new search start. The new start is vertex(A), so we search vertex(A)’s neighbors, which can be obtained from the adjacency matrix or adjacency list. After finding them we do three things: (1) Mark the found vertex as found (shown in gray here)(2) Set the found node’s distance to distance[A]+1 distance[B] = distance[A]+1 = 1 distance[C] = distance[A]+1 = 1 (3) Set the found node’s predecessor to vertex(A)(4) Push into the queue in the order the nodes were found(5) Remove vertex(A) from the queue Keep using the queue’s front as the new start to search. Now the new start is vertex(B), so we search vertex(B)’s neighbors. Step4 vertex(B) Search Neighbors
(1) Mark vertex(D), vertex(E) as found (shown in gray here)(2) Set the found nodes’ distances to distance[B]+1 distance[D] = distance[B]+1 = 2 distance[E] = distance[B]+1 = 2 (3) Set the found nodes’ predecessors to vertex(B)(4) Push into the queue in the order the nodes were found(5) Remove vertex(B) from the queue Since vertex(B) has been removed, the queue’s new front, vertex(C), becomes the new start. Step5 vertex(C) Search Neighbors
(1) Mark vertex(F) as found (shown in gray here)(2) Set the found node’s distance to distance[C]+1 distance[F] = distance[C]+1 = 2 (3) Set the found node’s predecessor to vertex(C)(4) Push into the queue in the order the nodes were found(5) Remove vertex(C) from the queue Then keep repeating the loop until the queue is emptied, which completes the graph’s BFS traversal. Following Steps
Code implementation#include <iostream>#include <vector>#include <queue>#include <algorithm>#include <climits>using namespace std;class Graph{ private: int num_vertex; vector<vector<int>> adjList; int *label, // 0: not found, 1: found, 2. removed *distance, // 0: starting point, MAX_INT: vertex that cannot be found by the starting point *predecessor; // -1: no predecessor, starting point public: Graph(): num_vertex(0) {}; Graph(int N): num_vertex(N){ adjList.resize(num_vertex); }; //member function void addEdgeList(int from, int to); void bfs(int start); // Getter functions for debugging int getNumVertex() const { return num_vertex; } int* getDistances() const { return distance; } int* getPredecessors() const { return predecessor; }};void Graph::addEdgeList(int from, int to){ adjList[from].push_back(to);}void Graph::bfs(int start){ // init the arrays label = new int[num_vertex]; distance = new int[num_vertex]; predecessor = new int[num_vertex]; for(int i=0; i<num_vertex; i++){ label[i] = 0; distance[i] = INT_MAX; predecessor[i] = -1; } queue<int> q; int i=start; for(int j=0; j<num_vertex; j++){ if(label[i]==0){ label[i]=1; distance[i]=0; predecessor[i]=-1; q.push(i); while(!q.empty()){ int u = q.front(); for(auto it=adjList[u].begin(); it!=adjList[u].end(); ++it){ if(label[*it]==0){ label[*it]=1; distance[*it] = distance[u] + 1; predecessor[*it] = u; q.push(*it); } } q.pop(); label[u] = 2; } } i =j; }}int main(){ //construct the graph Graph g1(8); g1.addEdgeList(0,1); g1.addEdgeList(0,2); g1.addEdgeList(1,0); g1.addEdgeList(1,3); g1.addEdgeList(1,4); g1.addEdgeList(2,0); g1.addEdgeList(2,5); g1.addEdgeList(3,1); g1.addEdgeList(3,4); g1.addEdgeList(3,6);g1.addEdgeList(3,7); g1.addEdgeList(4,1); g1.addEdgeList(4,3); g1.addEdgeList(4,5); g1.addEdgeList(3,7); g1.addEdgeList(5,2); g1.addEdgeList(5,4); g1.addEdgeList(5,6); g1.addEdgeList(6,3); g1.addEdgeList(6,5); g1.addEdgeList(6,7); g1.addEdgeList(7,3); g1.addEdgeList(7,4); g1.addEdgeList(7,6); g1.bfs(0); for (int i = 0; i < g1.getNumVertex(); i++) { cout << "Distance[" << i << "]: " << g1.getDistances()[i] << " | "; cout << "Predecessor[" << i << "]: " << g1.getPredecessors()[i] << endl; } return 0;}
Output: Distance[0]: 0 | Predecessor[0]: -1Distance[1]: 1 | Predecessor[1]: 0Distance[2]: 1 | Predecessor[2]: 0Distance[3]: 2 | Predecessor[3]: 1Distance[4]: 2 | Predecessor[4]: 1Distance[5]: 2 | Predecessor[5]: 2Distance[6]: 3 | Predecessor[6]: 3Distance[7]: 3 | Predecessor[7]: 3
Extended conceptWith the obtained predecessor array, we can know the order relationship of nodes starting from the start point and draw a predecessor subgraph. It usually has connected and acyclic properties, which makes the predecessor subgraph a tree rooted at the start vertex. This kind of tree is also called a Breadth-First Tree, and the edges connecting the vertices are called Tree Edges.
A graph’s Breadth-First Tree may not be unique, because the predecessor array is composed of the order in which vertices are discovered, and the discovery order is affected by the order the adjList is built. A different order produces a different Breadth-First Tree. Although the Breadth-First Tree structures differ, the distances between nodes remain the same in the end. (When using vector<vector<int>> as the adjacency list, the traversal order of neighbor nodes depends on their arrangement in the vector<int>, i.e. the insertion order.)
If the graph itself contains multiple connected components, you may be able to draw a Breadth-First Forest.
DFSI introduced Tree DFS before. One of the DFS traversal methods is Pre-order Traversal, which visits the node first, then its left subtree, then the root’s right subtree. This “visit the node when you reach it” property is the core spirit of graph DFS. In a graph, visit a node first, then use that node as the new search start, until all vertices connected by an edge are searched. And like tree traversal or walking a maze, as long as vertices are connected by edges, if one path doesn’t work, go back to the previous vertex and take another edge-connected path.
DFS guarantees that if there’s an edge connecting, a path can definitely be found, but it doesn’t guarantee the shortest path.
Algorithm introductionBefore running dfs(), for ease of explanation we need the following data structures:
time: dfs traversal has an order; think of it as a timeline. N nodes have 2N time points total (each node has a start and an end of search) discover array: records the time point when a vertex is discovered; if vertex(B) is found from vertex(A), then discover[B] = discover[A]+1 finish array: if vertex(B) has fully searched all vertices connected to it by valid edges, then the search starting from vertex(B) has ended, marked as finish[B] visited array: records which nodes are not discovered, or discovered but not yet finished searching, and finished states predecessor array: records which vertex a visited vertex was discovered from, usable to trace back paths
Step0 Initialize data structures
(1) time is 0(2) visited array initialized to 0(3) all discover, finish arrays initialized to 0(4) predecessor array initialized to -1 or null Step1 ~ Step8 visiting and backtracking nodes in order
Step1 - vertex(A) as the start(1) vertex(A) is marked visited (shown in green here)(2) Since vertex(A) is discovered, set discover[A] to ++time (so here discover[A]=1), meaning it’s the start of dfs(3) Next we search the nodes connected to vertex(A). Here we can observe that the first node connected to vertex(A) in the adjacency list is vertex(B), so the next start is vertex(B)
There’s no need to update finish[A] yet, because the search starting from vertex(A) is still in progress; not all edges connected to vertex(A) have been searched.
Step2 - vertex(B) as the start(1) vertex(B) is marked visited (shown in green here)(2) Since vertex(B) is discovered, set discover[B] to ++time (so here discover[B]=2)(3) Next we search the nodes connected to vertex(B). From the adjacency list we observe the next node is vertex(D) Step3 - vertex(D) as the start(1) vertex(D) is marked visited (shown in green here)(2) Since vertex(D) is discovered, set discover[D] to ++time (so here discover[D]=3)(3) Next we search the nodes connected to vertex(D). From the adjacency list we observe the next node is vertex(H) Step4~5 - vertex(H) as the start(1) vertex(H) is marked visited (shown in green here)(2) Since vertex(H) is discovered, set discover[H] to ++time (so here discover[H]=4)(3) Next we search the nodes connected to vertex(H). From the adjacency list we observe that vertex(H) has no next node, so we need to back off to the previous node, i.e. vertex(D)(4) vertex(H) is marked finished (shown in blue here)(5) Update finish to ++time (so here finish[H]=5) Step6 - vertex(D) as the start(1) Since it’s already marked visited, continue searching other connected but not-yet-visited nodes. From the adjacency list we observe that vertex(D) has no other connected nodes, so we need to back off to the previous node, i.e. vertex(B)(4) vertex(D) is marked finished (shown in blue here)(5) Update finish to ++time (so here finish[D]=6) Step7 - vertex(B) as the start(1) Since it’s already marked visited, continue searching other connected but not-yet-visited nodes. From the adjacency list we observe that vertex(B) has no other connected nodes, so we need to back off to the previous node, i.e. vertex(A)(4) vertex(B) is marked finished (shown in blue here)(5) Update finish to ++time (so here finish[B]=7) Step8 - vertex(A) as the start(1) Since it’s already marked visited, continue searching other connected but not-yet-visited nodes. From the adjacency list we observe that vertex(A)’s next connected node is vertex(C), so the next start is vertex(C) Step9 ~ Step16 visiting and backtracking nodes in order
Step9 - vertex(C) as the start(1) vertex(C) is marked visited (shown in green here)(2) Since vertex(C) is discovered, set discover[C] to ++time (so here discover[D]=8)(3) Next we search the nodes connected to vertex(C). From the adjacency list we observe the next node is vertex(F) Step10 - vertex(F) as the start(1) vertex(F) is marked visited (shown in green here)(2) Since vertex(F) is discovered, set discover[F] to ++time (so here discover[F]=9)(3) Next we search the nodes connected to vertex(F). From the adjacency list we observe the next node is vertex(E) Step11 - vertex(E) as the start(1) vertex(E) is marked visited (shown in green here)(2) Since vertex(E) is discovered, set discover[E] to ++time (so here discover[E]=10)(3) Next we search the nodes connected to vertex(E). From the adjacency list we observe that vertex(E)’s connected nodes have all been visited, so we go back to the previous node vertex(F)(4) vertex(E) is marked finished (shown in blue here)(5) Update finish to ++time (so here finish[E]=11) Step12 - vertex(F) as the start(1) Since it’s already marked visited, continue searching other connected but not-yet-visited nodes. From the adjacency list we observe that vertex(F)’s next connected node is vertex(G), so the next start is vertex(G) Step13 - vertex(G) as the start(1) vertex(G) is marked visited (shown in green here)(2) Since vertex(G) is discovered, set discover[G] to ++time (so here discover[G]=12)(3) Next we search the nodes connected to vertex(G). From the adjacency list we observe that vertex(G)’s connected nodes have all been visited, so we go back to the previous node vertex(F)(4) vertex(E) is marked finished (shown in blue here)(5) Update finish to ++time (so here finish[G]=13) Step14 - vertex(F) as the start(1) vertex(F)’s connected nodes have all been visited, so we go back to the previous node vertex(C)(2) vertex(F) is marked finished (shown in blue here)(3) Update finish to ++time (so here finish[F]=14) Step15 - vertex(C) as the start(1) vertex(C)’s connected nodes have all been visited, so we go back to the previous node vertex(A)(2) vertex(C) is marked finished (shown in blue here)(3) Update finish to ++time (so here finish[C]=15) Step16 - vertex(A) as the start(1) vertex(A)’s connected nodes have all been visited, and it’s already the graph’s start(2) vertex(A) is marked finished (shown in blue here)(3) Update finish to ++time (so here finish[A]=16) dfs() ends Here we can expand the timestamp each vertex costs, which looks like below:
You can see DFS is also a recursive structure, so in practice it’s implemented recursively.
Code implementation#include <iostream>#include <vector>#include <list>#include <iomanip>using namespace std;class Graph{ private: int num_vertex; vector<list<int>> adjList; int *visited, // 0: Not visited, 1: Visited, not finished, 2: Finished *predecessor, *discover, *finish; public: Graph(): num_vertex(0){}; Graph(int N): num_vertex(N){ adjList.resize(num_vertex); }; // Member functions void addEdgeList(int from, int to); void dfs(int start); void dfsVisit(int vertex, int &time); void printDiscoverAndFinishTimes();};void Graph::addEdgeList(int from, int to){ adjList[from].push_back(to);}void Graph::dfs(int start){ // Initialize arrays visited = new int[num_vertex]; predecessor = new int[num_vertex]; discover = new int[num_vertex]; finish = new int[num_vertex]; int time = 0; for(int i = 0; i < num_vertex; i++){ visited[i] = 0; predecessor[i] = -1; discover[i] = 0; finish[i] = 0; } // If vertices are unvisited, then visit them for(int i = start; i < num_vertex; i++){ if(visited[i] == 0){ dfsVisit(i, time); } }}void Graph::dfsVisit(int vertex, int &time){ visited[vertex] = 1; discover[vertex] = ++time; for(auto it = adjList[vertex].begin(); it != adjList[vertex].end(); ++it){ if(visited[*it] == 0){ predecessor[*it] = vertex; dfsVisit(*it, time); } } visited[vertex] = 2; finish[vertex] = ++time;}void Graph::printDiscoverAndFinishTimes(){ cout << "Vertex\tDiscover\tFinish" << endl; for(int i = 0; i < num_vertex; i++){ cout << i << "\t\t" << discover[i] << "\t\t" << finish[i] << endl; }}int main(){ Graph g2(8); g2.addEdgeList(0, 1); g2.addEdgeList(0, 2); g2.addEdgeList(1, 3); g2.addEdgeList(2, 5); g2.addEdgeList(3, 7); g2.addEdgeList(4, 1); g2.addEdgeList(4, 3); g2.addEdgeList(4, 7); g2.addEdgeList(5, 4); g2.addEdgeList(5, 6); g2.addEdgeList(6, 3); g2.addEdgeList(6, 7); g2.dfs(0); g2.printDiscoverAndFinishTimes(); return 0;}
