The way the tree is built is the same as BFS; the difference is this example is a directed graph. The program body consists of two functions, dfs and dfsVisit. First, look at dfs: it initializes the various variables and allocates memory based on num_vertex. And except for predecessor being initialized to -1, the other variables are initialized to 0. Then it iterates to check whether each node has been visited (if(visit[i]==0)); if a node hasn’t been visited yet (the white nodes in the figure above), it’s used as the start and passed to dfsVisit for visiting. This loop ensures every vertex in adjList is searched once. Once a vertex is discovered and it’s white, it enters dfsVisit. The first thing it does is update visited[vertex]=1, meaning the node is found but the search starting from it isn’t finished, then update the discovery time discover[vertex] = ++time. With the current vertex as the search start, it then looks among the vertices connected to this node by edges for ones that haven’t been searched yet (visited[i]==0). So it iterates with the current node for(auto it=adjList[vertex].begin(); it!=adjList[vertex].end(); ++it), searching in the build order of the nodes in adjList. Once it finds a node not yet visited, it updates the current node as the predecessor and uses that node as the new search start, recursing to search for other new nodes. Once there are no other connected vertices not yet visited, it marks the current node as search-complete visited[vertex]=2, and at this point also updates the search-complete time finish[vertex] = ++time. Output: Vertex Discover Finish0 1 161 2 72 8 153 3 64 10 115 9 146 12 137 4 5
You can observe that the output matches the result in the earlier algorithm introduction. Extended conceptLike BFS, DFS can also obtain a Predecessor Subgraph through the predecessor, which likewise forms a tree structure called a Depth-First Tree.
We can also derive a few properties about discover from the result:
If $discover[X] > discover[Y]$ and $finish[X] < finish[Y]$, then vertex(X) must be a descendant of vertex(Y). Because this means vertex(X) was discovered later than vertex(Y) and finished searching earlier. If $discover[X] < discover[Y]$ and $finish[X] > finish[Y]$, then vertex(X) must be an ancestor of vertex(Y). Because this means vertex(X) was discovered earlier than vertex(Y) and finished searching later.
Referencehttps://alrightchiu.github.io/SecondRound/graph-breadth-first-searchbfsguang-du-you-xian-sou-xun.htmlhttps://alrightchiu.github.io/SecondRound/graph-depth-first-searchdfsshen-du-you-xian-sou-xun.html

entry.title: Essential Problem-Solving Tool | Hash Table | LeetCode Notes
entry.content:
🌐 中文版：繁體中文
Basic introductionA hash table is a Key-Value mapping structure used for fast data lookup. Compared to the $O(\log n)$ time complexity of general search algorithms, its time complexity is $O(1)$. The main reason for the lightning speed is the hash function. If we first store n numbers in a hash table, then to check whether a number A is already in the hash table, we just throw A into the hash function and immediately know which slot in the hash table A maps to. When a Hash Table is not suitable When the data has a time-priority order for processing, a Queue (FIFO) structure is more suitable If you want the data to be sorted, a hash table isn’t suitable either https://www.reddit.com/r/learnprogramming/comments/29t4s4/when_is_it_bad_to_use_a_hash_table/
Conditions where a Hash Table is suitable The problem requires an $O(1)$ time-complexity algorithm to access elements The worst case is also $O(n)$ time complexity
Hash FunctionFor a hash function to hold, there are three conditions
The value computed by the hash function is a non-negative integer If key1 = key2, then hash(key1) = hash(key2) If key1 ≠ key2, then hash(key1) ≠ hash(key2)
A point to note is that putting multiple pieces of data in the same slot easily causes a collision, and the load factor is the factor used to measure how likely a collision is to happen. - $load factor = n / m$ - $n$ = number of input data items - $m$ = size of the hash table - If $load factor > 1$, a collision is very likely - https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/鴿巢原理 - In plain terms: if n > m, then some data must share a bucket with other data Implementing the hash function (division, stored with an array)First we can define each data item’s index in the hash table index = key % m // 0 <= index < m
Example: A ( Key = 11324)B ( Key = 6356)C ( Key = 345)D ( key = 4171 )
M (hash table size) = 6, so the hash table’s indices are as follows: Index of A : 11324 % 6 = 2Index of B: 6356 % 6 = 2Index of C: 345 % 6 = 3Index of D: 4171 % 6 =1
You can see that A and B collide, which is related to the choice of m. The choice of m should be as far as possible from $2^p$.
Implementing the hash function (multiplication, stored with an array)$index = [ m \cdot ((key \cdot A) \mod 1) ]$ $0 ≤ index < (m-1)$ Steps:
Multiply the key by an irrational number less than 1, i.e. A, where A is usually chosen as $\frac{\sqrt5 -1}{2}$; after multiplying you get a larger irrational number Take this irrational number mod 1, which removes the integer part and leaves only the decimal Multiply m by the decimal; this step gives an irrational number between $0$ and $(m-1)$ Use the floor function to take the integer of the irrational number https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/取整函数
The figure below explains it quite wellImage source: https://medium.com/@ralph-tech/%E8%B3%87%E6%96%99%E7%B5%90%E6%A7%8B%E5%AD%B8%E7%BF%92%E7%AD%86%E8%A8%98-%E9%9B%9C%E6%B9%8A%E8%A1%A8-hash-table-15f490f8ede6
What are the advantages of this more elaborate way of computing the index:
No constraint that m must be far from $2^p$ Can increase randomness
How to handle addressing collisions?1. Separate Chaining / Closed AddressingGenerate a new chained storage space within each storage slot, which can be implemented with a linked list or an array
Since extra pointers are needed, if the stored data is smaller than a pointer, using a linked list consumes double the memory to store the data. However, if the data to be stored is much larger than the size of a pointer, the extra cost of the pointer becomes negligible. In fact, we can modify the linked list to combine its back end with data structures like a red-black tree or a skip list, so that the final hash table’s lookup time only needs $O(\log n)$. This structure is suitable for storing large amounts of data where each item is relatively large, and it also supports more varied optimization strategies, usable in combination with a red-black tree, etc. 2. Open AddressingOpen addressing mainly uses probing to find unoccupied space, which can be divided into:
Linear Probing Quadratic probing
Linear ProbingWhen a collision occurs, check whether the next index position is free; if it’s empty, put the data in, if not, keep looking downward. When searching for an element, if a collision occurs, you also need to search backward, not stopping until you find an empty slot. Downside: a hash table supports deletion, but a deleted element needs to be marked, otherwise deleting it directly would interrupt subsequent search processes. Quadratic probingThis can be used to solve the inefficiency of linear probing. When many elements are inserted, linear probing is also slow during addressing. hash(key)+1, hash(key)+2, hash(key)+3,…..hash(key)+n
So with quadratic probing the addressing is changed to: hash(key)+ 1^2 , hash(key)+ 2^2, hash(key)+3^2 Each time it increases by n^2 to find a free slot Double hashingAlternatively, if a collision occurs, you can directly run another hash function, i.e. when a collision happens, keep hashing until the collision ends $index_{n} = F_{1}(k) + (n-1)* F_{2}(k)$ until the final index is found Pros and cons of open addressing:Pros: The open addressing method doesn’t use linked lists; all data is stored in an array, which helps speed up access through caching. Cons: Deleting data is more troublesome, requiring special marking of the data to be deleted.All data is stored in the same hash table, so the cost of a collision is higher, which means the load factor shouldn’t be too high, making this method more wasteful of memory. Hash Table implementation#include <stdio.h>#include <string.h>// in order to use bool function in C#include <stdbool.h>#define MAX_NAME 256#define TABLE_SIZE 10typedef struct{ char name[MAX_NAME]; int age;}person; person *hash_table[TABLE_SIZE];unsigned int hash(char *name);void init_hash_table();void print_table();bool hash_table_insert(person *p);bool hash_table_delete(person *p);int main(){ init_hash_table(); person Walt={.name="Walt",.age=26}; person Skyler={.name="Skyler",.age=27}; person Saul={.name="Saul",.age=28}; person Mike={.name="Mike",.age=29}; person Hank={.name="Hank",.age=30}; person Mary={.name="Mary",.age=31}; //add person into hash_table hash_table_insert(&Walt); hash_table_insert(&Skyler); hash_table_insert(&Saul); hash_table_insert(&Mike); hash_table_insert(&Hank); hash_table_insert(&Mary); print_table(); //delete persion in hash table hash_table_delete(&Walt); print_table(); return 0;}//define the hash functionunsigned int hash(char *name){ int length=strnlen(name, MAX_NAME); unsigned int hash_value=0; for(int i=0;i<length;i++){ hash_value+=name[i]; hash_value=(hash_value*name[i])%TABLE_SIZE; } return hash_value;}//initialize the hash table to NULL (let it be empty)void init_hash_table(){ for(int i=0;i<TABLE_SIZE;i++){ hash_table[i]=NULL; }}//print out the hash tablevoid print_table(){ printf("--------Start--------\n"); for(int i=0;i<TABLE_SIZE;i++){ //nothing in the hash table if(hash_table[i]==NULL) printf("\t%d\t---\n",i); //something in the hash table else printf("\t%d\t%s\n",i,hash_table[i]->name); } printf("--------End----------\n");}//insert the element into the hash_tablebool hash_table_insert(person *p){ //make sure not call this function with null ptr if(p==NULL) return false; //insert the person into the index return by hash_function int index=hash(p->name); //check the pointer at that index in the table is null or not if(hash_table[index]!=NULL) return false; //collision, somebody had occupied there already //if no one occupied there, then occupied the address hash_table[index]=p; return true;}bool hash_table_delete(person *p){ // to avoid null ptr if(p==NULL) return false; //get index int index=hash(p->name); if(hash_table[index]!=NULL){ hash_table[index] = NULL; } return true;}
Using the C++ STL makes problem solving much more convenient: #include <iostream>#include <unordered_map>#include <string>using namespace std;struct Person { string name; int age;};unordered_map<string, Person> hash_table;void init_hash_table();void print_table();bool hash_table_insert(const Person& p);bool hash_table_delete(const string& name);int main() { init_hash_table(); Person Walt = {.name = "Walt", .age = 26}; Person Skyler = {.name = "Skyler", .age = 27}; Person Saul = {.name = "Saul", .age = 28}; Person Mike = {.name = "Mike", .age = 29}; Person Hank = {.name = "Hank", .age = 30}; Person Mary = {.name = "Mary", .age = 31}; // Add persons into hash_table hash_table_insert(Walt); hash_table_insert(Skyler); hash_table_insert(Saul); hash_table_insert(Mike); hash_table_insert(Hank); hash_table_insert(Mary); print_table(); // Delete person from hash table hash_table_delete("Walt"); print_table(); return 0;}void init_hash_table() { hash_table.clear();}void print_table() { cout << "--------Start--------" << endl; for (const auto& pair : hash_table) { cout << "\t" << pair.first << "\t" << pair.second.name << endl; } cout << "--------End----------" << endl;}bool hash_table_insert(const Person& p) { auto result = hash_table.insert({p.name, p}); return result.second; // True if insertion took place, false if key already existed}bool hash_table_delete(const string& name) { return hash_table.erase(name) > 0; // True if element was removed, false if key didn't exist}
Adding collision handling#include <stdio.h>#include <stdlib.h>#include <string.h>#include <stdbool.h>#define MAX_NAME 256#define TABLE_SIZE 10typedef struct person { char name[MAX_NAME]; int age; struct person *next; // pointer to the next person in the list} person;person *hash_table[TABLE_SIZE];unsigned int hash(char *name);void init_hash_table();void print_table();bool hash_table_insert(person *p);person* hash_table_lookup(char *name);bool hash_table_delete(char *name);int main() { init_hash_table(); person Walt = {.name = "Walt", .age = 26}; person Skyler = {.name = "Skyler", .age = 27}; person Saul = {.name = "Saul", .age = 28}; person Mike = {.name = "Mike", .age = 29}; person Hank = {.name = "Hank", .age = 30}; person Mary = {.name = "Mary", .age = 31}; // Add persons into hash_table hash_table_insert(&Walt); hash_table_insert(&Skyler); hash_table_insert(&Saul); hash_table_insert(&Mike); hash_table_insert(&Hank); hash_table_insert(&Mary); print_table(); // Delete person from hash table hash_table_delete("Walt"); print_table(); return 0;}// Define the hash functionunsigned int hash(char *name) { int length = strnlen(name, MAX_NAME); unsigned int hash_value = 0; for (int i = 0; i < length; i++) { hash_value += name[i]; hash_value = (hash_value * name[i]) % TABLE_SIZE; } return hash_value;}// Initialize the hash table to NULL (let it be empty)void init_hash_table() { for (int i = 0; i < TABLE_SIZE; i++) { hash_table[i] = NULL; }}// Print out the hash tablevoid print_table() { printf("--------Start--------\n"); for (int i = 0; i < TABLE_SIZE; i++) { if (hash_table[i] == NULL) { printf("\t%d\t---\n", i); } else { person *tmp = hash_table[i]; while (tmp != NULL) { printf("\t%d\t%s\n", i, tmp->name); tmp = tmp->next; } } } printf("--------End----------\n");}// Insert the element into the hash_tablebool hash_table_insert(person *p) { if (p == NULL) return false; int index = hash(p->name); // Insert at the head of the list p->next = hash_table[index]; hash_table[index] = p; return true;}// Lookup a person in the hash table by nameperson* hash_table_lookup(char *name) { int index = hash(name); person *tmp = hash_table[index]; while (tmp != NULL && strncmp(tmp->name, name, MAX_NAME) != 0) { tmp = tmp->next; } return tmp;}// Delete a person from the hash table by namebool hash_table_delete(char *name) { int index = hash(name); person *tmp = hash_table[index]; person *prev = NULL; while (tmp != NULL && strncmp(tmp->name, name, MAX_NAME) != 0) { prev = tmp; tmp = tmp->next; } if (tmp == NULL) return false; if (prev == NULL) { hash_table[index] = tmp->next; } else { prev->next = tmp->next; } return true;}
When a collision occurs, here we use closed addressing (i.e. a linked list) to solve the problem. The concrete implementation is as follows: Linked List: Each person struct contains a next pointer to form a linked list.Each slot of the hash table (hash_table[index]) is the head pointer of a linked list.
Insert operation:
The hash_table_insert function, after computing the index, inserts the new person at the head of the linked list at the corresponding index.
Lookup operation:
The hash_table_lookup function traverses the linked list at the given index, looking for a person with a specific name.
Delete operation:
The hash_table_delete function finds and deletes a specific person in the linked list at the given index, while maintaining the linked list’s structure.This implementation uses a linked list to solve the hash collision problem in a hash table, ensuring that insertion, lookup, and deletion still work correctly when a collision occurs. Reference[1] https://medium.com/@ralph-tech/%E8%B3%87%E6%96%99%E7%B5%90%E6%A7%8B%E5%AD%B8%E7%BF%92%E7%AD%86%E8%A8%98-%E9%9B%9C%E6%B9%8A%E8%A1%A8-hash-table-15f490f8ede6[2] https://hackmd.io/@coherent17/Sk4fomSkt#%E9%9B%9C%E6%B9%8A%E8%A1%A8Hash-table[3] https://blog.techbridge.cc/2017/01/21/simple-hash-table-intro/[4] https://haogroot.com/2022/06/19/how-to-design-hash-table/

entry.title: Problem-Solving Notes | Graphs-3
entry.content:
🌐 中文版：繁體中文
IntroTo guarantee things like “you must take Calculus before you can take Engineering Mathematics”, this kind of graph problem with ordering dependencies is usually handled with Topological Sort.
Using DFS to find Strongly Connected Components (SCC)Strongly Connected Components (SCC) When vertices are connected by edges in both directions, for example going from vertex(A) to vertex(B) while vertex(B) also has an edge back to vertex(A), we say these two vertices are strongly connected.
You can usually determine which Strongly Connected Components exist in a directed graph through multiple DFS runs. The reason for multiple DFS runs is that a single DFS may not identify all the connected components, and depending on the search start point the result can differ. Each time you look for connected components you get a separate Depth-First Search Tree, and depending on the choice of search start point, a large Depth-First Search Tree may form. Using vertex(I)
Using vertex(A) as the search start point
From the figures above you can observe that using vertex(I), vertex(F), vertex(B) as start points finds three SCCs, each with its own Depth-First Search Tree. But using vertex(A) as the start point gives just one large SCC, and the true three SCCs aren’t separated. Component GraphHere, if a directed graph has multiple SCCs, you can treat each SCC as a larger vertex $V^{\text{SCC}}$, and the edges connecting the SCCs become the edges $E^{\text{SCC}}$ in the component graph, where $C_1 = {A,B,C,D}$$C_2 = {E, F}$$C_3 = {G, H , I}$$V^{\text{SCC}} = [C_1, C_2, C_3 ]$$E^{\text{SCC}} = [ (C,E),(D,F),(E,G),(F,G),(F,H) ]$
Properties:
For any directed graph, treating its SCCs as vertices forms a component graph. A component graph is always a directed acyclic graph (DAG): this is because if a cycle existed between C1 and C2, then they wouldn’t be separate SCCs and would merge into a larger SCC, so there is never a cycle between different SCCs.
So this comes back to the earlier problem: a single DFS with different start points can’t correctly distinguish the SCCs. How do we choose the start point so that the corresponding SCCs can be distinguished?
Different start points form different DFS treesStarting from C3, all SCCs are identified successfully Starting from C2, only two SCCs are identified Starting from C1, the three SCCs can’t be identified successfully
From the above we get a property: if DFS(), each time it looks for a “new search start point”, can follow the vertex order “from the tail to the head along a path”, then the predecessor subgraph can grow into a Depth-First Forest that distinguishes the SCCs.
So the next question is: how do we ensure that every time we can find “the vertex order from the tail to the head along a path”?
If you observe the recursion call (DFS tree) figures above, you’ll find that no matter how the search start point is chosen, in terms of the final finish time (the red dashed line) it’s always $C_1 > C_2 > C_3$. This isn’t actually any special principle, it’s super intuitive: if in a directed graph there exist vertex(A) and vertex(B) with edge(A, B), then vertex(A)’s finish time must be larger than vertex(B)’s. Either you pick vertex(A) as the start point, in which case you’ll reach vertex(B) first and vertex(A) finishes only after vertex(B); or you pick vertex(B) as the start, but vertex(B) doesn’t point to other nodes, so once it’s done you pick vertex(A) as the start, and its finish time is still the largest. Therefore
If edge(X,Y) exists in a directed graph, then the “maximum finish” of all vertices in set C1 must be larger than the “maximum finish” of all vertices in set C2.
So for the component graph above, finish[C1] > finish[C2] > finish[C3]. If we look at the earlier figure from the finish-time angle
C1=[A,B,C,D]finish[C1]= finish[B]=18C2=[E,F]finish[C2]=finish[F]=10C3=[G,H,I]finish[C3]=finish[I]=6
Here you can notice one thing: as long as you pick the vertices of the SCCs as DFS() start points in order of “finish time from small to large”, you can distinguish all the SCCs as a Depth-First Forest in the predecessor subgraph. So we can summarize three steps:
First run DFS on any vertex to obtain the finish information Based on the order obtained, decide the start-point order for the second DFS Run the second DFS to obtain the predecessor subgraph and thus the SCCs
There’s still a problem with point one: when picking the vertex in point one we have no prior knowledge of the SCCs, so the generated finish order doesn’t necessarily reflect the correct topological structure of the SCCs. If the first DFS fails to traverse the strongly connected components in some “global order”, the finish order may be unrelated to the true structure of the SCCs, which could cause a later SCC to go back to an earlier SCC via some edge.
We can solve this with the transpose. A later SCC might go back to an earlier SCC, which makes it hard to correctly distinguish SCCs purely by finish order from small to large. Through the transpose, in $G^T$ the directional dependency between SCCs is reversed, guaranteeing DFS can correctly separate the SCCs layer by layer in order of finish from large to small. Here you can see that $G$ and $G^T$ have the same components, but the finish order is completely reversed. So the finish times obtained after the first DFS are from large to small, and after transposing they become small to large. Therefore, picking start points by the “finish from large to small” order obtained from the first DFS() and running the second DFS on $G^T$, we first pick C1. Since we can’t walk from C1 back to C2, after DFS finishes searching all vertices in C1 it forms its own Depth-First Tree. Then we pick C2 and C3 in turn as start points and build each SCC’s Depth-First Tree. This finds all the SCCs in the directed graph. Algorithm Run DFS on $G$ Transpose $G$ to get $G^T$ Run DFS on $G^T$’s nodes in order of the first DFS’s finish “from large to small”; each DFS traverses one SCC Find the predecessor subgraph from the second DFS’s predecessors (if the directed graph has multiple SCCs, the predecessor subgraph is a Depth-First Forest where each Depth-First Tree is an SCC)
Code#include <iostream>#include <vector>#include <list>#include <stack>#include <algorithm>using namespace std;class Graph { private: int num_vertex; vector<list<int>> AdjList; void DFSVisit(int v, vector<bool> &visited, stack<int> &finishStack); void DFSVisitSCC(int v, vector<bool> &visited, vector<int> &component); public: Graph(int N): num_vertex(N) { AdjList.resize(num_vertex); } void AddEdgeList(int from, int to); Graph GraphTranspose(); void FindSCCs();};void Graph::AddEdgeList(int from, int to){ AdjList[from].push_back(to);}void Graph::DFSVisit(int v, vector<bool> &visited, stack<int> &finishStack){ visited[v] = true; for(int neighbor: AdjList[v]){ if(!visited[neighbor]){ DFSVisit(neighbor, visited, finishStack); } } finishStack.push(v);}void Graph::DFSVisitSCC(int v, vector<bool> &visited, vector<int> &component){ visited[v] = true; component.push_back(v); for(int neighbor: AdjList[v]){ if(!visited[neighbor]){ DFSVisitSCC(neighbor, visited, component); } }}Graph Graph::GraphTranspose(){ Graph gT(num_vertex); for(int i=0; i<num_vertex; i++){ for(int neighbor: AdjList[i]){ gT.AddEdgeList(neighbor, i); } } return gT;}// Kosaraju's Algorithm to find SCCsvoid Graph::FindSCCs(){ stack<int> finishStack; vector<bool> visited(num_vertex, false); // First DFS to get the finish order for(int i=0; i< num_vertex;i++){ if(!visited[i]){ DFSVisit(i, visited, finishStack); } } // Get transposed graph Graph gT = GraphTranspose(); //Second DFS to find SCCs in finishStack order // reinit visited array fill(visited.begin(), visited.end(), false); cout << "Strongly Connected Components: \n"; while(!finishStack.empty()){ int v = finishStack.top(); finishStack.pop(); if(!visited[v]){ vector<int> components; gT.DFSVisitSCC(v, visited, components); for(int node: components){ cout << node << " "; } cout << endl; } }}int main(){ //Test Graph g(9); g.AddEdgeList(0, 1); g.AddEdgeList(1, 2); g.AddEdgeList(1, 4); g.AddEdgeList(2, 0); g.AddEdgeList(2, 3); g.AddEdgeList(2, 5); g.AddEdgeList(3, 2); g.AddEdgeList(4, 5); g.AddEdgeList(4, 6); g.AddEdgeList(5, 4); g.AddEdgeList(5, 6); g.AddEdgeList(5, 7); g.AddEdgeList(6, 7); g.AddEdgeList(7, 8); g.AddEdgeList(8, 6); g.FindSCCs(); return 0;}
Execution result Strongly Connected Components: 0 2 1 3 5 4 6 8 7
Using DFS to find a DAG - Topological SortBack to what was mentioned earlier: if you have a problem like a school’s prerequisite/follow-up course schedule that needs to guarantee the ordering of vertices, you use Topological Sort. The basic theorem of Topological Sort:
In a DAG (Directed Acyclic Graph), if edge(X,Y) exists then vertex(X) must appear after vertex(Y)
It sounds like stating the obvious: in a directed graph, of course if an edge from X to Y exists, then during traversal X must appear after Y.
Topological Sort is only meaningful in a DAG. If a cycle appears it violates the rule mentioned above. For example,
If edge(YouTube, Dinner) exists, it means YouTube comes before Dinner: watch YouTube before eating. The overall sequence would be YouTube Dinner LeetCode Exercises, while the existence of edge(Dinner, LeetCode) would produce the sequence Dinner LeetCode Exercises Youtube, which violates the principle of watching YouTube before eating.
So if a cycle exists in a directed graph, Topological Sort is meaningless.
Back to our goal: we want to guarantee the order during traversal. Based on the conclusion of the previous section, if a path goes from vertex(X) to vertex(Y) then vertex(X)’s finish time must be larger than vertex(Y)’s (finish[X] > finish[Y]). So you only need to run one DFS and print in order of finish time from large to small, and that’s the Topological Sort.
Code Actually you only need to change part of the FindSCCs() logic, because the core idea of topological sort is to push a node onto a stack when DFS completes it, so we just output the contents of finishStack without running a second DFS.
#include <iostream>#include <vector>#include <list>#include <stack>#include <algorithm>using namespace std;class Graph {private: int num_vertex; vector<list<int>> AdjList; void DFSVisit(int v, vector<bool> &visited, stack<int> &finishStack);public: Graph(int N) : num_vertex(N) { AdjList.resize(num_vertex); } void AddEdgeList(int from, int to); void FindTopologicalSort(); };void Graph::AddEdgeList(int from, int to) { AdjList[from].push_back(to);}void Graph::DFSVisit(int v, vector<bool> &visited, stack<int> &finishStack) { visited[v] = true; for (int neighbor : AdjList[v]) { if (!visited[neighbor]) { DFSVisit(neighbor, visited, finishStack); } } finishStack.push(v); //Push to stack after DFS// Topological sortvoid Graph::FindTopologicalSort() { stack<int> finishStack; vector<bool> visited(num_vertex, false); // Perform DFS, push the finished node to the stack for (int i = 0; i < num_vertex; i++) { if (!visited[i]) { DFSVisit(i, visited, finishStack); } } // Output Result cout << "Topological Sort Order:\n"; while (!finishStack.empty()) { cout << finishStack.top() << " "; finishStack.pop(); } cout << endl;}int main() { Graph g(6); g.AddEdgeList(5, 2); g.AddEdgeList(5, 0); g.AddEdgeList(4, 0); g.AddEdgeList(4, 1); g.AddEdgeList(2, 3); g.AddEdgeList(3, 1); g.FindTopologicalSort(); // Topological Sort return 0;}
Output Topological Sort Order:5 4 2 3 1 0
Corresponding LeetCode problems 207. Course Schedule / Medium 210. Course Schedule II / Medium 310. Minimum Height Trees 269. Alien Dictionary / Hard / Premium 444. Sequence Reconstruction / Medium / Premium 1462. Course Schedule IV
Referenceshttps://alrightchiu.github.io/SecondRound/graph-li-yong-dfsxun-zhao-dagde-topological-sorttuo-pu-pai-xu.htmlhttps://hackmd.io/@bangyewu/BknWuaVlT#Topological-sort%E7%AF%84%E4%BE%8Bhttps://bclin.tw/2022/01/18/leetcode-207/

entry.title: A Logic Gate Shorted by Radiation | Ionized Transistangle | GaianSpace CTF 2026
entry.content:
Third post of the GaianSpace CTF 2026 “05-rad-hard-rampage” series. 🌐 中文版：繁體中文
The first two posts (SEU, SEL) were both single-event effects: one particle, one bit, one instant. This one is a cumulative effect: not a single hit, but months of radiation dose slowly wrecking the transistors. The failure model shifts from “data got changed” to “the logic itself is broken,” so the approach is completely different. Other post in the series: Sensor Drift / Degradift
What the challenge is about
Total ionizing dose does not flip a bit and move on — it leaves transistors shorted, stuck, permanently. The encoder now spits nonsense. We still have the original design, gate for gate, with the damaged nodes marked.
In plain terms: months of accumulated radiation dose have finally taken out Foundation One’s status encoder. Total Ionizing Dose (TID) doesn’t flip one bit and move on. It shorts transistors permanently and jams them. The encoder now spits out garbage. We still have the original design, gate for gate, with the damaged nodes marked. The encoder turns a string of probe words into a line of status words, but what’s measured on the board is garbage, because a few gates have shorted: no matter the input, their outputs are jammed. In other words, we need to reconstruct what the encoder was supposed to do: run the probe words through the “as-designed” logic, and the status line comes back. The file given is a gate-level netlist status_encoder.netlist, with the shorted gates marked and the probe words listed at the end.
Flag format: GAIANSPACE{...}.
Reading the netlistINPUTS i0 i1 i2 i3 i4 i5 i6 i7OUTPUTS o0 o1 o2 o3 o4 o5 o6 o7o0 = XOR i0 i7n1 = XOR i0 i2...n6 = XOR i0 i1 [SHORTED=0]...n15 = XOR i1 i3 [SHORTED=1]...PROBES 77 a6 ce a6 a7 e8 97 a6 61 b0 13 12 0a 12 35 f3 96 b2 8c 34 5d ab 5d 34 e4 96 9b 0a 7b 23 c2
8 inputs, 8 outputs, all XOR chains plus some NOTs. Two nodes, n6 and n15, are marked [SHORTED=0] and [SHORTED=1].
This is the challenge’s “transistors shorted, outputs permanently jammed at some value no matter the input.”
The short value is a lie, so use the design valueThis is the twist of the whole challenge, matching the hint “A short is a lie.” Total Ionizing Dose (TID) is a completely different radiation effect: not the instant event of one particle, but long-term accumulated charge trapped in the oxide layer, slowly drifting the transistors’ threshold voltage and leaking, until some gates “stick” at a fixed output and never respond to input again. So what’s measured on the board now is the two post-damage jammed values, which are the result of the fault, not the design intent. [SHORTED=0]/[SHORTED=1] are just recording what it’s broken into now, so when reconstructing you must completely ignore those markers and compute n6, n15 by their original logic (n6 = i0 XOR i1, n15 = i1 XOR i3), no different from any other healthy gate. Feed the probe words through the “as-designed” logicThe netlist comments spell out that each probe byte’s bits map to i7..i0 (bit 0 → i0, bit 7 → i7). Feed the 32 probes in order through the as-designed logic (ignoring the short markers), compute each group’s o0..o7, and reassemble into a byte. To see the damage’s effect clearly at the same time, I simulated both “run as damaged” and “run as designed”: def run(byte, damaged): v = {inputs[k]: (byte >> k) & 1 for k in range(8)} for lhs, op, a, b, shorted in gates: if damaged and shorted is not None: v[lhs] = shorted # jammed, ignore its inputs elif op == 'NOT': v[lhs] = 1 ^ v[a] else: v[lhs] = v[a] ^ v[b] # design value, don't use the SHORTED marker return sum(v[outputs[k]] << k for k in range(8))damaged = bytes(run(int(p,16), True) for p in probes)designed = bytes(run(int(p,16), False) for p in probes)
Put the two outputs side by side and the conclusion is obvious:
Interestingly, the damaged output’s first few characters still coincidentally show hints of GE and ENSPE (probably because some output bits happened not to be affected by those two jammed gates), but overall it’s not text at all. Only running fully as-designed (both gates treated as normal XOR) makes the 32 probes map to the complete, clean flag. FlagGAIANSPACE{t0tal_1onizing_d0se}
Takeaways “Stuck” and “flipped” are two completely different failure models. A flip (SEU) changes just one value, so you enumerate to recover it (see the first post); a stuck gate (TID) returns the same value for all inputs and propagates downstream. The solution isn’t to guess “what the correct value is,” but to directly reconstruct the as-designed logic. When the challenge explicitly says a marker is “the broken state,” don’t let it lead you around. The [SHORTED=...] value describes the fault; it’s not meant to be used, so treat it as noise to ignore. The real work here is “correctly turning the netlist into a simulator”; the logic itself is simple. Building both “run as damaged” and “run as designed” for comparison does more than verify understanding; it’s also vivid. You see at a glance how far the short corrupts the downstream signal, and it confirms your simulator isn’t buggy.

entry.title: Follow the Hops and Reassemble the Symbols | Hopscotch | GaianSpace CTF 2026
entry.content:
🌐 中文版：繁體中文 Seventh and final post in the series. Over the previous six posts the LoRa demodulator grew from single-frequency, fixed-parameter all the way to implicit header, different-SF-per-packet, and drift correction. Here the satellite does one last thing: it hops across multiple frequencies (FHSS), and the demodulator has to reassemble the symbols, scattered across different frequencies, back into time order before it can decode. Rest of the series: Channel Hop、True Color Is a Lie、Isodata Seven、Subsidy Claim、Two Voices、No Name on the Door
What the challenge is about The stranger has switched GAIAN-723’s downlink into a frequency-hopping mode, changing frequency every few symbols to shake off a recorder stuck on a single frequency. David opens the SDR’s bandwidth to the max and records the whole thing. Goal: decode the contents of this hopping downlink and pull out the flag. The files given are a wideband .sigmf-data and the ground-station notes. Flag format: GAIANSPACE{...} First, spot that it’s hoppingMake a wideband waterfall of the whole segment and you can see at a glance that the signal doesn’t stay on one frequency. It hops regularly between a few frequency slots. That’s FHSS (frequency-hopping spread spectrum):
Measure it: the carrier switches among a fixed set of channels, each dwell is roughly a fixed number of symbols, then it jumps to the next channel. The LoRa modulation parameters (SF, BW) are the same in every dwell; only the centre frequency changes. Reassemble the hop sequenceThe solution has two layers:
Estimate the hopping plan. Run an FFT over each time window to find the dominant frequency, giving you a time → frequency sequence. The channel set is a fixed handful of values, the dwell time is fixed, and the hop order is periodic (pseudo-random but repeating). Organize it into a hop table:
Follow the hops and stitch the symbols together. For each dwell, bring the signal back to baseband (multiply by exp(-j2πf·t) to move that channel to 0), decode that segment’s symbols with the same demodulator from the earlier posts, then join all the dwells’ symbols end to end in time order to recover the full symbol stream.
The trap here is the dwell boundary: there’s a short transition at the instant of a hop, so drop half a symbol at each end of a dwell and align each dwell’s symbol phase, so they don’t misalign when joined. After alignment, the whole symbol stream decodes through the standard pipeline (Gray → de-interleave → de-whiten XOR), and the packet ends with a CRC that checks out. FlagThe decoded downlink carries the flag directly: GAIANSPACE{h0p_sc0tch_AF44A6}
Takeaways The first step of FHSS is always “estimate the hopping plan.” A wideband waterfall plus a per-window FFT for the dominant frequency lets you plot “time → channel”; hopping is usually a periodic pseudo-random sequence, and once you spot the period the whole table is fixed. Hopping just scatters the symbols across frequencies; the decoding core is unchanged. After bringing each dwell back to baseband, it’s still the same LoRa demodulator, which is exactly why the earlier posts spent the effort getting the skeleton solid. Watch the dwell boundaries. There’s a transition at the moment of a hop, so leave a little margin at each end and align the phase before joining, or the symbols misalign at the seams. By this point, the LoRa demodulator hand-built since True Color Is a Lie can handle everything thrown at it: two transmitters, implicit headers, a different SF per packet, Doppler drift, and frequency hopping. One demodulator, seven challenges. That’s the most satisfying part of this whole series.

entry.title: initrd vs initramfs | Linux Kernel
entry.content:
🌐 中文版：繁體中文
IntroductionEarly in boot, a temporary filesystem is needed to perform initialization and configuration during the early boot stage. There are two mechanisms for using a temporary filesystem: initrd (Initial RAM Disk) and initramfs (Initial RAM Filesystem). initrd is the earlier approach, and most boot flows today use initramfs. initrd initrd (Initial RAM Disk) is a temporary root filesystem used in early Linux boot. It takes the form of a gzip-compressed block image, loaded at boot into a virtual RAM disk (e.g. /dev/ram0) and then mounted by the kernel as the initial root.
It usually contains:
The drivers needed to mount the real rootfs A linuxrc (an init-like early user-space script) Initialization scripts to mount /proc, /sys, and so on
Booting with initrdTo boot via initrd, it must be loaded into memory at the bootloader stage, and the bootloader must tell the kernel the initrd’s memory address. But how does it know the initrd address? Very old bootloaders told the kernel the initrd’s start address and size as parameters via the kernel command line; but in newer bootloaders (GRUB), the initrd is passed to the kernel through the boot protocol structure rather than the command line. console=tty0, 115200 root=/dev/nfs \ nfsroot=192.168.1.10:/home/testuser/sandbox/nfs-target \ initrd=0x10800000, 0x14af47
The kernel command line above means: set the console to tty0 at baud rate 115200, mount the rootfs over NFS (fetching the NFS rootfs from a private IP), and finally load and mount a RAM disk from physical memory address 0x10800000 with size 0x14af47. In the bootloader you can set the start memory addresses for the kernel image and initrd. Here’s an example with U-Boot: => setenv kernel_addr_r 0x80000=> setenv initrd_addr_r 0x1000000=> setenv initrd_size 0x800000# Read the kernel and initrd images (assuming FAT read from an mmc device)=> fatload mmc 0:1 ${kernel_addr_r} /boot/uImage=> fatload mmc 0:1 ${initrd_addr_r} /boot/initrd.img# Set the kernel command line, telling the kernel the rootfs and initrd info=> setenv bootargs "console=ttyS0,115200 root=/dev/mmcblk0p2 rw initrd=${initrd_addr_r},${initrd_size}"# Load and boot the kernel, passing the initrd image address and size=> bootm ${kernel_addr_r} ${initrd_addr_r}:${initrd_size}
U-Boot can also load the kernel image and initrd image over the network, saving the development time of flashing everything to flash ROM.
Overall flow: The bootloader loads the kernel image and initrd image into RAM The bootloader passes the initrd’s address and size via the boot protocol (or command line) After the kernel starts, it gets the initrd image from RAM It decompresses the initrd .gz into /dev/ram0 It mounts /dev/ram0 as the temporary root filesystem The kernel spawns an early process to run linuxrc linuxrc mounts /proc and /sys, loads drivers, and mounts the real rootfs linuxrc calls pivot_root or switch_root to switch to the real rootfs The initrd RAM disk is unmounted and its memory freed
This linuxrc is a script containing the commands needed before mounting the real root filesystem, such as mount -t proc /proc /proc or busybox sh.
After linuxrc finishes, the initrd early stage ends, at which point pivot_root / switch_root switches to the real rootfs, and only then is the initrd RAM disk freed. In the kernel source, the prepare_namespace() function in init/do_mounts.c decides where the rootfs is and where the mount point is. Within it:
initrd_load() checks whether an initrd exists, and if so decompresses and mounts it mount_root() mounts the real rootfs Finally init_chroot("/") completes the switch
initrd flowSwitch to light mode to view, button at bottom right
/* * Prepare the namespace - decide what/where to mount, load ramdisks, etc. */void __init prepare_namespace(void){ if (root_delay) { printk(KERN_INFO "Waiting %d sec before mounting root device...\n", root_delay); ssleep(root_delay); } /* * wait for the known devices to complete their probing * * Note: this is a potential source of long boot delays. * For example, it is not atypical to wait 5 seconds here * for the touchpad of a laptop to initialize. */ wait_for_device_probe(); md_run_setup(); if (saved_root_name[0]) ROOT_DEV = parse_root_device(saved_root_name); if (initrd_load(saved_root_name)) goto out; if (root_wait) wait_for_root(saved_root_name); mount_root(saved_root_name);out: devtmpfs_mount(); init_mount(".", "/", NULL, MS_MOVE, NULL); init_chroot(".");}
Let’s trace initrd_load, since it tries to load the initrd. Reading the code, we find: if the kernel enabled CONFIG_BLK_DEV_INITRD (initrd support, which you can check in the kernel config editor), it tries to load the early root filesystem from the initrd image passed in by the bootloader. On success it returns true, which tells the kernel: “I’ve already mounted the initrd, you don’t need to try mounting another rootfs.” On failure, or if not enabled, it returns false, and the kernel proceeds to mount_root() to mount the real rootfs. #ifdef CONFIG_BLK_DEV_INITRDbool __init initrd_load(char *root_device_name);#elsestatic inline bool initrd_load(char *root_device_name){ return false;}#endif
initramfsinitramfs’s purpose is actually similar to initrd:both provide a temporary root before the real root filesystem is mounted, letting us:
Load necessary drivers Do some early-userspace initialization Finally switch to the real rootfs
The difference is entirely in implementation:
initrd: a traditional filesystem image (e.g. ext2) that’s gzip-compressed. After the kernel decompresses it, it’s placed on a RAM disk like /dev/ram0 and mounted. initramfs: a cpio archive (usually gzipped too). The kernel unpacks the cpio directly into rootfs (ramfs or tmpfs), with no block device and no intermediate /dev/ram0 layer.
For a built-in initramfs (compiled into the kernel), its unpacking roughly happens at:
After start_kernel() calls a sequence of initializations Entering rest_init() → kernel_init() → kernel_init_freeable() which calls populate_rootfs() to unpack the compile-time initramfs cpio into rootfs
Later, do_basic_setup() calls do_initcalls() to initialize various drivers and subsystems. So roughly speaking: initramfs is unpacked and mounted before do_basic_setup(). kernel_init_freeableSwitch to light mode to view, button at bottom right
do_initcalls flowSwitch to light mode to view, button at bottom right
overall flowSwitch to light mode to view, button at bottom right
In the kernel source tree’s usr/ directory, you can see the initramfs-related files: kevin@MSI:~/linux-6.17.7$ ls -l usr/total 96-rw-rw-r-- 1 kevin kevin 7902 Nov 2 21:18 Kconfig-rw-rw-r-- 1 kevin kevin 2756 Nov 2 21:18 Makefile-rw-rw-r-- 1 kevin kevin 146 Nov 4 16:44 built-in.a-rw-rw-r-- 1 kevin kevin 153 Nov 2 21:18 default_cpio_listdrwxrwxr-x 2 kevin kevin 4096 Nov 2 21:18 dummy-include-rwxrwxr-x 1 kevin kevin 27248 Nov 4 16:44 gen_init_cpio-rw-rw-r-- 1 kevin kevin 15057 Nov 2 21:18 gen_init_cpio.c-rwxrwxr-x 1 kevin kevin 5888 Nov 2 21:18 gen_initramfs.shdrwxrwxr-x 2 kevin kevin 4096 Nov 2 21:18 include-rw-rw-r-- 1 kevin kevin 1243 Nov 2 21:18 initramfs_data.S-rw-rw-r-- 1 kevin kevin 512 Nov 4 16:44 initramfs_data.cpio-rw-rw-r-- 1 kevin kevin 1496 Nov 4 16:44 initramfs_data.o-rw-rw-r-- 1 kevin kevin 512 Nov 4 16:44 initramfs_inc_data
The flow is roughly:
You set INITRAMFS_SOURCE in the kernel config, which can be a directory or a cpio file list The build system calls gen_initramfs.sh to read your INITRAMFS_SOURCE Then gen_init_cpio produces a cpio archive initramfs_data.cpio This cpio is then converted to C/ASM data (initramfs_inc_data, initramfs_data.S) and finally linked into the kernel image
In other words: You can package a “mini rootfs” into the kernel at compile time, without separately preparing a standalone initrd image. BusyBox example, a minimal initramfs Suppose we want a super-minimal initramfs needing only: a busybox binary, an /init or /bin/sh to serve as init, and a /dev/console device node. Its file tree might look like: /├── init -> /bin/busybox├── bin│ ├── busybox│ └── sh -> busybox└── dev └── console
Here’s why there’s a symbolic link from init to /bin/busybox: when the kernel uses initramfs, it first looks for the /init executable in rootfs. If found, it runs it as the init process (PID 1); if not found, and neither rdinit= nor init= is specified, it proceeds to the subsequent root-mount flow to mount the real rootfs. You can see this default in init/main.c: static char *ramdisk_execute_command = "/init";
The ramdisk_execute_command char pointer points to this executable.
If you add rdinit=/bin/sh or rdinit=/bin/busybox to the kernel command line, you can override this behavior and directly specify the first program to run on the initramfs. This is a common usage: rdinit=/bin/sh with busybox drops you straight into a shell in early userspace to debug the boot flow.

entry.title: The Word Hidden Across Five Channels | Isodata Seven | GaianSpace CTF 2026
entry.content:
🌐 中文版：繁體中文 Third post in the series. After the demodulator got its skeleton in True Color Is a Lie, this one swaps in new parameters (implicit header) and upgrades the stego trick from subtracting two copies to clustering across multiple channels. Rest of the series: Channel Hop、Subsidy Claim、Two Voices、No Name on the Door、Hopscotch
What the challenge is about Since dawn the tractor has stopped listening to the mast and started listening to a different, unknown transmitter. The Johnripper terminal receives tiles under the dealer’s proprietary settings, and the dealer won’t publish those settings. Babb only has photocopies of pages 14 and 16 of the service manual. Page 15, in between, is missing. The shared SDR was moved into the tractor shed and recorded that channel. What the stranger sends to the tractor is a whole tile (all channels), and it looks real, except for one patch in the north field that Babb can’t explain. In the margin of the course notes, double-underlined: “count what actually grows here.”
Goal: find what the stranger planted in the tile. The files given are a ~213 MB .sigmf-data, manual pages 14/16, and the remote-sensing course notes. Flag format: GAIANSPACE{...}. This time it’s an implicit headerThe radio parameters (manual page 14) are 433.4 MHz, SF7, BW500k, CR4/5, sync word 0x2C, 10-symbol preamble, and no RF header (fixed-length frames). The missing page 15 holds the frame-length table, so we’ll have to infer it from the data. Reusing the demodulator skeleton from the last post, the difference here is the implicit header: the first 8 symbols are a low-rate block (CR4/8), after which every 5 symbols form a block; the length is inferred from how many symbols the packet spans in the air. Once all 779 frames pass the CRC-16 check from manual page 16, they reconstruct into five 128×128 grayscale images:
Looked at one channel at a time, that patch looks like random noise in every one, unlike the previous challenge. That’s probably exactly what the challenge means by “no band leaks anything.” First, understand what this “image” isA satellite doesn’t take an ordinary RGB camera photo. It records different wavelengths of light separately, storing each wavelength as its own channel (band). This challenge uses three kinds:
Visible light: the red/green/blue your eyes can see. A healthy plant’s chlorophyll absorbs red light, so vegetation looks dark in visible light while bare soil looks bright. Near-infrared (NIR): a bit longer in wavelength than red, invisible to the eye. Healthy leaf tissue reflects NIR strongly, so “high NIR” is almost the same as “this is a living plant.” Short-wave infrared (SWIR): longer still, and especially sensitive to water. More water (wet soil, after irrigation, moist leaves) absorbs SWIR and looks dark; dry ground looks bright in SWIR.
So every pixel carries a little fingerprint: bright or not in visible light, high or low in NIR, high or low in SWIR. Feed those fingerprints to a clustering algorithm and pixels with similar fingerprints get grouped together. ISODATA / k-means: count what grows hereThe course notes hint at using ISODATA with 7 classes (ISODATA is a common unsupervised clustering method in remote sensing, conceptually just k-means). Running k-means on the 5-dimensional pixels of the noisy patch, the error drops sharply at k=4 (adding more classes beyond that only lowers it slowly), which says the patch really has only 4 true classes. And those 4 aren’t random. They’re exactly the combinations of two switches, each with only two values:
Class Visible NIR SWIR
vegetation-like + SWIR low dark high low
vegetation-like + SWIR high dark high high
soil-like + SWIR high bright low high
soil-like + SWIR low bright low low
Read the table as two switches and it’s clear:
Switch A: does this patch “look like vegetation” or “look like soil” (decided by visible dark/bright and NIR high/low). Switch B: is SWIR “high” or “low.”
A × B = 2 × 2 = 4, which lines up perfectly with k=4. Here’s the key. Normally these two switches pair up naturally (real vegetation shows the combination you’d expect for A and B). But the stranger’s trick is to secretly flip switch B only on the pixels that “draw the text.” The result:
Looking at NIR alone: the text pixels and the background are both “vegetation” (same A), so there’s no visible difference → nothing leaks. Looking at SWIR alone: the text pixels just happen to have SWIR flipped, but SWIR is high and low all over the place anyway, so it looks like noise → nothing visible there either. Only by comparing “whether A and B agree“ does the text appear. In digital terms, you XOR the two switches: agree = 0, disagree = 1, and the text is painted exactly on the pixels where XOR = 1.
That’s why you must cluster rather than look at a single channel: clustering considers all channels’ fingerprints at once, so it naturally groups the self-contradictory pixels (“A says vegetation but B is flipped”) into their own small classes, and those small classes are the text. Running k=7 clustering over the whole image, those two “contradictory” small classes each show part of the text:
Merge those two classes and draw them, and three lines of text clearly emerge:
Reading the last lineThe font is a “bold” variant: each character is a 5×6 base glyph plus a copy shifted 1 pixel to the right. I used the already-known letters in the first two lines (GAIANSPACE{, 7TH-CLASS-) as a reference and confirmed the last line cell by cell. I hesitated between W/V here; W turned out to be correct. FlagGAIANSPACE{7TH-CLASS-XHTXWX}
Takeaways The “implant” here isn’t painted into one channel. It’s the text split into two noisy halves (XOR) spread across different bands. Any single channel is just noise; it only appears when you look at all channels at once (clustering), echoing the note’s line, “the computer only knows which pixels look alike in all channels at once.” The k-means error curve tells you how many classes really exist. The error plunges at k=4 and only crawls down afterwards, which is the implementation of the note’s “count what actually grows here.” You don’t need the missing manual page. Frame length, channel, and row number can all be inferred directly from the field layout in the data. For a tiny font, figure out the drawing rule before reconstructing the glyphs. This one is “bold, shifted 1 pixel right”. Once you know the rule, cell-by-cell comparison is more reliable than just eyeballing a zoomed image.

entry.title: AWS Lambda Notes: Provisioned Concurrency and Reserved Concurrency
entry.content:
🌐 中文版：繁體中文
RecapEarlier I covered a basic intro to Lambda, Lambda runtimes, permission configuration, and observing initialization time and function execution time from the logs. At the end I left one question:
What happens if we use the AWS CLI to invoke the function, opening three terminal tabs to invoke our Lambda at the same time?
Experiment 1: setting Reserved ConcurrencyWe run this command: aws lambda invoke \ --function-name TestInvocations \ --cli-binary-format raw-in-base64-out \ --payload '{ "name": "test" }' \ response.json
They all actually succeed, producing three log streams in CloudWatch.
But if we tweak something, setting Reserved Concurrency to 1 and clicking save, then rerun the CLI invocation, let’s see what happens.
Now only one request returns 200; the rest are throttled, returning a TooManyRequestsException error message: An error occurred (TooManyRequestsException) when calling the Invoke operation This brings us to Lambda’s mechanism for handling large volumes of simultaneous requests.
First, what is Reserved Concurrency? And what is Unreserved Concurrency?
Reserved ConcurrencyConcurrency means multiple requests at the same time. To handle these simultaneous requests, a Lambda function scales automatically. The nice thing about serverless is that you don’t have to think about how to configure scaling for Lambda, like setting up auto-scaling. In Lambda, for a single function, the user only needs to consider “how many instances do you need to reserve for this Lambda function at any time?“ That’s when you can consider setting Reserved Concurrency for your function. Reserved Concurrency is the maximum number of concurrent instances allocated to a function. When a function has Reserved Concurrency, no other function can use that concurrency. If you set Reserved Concurrency to 1 in the Lambda console, 1 is deducted from Unreserved Concurrency. This setting is a regional limit. If you set Reserved Concurrency to 100 for a function, the remaining 900 is shared by other functions in the region.
How much concurrency can you reserve for a function?
The answer is UnreservedConcurrency - 100 concurrency. That is, a function can’t monopolize all concurrency for itself; at least 100 concurrency is left for other functions to share.
How do you decide how much concurrency to reserve for your function?
You can decide by observing the CloudWatch metric ConcurrentExecutions [1]. This metric shows the number of concurrent requests to your function across different time periods in a day. If this function receives at most 30 requests at once per day and the function is important to you, you can consider reserving 30 Lambda instances to handle requests.
Also worth mentioning: setting Reserved Concurrency for a function is free.
Provisioned ConcurrencySome might wonder: if the function scales with requests, then starting a new execution environment introduces latency for time-sensitive requests, right?
Image source: AWS official docs
That thinking is correct; see number 4 in the figure above, which is exactly this situation. It means 3 execution environments are handling 3 requests, but when the 4th request comes in, a new Lambda execution environment must be initialized. That inevitably introduces latency, waiting for the runtime to start, the Lambda code and dependencies to download, and the code outside the handler to run (if any). The point of Provisioned Concurrency is “pre-initializing multiple environment instances for a function to help reduce cold-start latency”. Cold start latency is the uncontrollable delay while the Lambda execution environment is starting and loading (not including Function Init, the initialization time for code outside the handler). I’ll cover this part later. Back to Provisioned Concurrency: if it’s set, the figure looks more like the one below. Suppose Provisioned Concurrency is set to 4. Then four Lambda execution environments are initialized from the start, and subsequent requests reuse those four. This guarantees four initialized Lambda environments always exist, which suits time-sensitive requests so they don’t take the initialization delay hit.
So how do you set Provisioned Concurrency? [2]
Note: setting Provisioned Concurrency for a function costs money.
Experiment 2: setting Provisioned ConcurrencyThere’s a prerequisite before setting Provisioned Concurrency: publishing a version of your function. Every function defaults to $LATEST before a version is published, but Provisioned Concurrency can’t be set on the $LATEST version; that’s a limitation. First find Publish new version under Version on the main page. Then fill in this version’s description and click Publish. It redirects to the Version 1 Lambda console (slightly different from the $LATEST console). Now you should see the Provisioned Concurrency configuration screen; click it to set concurrency for Version 1.
Below, enter the number of Lambda concurrency instances you want to keep in a warm-start state.Notice “10 available”. Where does this number come from? That number is actually your function’s Reserved Concurrency count. Go back to the $LATEST version console.
Below you can see our setting is 10.
So the amount of Provisioned Concurrency we can set depends on the Reserved Concurrency set for that function.
Here we set Provisioned Concurrency to 5.
It takes some time to build the concurrency. Then let’s test the configured Provisioned Concurrency. First, here’s the test code (in the Version 1 function): import json, timetime.sleep(10)def lambda_handler(event, context): print("sleep for 3 secs") time.sleep(3) return { 'statusCode': 200, 'body': json.dumps('Hello from Lambda!') }
We trigger the Lambda function via the AWS CLI: aws lambda invoke \--function-name TestInvocations \--cli-binary-format raw-in-base64-out \--qualifier 1 \--payload '{ "key": "value" }' response.json
The --qualifier parameter takes a version name or alias name. Before actually triggering it, pause and observe the invocation logs in CloudWatch.
You’ll find multiple execution environments have already warmed up.
Why the count exceeds the Provisioned Concurrency number isn’t confirmed.Maybe for availability?
After opening multiple terminals to send requests, you’ll find the same thing: because the execution environments are already warm, there’s no need to re-init, and requests run on existing environments via container reuse.
Reserved Concurrency vs. Provisioned Concurrency
Image source: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/zh_tw/lambda/latest/dg/lambda-concurrency.html#reserved-and-provisioned
Here’s an official comparison figure explaining the difference between these two kinds of concurrency. Below is my summary of the difference:
RC (Reserved Concurrency) PC (Provisioned Concurrency)
Cost: Free Costs money
Characteristic: Ensures a certain number of Lambda execution environments exist Ensures a certain number of Lambda execution environments exist, with a certain number already initialized
Reaction at limit Throttled TooManyRequest If RC quota remains, scales up the environment count, but still with cold starts; if no quota, throttled
Also see the official comparison table [3].
Burst ConcurrencyBurst Concurrency also aims to handle sudden spikes in requests. But facing a sudden surge of many requests, Lambda may not be able to scale up immediately, in order to prevent the function from over-scaling and consuming too many resources. So to match the function’s surge rate, you can set Burst Concurrency to increase the maximum rate at which Lambda execution environments are created. This is an account-level setting. The Burst Concurrency limit differs by region:
us-west-2, us-east-1, and eu-west-1 are generally capped at 3000 ap-northeast-1, eu-central-1, and us-east-2 are capped at 1000 Other regions are 500
Taking us-east-1 as an example, Burst Concurrency scales 500 units per minute (additional Lambda execution environments) until demand is met or the 3000 cap is reached. Requests exceeding the limit are throttled (status code 429). If interested, see the official docs on Burst Concurrency [5]. Cold Start What does Lambda do during the Init phase?
When the Lambda service receives a request to start a Lambda function via the Lambda API, the service itself downloads the function code. This code is stored in Lambda’s internal S3 bucket. If the function is built as a container, the function code is stored in Amazon ECR. It then builds an environment with the specified memory size and runtime. It then runs the initialization code outside the function handler.
Per [4], all the steps above except running the function’s init code fall within the cold-start range. Running the code outside the handler counts as warm start, which is the part we can control.
How can a function stay “warm”?
The official docs explain it via a pinging mechanism. The main approach is setting an EventBridge rule to invoke the function once a minute to keep the execution environment active. The currently-recommended way to mitigate cold starts is still Provisioned Concurrency.There’s also SnapStart, which I’ll cover later. References[1] https://docs.aws.amazon.com/zh_tw/lambda/latest/dg/configuration-concurrency.html#estimating-reserved-concurrency[2] https://docs.aws.amazon.com/zh_tw/lambda/latest/dg/provisioned-concurrency.html[3] https://docs.aws.amazon.com/zh_tw/lambda/latest/dg/lambda-concurrency.html#comparing-reserved-provisioned[4] https://docs.aws.amazon.com/zh_tw/lambda/latest/operatorguide/execution-environments.html#cold-start-latency[5]https://docs.aws.amazon.com/zh_tw/lambda/latest/dg/burst-concurrency.html

entry.title: The One Bit Stuck High | Lunar Latch-Up | GaianSpace CTF 2026
entry.content:
Second post of the GaianSpace CTF 2026 “05-rad-hard-rampage” series. 🌐 中文版：繁體中文
The previous post, Cosmic Bit Blunder, was about a Single Event Upset (SEU): one bit knocked over, either 0↔1. This one is similar, but the failure mechanism is a bit different: a Single Event Latch-up (SEL), where a bit gets forced high and stuck there. The distinction is subtle, yet it’s enough to cut the search space in half again.
Other posts in the series: A Logic Gate Shorted by Radiation / Ionized Transistangle、Sensor Drift / Degradift
What the challenge is about
A single heavy ion hit the Foundation One power-management block and triggered a latch-up — a parasitic path that slams one bit high and holds it there, drawing current until someone cuts the rail. One bit in there is stuck high that should not be.
In plain terms: a heavy ion hit Foundation One’s power-management block and triggered a latch-up, a parasitic current path that forces a bit high and holds it there, drawing current until someone cuts the rail. In the dumped registers, one bit is stuck high that shouldn’t be, and everything downstream uses these registers as a key, so until that stuck bit is reset, the sealed mission payload can’t be opened. The only files given are reg_dump.bin (84 bytes) and a recovery_spec.md describing its format:
Offset Size Field
0x00 32 R0..R7, eight 32-bit registers (little-endian)
0x20 4 Integrity word: CRC-32 of these 32 bytes’ healthy state (zlib/ISO, little-endian)
0x24 rest Sealed payload: AES-128-ECB ciphertext of the flag (PKCS#7)
Key scheme: key = SHA-256(R0..R7 bytes)[:16].
The challenge spells out how to find the answer very plainly: use the only honest method: the single bit that makes the integrity word match again.
Flag format: GAIANSPACE{...}
Latch-up only “pushes a bit high,” never “pulls it low”This is the key to the whole challenge, matching the hint “One bit too high.” A quick intro to the physics of Single Event Latch-up (SEL): a particle triggers a parasitic PNPN (thyristor/SCR-like) conduction path in the CMOS structure, pulling a node high and self-sustaining it. The difference from the previous post’s SEU is that SEU can go 0→1 or 1→0, but latch-up slams one bit high. It can only stick a bit that was 0 at 1, and can never turn a bit that was 1 into 0. So that directionality cuts the search space in half again: the faulty bit must have been 0 before the damage and 1 after. I only need to check the bits currently equal to 1 (clearing them to 0 one at a time), and never touch the bits that are 0. Use the integrity word as a “search tool,” not just a verifierFor each bit currently set to 1 in the registers, try clearing it to 0, recompute the CRC-32 of those 32 bytes, and check whether it matches the integrity word stored in the file, 0xa70b003b: import struct, zlibdata = open('reg_dump.bin','rb').read()regs = bytearray(data[:32])crc_stored = struct.unpack('<I', data[32:36])[0]for i in range(256): bi, bit = i // 8, i % 8 if not (regs[bi] >> bit) & 1: continue # latch-up only pushes high → a 0-valued bit can't be the culprit r = bytearray(regs); r[bi] ^= (1 << bit) if zlib.crc32(bytes(r)) == crc_stored: print("found bit", i, bytes(r).hex())
This feels like the “only honest method” the challenge mentions: not guessing which bit is suspect, but letting the integrity check itself tell you the answer. Of all the bits currently set to 1, only one makes the CRC match after clearing, bit 37 (byte 4, i.e. the lowest byte of R1, 0x20 → 0x00):
recovery_spec.md actually plants a distractor: “R7’s reserved high nibble is where the clear routine often operates, but this event didn’t hit there”, which is the challenge kindly reminding you not to fixate on R7 out of preconception. The real fault is in R1. The registers are the keyMatching the second hint, “The registers are the key.” Compute SHA-256 of the repaired 32 bytes and take the first 16 as the AES-128 key: import hashlib, subprocessrepaired = bytes.fromhex("4d3c2b1a00000000efbeadde0df00000bebafeca785634120df0ad0beeffc000")key = hashlib.sha256(repaired).digest()[:16]# openssl enc -d -aes-128-ecb -K <key> -in <ciphertext>
AES-128-ECB decrypt the ciphertext (48 bytes = 3 blocks), strip the PKCS#7 padding, and out comes a clean, correctly-formatted flag, confirming once more that bit 37 was the right one. FlagGAIANSPACE{s1ngle_event_l4tchup}
Takeaways The fault’s directionality cuts the search space in half again. SEU requires checking 256 bits (either 0↔1); SEL only “pushes high,” so only bits currently set to 1 are candidates. Understanding the fault’s physics isn’t just flavour; it genuinely reduces the work. CRC isn’t only for “verifying” an answer; it can also “find” one. This challenge stores a CRC of the healthy state, so “try each candidate + filter by CRC” becomes a deterministic search algorithm, far more reliable than guessing which field is broken, exactly the challenge’s “only honest method.” A spec line like “this field is a common target, but not this time” is usually there to rule out a decoy. This challenge deliberately calls R7’s reserved nibble “the clear routine’s favourite spot” precisely so you don’t dive in. Binding the key to the repaired data itself gives built-in verification. The key is SHA-256(registers), so a correct repair decrypts correctly with valid padding, and a wrong one gives garbage. You know whether the answer is right without submitting it.

entry.title: 【Hiking Log】Qixing Mountain Main Peak + East Peak
entry.content:
🌐 中文版：繁體中文
IntroHaving grown up in Taipei for years without visiting Qixing Mountain’s main-peak triangulation marker, I took advantage of a rare day of good weather to go check it out. The main route for this Qixing Mountain hike was from the Xiaoyoukeng trailhead -> Qixing Mountain main peak -> Qixing Mountain east peak, then back the same way to the Xiaoyoukeng parking lot.
Qixing Mountain is the highest mountain within Taipei City, reaching an elevation of 1120 meters. Xiaoyoukeng geothermal ventThe sulfur smell near the geothermal vent is strong, but on a cold day it’s actually pretty warm close up. The gushing sulfur springs boil and bubble. Qixing Mountain main peakThe path to the main peak is almost all stone steps, but there are quite a few steep climbs along the way, so I recommend bringing trekking poles.
It’s silvergrass season in November, but it’s windy here and the silvergrass is all bent over by the wind, though the scenery is still pretty.
On weekends there are many hikers who come to take photos with this marker post, so decide for yourself whether to grab a memento. Qixing Mountain east peakFrom the main peak to the east peak is only another 0.3K, so you can collect both summits in one go. But some sections from the main peak to the east peak are slippery, so I recommend wearing anti-slip hiking shoes. The bushesBy the way, all along the trail there are many passable bush tunnels like the one below. If you check an offline map you can see there’s a path, and you can also find tied ropes. An old friend went in for a bit of exploring, but there was too much mud further on, so we didn’t go deeper.
Personally I thought the east peak’s scenery was so-so, but plenty of people still line up for photos.
Then I went back the same way to the parking lot, ending today’s trip.
Actually, most people go up from Xiaoyoukeng to the main peak then the east peak, then down via Lengshuikeng, or the reverse route. But since I drove, I could only go back and forth the same way.

entry.title: Essential Problem-Solving Tool | Linked List | LeetCode Notes
Kubernetes for DevOps Notes |【DevOps Skill Tree】
entry.content:
🌐 中文版：繁體中文
BasicExplain what Kubernetes is A platform for container orchestration and management, used for automated deployment and scaling of containers. What are Kubernetes’s main features?
Self-Healing: uses health checks to inspect running containers and takes corresponding action, e.g. restarting a container Load Balancing: distributes requests across different applications in the cluster Operations: applications packaged by Kubernetes can use the cluster’s API to update their state and trigger operations based on events and application state changes Automated Rollout: gradually updates applications, and can roll back when problems arise Scaling: horizontal scaling based on custom conditions Secrets: a mechanism to store usernames, passwords, and service endpoints privately, not viewable by every user of the cluster
What ways can you interact with Kubernetes resources? You can interact with a Kubernetes cluster using the kubectl command-line tool. When deploying an app to Kubernetes, which Kubernetes objects are used most?
Deployment: creates and monitors a group of Pods Service: routes traffic to Pods within the cluster Ingress: routes external traffic into the cluster
What are the common Kubernetes objects? Pod, Service, ReplicationController, ReplicaSet, DaemonSet, Namespace, ConfigMap, etc.
A container isn’t a Kubernetes object; the smallest object unit in Kubernetes is the Pod, which usually contains one or more containers.
Cluster and Architecture What is a Kubernetes cluster? A collection of nodes running containerized applications, mainly divided into master nodes and worker nodes. The master node is Kubernetes’s control center, containing several key components:
API Server: Kubernetes’s API entry point, responsible for receiving API requests like deploying apps and scaling containers. All resource operations go through the API Server. Scheduler: responsible for scheduling new Pods onto suitable worker nodes, mainly based on resource needs and policy choices Controller Manager: manages the various controllers that maintain the cluster’s desired state, e.g. ensuring a specified number of Pods keep running etcd: the distributed database in Kubernetes, holding the whole cluster’s state and configuration
A worker node runs applications in Kubernetes, mainly running these components:
kubelet: manages the Pods and containers on a node and monitors container state. It interacts with the master node via the API Server. kube-proxy: handles the node’s network configuration, ensuring every Pod in the cluster can communicate, and also handles load balancing container runtime: the container runtime (Docker, containerd) pulls images and runs containers
How do I tell whether the current Kubernetes environment is a master node or a worker node? kubectl get nodes -o wide
It may output info like: NAME STATUS ROLES AGE VERSIONmaster-1 Ready control-plane 20d v1.20.0worker-1 Ready <none> 20d v1.20.0worker-2 Ready <none> 20d v1.20.0
How do you manage multiple Kubernetes clusters? How do you quickly switch between clusters with kubectl? kubectl config use-context [CONTEXT_NAME] Each cluster has a context; you can view all available contexts with: kubectl config get-contexts
How do you avoid high memory usage causing a memory leak or OOM (Out Of Memory) in a Kubernetes cluster? Method 1Set resource requests and resource limits for Pods or containers to ensure containers don’t exceed their allowed resource usage, letting the app stop when it consumes too much and preventing node OOM. Resource requests ensure a Pod’s minimum resource requirement, which lets the Scheduler find a suitable node when scheduling the Pod. Conversely, resource limits cap the maximum resources a Pod can use. resources: requests: memory: "256Mi" cpu: "500m" limits: memory: "512Mi" cpu: "1000m"
Method 2Use other monitoring tools, e.g. Prometheus and Grafana, to monitor Pod memory usage. Method 3Enable the HPA (Horizontal Pod Autoscaler), which automatically adds or removes replicas based on CPU or memory usage. kubectl autoscale deployment [deployment_name] --cpu-percent=80 --min=2 --max=10
How do you list all API object types? kubectl api-resources
KubeletIf you disable the kubelet on a worker node, what happens to the running Pods? Since the kubelet communicates with the API Server, disabling it means the worker node can’t interact with the API Server. The node’s status is marked Not Ready, and the Pods on it become Unknown. Once the control plane detects a worker node has been Not Ready for too long (reaching the threshold time, usually 5 minutes), it evicts the Pods on that node and reschedules them onto other available nodes. PodsA Pod is the smallest object unit in Kubernetes, usually composed of one or more containers. A Pod shares network resources, storage, and the specification defining how containers run.
How do you deploy a Pod named my-pod using the nginx:alpine image? kubectl run my-pod --image=nginx:alpine
This isn’t the common way to run a Pod; you usually run Pods via a Deployment. How many containers are usually in a Pod? A Pod can contain multiple containers, but in most cases there’s one. You can also deploy a sidecar container into a Pod, usually for collecting logs. What phases can a Pod have? Briefly explain the Pod lifecycle A Pod may go through these phases in its lifecycle:
Value Description
Pending The Pod has been accepted by the cluster, but its containers may not be running yet; it may be waiting to be scheduled or waiting to download a container image
Running All containers have been created and at least one is running
Succeeded All containers in the Pod completed successfully and won’t restart
Failed All containers in the Pod were terminated, and at least one was terminated due to failure, with no restart
Unknown The Pod’s state can’t be obtained for some reason, usually due to a communication error between the Pod and the node
What happens when you run a Pod via kubectl? Explain the flow
Kubectl sends a request to the API Server to create the Pod The API Server validates the request etcd is updated
The Scheduler in the control plane learns there’s an unassigned Pod by watching the API Server The Scheduler chooses a node to assign the Pod to etcd is updated with this info
The Scheduler tells the API Server which Pod it chose The kubelet notices a Pod was assigned to its node but isn’t running The kubelet sends a request to the container engine (e.g. Docker) to create and run the container Once the Pod is running, the kubelet updates the status to the API Server
etcd is again notified by the API Server to update the info
Ref: https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/pod-lifecycle/
How do you know whether a container in a Pod is running? kubectl describe pod <POD_NAME> to check whether the container status is Running. Or use kubectl exec to run a command inside the container. When you find a Pod in CrashLoopBackOff, what could the error be? How do you check it? This usually means the Pod repeatedly starts then crashes, over and over. There are many possible causes, such as:
An application error forcing the container to exit A configuration error, like wrong environment variables or a missing config file Resource limits: the container doesn’t have enough memory or CPU allocated A health check failure: if the app doesn’t come up within the expected time, this error occurs too A container liveness probe / startup probe returning an error
For detailed troubleshooting, use kubectl describe pod <POD_NAME> to see the detailed cause, or kubectl logs <POD_NAME> to see the container’s logs.
What does the config below mean? livenessProbe: exec: command: - cat - /appStatus initialDelaySeconds: 10 periodSeconds: 5
First, what is a liveness probe: its purpose is to restart a container when it isn’t in the desired state. This YAML means: if the cat /appStatus command fails, Kubernetes kills the container and then applies the restart policy. initialDelaySeconds means the kubelet waits 10 seconds before first running the probe command (cat /appStatus), and from then on reruns it every 5 seconds (defined in periodSeconds). What does the config below mean? readinessProbe: tcpSocket: port: 2017 initialDelaySeconds: 15 periodSeconds: 20
A readiness probe usually determines whether a container is ready to accept traffic. So this defines that until the Pod can connect to the container’s port 2017, it won’t be marked Ready. The first probe runs 15 seconds after the container starts, and it keeps checking every 20 seconds until it can connect to the defined port. What happens when you delete a Pod?
Kubernetes sends a SIGTERM signal to the container in the Pod to terminate the container’s main process The container then has some time to finish its current task and release resources (this time can be defined in terminationGracePeriodSeconds); if it doesn’t shut down in time, a SIGKILL signal is sent to force termination
Why is there usually only one container per Pod? If each Pod has one container, Kubernetes can simply adjust the number of Pods to scale the service’s capacity. Multi-container Pods are harder to scale, since multiple containers must be replicated together. Static Pods Ref
https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/configure-pod-container/static-pod/ https://yuminlee2.medium.com/kubernetes-static-pods-734dc0684f31
What are static Pods? A kind of Pod managed directly by the kubelet daemon on a node, rather than by the control plane. A static Pod is usually defined directly in a designated directory on the node. The kubelet automatically detects the config files in that directory and starts the corresponding Pods. Since a static Pod is controlled directly by the kubelet, it can’t be replica-managed directly by a ReplicaSet or Deployment, and therefore a static Pod can only run on the node where its definition file resides, and won’t be automatically scheduled onto other nodes. Can you give a use case for static Pods? Static Pods are used to run control-plane components.
