Usually the control-plane components like the API Server, kube-scheduler, etcd, and kube-controller-manager all exist as static Pods on the master node. How do you know whether a Pod is a static Pod? kubectl describe pod <POD_NAME> -n <NAMESPACE> Check whether the result’s annotations or nodeName has a “mirror pod” annotation. If you find kubernetes.io/config.mirror in the metadata.annotations field, it means this Pod is a mirror Pod generated by a static Pod. NAMESPACE NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS AGEdefault web 1/1 Running 0 5h14mkube-system coredns-6f6b679f8f-s8l6l 1/1 Running 0 5h18mkube-system etcd-minikube 1/1 Running 0 5h18mkube-system kube-apiserver-minikube 1/1 Running 0 5h18mkube-system kube-controller-manager-minikube 1/1 Running 0 5h18mkube-system kube-proxy-9c8vm 1/1 Running 0 5h18mkube-system kube-scheduler-minikube 1/1 Running 0 5h18mkube-system storage-provisioner 1/1 Running 1 (5h18m ago) 5h18m~ ○ minikube 04:28:02 PM❯ kdp etcd-minikube -n kube-system
Output: Name: etcd-minikubeNamespace: kube-systemPriority: 2000001000Priority Class Name: system-node-criticalNode: minikube/192.168.58.2Start Time: Fri, 08 Nov 2024 11:09:17 +0800Labels: component=etcd tier=control-planeAnnotations: kubeadm.kubernetes.io/etcd.advertise-client-urls: https://192.168.58.2:2379 kubernetes.io/config.hash: 0f576c7626af2d96b08f13e09b83eb08 kubernetes.io/config.mirror: 0f576c7626af2d96b08f13e09b83eb08 kubernetes.io/config.seen: 2024-11-08T03:09:16.930402512Z kubernetes.io/config.source: fileStatus: RunningSeccompProfile: RuntimeDefaultIP: 192.168.58.2IPs: IP: 192.168.58.2Controlled By: Node/minikubeContainers:.....
You can see the mirror pod annotation is indeed there. Where is a static Pod’s manifest file usually? Usually in /etc/kubernetes/manifests; to delete a static Pod you usually just delete the related manifest file. ❯ minikube sshdocker@minikube:~$ ls /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml kube-apiserver.yaml kube-controller-manager.yaml kube-scheduler.yamldocker@minikube:~$
Pods CommandsHow do you confirm which worker node a Pod was scheduled onto? kubectl get pods -o wide
Delete a Pod kubectl delete pod <POD_NAME>
List all Pods across all namespaces kubectl get pods --all-namespaces
Pods Troubleshooting and DebuggingWhen you run a Pod but it stays Pending, what could the cause be? One possibility is that the Scheduler responsible for scheduling Pods isn’t running. You can confirm with kubectl get pod -A | grep scheduler. What can the kubectl describe pod command do? It shows various detailed info about the Pod, sometimes including the error cause. Create a static Pod using the python image, running the command sleep 20 kubectl run some-pod --image=python --command sleep 20 --restart=Never --dry-run=client -o yaml > statuc-pod.yaml
Labels and SelectorsWhat is a label? A label is a key-value tag attached to a Kubernetes object to mark its characteristics (e.g. app=nginx, env=prod). A label itself doesn’t affect how an object runs, but it lets a selector filter objects by these tags. kubectl get pods -l app=nginx # list pods with app=nginxkubectl label pod my-pod tier=frontend # add a label to a pod
What’s the difference between a label and an annotation? Both are key-value, but their purposes differ:
Label: for filtering and grouping, queried by selectors, with length and character restrictions on values Annotation: for storing non-identifying metadata (e.g. build info, hints), not used by selectors, able to hold longer, more complex data
What is a selector? A selector selects a group of objects by label, commonly used when a Service finds which Pods to route to, or a Deployment decides which Pods to manage. Types:
Equality-based: app=nginx, env!=prod Set-based: env in (prod, staging), tier notin (frontend)
DeploymentWhat is a Deployment? A Deployment declaratively manages a group of stateless Pods. You describe the “desired state” (how many replicas, which image), and the Deployment uses a ReplicaSet underneath to ensure the actual state matches, supporting rolling updates and rollback. kubectl create deployment nginx --image=nginx --replicas=3kubectl scale deployment nginx --replicas=5kubectl set image deployment/nginx nginx=nginx:1.25 # rolling updatekubectl rollout status deployment/nginxkubectl rollout undo deployment/nginx # rollback
What’s the relationship between a Deployment, ReplicaSet, and Pod? A Deployment manages a ReplicaSet, and a ReplicaSet manages Pods. Each time you update the image, the Deployment creates a new ReplicaSet and gradually replaces the old ReplicaSet’s Pods with new ones. That’s a rolling update. How do you control how many Pods are replaced at once during a rolling update? Via strategy.rollingUpdate‘s maxSurge (how many extra Pods beyond the desired count) and maxUnavailable (how many Pods can be unavailable). strategy: type: RollingUpdate rollingUpdate: maxSurge: 1 maxUnavailable: 0
ServicesWhat is a Service? Why do you need it? A Pod’s IP changes when it’s recreated. A Service provides a stable virtual IP (ClusterIP) and DNS name, and load-balances traffic to a group of Pods via a label selector. What Service types are there?
Type Purpose
ClusterIP default, accessible only within the cluster
NodePort opens a fixed port (30000-32767) on every node, accessible from outside via <NodeIP>:<NodePort>
LoadBalancer requests an external load balancer from the cloud provider
ExternalName maps the Service to an external DNS name (CNAME)
kubectl expose deployment nginx --port=80 --target-port=80 --type=ClusterIP
How does a Service know which Pods to send traffic to? It matches Pods’ labels via a selector, and the matching Pods’ IPs are recorded in the corresponding Endpoints (or EndpointSlice) object, which kube-proxy then uses to set iptables/IPVS rules for load balancing. IngressA Service’s LoadBalancer already exposes things externally, so why do you need Ingress? Opening a LoadBalancer per service is expensive and hard to manage. Ingress provides a “layer-7 (HTTP/HTTPS) entry point” that routes traffic to different Services from a single entry by host or path, and can handle TLS termination centrally. Does Ingress work on its own? No. An Ingress object is just a “declaration of routing rules”; what actually executes them is an Ingress Controller (e.g. nginx-ingress, Traefik, AWS ALB Controller), which must be deployed first for the rules to take effect. apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1kind: Ingressmetadata: name: webspec: rules: - host: example.com http: paths: - path: /api pathType: Prefix backend: service: name: api-svc port: number: 80
ReplicaSetsWhat is a ReplicaSet? A ReplicaSet ensures a specified number of Pod replicas are “always running.” If a Pod dies, it automatically creates a new one; if there are too many, it deletes the extras. So should I use a ReplicaSet directly? Usually not. A ReplicaSet is almost always created and managed by a Deployment, since a Deployment adds rolling-update and rollback capabilities. Operating a ReplicaSet directly is rare. DaemonSetsWhat is a DaemonSet? When do you use it? A DaemonSet ensures “exactly one Pod runs on every (or every matching) node.” It’s commonly used for node-level system services, such as:
Log-collection agents (Fluent Bit, Filebeat) Monitoring agents (node-exporter) Network plugins (CNI), kube-proxy
When a new node joins the cluster, the DaemonSet automatically creates the corresponding Pod on it. StatefulSetHow is a StatefulSet different from a Deployment? A Deployment suits “stateless” apps (Pods are interchangeable). A StatefulSet suits “stateful” apps, providing:
Stable, fixed network identity: Pod names are <name>-0, <name>-1, which don’t change Stable persistent storage: each Pod binds its own dedicated PVC and remounts the same data after recreation Ordered deployment and scaling: created in order (0→1→2), deleted in order
What scenarios use a StatefulSet? Databases (MySQL, PostgreSQL) and distributed systems (Kafka, Zookeeper, Elasticsearch), where each node has a distinct identity and needs to keep its own data. StorageWhat are PV and PVC?
PersistentVolume (PV): an actual storage resource in the cluster (NFS, cloud disk, Ceph, etc.), provided by an admin or a StorageClass PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC): a user’s “request” for storage, describing how much is needed and what access mode, which Kubernetes binds to a suitable PV
This design decouples “storage provisioning” from “storage consumption.” What is a StorageClass? A StorageClass defines the method for “dynamic provisioning.” When a PVC specifies a StorageClass, Kubernetes automatically creates the corresponding PV (e.g. automatically provisioning an EBS disk), without an admin pre-creating it manually. What access modes are there?
ReadWriteOnce (RWO): can be mounted read-write by a single node ReadOnlyMany (ROX): can be mounted read-only by multiple nodes ReadWriteMany (RWX): can be mounted read-write by multiple nodes (requires underlying storage support, like NFS)
NetworkingWhat are the basic principles of Kubernetes networking? Kubernetes requires:
Every Pod has its own IP All Pods can communicate directly without NAT An agent on a node (like the kubelet) can communicate with the Pods on that node
These are implemented by CNI (Container Network Interface) plugins (Calico, Flannel, Cilium, etc.). How does in-cluster DNS work? CoreDNS provides in-cluster DNS. A Service has a DNS name <service>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local, so Pods can access each other by name instead of IP.
https://sean22492249.medium.com/networking-in-kubernetes-pod-%E8%88%87-pod-%E7%9A%84%E7%B6%B2%E8%B7%AF%E9%80%A3%E9%80%9A-216cfe6de471
PoliciesWhat is a NetworkPolicy? By default, all Pods can communicate with each other. A NetworkPolicy lets you use label selectors to define “which Pods can communicate with which Pods (or namespaces, IP ranges),” acting like a Pod-level firewall. Note: a NetworkPolicy requires CNI plugin support (e.g. Calico, Cilium) to take effect. What are ResourceQuota and LimitRange?
ResourceQuota: limits the total resources available in a namespace (e.g. total CPU, memory, Pod count) LimitRange: sets default and min/max resource values for individual Pods/containers in a namespace
EtcdWhat role does etcd play in Kubernetes? etcd is a distributed key-value database, the “single source of truth” for the whole cluster. All object state (Pods, Services, ConfigMaps, Secrets…) lives in etcd, and the API Server is the only component that talks to etcd directly. Why is backing up etcd important? If etcd data is lost, the entire cluster’s state is gone, so production usually backs up etcd snapshots regularly. ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl snapshot save snapshot.db \ --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 \ --cacert=... --cert=... --key=...
NamespacesWhat is a Namespace? A Namespace lets you carve multiple “virtual clusters” out of one physical cluster, to isolate the resources of different teams, environments, or projects. Combined with ResourceQuota and RBAC, it achieves resource and permission isolation. kubectl create namespace devkubectl get pods -n dev
Which resources are cluster-scoped and don’t belong to any namespace? Most resources (Pod, Service, Deployment) belong to a namespace, but some are cluster-level and don’t belong to any namespace, such as Node, PersistentVolume, Namespace itself, and ClusterRole. OperatorsWhat is an Operator? An Operator is a pattern for encoding “the operational expertise of running an application” as code. It extends the Kubernetes API with Custom Resource Definitions (CRDs), paired with a Controller that continuously watches these custom resources and reconciles the actual state to the desired state. Can you give an example? For example, to run a PostgreSQL cluster on K8s, after installing a PostgreSQL Operator, you just create a kind: PostgresCluster custom resource, and the Operator automatically handles creation, backup, failover, version upgrades, and other operational work. SecretsWhat’s the difference between a Secret and a ConfigMap? Both separate config from the image; the difference is:
ConfigMap: stores general, non-sensitive config (config files, environment variables) Secret: stores sensitive data (passwords, tokens, certificates)
Is a Secret really secure? Note: a default Secret is just base64-encoded, not encrypted, so anyone who can read the Secret can decode its contents. For real protection, you need to additionally enable etcd encryption at rest and strictly limit who can read Secrets via RBAC. kubectl create secret generic db-cred \ --from-literal=username=admin --from-literal=password=p@ss
VolumesWhat’s the difference between a Volume and a PersistentVolume?
An ordinary Volume‘s lifecycle is tied to the Pod; once the Pod is deleted, data in a volume like emptyDir is gone A PersistentVolume‘s lifecycle is independent of the Pod, so the data survives Pod deletion
What are common Volume types?
emptyDir: scratch space for the Pod’s lifetime, often used to share data between containers in the same Pod hostPath: mounts a path on the node (be careful, it couples to the node) configMap / secret: mounts a ConfigMap/Secret into the container as files persistentVolumeClaim: mounts a PVC (real persistent storage)
Access ControlHow does Kubernetes do permission control? Mainly through RBAC (Role-Based Access Control). The four core objects:
Role / ClusterRole: define “what actions on which resources are allowed” (Role is namespace-scoped, ClusterRole is cluster-wide) RoleBinding / ClusterRoleBinding: bind a Role to a User, Group, or ServiceAccount
kubectl create role pod-reader --verb=get,list,watch --resource=podskubectl create rolebinding read-pods --role=pod-reader --user=kevin
What is a ServiceAccount? A ServiceAccount is an identity for “programs inside a Pod” (as opposed to a User for people). A Pod can use its ServiceAccount’s token to call the API Server, governed by RBAC. What checks does a request to the API Server go through? Authentication (who you are) → Authorization (RBAC, whether you can do it) → Admission Control (extra admission control, e.g. validating or mutating the request). CronJobWhat’s the difference between a Job and a CronJob?
Job: runs a one-off task that “finishes” (e.g. data migration, batch computation), ensuring it completes successfully the specified number of times CronJob: adds scheduling on top of a Job, creating Jobs on a schedule via cron syntax (e.g. a backup every night)
apiVersion: batch/v1kind: CronJobmetadata: name: backupspec: schedule: "0 2 * * *" # daily at 02:00 jobTemplate: spec: template: spec: containers: - name: backup image: backup-tool:latest restartPolicy: OnFailure
HelmWhat is Helm? Helm is Kubernetes’s “package manager,” similar to apt/yum. It packages a set of K8s manifests into a Chart, supporting parameterization via values.yaml, version management, and one-command install/upgrade/rollback. helm install my-release bitnami/nginxhelm upgrade my-release bitnami/nginx --set replicaCount=3helm rollback my-release 1helm uninstall my-release
Why use Helm instead of just kubectl apply? When an application is made of many manifests and deployed to multiple environments (dev/staging/prod with different parameters), Helm’s templating and version management are far more convenient than hand-maintaining a pile of YAML. SecurityWhat are some common Kubernetes security practices?
Principle of least privilege: strictly limit ServiceAccount and user permissions with RBAC Don’t run containers as root: set securityContext.runAsNonRoot: true Encrypt Secrets: enable etcd encryption at rest and restrict Secret access NetworkPolicy: default deny, open only necessary Pod-to-Pod communication Image scanning: scan images for vulnerabilities, use only trusted sources Pod Security Admission: use the built-in Pod Security Standards (privileged / baseline / restricted) to limit Pod privileges
What is a securityContext? A securityContext sets security-related attributes for a Pod or container, such as which UID to run as, whether privileged mode is allowed, and whether the root filesystem is read-only. securityContext: runAsNonRoot: true runAsUser: 1000 readOnlyRootFilesystem: true allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
MiscWhat are some handy kubectl debugging commands? kubectl describe <resource> <name> # see detailed status and eventskubectl logs <pod> [-c container] # see container logskubectl logs <pod> --previous # see the previous crashed container's logskubectl exec -it <pod> -- sh # enter the containerkubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestampkubectl top pod / kubectl top node # see resource usage (needs metrics-server)
What’s the difference between kubectl’s imperative and declarative styles?
Imperative: directly issue commands to change state, e.g. kubectl create, kubectl run Declarative: write the desired state as YAML and let Kubernetes reconcile it with kubectl apply -f. Production usually uses the declarative style with GitOps (version-controlling all manifests).

entry.title: 🗃️Deep Dive: How the malloc Function Allocates Memory
entry.content:
🌐 中文版：繁體中文
Deep Dive: How does the malloc function allocate memory?PrefaceDynamic memory allocation is an important concept. It lets a program allocate and free memory dynamically as needed during execution, rather than relying on statically-allocated blocks set up in advance. This flexibility lets a program use memory resources more efficiently and handle problems of various sizes and complexities. C’s malloc function is a widely-used dynamic memory allocator. It lets programmers dynamically allocate memory blocks of a specified size at runtime. An important property of malloc is that it ensures the allocated block is valid and accessible while in use, while freeing it appropriately to avoid memory leaks. But you might be curious how malloc implements allocation at a low level, and how it accurately allocates the freed-up memory to the caller. That’s the topic we’ll dig into here. We’ll focus on malloc’s low-level implementation, especially how the system decides on and allocates a suitable memory address for us when we call malloc. Before exploring this, let’s review the basics of dynamic memory allocation. In C, we can use malloc to allocate memory dynamically. Its prototype is: void* malloc(size_t size); malloc takes a positive integer size, representing the size (in bytes) of the block we want to allocate. It tries to find a contiguous block large enough and marks it as allocated. If it finds a suitable block, malloc returns a pointer to the start of that block; otherwise it returns NULL to indicate failure. Although malloc looks relatively simple, its low-level implementation is a complex task. Different operating systems and compilers may use different algorithms and strategies to perform memory allocation. So we’ll dig into these internal mechanisms to understand how malloc allocates memory, and discuss the trade-offs and performance implications. Next, we’ll enter the low-level world of malloc and lift the veil behind it. We’ll look at several common memory allocation algorithms, including fixed partitioning, dynamic partitioning, and paging. These algorithms will help us understand how malloc works and how to optimize memory usage performance.
With this question, we can dig into the principles. How memory is allocatedMemory allocation in an operating system is mainly implemented by a memory allocator. In the early days, glibc’s default allocator was dlmalloc. But dlmalloc has a problem: once multiple threads call malloc, only one thread can enter the critical section. The improvement to this is ptmalloc2, forked from dlmalloc: once multiple threads call malloc, memory is allocated to each thread immediately. Since memory allocation fundamentally happens across multiple threads, dlmalloc easily causes poor performance. In ptmalloc2, when multiple threads call malloc at the same time, memory is allocated immediately, because each thread maintains its own separate heap segment, and the freelist data structure maintaining each heap segment is also independent. This behavior of maintaining per-thread freelist structures and heap segments is called a per-thread arena. /* Per thread arena example. */#include <stdio.h>#include <stdlib.h>#include <pthread.h>#include <unistd.h>#include <sys/types.h>void* threadFunc(void* arg) { printf("Before malloc in thread 1\n"); getchar(); char* addr = (char*) malloc(1000); printf("After malloc and before free in thread 1\n"); getchar(); free(addr); printf("After free in thread 1\n"); getchar();}int main() { pthread_t t1; void* s; int ret; char* addr; printf("Welcome to per thread arena example::%d\n",getpid()); printf("Before malloc in main thread\n"); getchar(); addr = (char*) malloc(1000); printf("After malloc and before free in main thread\n"); getchar(); free(addr); printf("After free in main thread\n"); getchar(); ret = pthread_create(&t1, NULL, threadFunc, NULL); if(ret) { printf("Thread creation error\n"); return -1; } ret = pthread_join(t1, &s); if(ret) { printf("Thread join error\n"); return -1; } return 0;}
Compile and run: gcc -c mythread -lpthread -o mythread./mythread
We can check the process’s memory allocation by PID.Per the program output above, its PID is 74: cat /proc/PID/maps
You can see the heap segment is: 55590b2c9000-55590b2ea000 rw-p 00000000 00:00 0 [heap]7fd7ddf25000-7fd7ddf28000 rw-p 00000000 00:00 0 After calling malloc, check the memory allocation again:
We find that after freeing, the allocated memory isn’t released immediately. It’s first returned to the glibc malloc library, and the freed block (chunk) is added to the main arena’s bin (in glibc malloc, the freelist is called a bin). Then if the user requests a new block, malloc won’t ask the kernel for new memory but instead looks for a free chunk in the bin; only if the bin has no available chunk does it ask the kernel again.
A later post will analyze further: which system call is used?
mmap brk
Referenceshttps://sploitfun.wordpress.com/2015/02/11/syscalls-used-by-malloc/https://hanfeng.ink/post/understand_glibc_malloc/https://sploitfun.wordpress.com/2015/02/10/understanding-glibc-malloc/comment-page-1/

entry.title: High SF, Dragged Down by Drift | No Name on the Door | GaianSpace CTF 2026
entry.content:
🌐 中文版：繁體中文 Sixth post in the series. In the previous post, Two Voices, the satellite was still using a standard SF9. Here the stranger has changed its downlink config into implicit header + a different SF per packet, and because high-SF symbols are long, Doppler/clock drift makes the decode start going wrong partway through. This is the post where the demodulator is finally forced to add drift correction. Rest of the series: Channel Hop、True Color Is a Lie、Isodata Seven、Subsidy Claim、Hopscotch
What the challenge is about 01:40. The stranger is still talking to GAIAN-723, and the satellite responds every few minutes, but every response uses a voice the ground-station modem “refuses to listen to.” GAIAN-723 has changed how it speaks: packets no longer mark their length, and every packet sounds slightly different from the last. The ground-station log has a line at 01:31: DL CFG CHANGED BY TC — NOT FROM MOC. Goal: find the CO₂ reading GAIAN-723 reported when it acknowledged the stranger’s command at 01:37, and how long it says it’s been awake. Flag format: GAIANSPACE{[CO2 in ppm]_[uptime in seconds]}. Every packet has a different SFThe log shows the downlink config was changed by a telecommand at 01:31, after which “the header is gone and the length is unknown”, i.e. an implicit header. This recording is a fresh segment after the 01:36 roll-over, starting at 01:36:45, so 01:37 is after the 15-second mark in the recording. Measuring per-band energy, I find 8 satellite packets, then search the preamble peaks over SF 7–12, and it turns out every packet has a different SF (SF7, 8, 9, 10 in rotation), which should be what the challenge means by “each one sounds slightly different”:
Start (s) Length SF
7.50 0.84 s 10
13.07 0.57 s 8
34.88 0.84 s 10
… … …
The stranger’s commands are short, strong pulses (SF7, BW250k). Recording start 01:36:45 + 34.65 s ≈ 01:37:19, so the satellite packet closest after that command (34.88 s, SF10) is the ACK the challenge wants. Drift correction for high SFThe hardest packet here is SF10. The bigger the SF (Spreading Factor), the longer each symbol. An SF10 symbol takes 4096 samples (SF7 is only 512), so the longer a symbol drags on, the more deadly the following problem becomes. What is drift? The satellite flies overhead at several kilometres per second, so the frequencies on each end keep shifting due to the Doppler effect (like an ambulance’s pitch changing as it passes). Add the clock error of each side’s quartz oscillator, and the signal’s frequency isn’t off by a fixed amount. It slides slowly the whole time. The longer a symbol, the more it slides within a single packet. How does that hurt decoding? Recall the demodulation skeleton: after dechirping each symbol you get an FFT peak, and whichever integer bin the peak lands in is the symbol’s value. But drift makes the peak not land exactly on an integer bin. It carries a fraction (e.g. bin 100.2, 100.35, 100.5…), and that fractional part grows steadily over time.
I measured it drifting from −0.2 slowly to −0.5, then flipping to +0.5.
At first, off by 0.2, rounding still lands in the right bin; but as it approaches 0.5, rounding jumps to the wrong bin, so the first half of the packet decodes correctly and the second half turns to garbage right around CO2=. That’s why “a single fixed offset collapses partway through.” So first confirm the problem is purely drift: this ACK packet’s spectrogram is a clean chirp, with no frequency hop or interference midway:
The fix is three steps:
Extract each symbol peak’s fractional part and line them up over time into a curve; Because the fraction “wraps around” when it crosses ±0.5, use np.unwrap to stitch those jumps into a continuous curve; Fit it with a quadratic polynomial (drift is smooth, so quadratic is enough), then subtract that fitted curve from each symbol’s bin, and the peaks settle back onto integer bins.
The left panel shows the symbol peaks’ drift (blue dots) and the quadratic fit (red line); the right panel shows the timeline of packets and commands:
With the drift subtracted, the whole packet decodes cleanly. This packet also ends with a CRC-16 (*18FC), which I recomputed with CCITT parameters and matched exactly, a stamp of approval on “decoded correctly.” ResultTM,ACK,1,GET HK,HK,V=4.51,I=0.1,T=21.82,P=996.24,CO2=432,UP=132*18FC
The challenge wants CO₂ and UP (uptime in seconds): CO2=432, UP=132. There’s a trap here: the ACK at 01:36:52 is almost identical (CO2=424,UP=105), and the only way to tell them apart is by time, so you have to convert the recording’s start into real time to land on the 01:37 one. The two UP values differ by 27 seconds, matching the gap between the two responses, which cross-checks nicely. FlagGAIANSPACE{432_132}
Takeaways “Every packet is different” usually means SF or BW is hopping. Do an independent parameter search per packet; don’t assume the previous packet’s parameters carry over. An implicit header has no length and no CR: infer the length from the symbol count on the air, and pick the CR by “which one decodes clean text or passes CRC.” First few bytes matching but the rest garbled is often a CR or drift issue, not a wrong overall direction. High-SF symbols are long and very sensitive to drift. Plot the trend of the symbol peaks’ fractional part and the drift is obvious; correct it with unwrap + polynomial fit. Two identical-looking ACKs can only be told apart by time. Convert the recording’s start to real UTC first, then match the moment the challenge states, so you don’t grab the wrong one. In the next post, Hopscotch, the satellite goes one step further: it hops across multiple frequencies (FHSS), and the demodulator has to reassemble the hop sequence before it can decode.

entry.title: 🗂️Paper Review: O-RAN and Virtualized 5G Networks
entry.content:
🌐 中文版：繁體中文
This is a survey paper.Title: “Open, Programmable, and Virtualized 5G Networks: State-of-the-Art and the Road Ahead”College: Institute for the Wireless Internet of Things, Northeastern UniversityAuthors: Leonardo Bonati, Michele Polese, Salvatore D’Oro, Stefano Basagni, Tommaso MelodiaCitation: 24
Abstract5G brings many benefits, and software-defined cellular networks bring many changes. There are currently many open-source 5G projects, and this paper introduces many current open-source 5G projects and their internal details, along with their frameworks and corresponding hardware environments and testbeds. Introduction5G applications are diverse: VR, remote surgery, high-resolution streaming video, private cellular networks. But traditional mobile-network architecture is relatively inflexible and inelastic, unable to meet the conditions for realizing 5G applications. Current mobile networks’ black-box approach brings many limitations; for example, hardware/software is plug and play but lacks reconfiguration ability and can’t control a large amount of available resources, making it hard to achieve real-time traffic control in network operations, hard to manage resources, with unoptimized performance, and hard to realize Connectivity-as-a-Service (CAAS) technologies like private cellular networks. Both industry and academia believe 5G should change this plug-and-play approach, adopting programmable, open, resource-sharing, edge-oriented network solutions, such as SDN, network virtualization, and MEC (Multi-access Edge Computing), which make dynamic network control and agile management possible. Likewise, network slicing and C-RAN (Cloud RAN) have proven that infrastructure sharing can not only maximize resource utilization but also bring new market opportunities. Traditional closed telecom networks are hard for ordinary people to access, but today software examples defined by GNU Radio Libraries have been incorporated into OpenAirInterface (OAI) and srsLTE, and can be quickly deployed on commercial SDR devices. Software frameworks like O-RAN run on white-box servers and allow reconfiguration and optimization of network and transceiver functions. Architectural enablers of 5G cellular networksArchitectureMobile networks have changed their overall architecture, from the old black-box hardware with dedicated firmware to an architecture based on open software running on SDRs or other hardware, but this has actually been discussed continuously since the 4G era. 5G, from its spec, has great agility and flexibility for deployment, and in the early stages software-ized services were also being built. This flexibility-by-design made 5G cooler from the start. This chapter introduces the network architecture from 4G to 5G, RAN, core network, deployment examples, SDN, NFV, network slicing, MEC, and intelligent networks. From this figure, 4G and 5G deployments seem no different, but the internal composition and configuration of the core network differ a lot.
Composition 4G 5G
RAN LTE NR
Core EPC 5GC
In the 4G EPC, many components used to run on proprietary hardware and only recently started being deployed in software.5GC, on the other hand, was designed from the start based on a service-based approach: the EPC server is split into many virtual network functions providing specific functions, communicating with each other through open standard interfaces; 5G RAN has a similar split principle (CU/RU), etc. NR wider range of carrier frequencies (mmWave Spectrum) frame structure: OFDM-based, more flexible, with a variable number of symbols delivered in each sub-frame, and able to use larger bandwidths than LTE (400MHz per carrier) integration of signals and procedures to manage mmWave directional transmission 5G RAN can connect to a 4G EPC (non-standalone config) and a 5G 5GC (standalone config) NR base stations = gNodeBs allow distributed deployment: different parts of the protocol stack can be distributed across different hardware components In NR’s protocol stack, an SDAP (Service Data Adaptation Protocol) layer is stacked on top of PDCP, managing QoS for point-to-point traffic and mapping it to local resources on the gNodeB-UE link; other layers are updated to achieve NR functionality
CU/DU split and the virtualized RAN architectureThe most innovative thing in NR is splitting the higher layers of the 3GPP stack (PDCP, SDAP, RRC) from the lower layers (RLC, MAC, PHY) into two different logical units, the CU (Control Unit) and DU (Distributed Unit), which can be deployed in different places. The lower part of the physical layer can be separated from the DU into an independent RU (Radio Unit); the CU, DU, and RU can communicate with each other at different data rates and latencies via well-defined interfaces.This architecture appears in 3GPP and makes a virtualized RAN (vRAN) possible:antenna elements $\longrightarrow$ RUbaseband, signal processing units $\longrightarrow$ CU, DUAll of the above can run on general-purpose or multi-vendor platforms or hardware components, and if the interfaces between different RAN components are open, deployment follows the O-RAN model. The 5G CoreWith the service-based approach, control- and user-plane core functions are split into multiple network functions, and 3GPP defines APIs for these, enabling flexible network deployment and network slicing.
UPF (User Plane Function): the gateway between the user and the network, acting as the mobility anchor and the QoS classifier CPF (Control Plane Function): the 4G MME is mostly distributed into the AMF (Access and Mobility Management Function); the SMF (Session Management Function) allocates IP addresses to UEs and orchestrates user-plane services (e.g. which UPF the UE should use)
Enabling technologies for softwarized 5G cellular networks5G integrates different functional components, and the architecture will be very large, with management being a challenge. 5G networks reference the broad and complete processes and architectures of the cloud-computing ecosystem, integrating virtualization and softwarization to abstract services and functions from the original hardware. Softwarization and software-defined networkingTo integrate functions and configuration parameters across different vendors’ hardware components, 5G systems rely on softwarization:
SDN OpenFlow protocol
SDN: decouples network control from the data plane, separating routing and controlling procedures from the original hardware-based forwarding operations. In 5G, it separates RAN and edge hardware components from their network and service functions.
In the RAN architecture, only the RU retains basic transmit/receive functions; the rest of the control and processing is controlled by software via open interfaces and APIs. Network function virtualization (NFV)Each network function is implemented in software via a VNF (Virtual Network Function) running on a VM (built on general-purpose hardware). One advantage of NFV is that each VNF provides atomic-level functionality, so multiple VNFs can be combined to create more complex, specific network functions.
The Network Orchestrator: manages the VMs on the object infrastructure and the services they run VNF: runs on a VM and performs a network function NFVI (Network Function Virtualization Infrastructure): composed of various general-purpose hardware
open-source network virtualization project: Open Platform for NFV (OPNFV)provides testing tools and validation programs to accelerate enterprises’ and service providers’ network transformation to NFV
RAN and Core Network slicingNetwork slicing is a multi-tenancy virtualization technology in which network functions are abstracted from hardware and software and provided as slices to so-called tenants. The physical infrastructure (base stations, fiber) is shared among multiple tenants, and a tenant may receive one or more slices. Each slice is allocated specific physical resources, and an independent virtual network is instantiated on those physical resources. Although tenants have resource control over their own slices, they can’t interact with other slices, which is called slice isolation/orthogonality. Each slice covers specific network functions of the RAN and core parts, and a tenant can provide CaaS (for private cellular networking) to mobile users via RAN slice instantiation on selected base stations. RAN slices can also be allocated to specific services, users, and applications, e.g. allocating a slice to a resource-demanding application (AR/VR). This figure shows how slicing lets infrastructure resources be shared and supports instantiating multiple slices embedded in infrastructure components, and lists the related open-source software projects and which parts of this architecture each controls, configures, and instantiates. Advantages of network slicing: Each slice can be reserved to handle a specific traffic class with different security requirements and allocated a different amount of resources, achieving infrastructure-level service differentiation Slices are software-controlled, enabling real-time, on-demand instantiation, reconfiguration, and revocation of network slices to adapt to time-varying traffic demands and meet SLAs (Service Level Agreements) Underutilized resources can be rented out as network slices to MVNOs (Mobile Virtual Network Operators) to maximize resource utilization and give infrastructure providers new monetization opportunities
Network slices need to be dynamically orchestrated, instantiated, and revoked, meet SLAs, and have strong tolerance for faults or interruptions. OSSs (Operations Support Systems)OSS can serve as a tool to guarantee service fulfillment through closed-loop control and management of network slices.Meanwhile, operators and infrastructure owners providing slice services to vertical industries must generate diverse offerings through slices dedicated to reflecting vertical-industry needs.BSSs (Business Support Systems)BSS will need to control this diverse environment and implement dynamic billing and pricing mechanisms for each slice. Multi-access edge computing5G’s high-performance signal processing, transmission mechanisms, and data rates still can’t meet its throughput and low-latency requirements, such as handling real-time applications like VR/AR, and MEC can solve this. MEC moves the architecture’s basic components closer to the user; built on edge computing, content caching, NFV, and SDN, MEC provides an effective solution for 5G applications’ latency and throughput needs.
Since content and data are processed at the edge, data only needs to be transmitted to the CN occasionally, reducing transmission latency and the CN’s burden. It supports localized service provisioning, providing cellular private networks for health, environmental monitoring, edge IoT computing, etc.
Intelligence in the networkML/AIData-driven, automated 5G networks become possible, and different use cases can be used to train and optimize the RAN. Use cases range from predicting traffic demand to scale CN resources, to reducing latency in ultra-reliable low-latency communication (URLLC). The framework realizing this is O-RAN, which monitors data, learns, and executes closed-loop control via a RIC that interacts with the gNB and eNB. The radio access network This chapter describes the open-source libraries and frameworks for deploying 4G/5G; the details can be found on the projects’ official sites, so they aren’t elaborated here.
OpenAirInterfacehttps://openairinterface.org/ srsLTEhttps://www.srslte.com/ Radisys open source RAN contributionshttps://www.radisys.com/solutions/openran Core NetworkThis chapter describes the mainstream open-source solutions for 4G/5G, i.e. EPC and 5G Core. Evolved Packet Core (EPC)The 4G EPC implementation was discussed in section 2.1 and usually includes - MME(Mobile Management Entity)- Home Subscription Server(HSS)- Service Gateway(SGW)- Packet Gateway(PGW)
MME (Mobility Management Entity)
control messages for establishing a connection with the UE paging and mobility procedures NAS signaling security functions like tracking-area-list management PGW/SGW selection UE authentication reachability procedures bearer managementi.e. the tunnel between UE and PGW in the EPC case, and between UE and UPF in the 5GC case supports the control-plane signaling protocol between EPC and E-UTRAN reliable message-delivery service supports tunneling protocols for UDP control messages supports protocols for authenticating, authorizing, and accounting the UE
HSS (Home Subscription Server)
User Database: stores subscriber data (id and key) User Authentication provides the interface between the user and the MME
The SGW and PGW components deliver data for the user and control planes via GTP,i.e. GPRS Tunneling Protocol User Plane (GTP-U) and GPRS Tunneling Protocol Control Plane (GTP-C), using UDP as the transport-layer protocol. GTP is also implemented in 5G, and a vulnerability was disclosed last year. https://www.ithome.com.tw/news/138340 https://itw01.com/8JS4VEH.html
It supports packet routing and forwarding, allocating IP addresses to UEs, and paging. Open-source projects supporting the LTE EPC are: - OpenAirInterface(with OAI-CN)- srsLTE(with srsEPC)- Open5GS- Open Mobile Evolved Core(OMEC)
Each open-source project’s implementation status for the EPC interfaces 5G Core The current open-source project implementing the 5G core is Free5GC, implemented based on NextEPC (now Open5GS), providing:
user access, mobility, session (AMF and SMF) management service discovery provided by other NFs (NRF) NFs to select the slice allocated to the UE (Network Slice Selection Function) managing, storing, retrieving user data (UDM, UDR) UE authentication (AUSF) core-network operations and management (Operations, Administration and Maintenance (OAM)) network orchestration, etc.
3GPP interfaces implemented by free5gc:
N1/N2: connect the AMF to the UE and RAN respectively, for session and mobility management N3/N4/N6: connect the UPF to the RAN, SMF, and data network respectively N8: connects the UDM and AMF, for user-authentication procedures N10/N11: connect the SMF to the UDM and AMF respectively, handling subscription and session-management requests N12/N13: connect the AUSF to the AMF and UDM respectively, enabling authentication services
RAN and core frameworksThis chapter describes several open frameworks used in the RAN and core network.Although the software in chapters 3 and 4 can perform specific functions, the frameworks introduced below are more general and broader in scope, used with the RAN and CN for management, control, and coordination. Open frameworks and architectures summary O-RANThe open-standard definition for vRAN championed by the O-RAN Alliance, with two major goals.The first is integrating ML and AI technologies via intelligent controllers deployed at the edge.The second is the definition of openness and agility, achieved by defining clear interfaces between the RAN’s different components.Since O-RAN must expose the same APIs, it’s easy to replace a component with another of the same function, which lets 5G O-RAN integrate components from different vendors.
O-RAN architectureAt the very top, the SMO runs a non-RT RIC, which makes control decisions at a granularity above 1 second. It can provide O-RAN’s various functions, for example training different algorithms on the data the RAN provides. The near-RT RIC, however, runs a control loop with a tighter time interval (decision < 10 ms), varying depending on the RAN’s different start, stop, override, or control types, e.g. radio resource management. These APIs can be used by applications installed on the near-RT RIC (called xApps).These xApps can be developed by third-party entities and obtained from a public marketplace.For example, via the near-RT RIC and its xApps, operators can control user mobility processes (i.e. handovers), allocate network resources based on predicted paths of connected vehicles and drones, perform load balancing and traffic steering, and optimize scheduling policies. The near-RT RIC can also use algorithms trained in the non-RT RIC to do things. O-RAN’s other components like CU/DU/RU: like the 5G gNB being split into CU/DU/RU and the 4G eNB. The CU is further split into a control-plane CU and a user-plane CU. Per 3GPP’s definitions of different splits, O-RAN chooses split 7-2x for the DU/RU split; so encoding, modulation, and resource mapping are done by the DU; while demodulation, cyclic prefix addition, and digital-to-analog are implemented in the RU, and precoding can be done in both. O-RAN interfacesThe interface between the two RICs is the A1 interface, and the non-RT RIC uses the O1 interface to interact with the RIC and 4G eNB.
The A1 interface lets the non-RT RIC provide:
policy-based guidance to the near-RT RIC (in case it detects that its operations don’t achieve the RAN’s performance targets) ML Model management rich information to the near-RT RIC, e.g. from sources external to the RAN, to further refine RAN optimization
The O1 interface has operations and management functions, striving to be compatible with existing standards for perfect integration with existing frameworks, e.g. relying on NETCONF or other 3GPP-defined APIs.
The non-RT RIC uses the O1 interface for:
provision management fault supervision performance assurance services starting, registering, and updating physical equipment managing communication-monitoring equipment
The near-RT RIC also exposes the E2 interface to various other components (CU, DU, eNB); this interface focuses only on deploying
the near-RT RIC’s control operations on E2-interface endpoints managing the interaction behavior between the RIC and these nodes
The E1 and F1 interfaces conform to 3GPP specifications.
The E1 interface runs between the control-plane and user-plane CUs; its main function is UE-specific trace collection and bearer setup and management.The F1 interface runs between the CU and DU; it has two different versions, one connecting to the control-plane CU and the other to the user-plane CU; F1 is responsible for transmitting signaling and data between the CU and DU to perform RPC procedures and PDCP-RLC exchange. Finally, the interface with the RU is defined by O-RAN’s internal Open Fronthaul working group; this interface carries compressed IQ samples for the data plane and control messages for beamforming and other physical-layer procedures. O-RAN Deployment OptionsO-RAN envisions different deployment strategies: in the regional or edge cloud, or at operator-owned cellular base stations. Each facility can run an O-Cloud (i.e. containers and VMs) that uses open interfaces to execute O-RAN programs, or a dedicated site can use O-RAN’s open APIs but run closed-source code. Both cases are described in the figure, which describes 6 different O-RAN deployment combinations.
In Scenario A, all components except the RU are deployed at the network edge, co-located in the same data center connected by fronthaul fiber. Other deployment strategies have the RIC and CU co-deployed in regional cloud facilities, with the DU and RU at the network edge or cellular base stations, and the preferred strategy is Scenario B. RIC in the regional cloudCUs, DUs at the edgeOnly the RU at the operator's cellular base station
The O-RAN Software CommunityBesides standardization activities, O-RAN also has a software community (OSC) that collaborates with the Linux Foundation to contribute 5G software conforming to O-RAN specifications. The first release was the 2019 Amber release.The second was the 2020 Bronze release. These releases include Docker containers and open-source software for multiple O-RAN components:
non-RT RIC: with an A1 interface controller and the ability to manage AI models near-RT RIC platform: with multiple applications, such as: admission control UE manager performance and measurement monitor able to communicate with the DU via the E2 interface
DU: an initial version of the fronthaul library
a framework for operations, management, maintenance, and virtualized architecture simulator: for testing various interfaces
The cherry release attempts to complete the integration between different RAN components via the RIC.
The current latest release is the F-Release.
The SD-RAN project is also leading and developing an effort to realize an open-source, 3GPP-compliant RAN integrated with the O-RAN RIC interfaces. Open Networking Foundation frameworksA consortium of multiple telecom operators who provide open-source programs and frameworks for deploying their networks, including: OMEC, SD-RAN, ONOS.Component Projects are frameworks and software for specific purposes, while an Exemplar contains many Component Projects. Other frameworks and projectsBesides O-RAN and ONF solutions, many open-source communities have released frameworks and projects for connectivity, slicing, and core. 5G-EmPOWERAn operating system for heterogeneous RAN architectures, consisting of an open-source, reprogrammable software platform that abstracts the physical infrastructure and provides high-level APIs to manipulate RAN functions. 5G-EmPOWER also separates the control plane from the user plane, a separation actually composed of two main components: a central controller and a set of agents.Central controller:
acts as the OS and has full knowledge of the physical infrastructure’s functions sends control commands via the OpenEmpower protocol to orchestrate the agents’ behavior
Agents:
run on each network unit abstract the underlying RAN-specific protocol (LTE, Wifi) implementation to the controller modify underlying protocol parameters per the controller’s commands
5G-EmPOWER currently supports multiple Radio Access Technologies (RATs), including LTE, Wifi, LoRa (5G NR not yet supported). There are also these projects:
FlexRAN Magma LL-MEC LightEdge OpenRAN (not equal to O-RAN Projects) Akraino REC NVIDIA Aerial
Open virtualization and management frameworksBesides RAN and CN software, virtualization and management frameworks also play an important role.
ETSI defines the common features an NFV MANO (Management and Orchestration) framework should have, mainly for orchestrating network functions (NFs).
The figure above shows which part of the 5G ecosystem these NFV pieces correspond to NFV Orchestrators are responsible for providing network services, i.e. combining physical and virtual network functions (PNF/VNF) connected through a specific topology, to manage their lifecycle. Per the ETSI architecture, an NFV Orchestrator consists of:
a subsystem managing the virtualization infrastructure (e.g. a VIM (Virtualization Infrastructure Manager) framework like OpenStack, Kubernetes, Docker) and its connection to physical hardware an actual MANO framework the set of VNFs it managesThese frameworks have northbound and southbound APIs to interact with other cellular-network components.This chapter discusses virtualization techniques, VIMs, and popular MANO frameworks like ONAP, OSM, and Open Baton.
Virtualization techniquesNFV separates the services deployed in the network from the hardware infrastructure they run on, and applications are packaged into VMs separated from the hardware. NFV removes the need for each NF to require specific hardware, enabling network scalability. This is a high-level NFV architecture, showing multiple implementation approaches Traditional Virtual MachineHardware-level virtualization, providing machine-level isolation, emulating a computer system via a guest OS and kernel.Since VNFs have many hardware-virtualization requirements, traditional VMs are considered resource-intensive. Bare-metal hypervisorsThe bare-metal hypervisor VM approach is similar to the traditional VM approach, but here the hypervisor runs directly on the host’s hardware without a host OS, and can also be used to manage and run containers or unikernels rather than entire VMs. ContainersPackage a specific program and its dependencies, running applications and services in a virtualized environment.Containers are isolated from each other and share the host OS and access to the kernel; compared to a VM, they don’t need to virtualize the underlying hardware and are much lighter. Containers can be maintained via a container manager connected to the host OS, or run directly on a bare-metal host machine via a hypervisor. Open-source container systems:
LXC: the main implementation of modern containers, isolating via cgroups and namespaces to create a virtual environment with independent network and process spaces Docker: allows creating containers, using OS-level virtualization to deploy them on a machine; unlike LXC, it decomposes services, applications, and dependencies into modular units and layers within each container, and these layers can be shared across multiple containers, increasing container-image efficiency.
UnikernelsUnikernels are tiny, lightweight, specialized images whose sole purpose is to run a specific application. They compile the application service and its dependencies into an executable virtual image, without including unnecessary components, so unikernels can achieve better performance than traditional containers and VMs; because a unikernel only includes the software components necessary to run the target application, it exposes fewer features that could be maliciously attacked, improving system security. Known unikernel systems: ClickOS, IncludeOS, OSv, MirageOS, Unik Cellular-network-related unikernel applications (papers):
integrating Android libraries into OSv to reduce the mobile-computing burden of MCC (Mobile Cloud Computing) and MFC (Mobile Fog Computing) unikernel-based 5G network CDNs, like ClickOS, OSv, MirageOS one paper compares the performance of instantiating a 5G application as a VNF with the IncludeOS unikernel vs Docker
HypervisorsA set of software for running virtual machines (guest machines) on a physical machine (host machine).The hypervisor’s key tasks are:
providing virtualization between host and guest machines managing the allocation and reallocation of guest-machine resources (CPU, memory, storage) scheduling resources between host and guest machines
There are two types of hypervisor: Type 1, Type 2.Type 1: the hypervisor runs directly on the bare-metal host machine, acting as the OS on the host.Example: Xen, VMware ESXiType 2: runs as a software layer on the host OS.Example: Linux Kernel-based VM (KVM), BSD bhyve, Oracle VirtualBox Virtualization infrastructure managers (VIM)A VIM controls and manages the NFV infrastructure and its resources, like storage, compute, and network resources, and coordinates the instantiation of guest machines on the host hardware. A VIM is part of the MANO framework, discussed earlier. Examples of VIMs: OpenStack, Kubernetes
OpenStack: a cloud-computing platform able to control a large amount of heterogeneous resources like compute, storage, and network. Among its many functions, it can act like a VIM, managing network infrastructure, VMs, containers, unikernels, VNF services, and applications Kubernetes: provides automated deployment, scaling, and management of VMs, containers, unikernels, and their applications; it abstracts and expresses system state through a series of objects, persistent entities describing the VNFs and applications running on a K8s-managed cluster, their available resources, and policies about their intended behavior. Over the years, several projects have interacted with k8s to handle complex Layer 2/Layer 3 protocol problems, like Istio and NSM (Network Service Mesh) Istio mesh service: implements traffic management, policy enforcement, and telemetry collection NSM: supports advanced use cases via the Kubernetes API and promotes adoption of new cloud-native solutions, and also lets network admins seamlessly perform tasks like requesting network interfaces and adding radio services
The Open Network Automation PlatformAn NFV framework mainly developed by the Linux Foundation, with many supporting operators.ONAP is deployed in multiple commercial cellular networks, with vendors like Ericsson, Nokia, Huawei, and ZTE providing ONAP support and integrating it into their products. ONAP is the best software-based solution for commercial cellular networks.ONAP handles the design, creation, and lifecycle management of a large number of network services. Network operators can use ONAP to orchestrate the PNFs and VNFs deployed in their networks. Besides the functions common to NFV orchestrators (automated, policy-based management of virtual infrastructure or network services), ONAP also provides a design framework to model network applications and services, and a data-analytics framework to monitor service healing and scaling. ONAP also provides many reference designs (i.e. blueprints) that can be used to deploy the ONAP architecture for specific scenarios (5G Networks, VoLTE, etc.).
Main components of the ONAP architecture:
Management Framework: also called OOM (ONAP Operations Manager), responsible for orchestrating and monitoring the lifecycle of ONAP components. OOM uses K8s and Consul to support service control, discovery, configuration, and segmentation. Among its notable functions: Component deployment, dependency management, and configuration real-time health monitoring service clustering and scaling component upgrade, restart, and deletion
Design Framework: allows creating network services using a declarative modeling language, enabling specification of each service’s requirements and functions. allows modeling resources, services, products, and their management and control functions through a set of common specifications and policies. also includes service-design and creation modules for defining, simulating, and certifying system assets, processes, and policies. modules also provide a database of existing services and APIs for validating network functions
Run-time Framework composed of many software frameworks for most management and orchestration functions at run-time, the Microservices Bus allows messaging and data communication and routing between the different network functions (NFs) managed by ONAP the run-time framework uses an automated control loop to schedule and terminate microservices, and collects and analyzes data from the platform run-time components have public APIs, a dashboard, and command-line tools to control the network infrastructure through a unified interface
Underneath these frameworks can be integrated with external controllers, operating systems, and cloud environments; northbound APIs are provided to OSS/BSS, big data, and related services. Integration with 5G networksBesides general mobile-network orchestration and management frameworks, ONAP provides important functions related to 5G deployment.Operators’ main requirement is usually supporting a hybrid infrastructure:
must include software and hardware equipment edge automation, with the cloud distributed across geographically different edge locations real-time analytics (must use an automated control loop)
The Frankfurt release (June 2020) integrated with O-RAN. Open Source NFV Management and OrchestrationOpen Source NFV Management and Orchestration (OSM) is a MANO framework developed by a group of network operators.Similar to ONAP, it’s also developed and deployed in cellular networks. OSM’s architecture
The information model: models NFs and slices as templates called packages, enabled by the well-defined information model provided by the ETSI MANO framework. Similar to ONAP’s design components, it lets telecom operators analyze network requirements and model the resources that need to be deployed for functions, services, and slices. The OSM Automation Framework: automates the NF lifecycle, from initialization to scaling to deletion, by applying the information model to the actual deployed infrastructure (see figure above), exposing a northbound interface to the different modeling components via the automation framework
Like ONAP, OSM’s southbound and northbound APIs can be exposed to external services, like other orchestrators and OSS/BSS. Software-defined radio support for open source radio unitsSDR devicesUSRP, BladeRF, LimeSDR, Iris TestbedsIntroduces testbeds that use open-source applications, frameworks, and hardware components to instantiate and softwarize 5G networks.
Softwarized 5G: Limitations and road ahead Keep pace with the standards Latency and scalability issues. Limited contributions for RAN open source software
Paper link: https://ece.northeastern.edu/wineslab/papers/bonati2020open.pdf

entry.title: Python for DevOps Notes |【DevOps Skill Tree】
entry.content:
🌐 中文版：繁體中文
Basic Data Typesdata type You can get an object or variable’s data type with type()
>>> var = "This is a string">>> print(type(var))<class 'str'>
Variables x valid x_y valid x-y invalid Python variables are case-sensitive VAR is not equal to var
What happens when you type x=1? It creates an integer object with value 1 So a fixed-size address is allocated in memory to store 1 And the name x points to the reference for that object
>>> x =123>>> y =x>>> print(id(x))4298889392>>> print(id(y))4298889392
In Python, a variable is a reference to an object, meaning the variable name points to an object in memory, but the variable itself doesn’t contain the memory address So when you assign one variable to another, both use the same reference Multiple variables initialized to the same value can be declared like a = b = c = 1
Booleansbool(0), bool(), bool("") -> Falsebool(1), bool(456), bool("Hello") -> True
Strings How to convert “2 0 1 7” to the list [2, 0, 1, 7]? int(i) for i in "2 0 1 7".split()
Lists & Tuples What is a tuple in Python? What is it used for? An ordered, immutable collection of elements in Python, basically for holding multiple items in a single variable Its biggest difference from a list is that once a tuple is created, its values can’t change coordinates = (120.5, 23.5 )
List Basic Operations >>> x = [1,2,3]>>> y = [4,5,6]>>> print(x[-1])3>>> x.append(4)>>> print(x)[1, 2, 3, 4]>>> x[0:2] = []>>> print(x)[3, 4]>>> y.extend(x)>>> print(y)[4, 5, 6, 3, 4]>>> y.insert(0, 123)>>> print(y)[123, 4, 5, 6, 3, 4]>>> y.sort()>>> print(y)[3, 4, 4, 5, 6, 123]>>> y.sort(reverse=True)>>> print(y)[123, 6, 5, 4, 4, 3]
How do you iterate a list?
for item in list: print(item)
How do you iterate a list by index?
for i , item in enumerate(list): print(i)
How do you iterate a list in reverse?
for i reversed(list): print(i)
How do you merge two sorted lists? sorted(list1, list2) What is a list comprehension? A more concise, convenient way to build a list Syntax: [expression for item in iterable if condition]
squares = [x**2 for x in range(10)]print(sqaures) ## Output [0, 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49, 64, 81]
https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/datastructures.html#list-comprehensions
DictionariesHow do you create a dictionary? >>> my_dict = dict(x=1, y=2)>>> print(my_dict){'x': 1, 'y': 2}
How do you delete a specific key? dictName.pop(KEYNAME) >>> print(my_dict){'x': 1, 'y': 2, 'k': 3}>>> my_dict.pop('y')2>>> print(my_dict){'x': 1, 'k': 3}
How do you merge two dictionaries? dict1.update(dict2)
IteratorsOOP, ClassObjectWhat information an object in Python holds? or what attributes an object has? a. Explain each one of them An object is a collection of attributes and methods acting on some data.
Attributes E.g. self.name, self.age Methods E.g. def greet(self): Class Variable: a variable shared across instances of a class E.g. class_variable =0 Special Methods (Magic Methods): __init__, __str__, __repr__ Docstring: a string describing a class or method: """This is a method""" Class Name: the name of the class an object belongs to, accessible via __class__, e.g. object.__class__.__name__ Module Name: which module an object’s class is defined in, accessible via __module__, e.g. object.__module__ Dictionary containing all an object’s attributes and methods, usable for dynamic access, e.g. object.__dict__
ClassesPython Built-In FunctionsExplain the difference between repr, any, and all? __repr__() is a special method in Python used to tell others about an object’s contents. class Person: def __init__(self, name, age): self.name = name self.age = age p = Person("Kevin", 26)print(p)## output: <__main__.Person object at 0x102934370>
When the code above runs, it prints the object’s memory address, which doesn’t describe the object itself, but repr can describe the object. class Person: def __init__(self, name, age): self.name = name self.age = age def __repr__(self): return f"Person(name='{self.name}', age={self.age})" p = Person("Kevin", 26)print(p)## Output: Person(name='Kevin', age=26)
any() returns True if at least one element in the iterable is True. It returns False if the iterable is empty or all elements are False. all() returns True if all elements in the iterable are True. It returns False if the iterable is empty or any element is False. InheritanceInheritance is a feature all object-oriented languages have: a class can inherit the corresponding attributes and methods from another class. Raises exception What is an error? What is an exception? What types of exceptions are you familiar with? The errors you may get are Syntax Error and Exception A Syntax Error means the code doesn’t follow the syntax rules, which the Python interpreter catches during parsing and reports An Exception is an error during execution, usually from unexpected situations, like dividing an integer by 0 or accessing an empty file But exceptions can be caught and handled with try and except
Common exceptions ZeroDivisionError ValueError TypeError IndexError KeyError FileNotFoundError AttributeError ImportError
Example try: result = 10/0except ZeroDivisionError: print("Cannot divide zero")else: print(f"Result:{result}")finally: print("Completely")
Cannot divide zeroCompletely
Async && Concurrency For the concepts of synchronous and asynchronous, see this article.
Files ManipulationHow do you write to a file? with open("example.txt", 'w') as file: file.write("This is a test file.")
Given a text file, print every third line def print_3rd_line(file_path) ->str: result = [] with open(file_path, 'r') as file: for i, line in enumerate(file): if (i+1)%3 == 0: print(line) result.append(line) return '\n'.join(result)
Given a text file, print how many lines it has def print_line(file_path) ->str: result = 0 with open(file_path, 'r') as file: for i, line in enumerate(file): result = i return result
Given a text file, print how many words it has def print_word(file_path) ->str: with open(file_path, 'r') as file: text =file.read() words = text.split() return len(words)
Write a piece of text to the end of an already-open file text = "A brown fox jumped over the lazy dog."with open('example.txt', 'a') as file: file.write('\n' +text + '\n')
How do you write a dictionary to a file? import jsondef write_dict(file_path) ->str: myDict = dict(x=1, y=2) with open(file_path, 'w') as file: file.write(json.dumps(myDict))
Read a JSON file import jsonfrom pprint import pprintwith open("example.json", "r") as file: data = json.load(file) pprint(data)
Write a JSON file import jsonfrom pprint import pprintinput = '''{ "user": { "id": 12345, "name": "Alice Johnson", "email": "alice.johnson@example.com", "isActive": true, "age": 29, "address": { "street": "123 Main St", "city": "Wonderland", "postalCode": "12345", "country": "Fantasyland" }, "preferences": { "notifications": { "email": true, "sms": false }, "theme": "dark" }, ...'''# Convert to dictionarydata = json.loads(input)with open("example.json", "w") as file: json.dump(data, file)pprint(data)
Using PathlibPrint the contents of a file in the current directory import pathlibimport ospath = pathlib.Path(os.getcwd()+'/example.txt')text = path.read_text()print(text)
Write a string to a file import pathlibimport ostext = "A quick brown fox jumped over the dog."path = pathlib.Path(os.getcwd() + '/example.txt')path.write_text(text)story = path.read_text()print(story)
OS operationsPython’s os module provides many low-level operating-system system calls, with a unified calling interface across multiple operating systems. Methods the os module provides os.listdir('DIRECTORY PATH')os.rename('Bpple','Apple')os.chmod('script.py', 0o777)os.mkdir('/tmp/devops')os.remove('script.py')os.rmdir('/tmp/devops')os.stat('/tmp/devops') # get file or directory info, like permissions, access time, etc.
How do you print the current directory? import osprint(os.getcwd())
Given the file path /dir1/dir2/file1, print the file name import osprint(os.path.basename('/dir1/dir2/file1'))
How do you run a shell command from Python? import osos.system("ls -l")
How do you join different paths together? import osprint(os.path.join(Dir_Path1, Dir_Path2))
Traversing a folder with os.walkThe os module provides a handy method called os.walk to traverse an entire file tree. This function returns a generator that yields a tuple on each iteration, containing the current directory, the directory list, and the file list. def walk_dir(parent_path): for parent_path, dir, files in os.walk(parent_path): print(f"Checking: {parent_path}") for fileName in files: file_Path = os.path.join(parent_path, fileName) last_access = os.path.getatime(file_Path) size = os.path.getsize(file_Path) print(f"File: {file_Path}") print(f"Last accessed: {last_access}") print(f"Size: {size} bytes")
Regular expressionsPython’s re module provides regular-expression operations. Suppose there’s a collection of strings: mail-list = '''kevin@amazon.com,kev.mgry@jabber.rukev.mgry@jabber.rualkhobar_boy@ayna.comrami_moman@hotmail.comhazeen@cam.comwaleed_97@hotmail.comal_aned@hotmail.comwldabooh@hotmail.comb_m_attar@yahoo.commohscript@hotmail.commalarifi@usa.comsalehsul@yahoo.comaljwhra@hotmail.comethaer@hotmail.comben_njem@hotmail.commaas2000@maktoob.comaboa7med@yahoo.comsaud124@hotmail.comhm_2002_ad@hotmail.comhm2002ad@maktoob.comdark_eyess@hotmail.comwali999@hotmail.commateb_2001@ayna.comdevil2100@maktoob.comahmedshatoor@hotmail.comfaisal20o0@hotmail.comm_sh4ever@hotmail.comshaib2005@maktoob.comf-tp@maktoob.comkevin@amazon.comsmartstar_sa@yahoo.comswaah99@hotmail.comdo7me2002@hotmail.combleaks20@hotmail.comzaeem@ksatoday.comsarah_21_ksa@hotmail.comraheema@ayna.comtoyota@444.netmajeed97@hotmail.comkhabom2@hotmail.coma2685@yahoo.comab_alraddadi@yahoo.comturky_net2002@hotmail.comabu_fahad22@hotmail.comyah1418@maktoob.comnew_sa1@yahoo.comanoooooooos@hotmail.comfem_kinani@hotmail.comalbqaawi@ayna.comalhazenh@hotmail.comuea1@hotmail.comazoo1ooz@hotmail.com00@factmail.calove-1@maktoob.comrami_shut@yahoo.comthe_husaam@hotmail.comvip9999@ayna.comnoor_99_99@yahoo.comalma7roomm@hotmail.comjawad76ly@yahoo.comhemdan_na@hotmail.comi@stc.combuok6977@ayna.comehwaawy@yahoo.comaseer2@maktoob.combin_000@hotmail.comabeyr@ayna.comal_maknun2001@maktoob.comahmsh@naseej.comfar_alsekak@hotmail.commos011@yahoo.comsaud1900@hotmail.comessa1420@yahoo.comalmonta7er@hotmail.comzayd2002-2000@maktoob.comkh_mahfouz@hotmail.coml3yonha@hotmail.comhat1972@hotmail.commk8n@hotmail.comsoul_devil14@hotmail.comkhater_love@hotmail.commohdbahrawi@hotmail.comnaaader@hotmail.comfaisal_war@yahoo.comarramalomari@hotmail.comgmmare@hotmail.comthamir5@hotmail.comseilver@hotmail.comaboghadi@hotmail.comlatte2001@maktoob.comlotfy_s@hotmail.comhamadah990@hotmail.com'''
Say you want to find kevin@amazon.com but only know the email starts with k. How do you find it? import reprint(re.search(r'[A-Za-z]+@[A-Za-z]+\.[a-z]+', mail_list))## Output# <re.Match object; span=(1, 17), match='kevin@amazon.com'> This means any letter from the character sets A-Z and a-z, then + means the preceding character appears one or more times in the match. Since . is a wildcard, it needs to be escaped with a backslash \. The re module represents the common character set [a-zA-Z0-9_] with \w, and ordinary digits [0-9] with \d. So the code above can be rewritten as: import reprint(re.search(r'\w+@\w+\.\w+', mail_list))## Output# <re.Match object; span=(1, 17), match='kevin@amazon.com'>
To access the returned match object better, you can define groups of the match result with parentheses, and get the matched group directly from the returned object by number. import rematch = re.search(r'(\w+)@(\w+)\.(\w+)', mail_list)print(match.group(0))## Output# kevin@amazon.com
To access the returned match object even more conveniently, you can name groups with ?P<NAME>. import rematch = re.search(r'(?P<name>\w+)@(?P<SLD>\w+)\.(?P<TLD>\w+)', mail_list)print(match.group("name"))## Output# kevin
How do you find all IP addresses in a file? For an input like this: In the ever-evolving digital landscape, tracking online data often requires observing user interactions from various regions. For instance, a significant number of logins were recorded from IP addresses like 24.31.173.2 and 82.33.11.118, which reflect diverse user origins. Security teams frequently monitor these access points, noting unusual activity from IPs such as 45.56.148.51 and 99.116.96.74.On an average day, they might encounter new sessions from endpoints like 24.15.139.93 or 67.166.35.191, each needing real-time analysis to ensure data protection. In one case, an IP address from the Asia-Pacific region, 180.215.121.104, demonstrated a high frequency of requests, which raised some flags in the system.Europe is also represented in traffic logs, with IPs such as 64.130.155.78 and 186.176.159.218 originating from locations that maintain stringent data compliance regulations. The North American region had frequent logins from addresses like 71.239.86.182 and 69.43.251.147, where several were validated for secure access.Moreover, a pattern was observed with IPs like 100.12.201.224 and 85.164.201.224 accessing confidential systems during peak hours. Meanwhile, analysts in cybersecurity teams often encounter unusual log requests from regions like 120.156.7.200, necessitating further investigation.The logs also revealed consistent access from IPs like 24.61.142.106, which had been previously flagged for unauthorized attempts. Similarly, 99.58.40.206 and 70.15.237.26 showed a surge in activity, prompting immediate protocol checks. Another example is the IP 108.205.48.11, detected during an audit of high-value transactions.Many more instances, such as connections from 72.168.129.149 and 189.224.44.46, add complexity to monitoring systems. Security teams must evaluate each source, even those with benign records like 68.60.26.228 or frequent accesses from 24.236.160.189.Moreover, the system recorded remote sessions from addresses like 100.36.162.76 and 47.16.121.249, both requiring location verification steps. High-risk IPs, such as 184.4.175.60 and 62.19.65.98, were flagged during the latest vulnerability scan, which further highlighted global risks.Unusual activity from Latin America was seen with addresses like 186.35.108.144, while other regions showed minimal access, as with 189.24.118.68. IPs from North America, like 71.75.81.146 and 72.89.236.44, represent legitimate access but require continuous monitoring. For example, sessions from 174.125.174.95 often triggered notifications, especially those attempting to access privileged systems.A deeper look at international traffic unveiled access from IP 190.244.119.142, a significant address due to its activity level. Occasional spikes were noted from Europe, with entries from IP 84.26.122.138, which was scrutinized during regular audits.Lastly, domestic IPs like 65.112.10.60 and overseas ones such as 108.71.92.240 reveal the complexity of maintaining cybersecurity in a global context. One user from an IP at 1.43.41.29 exhibited typical behavior but underscored the need for constant vigilance.
import redef find_IP(file_Path): with open(file_Path, "r") as file: text = file.read() match = re.findall(r'(\d+)\.(\d+).(\d+)\.(\d+)', text) ip_list = ['.'.join(ip) for ip in match] return ip_listprint(find_IP('example.txt'))
Again using the re module to find the IP addresses in the text. Various ways to make requestsTo send a request to a server in Python, you’ll mostly use the requests module. import requestsresponse = requests.get("https://google.com")print(response.text)
Available HTTP methods
HTTP Method Request Description
GET requests.get(url) can additionally set a params dictionary
POST requests.post(url) can additionally set a data dictionary
PUT requests.put(url) can additionally set a data dictionary
DELETE requests.delete(url) delete the specified resource
HEAD requests.head(url) request only the resource’s response header
OPTIONS requests.options(url) request all HTTP methods the resource supports
You can also use the http.client module to send requests; this module is part of the Python standard library.
Encrypting dataIn Python you can encrypt text with the cryptography package, and hash with hashlib. Hashing with Hashlibhashlib provides several hash functions: SHA1, SHA224, SHA384, SHA512, and MD5. import hashlibsecret = "This is the message"bsecrets = secret.encode()m = hashlib.md5()m.update(bsecrets)print(m.hexdigest())
Before hashing text, you first convert it to a binary string with encode. Then create an MD5 hash object, which processes our message and computes the MD5 hash value. Then update the hash object, passing the binary string via update to hash, and output the 16-byte MD5 hash. Output 87f77fdd7fa847899a10a7aab651bd75
Misc QuestionsWhat do Python Interpreter do?
Parsing In this phase the Python interpreter converts the code into an AST (Abstract Syntax Tree) The conversion involves lexical analysis and syntax analysis Syntax errors are usually caught in this phase
Compilation The AST is converted into bytecode that the Python Virtual Machine (PVM) can execute
Execution The PVM interprets and executes this bytecode The PVM is a stack machine that manages and executes bytecode line by line
For the detailed flow, see this article.
What is Python Global Interpreter Lock(GIL)?
The Python GIL is a mutex in the Python interpreter (only in CPython) that ensures only one thread executes Python bytecode at a time, which helps solve memory-management problems such as race conditions
How GIL effect the multi-threading application?
The GIL limits the concurrency of multi-threaded applications; it doesn’t help much with CPU-bound tasks, since a CPU has multiple cores to share the computation You can use multiprocessing to bypass the GIL’s limitation, or switch to a Python without a GIL, like IronPython
https://yhtechnote.com/global-interpreter-lock/https://chtseng.wordpress.com/2024/02/29/python%E9%9D%9E%E5%90%8C%E6%AD%A5%E8%88%87%E5%B9%B3%E8%A1%8C%E8%99%95%E7%90%86/
Explain the difference between Concurrency and Parallelism in detail Concurrency means execution on a single CPU/core where multiple tasks run interleavedParallelism means execution on multiple CPUs/cores, possibly containing multiple concurrent tasks Referencehttps://github.com/bregman-arie/python-exercises

entry.title: Building and Analyzing a Satellite Ground Station with SatNOGS
entry.content:
🌐 中文版：繁體中文
IntroductionI’ve long been fascinated by how satellites communicate with ground stations, including how satellites are tracked, how a ground station obtains orbital data (e.g. TLE, and the signal the SDR receives), and how the received signal is converted into a decodable IF frequency, and so on.
So I decided to use SatNOGS (Satellite Networked Open Ground Station) as my entry point, building a complete ground station that can automatically schedule, track, and receive satellite signals.
The hands-on process gave me a concrete understanding of how satellite missions operate and of the ground segment.
