Once you confirm the server returns exception content verbatim to the client, a deliberate raise is more useful than a normal return for probing unknown calling conventions, since you don’t need to know the correct response format in advance. The implanted payload has to be fast enough. Recon code that’s too slow can hit an unrelated timeout / protection first, making the whole attack look like a failure and masking the fact that the injection already succeeded. When debugging, separate “is my code running at all” (a fast, simple probe) from “what can my code reach” (the real payload).

entry.title: A Tumbling Satellite and an Answer Blocked by Floating-Point Error | Tumbling Through Space | STARPWN 2026
entry.content:
🌐 中文版：繁體中文 Like Time to Intercept, this is an interactive orbital-mechanics challenge where you talk to a server over nc. The difference is that here the server practically writes the formula out for you in the hints. What actually blocked me was something boring that every engineer has run into: floating-point precision.
What the challenge is about Our friends are having difficulties with one of their satellites. It appears it has been struck by space debris and is now tumbling out of control. This is where you come in. The Attitude Determination and Control System (ADCS) is still online, but the automated detumbling sequence has failed. You will have to compute the correct control torques manually.
In plain terms: a satellite has been hit by space debris and is tumbling out of control. Its ADCS (Attitude Determination and Control System, the subsystem that senses and controls which way the satellite points) is still alive, but the automated detumbling routine (stopping a tumbling object’s rotation) is broken, so you need to compute the correct control torques by hand to stabilize it. After connecting, the server tells you the satellite’s moments of inertia (Ixx, Iyy, Izz, roughly “how much the object resists rotation,” determined by how mass is distributed across the three axes) and its current angular velocity (ωx, ωy, ωz, how fast it’s spinning about each axis). You send back four numbers: Tx Ty Tz duration
Tx/Ty/Tz are the three-axis control torques (N·m), and duration is the burn time (between 0 and 100 seconds). The torque vector’s magnitude (not the individual axis values) is capped at 1.0 N·m. Success means driving the angular velocity magnitude |ω| below 0.01 rad/s, with 5 attempts per connection. The server practically writes the answer in the hintsWhat you see on connecting: Moment of Inertia (kg*m^2): Ixx = 15.598269 Iyy = 13.194180 Izz = 15.434869Angular Velocity (rad/s): omega_x = +0.357402 omega_y = -0.285910 omega_z = -0.261535 |omega| = 0.527145Angular Momentum (kg*m^2/s): Lx = +5.574857 Ly = -3.772351 Lz = -4.036764HINTS:1. To stop rotation, you need to cancel angular momentum: L = I * omega2. Torque changes angular momentum: dL/dt = T3. For detumbling: T = -L / t (where t is application time)
The server has already computed and printed the angular momentum (L = I * ω, essentially “momentum for rotation,” inertia times angular velocity), and hint 3 spells the control law out directly as T = -L / t. There’s no need to derive any dynamics here. The only real work is choosing the burn time t under the constraint that torque magnitude cannot exceed 1.0 N·m. The physics: cancel all the angular momentum in one burnFor a body whose inertia tensor is diagonal (Ixx, Iyy, Izz independent, with no cross-coupling), the angular momentum is: L = (Ixx·ωx, Iyy·ωy, Izz·ωz)
Applying a constant torque T for a time t subtracts an impulse T·t from the angular momentum. So to zero out the angular momentum in a single burn: T · t = -L => T = -L / t
The only constraint is the torque vector’s magnitude (not each axis’s absolute value), so |T| ≤ 1.0 N·m. To solve it in one burn with as short a burn as possible (a shorter burn means a smaller window for error between the real dynamics and this simplified linear model), the ideal move is to burn at the full torque limit and back out how long that takes to cancel L: |T| = |L| / t = 1.0 => t = |L|T = -L / |L| (that is, -L normalized to a unit vector, times 1.0 N*m)
Computing the numbersimport mathLx, Ly, Lz = 5.574857, -3.772351, -4.036764L_mag = math.sqrt(Lx**2 + Ly**2 + Lz**2) # 7.848893Tx = -Lx / L_magTy = -Ly / L_magTz = -Lz / L_magduration = L_magprint(Tx, Ty, Tz, duration)# -0.710273 0.480622 0.514310 7.848893
First attempt: blocked by floating-point error> -0.710273 0.480622 0.514310 7.848893ERROR: Torque magnitude exceeds thruster capability (max 1.0 N*m)
In theory this torque vector’s magnitude is exactly 1.0, but what actually gets sent are values rounded to six decimal places. Recomputing sqrt(Tx²+Ty²+Tz²) from those rounded numbers lands just barely above 1.0 (something like 1.000000008), and the server’s check is ≤ 1.0, so it gets rejected. The server checks the literal numbers you actually sent, so when designing a numerical solution, don’t sit exactly on a limit boundary. Leave yourself some margin. Second attempt: leave a safety marginScale the whole solution down by a small factor (0.999) so the torque magnitude is clearly under the cap, and scale the burn time up by the same factor to keep the impulse (and therefore the cancellation) unchanged: Tx_safe = Tx * 0.999Ty_safe = Ty * 0.999Tz_safe = Tz * 0.999duration_safe = L_mag / 0.999# -0.709563 0.480141 0.513796 7.856750
> -0.709563 0.480141 0.513796 7.856750Applying control torques...UPDATED TELEMETRY:Angular Velocity (rad/s): omega_x = +0.002581 omega_y = -0.002065 omega_z = -0.001889 |omega| = 0.003808SUCCESS! SATELLITE STABILIZED!Here is your flag: STARPWN{d3tumbl3_m4st3r_sp4c3_0p5}
|ω| dropped from the original 0.527145 to 0.003808, far below the 0.01 threshold, which also proves this linear model (ignoring gyroscopic coupling terms) is plenty accurate over a burn of this length. FlagSTARPWN{d3tumbl3_m4st3r_sp4c3_0p5}
Takeaways Hints aren’t decoration; they can be formulas to copy directly. The server prints the control law T = -L/t outright, so this challenge needs no control theory derivation, only correct arithmetic and unit handling. A “magnitude cap of 1.0” means the vector magnitude, not individual axes. Normalizing -L to a unit vector, multiplying by the maximum allowed torque, and cancelling in one burn with duration = |L| is the most natural solution. When floating point is involved, never sit exactly on a hard limit. A vector whose magnitude is theoretically exactly 1.0 can easily come back as 1.000000008 once formatted to six decimals and parsed again. Multiplying by a small safety factor (say 0.999) before submitting avoids wasting an attempt, which matters when a connection only gives you 5. Five attempts is generous for a converging linear model. Even without perfect precision, the first burn usually brings |ω| close to the threshold, and a second corrective burn (here, literally the same solution retried with a safety margin) is enough to cross the 0.01 rad/s line.

entry.title: Using a Hash Table | LeetCode#1 Two Sum
A Downlink Hijacked in the Dead of Night | Two Voices | GaianSpace CTF 2026
entry.content:
🌐 中文版：繁體中文 Fifth post in the series, and the storyline shifts to “the night shift”: GaianSpace Mission Control’s GAIAN-723 satellite has been hijacked. The first four posts (the farm arc) got the LoRa demodulator well-practiced; these three (this one, No Name on the Door, Hopscotch) throw increasingly nasty situations at that same demodulator. This post’s theme: within one recording, two LoRa transmitters with completely different parameters are talking to each other. Rest of the series: Channel Hop、True Color Is a Lie、Isodata Seven、Subsidy Claim
What the challenge is about On the night shift, GAIAN-723 dropped off the telemetry terminal at 01:12, yet the schedule says it’s overhead right now. David Aroz is alone in the SOC; the ground-station modem reports nothing, but the station’s raw recorder has been running the whole time, and he pulls out the last 40 seconds of the band. The waterfall isn’t empty. There are two voices in it: one is GAIAN-723, and the other isn’t on any GaianSpace frequency plan, and it’s talking to the satellite. The old frequency sheet on the desk still says 433.000 MHz. Goal: find what GAIAN-723 answered when the stranger made its first call. The file given is a ~180 MB .sigmf-data (2 MS/s, 433.55 MHz) plus the desk notes. Flag format: GAIANSPACE{...} Two voices with different “accents”The 433.000 MHz on the old sheet isn’t where any signal actually is (the note itself says “might be wrong”). Looking at the waterfall and the per-band energy, there are two transmitters, repeating a cycle about every 12 seconds:
A (satellite) B (stranger)
Frequency ~433.170 MHz ~433.920 MHz
Modulation LoRa SF9, BW125k LoRa SF7, BW250k
Sync word 0x12 (public) 0x34 (LoRaWAN)
Preamble 12 symbols 8 symbols
This is the “different accents” the challenge mentions: the sync word, SF, and bandwidth are all different. So you can’t decode both sides with the same parameters; the demodulator has to run against each parameter set separately. Zoom into one cycle and the order is: A long packet → B strong pulse → A short packet:
Decoding the conversationRunning the demodulator with each parameter set, all packets decode cleanly with parity check 0. The conversation (TC = telecommand, TM = telemetry response):
Time Who Content
4.017 s B TC HELLO (seq 0)
4.224 s A TM,ACK,0,HELLO,GAIANSPACE{...}
15.89 s B TC GET HK; A replies with housekeeping
28.25 s B TC GET CFG; A replies NAK
39.08 s B TC SET DLCFG B; A replies OK,DLCFG=B
B is the stranger: it says hello, queries status and config, and finally switches the satellite’s downlink config to B, which explains why the ground-station modem, stuck on the old config, stopped receiving anything. The challenge asks what the satellite answered on the stranger’s “first call,” which is the ACK at 4.224 s, and it coughs up the flag directly. FlagGAIANSPACE{tw0_v01c3s_0B0EFE1A}
Takeaways “Two voices” means compare modulation parameters. Here the two sides differ in SF, BW, sync word, and preamble length; building out all the transmitters and a timeline first, then decoding each, is more efficient than trying parameters one at a time. The old frequency sheet is wrong, so trust the recorded data, not the documents. Very common in SDR challenges. Pair commands with responses using the sequence number. TC/TM looks like a protocol, and the seq in TM,ACK,<seq>,... lets you pin down the “first call” answer exactly. Here the satellite side used SF9 and the stranger SF7, both fairly standard. In the next post, No Name on the Door, the satellite switches to no header, with every packet looking different, and the demodulator has to evolve again.

entry.title: Horizontally Scaling ActiveMQ
entry.content:
🌐 中文版：繁體中文
Amazon MQAmazon MQ offers managed ActiveMQ, a message-queue service. I recently ran into the question of how to do horizontal scaling on Amazon MQ. First, a quick explanation of the difference between vertical scaling and horizontal scaling. Scaling means expanding. Vertical scaling focuses on boosting a single instance’s compute power, so vertical scaling might be a better CPU/GPU, larger memory capacity, and so on. In terms of AWS services, it might be swapping the instance; for MQ it would be switching from t3.Micro to m5.large.
[+] Instance types - https://docs.aws.amazon.com/zh_tw/amazon-mq/latest/developer-guide/broker-instance-types.html
Horizontal scaling usually means the architecture receives more messages, so you need to scale based on traffic/message volume and share the load off a single instance. ActiveMQ network of brokersThis is a native ActiveMQ feature. A network of brokers contains multiple brokers connected together; the brokers can share info about the clients and destinations they host, and can route messages between each other over the network. A broker can be:
A single-instance broker (unavailable if the node fails, unless restarted) Active/Standby brokers (the network has a standby broker that can share storage; if the active node fails, the standby takes over)
Generally, if there’s a need for horizontal scaling, a network of brokers is used.
[+] Amazon MQ network of brokers - https://docs.aws.amazon.com/zh_tw/amazon-mq/latest/developer-guide/network-of-brokers.html
Below are the step-by-step build steps. Steps
Choose Next
Here you can download the CloudFormation template, convenient for modifying the configuration and redeploying later. Estimated deployment time: 25 minutes
You can see all three brokers deploying.
You can click into a broker to view its detailed configuration.
In the config file, you can design the MQ topology by editing the attributes within <networkConnector></networkConnector>. Here are the current brokers’ configurations.
Broker1’s configuration
<networkConnectors> <networkConnector conduitSubscriptions="false" consumerTTL="1" messageTTL="-1" name="QueueConnectorConnectingToBroker2" uri="masterslave:(ssl://b-88e0e40a-d67a-4476-ac04-9015b4a491e5-1.mq.us-east-1.amazonaws.com:61617,ssl://b-88e0e40a-d67a-4476-ac04-9015b4a491e5-2.mq.us-east-1.amazonaws.com:61617)" userName="Kevin"> <excludedDestinations> <topic physicalName="&gt;"/> </excludedDestinations> </networkConnector> <networkConnector conduitSubscriptions="true" consumerTTL="1" messageTTL="-1" name="TopicConnectorConnectingToBroker2" uri="masterslave:(ssl://b-88e0e40a-d67a-4476-ac04-9015b4a491e5-1.mq.us-east-1.amazonaws.com:61617,ssl://b-88e0e40a-d67a-4476-ac04-9015b4a491e5-2.mq.us-east-1.amazonaws.com:61617)" userName="Kevin"> <excludedDestinations> <queue physicalName="&gt;"/> </excludedDestinations> </networkConnector> <networkConnector conduitSubscriptions="false" consumerTTL="1" messageTTL="-1" name="QueueConnectorConnectingToBroker3" uri="masterslave:(ssl://b-52af7fc7-4bb2-4c0d-b427-11a1c965434f-1.mq.us-east-1.amazonaws.com:61617,ssl://b-52af7fc7-4bb2-4c0d-b427-11a1c965434f-2.mq.us-east-1.amazonaws.com:61617)" userName="Kevin"> <excludedDestinations> <topic physicalName="&gt;"/> </excludedDestinations> </networkConnector> <networkConnector conduitSubscriptions="true" consumerTTL="1" messageTTL="-1" name="TopicConnectorConnectingToBroker3" uri="masterslave:(ssl://b-52af7fc7-4bb2-4c0d-b427-11a1c965434f-1.mq.us-east-1.amazonaws.com:61617,ssl://b-52af7fc7-4bb2-4c0d-b427-11a1c965434f-2.mq.us-east-1.amazonaws.com:61617)" userName="Kevin"> <excludedDestinations> <queue physicalName="&gt;"/> </excludedDestinations> </networkConnector> </networkConnectors>

<networkConnectors> <networkConnector conduitSubscriptions="false" consumerTTL="1" messageTTL="-1" name="QueueConnectorConnectingToBroker1" uri="masterslave:(ssl://b-853601ab-b005-4305-b511-283b560a6ddb-1.mq.us-east-1.amazonaws.com:61617,ssl://b-853601ab-b005-4305-b511-283b560a6ddb-2.mq.us-east-1.amazonaws.com:61617)" userName="Kevin"> <excludedDestinations> <topic physicalName="&gt;"/> </excludedDestinations> </networkConnector> <networkConnector conduitSubscriptions="true" consumerTTL="1" messageTTL="-1" name="TopicConnectorConnectingToBroker1" uri="masterslave:(ssl://b-853601ab-b005-4305-b511-283b560a6ddb-1.mq.us-east-1.amazonaws.com:61617,ssl://b-853601ab-b005-4305-b511-283b560a6ddb-2.mq.us-east-1.amazonaws.com:61617)" userName="Kevin"> <excludedDestinations> <queue physicalName="&gt;"/> </excludedDestinations> </networkConnector> <networkConnector conduitSubscriptions="false" consumerTTL="1" messageTTL="-1" name="QueueConnectorConnectingToBroker2" uri="masterslave:(ssl://b-88e0e40a-d67a-4476-ac04-9015b4a491e5-1.mq.us-east-1.amazonaws.com:61617,ssl://b-88e0e40a-d67a-4476-ac04-9015b4a491e5-2.mq.us-east-1.amazonaws.com:61617)" userName="Kevin"> <excludedDestinations> <topic physicalName="&gt;"/> </excludedDestinations> </networkConnector> <networkConnector conduitSubscriptions="true" consumerTTL="1" messageTTL="-1" name="TopicConnectorConnectingToBroker2" uri="masterslave:(ssl://b-88e0e40a-d67a-4476-ac04-9015b4a491e5-1.mq.us-east-1.amazonaws.com:61617,ssl://b-88e0e40a-d67a-4476-ac04-9015b4a491e5-2.mq.us-east-1.amazonaws.com:61617)" userName="Kevin"> <excludedDestinations> <queue physicalName="&gt;"/> </excludedDestinations> </networkConnector> </networkConnectors>
The conduitSubscriptions attributePer the ActiveMQ official docs
https://activemq.apache.org/networks-of-brokers
Multiple consumers subscribing to the same destination are treated as one consumer by the network, to avoid receiving the same message multiple times. ActiveMQ relies on information about active consumers (subscribers) to pass messages in the network. With conduit subscriptions, if there are multiple remote subscriptions, the remote broker treats each message’s copy as valid, which can cause message duplication. So the default conduit behavior consolidates all matching subscription info to prevent duplication from propagating in the network. This way, N subscriptions on a remote broker look like a single subscription to the network broker.
However, if only queues are used, duplicate subscriptions are a useful feature, since the load-balancing algorithm will try to distribute the message load evenly; only when conduitSubscriptions=false will consumers across the network evenly share the message load.
For example, there are two brokers, A and B, connected to each other via a proxy bridge. A consumer connected to broker A subscribes to a queue named Q.TEST, and two consumers connected to broker B also subscribe to Q.TEST, so there are three consumers, and assume all have equal priority. Then, start a producer on broker A, writing 30 messages to Q.TEST. By default (conduitSubscriptions=true), 15 messages are sent to the consumer on broker A, and the remaining 15 to the two consumers on broker B. But also because by default broker A treats the two subscriptions on broker B as one, the message load isn’t evenly distributed among all three consumers. But if you set conduitSubscriptions to false, each of the three consumers gets 10 messages. References[+] Instance types - https://docs.aws.amazon.com/zh_tw/amazon-mq/latest/developer-guide/broker-instance-types.html[+] Amazon MQ network of brokers - how does it work? - https://docs.aws.amazon.com/zh_cn/amazon-mq/latest/developer-guide/network-of-brokers.html#how-does-it-work[+] ActiveMQ - NetworkConnectors - https://activemq.apache.org/networks-of-brokers
